case_title: Vacc Synbiotech vs Bank of India & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vacc-Synbiotech is the Corporate Debtor/Appellant; Bank of India is the Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loan facility sanctioned by Bank of India on 30th March 2015 for Rs. 20,50,00,000/-, later reviewed and reduced to Rs. 18,95,00,000/- on 08th January 2018, secured by hypothecation of goods and security documents. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial Creditor claimed outstanding default in excess of Rs. 24 Crores; Corporate Debtor admitted outstanding dues of Rs. 20.30 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Term loan sanctioned on 30th March 2015; account classified as NPA on 28.09.2016/30.09.2016; notice under Section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act issued; Section 7 IBC application CP (IB) No. 2947/MB/2019 filed on 29th August 2019; NCLT Mumbai admitted application. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Written acknowledgment of debt letter dated 05th March 2018; reversal of Rs. 71,46,859/- overcharged interest on 30th December 2017; bank account statements establishing disbursed amounts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor appeared before NCLT Mumbai Bench on 27th September 2019 and 05th December 2019 but failed to file a reply or appear on the final adjourned date of 04th February 2020; NCLT admitted the Section 7 petition; Corporate Debtor appealed citing counsel's scheduling error and interest disputes.
legal_issues: Whether disputes concerning quantum of disbursement, overcharging of interest, EMI calculations, or the precise date of NPA classification bar the admission of a Section 7 IBC application where default exceeds the statutory threshold and an acknowledgment of debt exists.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In an application under Section 7 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority is not required to adjudicate disputes regarding quantum of debt, excess interest charges, or exact NPA dates, provided there is an admitted debt and default exceeding the statutory threshold under Section 4. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 mandates admission once the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that a financial default has occurred and the application is complete; a dispute regarding the exact quantum does not prevent insolvency commencement if the debt meets the statutory threshold. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of loan sanction, subsistence of default above the statutory threshold, and valid written acknowledgment of debt within limitation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Even by the debtor's own admission, an outstanding default of over Rs. 20 Crores existed, supported by a valid acknowledgment of debt dated 05th March 2018, rendering the Section 7 admission legally unimpeachable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed at the stage of admission; no orders as to costs.
summary: Bank of India initiated CIRP against Vacc-Synbiotech under Section 7 of the IBC for outstanding defaults exceeding Rs. 24 Crores on a term loan sanctioned in March 2015. NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the application after the debtor failed to file a reply or appear on the adjourned hearing date. On appeal, the Corporate Debtor contended that the Bank had overcharged interest, collected excessive EMIs, disbursed less than sanctioned, and that its counsel missed the hearing due to date confusion. NCLAT dismissed the appeal at the admission stage, holding that disputes relating to interest calculations, exact debt quantum, or NPA dates are irrelevant under Section 7 when the existence of financial debt and default above the Section 4 threshold is undisputed and backed by an acknowledgment of debt.

case_title: M. Karishma Bothra & Ors vs S. Rajendran, RP of PRC International Hotels Pvt. Ltd. & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Late S. Mukanchand Bothra was an Unsecured Financial Creditor, succeeded by legal heirs M. Karishma Bothra, M. Gagan Bothra, and M. Sandeep Bothra (Appellants); PRC International Hotels Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor; S. Rajendran is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2); M/s Sai Baba Business Solutions Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 1. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim lodged in Form C by Late Mukanchand Bothra for financial debt against the Corporate Debtor during CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim submitted was for Rs 15 Crores; pursuant to the approved Resolution Plan, an admitted payout of Rs 4,12,95,002/- (constituting 27.53% payout) was allocated to Late Mukanchand Bothra. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Mukanchand Bothra died on 17th April 2019; NCLT Chennai allowed substitution of legal heirs on 03rd May 2019 in MA/518/2018; Resolution Plan approved on 27th August 2019 in MA No. 651/2019; NCLT Chennai passed impugned directions in MA No. 927 of 2019 on 11th October 2019 ordering newspaper publication. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan containing a binding payout of Rs 4,12,95,002/-; NCLT order dated 03.05.2019 recording the RP's express 'no objection' to impleading the three legal heirs; affidavits affirming that the mother of the appellants attained sainthood. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai approved the plan on 27.08.2019, but subsequently in MA No. 927 of 2019 ordered newspaper publications in 'The Hindu' and 'Dinamalar' before disbursing funds; Appellants appealed the publication order (CA 1275/2019), and the RP appealed the earlier CoC reconsideration order dated 02.07.2019 (CA 844/2019).
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional and Adjudicating Authority can demand succession certificates, probates, or require newspaper publications prior to disbursing approved resolution plan payouts to legal heirs who have already been formally substituted on record with the consent of the Resolution Professional.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once legal heirs are formally substituted on record in CIRP proceedings with the consent of the Resolution Professional and an approved Resolution Plan confirms their allocated payout, the Resolution Professional cannot demand succession proof, probates, or newspaper publications as a condition precedent to disbursing the funds. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: An approved Resolution Plan becomes final and binding on all stakeholders; the RP has no statutory authority to re-agitate succession issues at the distribution stage, and an appeal filed by an RP challenging an order that culminated in an unchallenged, approved plan is non-maintainable as the RP is not an 'aggrieved person' under Section 61. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Judicial verification of prior unchallenged substitution orders and the distribution matrix embedded in the approved Resolution Plan. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants were duly substituted on record without objection and are entitled to their one-third equal shares of Rs 4,12,95,002/- without furnishing further proof of succession or causing newspaper advertisements.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1275 of 2019 is allowed, the order requiring newspaper publication is set aside, and the RP is directed to disburse the funds without requiring succession proof; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 844 of 2019 is rejected as infructuous and non-maintainable without costs.
summary: Late S. Mukanchand Bothra lodged an unsecured financial claim of Rs 15 Crores in the CIRP of PRC International Hotels Pvt. Ltd., which resulted in an approved allocation of Rs 4,12,95,002/- under the resolution plan. Following his death, his three legal heirs were substituted on record by NCLT Chennai without objection from the RP. However, when disbursing funds, the RP insisted on succession certificates and probates, and NCLT directed newspaper publications. On appeal, NCLAT held that once legal heirs are validly brought on record and the resolution plan attains finality, demanding succession documents or newspaper publications is illegal and baseless. The directions were modified, ordering immediate distribution to the legal heirs, while the RP's cross-appeal was rejected.

case_title: Swwapnil Bhingardevay vs Khandoba Prasanna Sakhar Karkhana Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Khandoba Prasanna Sakhar Karkhana Limited is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 1); Swwapnil Bhingardevay is the Appellant (Promoter/Director); M/s Sai Agro (India) Chemicals is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 2); M/s Sarvadnya Industries Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 3 (owner of plant machinery); Jitendra Palande is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 5). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor held a license to produce ethanol from rectified spirit; however, the crucial ethanol plant and machinery installed on its premises belonged to third party M/s Sarvadnya Industries Pvt. Ltd.. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial Creditor (Karad Urban Co-operative Bank Ltd.) initiated Section 7 proceedings upon NPA default; RP calculated average liquidation value at Rs 13.53 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Public notice published on 30th March 2018; resolution plan submitted with printed date 07th February 2019 and partners' declaration dated 09th February 2019; approved by CoC on 09th February 2019 within three hours; NCLT Mumbai approved plan on 01st August 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Newspaper publication dated 30.03.2018 improperly inviting bids for 'outright sale of the company as a going concern' instead of inviting resolution plans/EOI; SRA's plan showing knowledge of the exact confidential liquidation value of Rs 13.53 Crores matching Form H; appellate order in CA 897/2019 permitting Respondent No. 3 to take possession of the ethanol plant. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved Sai Agro's resolution plan on 01st August 2019; Suspended Director appealed alleging material irregularity and lack of feasibility/viability under Section 61(3)(ii).
legal_issues: Whether publishing a public notice for outright sale instead of an expression of interest under Regulation 36A, leaking confidential liquidation value to the resolution applicant in breach of Regulation 35(2), and approving a business plan based on essential plant machinery owned by a third party constitutes material irregularity rendering the plan non-feasible and unviable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan that presumes ownership over essential production machinery owned by a third party lacks feasibility and viability under Section 30(4); furthermore, publishing notices for 'outright sale' rather than inviting expressions of interest and breaching statutory confidentiality by leaking liquidation values to an applicant constitutes material irregularity under Section 61(3)(ii) vitiating the approval process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 35(2) and Section 30(2) require strict confidentiality of liquidation value; a rushed approval within hours without independent verification of asset ownership invalidates the CoC's feasibility determination under Section 30(4). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Exact numerical match of confidential liquidation value in the SRA's plan alongside judicial orders establishing third-party title over the corporate debtor's sole operational machinery. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CIRP was tainted by material irregularities, confidentiality breaches, and fatal structural defects regarding the plant's operational viability, requiring the plan's approval to be set aside.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order dated 01st August 2019 is set aside, and the matter is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to send back the Resolution Plan to the CoC for resubmission and reconsideration in accordance with law; no costs.
summary: A promoter/director of Khandoba Prasanna Sakhar Karkhana Ltd. challenged the approval of a resolution plan submitted by Sai Agro (India) Chemicals. The appellant established that the CIRP was plagued by fatal irregularities: the RP published an advertisement for 'outright sale' instead of issuing a proper EOI under Regulation 36A, the SRA possessed exact confidential liquidation figures (Rs 13.53 Crores) in violation of Regulation 35(2), and the plan was rushed through CoC approval in three hours on the erroneous premise that the debtor owned the ethanol plant machinery, which actually belonged to a third party. NCLAT held that the plan lacked feasibility and viability under Section 30(4) and suffered from material irregularities under Section 61(3)(ii), set aside the approval, and remitted the matter for reconsideration.

case_title: Naik Environmental Engineers Pvt. Ltd vs Indiabulls Construction Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Naik Environmental Engineers Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor/Appellant; Indiabulls Construction Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Issuance of 3 Purchase Orders and 2 Work Orders for comprehensive maintenance, operation, and repair of Sewage Treatment Plants (STP) and supply of consumables across project sites at Hyderabad (Centrum Project) and Panvel (Greena Panvel Project). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid invoices amounting to Rs 48,06,944/- with interest of Rs 14,69,242/- aggregating to Rs 62,76,186/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Purchase/work orders executed between 21.12.2012 and 13.03.2014; separate Section 8 demand notices re-issued on 16.04.2018 for Hyderabad and Panvel sites; replies sent by Corporate Debtor on 23.04.2018; Section 9 application CP No. IB-889(N.D.)/2018 dismissed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-III on 14.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Seven unpaid invoices and separate purchase/work orders having independent dispute resolution clauses; reply to demand notice asserting deficiency of service and performance defects solely in respect of a completely separate project (Sky Forest Project, Parel, Mumbai under distinct WOs 3228108736 and 3200100371), while admitting lack of disputes for the Panvel PO. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-III rejected the Section 9 petition holding that a running composite account existed between parties and cross-project disputes at Sky Forest constituted a pre-existing dispute; Operational Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a dispute concerning performance deficiencies in a separate and independent contract/project can be imported as a 'pre-existing dispute' to reject a Section 9 application filed for unpaid dues under distinct purchase orders and work orders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Separate purchase orders and work orders with independent terms and dispute resolution mechanisms constitute independent contracts; a dispute regarding one contract cannot be imported to claim a pre-existing dispute against unpaid, undisputed claims arising out of distinct contracts, in the absence of a proved composite running account. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(2)(d) read with Mobilox Innovations mandates rejection only when a plausible, bona fide dispute exists regarding the specific debt in question; asserting defects in an un-demanded, distinct project constitutes a spurious defence to evade statutory insolvency liability. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of individual purchase orders, distinct project locations, and replies to demand notices confirming that complaints were confined to unrelated sites. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: No dispute existed regarding the Hyderabad and Panvel work orders, which fulfilled all Section 9 criteria; NCLT's finding of a running composite account was baseless.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order dated 14th June 2019 is set aside, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to pass an order of admission within seven days from submission of certified copy of this order; no costs.
summary: Naik Environmental Engineers Pvt. Ltd. filed a Section 9 IBC application claiming unpaid operational debts of Rs 62.76 Lakhs for sewage treatment plant works executed at Hyderabad and Panvel under separate purchase and work orders. NCLT New Delhi Bench-III rejected the application, holding that a composite running account existed and that disputes over an STP installed at a third site (Sky Forest Project, Parel, Mumbai) constituted a pre-existing dispute. On appeal, NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that each work order formed an independent contract. Since the Corporate Debtor raised no grievance regarding the Hyderabad or Panvel works, deficiencies alleged at an unrelated project could not bar admission under the rule in Mobilox Innovations. NCLAT directed NCLT to admit the petition.

case_title: Simplex Infrastructures Limited vs Nitesh Estates Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Simplex Infrastructures Limited is the Operational Creditor/Appellant; Nitesh Estates Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent; Nitesh Residency Hotels Private Limited (NRHPL) is the subsidiary/associate owner company. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Contract agreement dated 19th March 2008 for construction of the Ritz Carlton Hotel in Bangalore. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Balance claimed unpaid sum of Rs 6,03,55,646/- under a Final Payment Certificate/Reconciliation Statement dated 31st October 2014. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Hotel construction completed in 2012 and operational in 2013; Taking Over Certificate issued on 07th April 2014; Final Payment Certificate dated 31st October 2014; Section 8 notice issued on 28th September 2017; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 02/BB/2018 filed on 22nd December 2017 simultaneously with arbitration notice; NCLT Bengaluru dismissed petition on 29th May 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Conditions of Contract specifically naming subsidiary NRHPL as the 'Employer'; email dated 21st January 2016 from Ritz Carlton's Chief Engineer detailing major leakages, seepages, and damages in hotel rooms; recommendatory nature of the DLKPK reconciliation statement unsigned by Respondent; simultaneous invocation of tripartite arbitration. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru rejected the Section 9 petition on 29th May 2019 on grounds of pre-existing dispute, limitation, and lack of privity; Operational Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 IBC application is maintainable where the contractual definition of 'Employer' points to a subsidiary requiring tripartite adjudication, whether simultaneous invocation of arbitration and prior correspondence regarding construction defects evidence a pre-existing dispute, and whether the claim is barred by limitation when filed more than three years after project completion.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the underlying contractual identity of the liable employer requires complex interpretation across corporate entities, and contemporaneous documentary evidence establishes pre-existing disputes regarding defects in construction works, a summary proceeding under Section 9 IBC cannot be maintained; furthermore, claims filed beyond three years from completion of works are barred by limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 summary jurisdiction cannot be invoked as a substitute for debt recovery or complex tripartite contractual disputes; pre-existing communications concerning defective construction quality satisfy the threshold of genuine dispute barring admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of contemporaneous pre-notice emails detailing construction defects, contract definition clauses, and the date of completion/handover against statutory limitation periods. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The dispute regarding defective works was raised in 2016 prior to the Section 8 notice, the claim was barred by limitation since completion occurred in 2012/2014, and the liability of the respondent was disputed, justifying dismissal.
operative_order: The appeal is rejected, confirming the NCLT Bengaluru order dated 29th May 2019; no orders as to costs.
summary: Simplex Infrastructures Ltd filed a Section 9 application against Nitesh Estates Ltd seeking recovery of Rs 6.03 Crores for constructing the Ritz Carlton Hotel in Bangalore, relying on a 2014 reconciliation certificate. The Adjudicating Authority dismissed the petition due to pre-existing disputes, limitation, and tripartite issues involving subsidiary NRHPL. On appeal, NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that emails dating back to January 2016 from the hotel's chief engineer detailing leakages and defects proved a genuine pre-existing dispute. Furthermore, NCLAT held that the petition filed in December 2017 was time-barred since construction was completed in 2012 and taken over in April 2014, and that summary proceedings under IBC cannot resolve disputed contractual employer identities.

case_title: Excel Infralogistics Private Limited vs Karnani Solvex Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Excel Infralogistics Private Limited is the Operational Creditor/Appellant; Karnani Solvex Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial contract for providing cargo storage, clearing, and transportation services. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed in Part IV was Rs 37,51,623/- with interest @ 18% p.a. of Rs 8,77,731/-; admitted service bills raised were Rs 29,18,599/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued on 20th March 2019 and served on 27th March 2019; Corporate Debtor sent no reply to demand notice; CP No. 110/9/JPR/2019 filed under Section 9; NCLT Jaipur rejected the petition on 01st October 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Regular godown-wise stock reports shared by Appellant; email dated 10.02.2018 disclosing moisture loss of ~75 MT and email dated 28.11.2018 requesting removal of 30 MT rejected cargo; counter-invoice of Rs 40,17,321/- raised by Corporate Debtor belatedly on 31.03.2019 alleging missing cargo from 2013; NCLT's own finding that the 2013 cargo loss claim was time-barred. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Jaipur Bench rejected the Section 9 application on 01st October 2019 finding existence of dispute over lost and rejected cargo; Operational Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a stale, time-barred counterclaim relating to missing cargo from 2013, raised after service of demand notice without prompt contemporaneous action to stock loss intimations, constitutes a bona fide pre-existing dispute under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate debtor cannot defeat a Section 9 application by manufacturing a stale, time-barred counterclaim or raising retrospective disputes where it failed to contemporaneous protest against periodic stock reports and neglected to reply to a Section 8 demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 mandates admission when debt and default exceed statutory limits, unless the debtor establishes a bona fide pre-existing dispute under Section 9(5)(2)(d); illusory claims barred by limitation do not meet the Mobilox standard of a plausible dispute requiring investigation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Analysis of regular stock reporting without contemporaneous objection versus belated counter-invoices raised on the eve of litigation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was due, unpaid, and above statutory minimums; the corporate debtor's defense was an afterthought and barred by limitation, warranting admission of the application.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned judgment dated 01st October 2019 is set aside, and the case is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to admit the Section 9 application after giving notice to enable the Corporate Debtor to settle the matter prior to admission; no costs.
summary: Excel Infralogistics Pvt. Ltd. filed an application under Section 9 of the IBC against Karnani Solvex Pvt. Ltd. claiming operational dues of Rs 37.51 Lakhs plus interest for cargo storage and transportation services. The Corporate Debtor did not reply to the Section 8 demand notice, but before NCLT Jaipur asserted a pre-existing dispute, claiming 75 MT cargo loss and raising a counter-invoice for missing trucks dating back to 2013. NCLT dismissed the application on grounds of a disputed claim. On appeal, NCLAT reversed the order, holding that the debtor failed to raise contemporaneous objections despite receiving stock reports and that the alleged 2013 dispute was time-barred and illusory under the Mobilox doctrine. The matter was remitted to NCLT for admission.

case_title: Mr. Sandip Patel vs. Central Bank of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Sandip Patel is the Appellant/Financial Creditor; Central Bank of India is Respondent No. 1/Financial Creditor; M/s Cure Life Care Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 2/Corporate Debtor; Mr. Premraj Ramratan Laddha is Respondent No. 3/Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claimed financial debt advanced by the Appellant, alongside loan and credit facilities extended by Respondent No. 1 Bank to the Corporate Debtor secured against corporate assets. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Exact amounts of default are not quantified in the order; the defaults arose from failure to service the respective financial debts, leading to Section 7 petitions. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP(IB) No. 388/2018 was admitted under Section 7 on 31.05.2019; Public Announcement was issued on 07.06.2019 with a claim submission cut-off date of 21.06.2019; Appellant submitted proof of claim via email on 28.06.2019 and a modified claim on 09.07.2019; CoC was constituted on 05.07.2019 and passed a 100% vote to withdraw on the same date; I.A. No. 399 of 2019 was allowed by NCLT on 11.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Annexure-C Form-C email delivery receipt dated 28.06.2019 at 10:52 AM IST; Minutes of the 1st CoC Meeting held on 05.07.2019 explicitly acknowledging receipt of claims after the deadline that remained under process of verification; Sale Confirmation letter dated 23.05.2019 and Sale Certificate dated 16.07.2019 evidencing e-auction realization of corporate assets by Respondent No. 1. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant initially filed CP(IB) No. 157/7/NCLT/AHM/2017 against the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 1 later filed CP(IB) No. 388/NCLT/AHM/2018, which was admitted on 31.05.2019; Appellant's original petition was disposed of as infructuous on 04.06.2019 with express liberty to lodge claims before the Resolution Professional; NCLT Ahmedabad allowed the IRP's application I.A. No. 399 of 2019 under Section 12A on 11.07.2019, permitting withdrawal of CIRP because Respondent No. 1 recovered its debt through asset sale, without hearing the Appellant or verifying his submitted claim.
legal_issues: Whether a Committee of Creditors comprised solely of a single financial creditor can resolve to withdraw CIRP under Section 12A of the IBC, and whether the Adjudicating Authority can sanction such withdrawal, while pending claims of other financial creditors (who previously had their Section 7 petitions disposed of as infructuous with liberty to lodge claims) remain unverified and without affording them an opportunity of being heard.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for withdrawal under Section 12A of the IBC cannot be sustained or allowed arbitrarily where the sole member of a Committee of Creditors resolves to terminate CIRP after satisfying its own debts, while unverified claims submitted by other creditors whose prior insolvency applications were dismissed as infructuous remain pending. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12A read with Regulation 30A of the CIRP Regulations does not permit an exit mechanism to operate in derogation of basic principles of natural justice or to defeat the rights of other creditors whose claims are under active verification. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the CoC minutes record that claims were received and under process of verification, resolving to withdraw without adjourning to complete claim verification constitutes an arbitrary act contrary to legal conscience. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The withdrawal allowed by the Adjudicating Authority without granting a hearing to the Appellant was unsustainable; the order was set aside and the petition restored with directions to afford a proper hearing to the Appellant.
operative_order: The order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 11.07.2019 passed in IA No. 399 of 2019 in CP(IB) No. 388/NCLT/AHM/2018 is set aside; CP(IB) No. 388/NCLT/AHM/2018 is restored to its original position; the Adjudicating Authority is directed to afford an opportunity of being heard to the Appellant before deciding on withdrawal; parties are directed to appear before the Adjudicating Authority on 09.07.2020; no orders as to costs.
summary: Mr. Sandip Patel appealed against an order of NCLT Ahmedabad allowing an application under Section 12A of the IBC filed by Central Bank of India to withdraw the CIRP against Cure Life Care Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant had earlier filed a Section 7 petition which was disposed of as infructuous upon admission of the Bank's petition, with liberty to file a claim before the Resolution Professional. Despite the Appellant lodging his claim, the Bank, acting as the sole member of the CoC, resolved in its first meeting to withdraw CIRP after realizing its own dues through an asset sale. Holding the procedure arbitrary and violative of natural justice, NCLAT set aside the withdrawal and restored the petition.

case_title: Regional Provident Fund Commissioner vs. T.V. Balasubramanian, Resolution Professional Representing Corporate Debtor Sholingur Textiles Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, EPFO Regional Office Chennai (Appellant/Statutory Creditor/Recovery Authority); T.V. Balasubramanian (Respondent/Resolution Professional); Sholingur Textiles Limited (Corporate Debtor); Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory provident fund dues assessed and recoverable against the Corporate Debtor under the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding statutory PF arrears amounting to Rs. 53,80,21,376.31, leading to attachment under Section 8B of the EPF & MP Act, 1952. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Recovery Officer issued attachment order EPFCP-16 on 04.08.2017 (received by Sub-Registrar on 16.08.2017); Reminder letters sent to Sub-Registrar on 10.05.2018 and 29.11.2018; Section 7 petition was admitted against the Corporate Debtor on 04.02.2019; Encumbrance was formally recorded by Sub-Registrar during CIRP on 28.03.2019; Notice on MA No. 830/2019 issued on 05.09.2019; Reply filed by EPFO on 11.10.2019; Impugned order passed on 11.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Recovery Certificate and attachment order EPFCP-16 bearing reference No. T.N./VL/6294/Recovery/2017 dated 04.08.2017 (Annexure A-4); Sub-Registrar reminder letters dated 10.05.2018 (Annexure A-5) and 29.11.2018; Web records from tnreginet.com; Proof of reply filed in NCLT Chennai registry on 11.10.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor through the RP filed MA No. 830 of 2019 before NCLT Chennai seeking cancellation of the encumbrance created by EPFO's attachment. On 11.10.2019, NCLT Chennai disposed of the application on the same day without taking into consideration the objections filed by EPFO, holding that the encumbrance registered during moratorium violated Sections 14 and 238 of the IBC.
legal_issues: Whether the statutory attachment of immovable property of a Corporate Debtor executed by the EPFO prior to the commencement of CIRP violates the moratorium under Section 14(1) of the IBC merely because its administrative entry in the Sub-Registrar's register was carried out after CIRP initiation, and whether the Adjudicating Authority violated principles of natural justice by disposing of the application without considering the reply filed by the statutory authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory attachment of immovable property effected prior to the initiation of CIRP does not violate Section 14 of the IBC, as subsequent ministerial entry in public land registers is merely the recording of an antecedent valid attachment rather than the creation of a fresh encumbrance; furthermore, an order passed without considering objections properly placed on record violates natural justice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1) of the IBC prohibits transferring, encumbering, alienating, or disposing of assets by the Corporate Debtor during the moratorium, but does not retrospectively invalidate statutory attachments perfected prior to the admission of the insolvency petition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documentary proof establishing that the order of attachment under Section 8B of the EPF & MP Act was passed and served on the registration authority prior to Section 7 admission conclusively proves the pre-existing nature of the attachment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in passing the order in haste without considering the EPFO's reply and incorrectly concluded that the registration constituted an illegal post-moratorium encumbrance; the attachment was pre-existing and lawful.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 11.10.2019 passed in MA No. 830 of 2019 in CP/1037/(I.B.)/2018 is set aside; no order as to costs.
summary: The Regional Provident Fund Commissioner appealed an order of NCLT Chennai which cancelled an encumbrance registered over the immovable properties of Corporate Debtor Sholingur Textiles Limited. The Resolution Professional contended that the registration of the encumbrance on 28.03.2019 violated the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC following CIRP admission on 04.02.2019. NCLAT held that the attachment was legally executed by EPFO on 04.08.2017, long before CIRP initiation, and subsequent entry by the Sub-Registrar was merely ministerial recording of an existing order. NCLAT further held that NCLT violated natural justice by ignoring EPFO's timely filed reply, and consequently allowed the appeal, setting aside the cancellation.

case_title: Abhishek Agarwal & Ors. vs. M/s. Manasadevi Bakers Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Abhishek Agarwal, Ashish Kumar Agarwal, Neha Agarwal (Appellants/Purported Financial Creditors); M/s Manasadevi Bakers Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor); Ajay Kumar Agarwal and Vishnu Dutt Gupta (Contending Directors/Shareholders); Canara Bank (Secured Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Disbursement of unsecured loans based on MOU dated 29.04.2007 and Agreement dated 08.02.2012 for which equity shares were to be allotted without any stipulated repayment date, alongside execution of a Subordination Agreement in favor of Canara Bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal unsecured loan of Rs. 66,75,000 disbursed on different dates; total amount claimed with interest was Rs. 1,47,81,477 (or Rs. 1,47,881,477 as cited in record); default claimed upon non-payment following expiration of demand notices. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notices issued on 10.06.2016 and 10.08.2017; Corporate Debtor's reply dated 18.12.2017 requesting six months; Further notice issued on 26.06.2018; Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 30/7/HDB/2019 filed on 17.12.2018; Board removed Vishnu Dutt Gupta on 06.02.2019; Impugned rejection order passed on 22.08.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Annual Financial Statements of Corporate Debtor from 2006-2007 to 2016-2017 showing interest-free unsecured loans without any provision for interest; MOU dated 29.04.2007 and Agreement dated 08.02.2012; Subordination Agreement dated 26.08.2014 executed by Appellants in favor of Canara Bank agreeing not to claim or receive payments until Canara Bank's debt is satisfied; ROC charge registered by Canara Bank on 25.09.2014; Affidavit and counter filed by Canara Bank Officer in I.A. 432 of 2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed Section 7 application before NCLT Hyderabad. One director admitted default while another director opposed, producing the Subordination Agreement. On 22.08.2019, NCLT Hyderabad dismissed the petition holding that the loan was interest-free, lacked consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8), and was not legally payable due to the binding Subordination Agreement.
legal_issues: Whether an interest-free unsecured loan advanced without any agreed schedule for repayment and tied to the issuance of equity shares constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and whether an actionable 'default' can occur when creditors have executed a Subordination Agreement undertaking not to collect dues until institutional bank borrowings are cleared.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interest-free loan with no defined repayment schedule and disbursed against an understanding for allotment of equity shares lacks the commercial effect of borrowing and consideration for the time value of money, failing the definition of financial debt under Section 5(8); furthermore, where creditors covenant under a subordination agreement not to collect dues prior to full satisfaction of primary institutional debt, the subordinated debt is not legally payable and no default can be established. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Financial debt' under Section 5(8) strictly mandates disbursement against consideration for the time value of money. 'Default' under Section 3(12) requires non-payment of a debt that has become legally due and enforceable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented subordination covenants and supporting affidavits from institutional lenders outweigh bare denials of execution in summary Section 7 proceedings; the tribunal need not resolve internal management faction disputes when the petition is driven by purposes extraneous to resolution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants failed to establish the existence of a financial debt and an enforceable default, rendering the dismissal of the Section 7 petition sound and unassailable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; no orders as to costs.
summary: Appellants challenged the NCLT Hyderabad order dismissing their Section 7 application against Manasadevi Bakers Pvt. Ltd. for default of Rs. 1,47,81,477. NCLT found that the funds were advanced as interest-free unsecured loans with no repayment terms and were intended for equity allotment. Furthermore, Appellants had executed a Subordination Agreement in favor of Canara Bank, agreeing not to claim repayment until the Bank's facilities were cleared. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the advances lacked consideration for the time value of money to qualify as financial debt under Section 5(8), and because the debt was subordinated and not currently payable, no default existed under the IBC.

case_title: M/s. Kotak Resources vs. Dharmendra Dhelaria & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Kotak Resources (Appellant/Financial Creditor/CoC Member); Dharmendra Dhelaria (Respondent No. 1/Resolution Professional); ARCIL (Financial Creditor/CoC Member); M/s Raninga Ispat Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities advanced to the Corporate Debtor resulting in an application for initiation of CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Ratified CIRP cost liability of Rs. 12,12,831 incurred by the Resolution Professional in managing the operations of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted by NCLT Ahmedabad on 21.02.2018; RP confirmed in CoC meeting on 22.03.2018; CIRP costs ratified in CoC meeting on 07.08.2018; NCLAT set aside CIRP admission order on 29.08.2018; RP filed application under Section 60; NCLT passed cost apportionment order on 24.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the CoC meeting dated 07.08.2018 formally approving and ratifying resolution costs of Rs. 12,12,831; Records of the RP managing the Corporate Debtor's operations as a going concern during the active CIRP period. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After NCLAT set aside the Section 7 admission order on 29.08.2018, the RP approached NCLT Ahmedabad under Section 60 for reimbursement of CIRP costs. On 24.02.2020, NCLT Ahmedabad directed the CoC members (Kotak Resources and ARCIL) to reimburse Rs. 12,12,831 in equal proportion. Kotak Resources appealed, arguing lack of jurisdiction and denying liability.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under Section 60 of the IBC to direct the Committee of Creditors to reimburse ratified CIRP costs to the Resolution Professional upon closure of proceedings after admission is set aside on appeal, and whether such costs must be borne equally among CoC members rather than saddling the Corporate Debtor or a single creditor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an order admitting an insolvency application is set aside on appeal and CIRP is closed, the Adjudicating Authority retains jurisdiction to direct the members of the Committee of Creditors to reimburse approved CIRP costs to the Resolution Professional; such costs cannot be saddled on the Corporate Debtor and must be shared equally among the CoC members. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60 of the IBC confers comprehensive jurisdiction upon the Adjudicating Authority to resolve incidental questions and issue consequential orders concerning CIRP expenses and their apportionment upon termination of proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Approval and ratification of incurred CIRP costs by the Committee of Creditors in its formal meetings serves as conclusive proof of the legitimacy of the expenditure. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority acted within its statutory jurisdiction; the requirement that both CoC members reimburse the ratified CIRP costs in equal proportion was fully justified.
operative_order: The appeal lacks merit and is dismissed at the threshold stage; no order as to costs.
summary: Kotak Resources appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad order directing the two CoC members—Kotak Resources and ARCIL—to reimburse CIRP costs of Rs. 12,12,831 in equal proportion to Resolution Professional Dharmendra Dhelaria. The CIRP against Raninga Ispat Pvt. Ltd., triggered under Section 7 by Kotak Resources, had earlier been set aside in appeal by NCLAT. Kotak Resources argued that NCLT had no jurisdiction to saddle it with CIRP costs. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority possesses full jurisdiction under Section 60 to direct reimbursement of ratified costs, that the Corporate Debtor cannot be burdened with these expenses, and that CoC members must share them equally. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Naveen Kumar Jha vs. Randstad India Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Naveen Kumar Jha, member of suspended Board of Directors of Dalmia Biz Medicare Ltd. (Appellant/Corporate Debtor); Randstad India Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Operational Creditor); Madhu Juneja (Interim Resolution Professional/Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of recruitment and staffing services by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor under a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Invoices raised in June 2017 amounted to Rs. 20,20,349.13; after agreeing to an instalment plan of six equal monthly payments of Rs. 2,57,627.33, the Corporate Debtor paid only three instalments, leaving an unpaid default amount of Rs. 7,72,882. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised in June 2017; Payment plan agreed July 2017; Section 8(1) demand notice issued subsequently; Corporate Debtor set ex parte before NCLT on 08.08.2019; NCLT admission order passed on 13.01.2020; IRP issued public announcement email on 20.01.2020; Appeal filed on 05.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor's invoices and July 2017 instalment plan; Bank records showing clearance of only three instalments; Section 8 demand notice and Corporate Debtor's reply alleging quality defects without any contemporaneous supporting pre-notice emails or correspondence. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 application before NCLT New Delhi. Although represented by counsel initially, Corporate Debtor failed to file a reply and was proceeded ex parte on 08.08.2019. More than five months later, on 13.01.2020, NCLT admitted the petition, initiated CIRP, and appointed the IRP. Appellant appealed alleging breach of natural justice and a pre-existing dispute regarding service quality.
legal_issues: Whether a claim of service deficiency raised for the first time in response to a Section 8 demand notice, without contemporaneous prior correspondence, constitutes a genuine pre-existing dispute, and whether an ex parte Section 9 admission order violates natural justice when the Corporate Debtor failed to file a reply or seek recall of the ex parte order for over five months.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An uncorroborated allegation of deficiency of service raised for the very first time in a reply to a Section 8 demand notice constitutes a spurious defense and does not qualify as a pre-existing dispute under the IBC; furthermore, a party that fails to file a reply or apply to set aside an ex parte order for several months cannot claim violation of natural justice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 8 and 9 require the dispute to be genuine, bona fide, and pre-existing prior to the issuance of the demand notice; an afterthought defense raised post-notice cannot thwart insolvency admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The defense must not be spurious, hypothetical, or an afterthought; the total absence of prior contemporaneous communications establishes the defense as spurious. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor failed to establish any pre-existing dispute and neglected procedural remedies before the Adjudicating Authority; the admission of CIRP under Section 9 was lawful and warranted.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the dismissal shall not prevent the Corporate Debtor from exploring a settlement with the sole creditor under the Section 12A framework.
summary: Naveen Kumar Jha, director of Dalmia Biz Medicare Ltd., challenged the NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Randstad India Pvt. Ltd. for an unpaid debt of Rs. 7,72,882. The Appellant argued that NCLT breached natural justice by passing an ex parte order and contended that a pre-existing dispute existed regarding service quality. Rejecting the appeal, NCLAT observed that the Corporate Debtor had appeared through counsel but failed to file a reply or apply to recall the ex parte order for five months. Moreover, because no contemporaneous correspondence documented complaints prior to the Section 8 demand notice, the defense was spurious. The Section 9 admission was upheld.

case_title: Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs vs. Oriental Bank of Commerce
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Union of India through the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA); the Respondent is Oriental Bank of Commerce, a financial creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying insolvency proceedings were initiated under the IBC against a Corporate Debtor in CP (IB)-939(PB)/2018, during which the Resolution Professional filed Application No. 2024 of 2019 addressing compliance difficulties under the Companies Act, 2013 and ROC master data updates. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not directly at issue in this appeal; the appeal arose out of a broad administrative/procedural direction issued during the CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT Principal Bench passed the impugned order on 22.11.2019 directing MCA's impleadment; the appellate judgment was delivered on 22.05.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT order dated 22.11.2019 directed that in all cases under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and Company Petitions across India, the Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs through the Secretary, must be impleaded as a party respondent to make authentic records available. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In (IB)-939(PB)/2018, the NCLT Principal Bench issued a nation-wide blanket direction commanding all NCLT benches to implead MCA as a respondent; UOI appealed against this order.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) possesses the inherent power or jurisdiction to issue an omnibus, blanket direction mandating that the Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs through its Secretary, be impleaded as a party respondent in all IBC applications and Company Petitions across all benches nationwide.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicating tribunal lacks jurisdiction to issue blanket, nationwide administrative or quasi-legislative mandates requiring government ministries to be made compulsory parties in every litigation; impleadment of necessary or proper parties is a case-by-case judicial discretion governed by principles of natural justice and the dominus litis rule. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60 and related provisions of the IBC and the Companies Act, 2013 do not grant rule-making powers to the NCLT under the guise of an order; wholesale impleadment without a specific relief sought against the Union of India is otiose. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Necessary or proper party tests require assessing whether an effective order can be passed without that party or if their presence is indispensable to adjudicating the real controversy in a specific case; absent any specific relief claimed or hearing afforded, impleadment violates natural justice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's blanket directive exceeded its statutory authority, infringed upon the Central Government's exclusive rule-making power, violated natural justice, and constituted material irregularity and patent illegality.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 22.11.2019 passed by NCLT New Delhi (Principal Bench) in (IB)-939(PB)/2018 is set aside with no order as to costs.
summary: The Union of India challenged an order by the NCLT Principal Bench mandating that the Ministry of Corporate Affairs be impleaded as a party respondent in all IBC and Company Petition matters across all NCLT benches nationwide to facilitate authentic records. The NCLAT held that the NCLT exceeded its powers by effectively legislating a new rule rather than exercising judicial discretion on a case-by-case basis. Finding that such an omnibus, blanket directive infringed on the exclusive rule-making domain of the Central Government and violated the principles of natural justice, the NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned direction.

case_title: Bank of India vs. M/s. IRIS Electro Optics Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Bank of India is the sole secured financial creditor; Respondent No. 1 is M/s IRIS Electro Optics Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional; Respondent No. 3 is Laxmi Kantha Rao Thota (alleged related party Financial Creditor and husband of suspended Director Mrs. Archana Thota). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial debt arising under a loan agreement wherein Respondent No. 3 purportedly advanced a loan of Rs. 62,97,825/- to the Corporate Debtor at 24% interest per annum. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 62,97,825/- along with 24% per annum interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respondent No. 3 filed a Section 7 petition on 20.03.2019; Corporate Debtor filed an admission reply on the same day (20.03.2019); Section 7 petition was admitted on 28.03.2019; first CoC held on 01.05.2019; second CoC held on 28.05.2019; I.A. 461/2019 disposed on 19.08.2019; impugned order passed on 27.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's reply admitting liability immediately on the date of petition filing; resignation of Mrs. Archana Thota dated 30.11.2018 accepted by MD on 01.12.2018 but never filed with the ROC; exclusion of sole secured creditor Bank of India from initial CoC; voting share reconfiguration allocating 63.95% to Bank of India and 36.05% to Respondent No. 3 to prevent replacement of RP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 181/7/HDB/2019 admitted on 28.03.2019; Appellant filed I.A. No. 785/2019 under Section 65 alleging fraudulent initiation to thwart SARFAESI proceedings; NCLT Hyderabad Bench declined to decide the collusion and recall issues, deferring them while liquidation loomed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in deferring the adjudication of an application under Section 65 of the IBC alleging collusive and fraudulent initiation of CIRP by a related party to defeat a secured creditor's rights, while proceeding toward liquidation of the Corporate Debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When substantive allegations of fraudulent or collusive initiation under Section 65 are raised by a secured creditor against an alleged related-party applicant, the Adjudicating Authority cannot abdicate its duty by deferring adjudication to a later stage while letting the resolution process advance toward liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 65 of the IBC mandates determination of whether an application is filed with fraudulent or malicious intent for any purpose other than resolution of insolvency; a related party cannot usurp CoC control or voting share through clandestine insider arrangements. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Material irregularity and prima facie indicators of collusion (e.g., immediate admission of liability on the day of filing, unfiled ROC resignation of a director-spouse, and deliberate exclusion of the sole secured financial creditor from the CoC) demand immediate judicial enquiry. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Deferment of the Section 65 enquiry while allowing an alleged related party to hold voting shares and forcing the secured creditor into an adverse position constituted a failure of jurisdiction and a grave miscarriage of justice.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned order dated 27.11.2019 is set aside. The matter is remanded to the Adjudicating Authority to accord fresh consideration to I.A. No. 785 of 2019 and determine whether Respondent No. 3 is a related party and whether CIRP was fraudulently initiated under Section 7. The period of judicial intervention and lockdown is excluded from the CIRP timeline.
summary: Bank of India, the sole secured financial creditor, challenged the NCLT Hyderabad Bench's order declining to decide its application under Section 65 of the IBC. The Bank alleged that Respondent No. 3, the husband of a director of the Corporate Debtor, collusively triggered Section 7 CIRP to stall SARFAESI proceedings and manipulated the CoC by excluding the Bank. The NCLAT held that the NCLT abdicated its jurisdiction by deferring the critical issue of collusion and related-party status until final hearing while the Corporate Debtor was being pushed into liquidation. The NCLAT set aside the order and remanded the matter for urgent fresh adjudication.

case_title: Amitabh Kumar Jha vs. Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Amitabh Kumar Jha, Director of TD Toll Road Private Limited (Corporate Debtor, an SPV of Reliance Infrastructure Ltd); Respondent No. 1 is Bank of India (Financial Creditor); other consortium lenders include Canara Bank, Corporation Bank, IIFCL, OBC, and UCO Bank. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Common Rupee Loan Agreement dated 28.03.2008 executed with a consortium of six banks for Rs. 322.40 Crores to execute a four-laning road project of Trichy-Dindigul Road awarded by NHAI; Bank of India advanced Rs. 25 Crores (7.75% share). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 21,68,44,477/-; account classified as Non-Performing Asset on 29.10.2018; default date specified as 16.07.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice issued on 12.11.2018; Section 7 petition CP (IB) 2803/MB/2019 filed and admitted on 25.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Common Rupee Loan Agreement (CLA), Security Trustee Agreement (STA), and Inter-Creditor Agreement (ICA) dated 28.03.2008; Clause 2.2 of CLA explicitly preserving independent enforcement rights of lenders; Clause 1.3 of ICA preserving Rupee Lenders' rights against the borrower. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Bank of India filed a Section 7 petition before NCLT Mumbai Bench; NCLT admitted the petition on 25.11.2019 holding that ICA does not override statutory rights under Section 7 read with Section 238; Appellant appealed against the admission.
legal_issues: Whether an Inter-Creditor Agreement entered into by a consortium of lenders bars an individual consortium bank from independently triggering CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC without the consent or collective action of the other consortium members.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An individual financial creditor's statutory right to initiate CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC cannot be curtailed, restricted, or made subservient to private inter-se arrangements such as an Inter-Creditor Agreement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: By virtue of Section 238 of the IBC, statutory rights created under the Code override non-statutory contractual mechanisms; moreover, an ICA regulates rights inter se lenders and cannot be leveraged by a defaulting borrower to defeat statutory enforcement. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The satisfaction test requires only proof of debt and default; where existence of financial debt and default are admitted and payable in law/fact, contractual inter-creditor terms cannot impede admission. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor had no locus standi to invoke the ICA against an individual lender; Bank of India was fully entitled to file under Section 7 independently.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as being frivolous, with no order as to costs.
summary: A director of the Corporate Debtor challenged the admission of a Section 7 application by Bank of India, contending that under an Inter-Creditor Agreement (ICA) among consortium lenders, no individual lender could initiate recovery or insolvency proceedings without collective consortium action. The NCLAT held that the statutory right of a financial creditor to initiate CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC cannot be curtailed by an ICA. Furthermore, the borrower has no locus standi to rely on internal lender agreements, and Section 238 overrides conflicting contractual arrangements. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Allahabad Bank vs. Poonam Resorts Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Allahabad Bank (Financial Creditor); Respondents are Poonam Resorts Limited (Corporate Debtor in CA 1303/2019) and Link House Industries Limited (Corporate Debtor in CA 1304/2019). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by Allahabad Bank to the two Corporate Debtors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Poonam Resorts Limited admitted liability to the extent of Rs. 44,60,09,790/-; Link House Industries Limited admitted liability to the extent of Rs. 6,52,03,922/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 applications filed on 05.09.2018; matters pending since 18.09.2019; impugned interim forensic audit orders passed on 16.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Common written submissions of Corporate Debtors admitting debt liabilities of Rs. 44.60 Crores and Rs. 6.52 Crores respectively; applications filed by Corporate Debtors under Section 75 alleging false information. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP (IB)-3631(MB)/2018 and CP (IB)-3621(MB)/2018, the NCLT Mumbai Bench, on applications filed under Section 75, appointed PricewaterhouseCoopers Services LLP as Forensic Auditor to investigate loan utilization before deciding admission under Section 7; Allahabad Bank appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction at the pre-admission threshold of a Section 7 application to bypass statutory timelines and direct a forensic audit of the Corporate Debtor's accounts upon an application filed under Section 75 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority cannot direct a forensic audit or initiate an exhaustive pre-admission investigative inquiry into loan utilization before deciding whether to admit a Section 7 petition, as speed and adherence to strict statutory timelines are paramount under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 7(4) and 7(5), the Adjudicating Authority's duty is strictly circumscribed to ascertaining the existence of debt and default within 14 days based on Information Utility records or other evidence furnished by the creditor; Section 75 is a penal provision for offences and cannot be deployed to derail admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where debt and default are admitted or apparent from record, disputes regarding claim amounts or assertions under Section 65/75 cannot stall CIRP admission unless patent forgery or falsification of documents is prima facie established. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Ordering a forensic audit at the pre-admission stage is impermissible and violates the core scheme and timeline of the IBC.
operative_order: Both appeals are allowed; the impugned orders dated 16.10.2019 directing a forensic audit are set aside. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to address admission of the Section 7 applications without further loss of time, with an opportunity granted to the parties to settle claims.
summary: Allahabad Bank challenged orders of the NCLT Mumbai Bench appointing a forensic auditor (PwC) at the pre-admission stage of Section 7 applications, following applications filed by the Corporate Debtors under Section 75 alleging false information. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority cannot travel beyond the statutory mandate of Section 7(4) and (5) to order a long-drawn forensic audit. Reiterating the Supreme Court's ruling in Innoventive Industries, the Appellate Tribunal held that the tribunal's sole role at the threshold stage is to ascertain default within the prescribed 14 days, and penal provisions like Section 75 cannot thwart admission when default is admitted. The appeals were allowed.

case_title: Gopal Krishan Bathla vs. Crown Realtech Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Gopal Krishan Bathla, Ex-Director of M/s Crown Realtech Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 2 is Mohan Agarwal (Allottee / Financial Creditor); Intervenors are other homebuyer allottees. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement to sell for commercial space (Flat Nos. 409, 410, and 411, 4th Floor, Tower B-2, Sarai Khawaja, Faridabad) in the project 'Abacus Technopark' for Rs. 2,08,98,830/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total consideration paid was Rs. 2,08,60,200/-; possession due by December 2012 (with 3-month grace period); failure to deliver attracted interest @20.50% per annum compounded annually. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreed possession date December 2012; Section 7 petition filed in November 2018; Section 7 admitted on 06.12.2019; CoC constituted on 03.01.2020; alleged settlement dated 03.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Complete failure to deliver possession for over 6.5 years with only 80-85% construction completed; no settlement agreement placed on record or communicated to the NCLT prior to admission or CoC constitution; intervention by multiple homebuyers showing pending claims. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 2 filed CP (IB) No. 1565 (PB) OF 2018 under Section 7; admitted by NCLT Principal Bench on 06.12.2019; Appellant appealed seeking to set aside admission under Rule 11 on the basis of an unrecorded bilateral settlement.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal should exercise inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 to set aside an admission order based on an alleged bilateral pre-admission settlement between a real estate corporate debtor and a single allottee where other allottees' claims are pending and CoC has been constituted.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Inherent powers under Rule 11 to allow withdrawal or exit from CIRP upon settlement cannot be exercised mechanically where the settlement is not evidenced on record, was not disclosed to the Adjudicating Authority, and operates to the prejudice and detriment of numerous other similarly placed financial creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 insolvency proceedings are collective proceedings in rem; Rule 11 powers of the NCLT/NCLAT as recognized in Swiss Ribbons must be exercised judicially considering all relevant factors, public interest, and stakeholder rights. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The appellant must present credible, contemporaneous documentary evidence of a genuine pre-admission settlement; an unproven, clandestine bilateral understanding designed to exit CIRP while stranding other creditors cannot be recognized. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The alleged settlement was a ploy to defeat the legitimate interests of other homebuyers and avoid the threshold requirements of the 2019 Amendment Ordinance; exercise of Rule 11 was unwarranted.
operative_order: The appeal lacks merit and is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: An ex-director of Crown Realtech Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the admission of a Section 7 petition filed by a commercial space allottee, claiming the parties had settled the matter on 03.12.2019, prior to admission on 06.12.2019, and seeking termination of CIRP under Rule 11. Multiple other homebuyers intervened, opposing termination. The NCLAT held that insolvency proceedings are collective proceedings in rem and inherent powers under Rule 11 cannot be used to sanction a clandestine, unrecorded settlement that defrauds or prejudices other stakeholders. Finding no supporting evidence of an all-encompassing settlement, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Chhattisgarh Distilleries Ltd. vs. Dushyant Dave & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Chhattisgarh Distilleries Ltd. (unsuccessful second Resolution Applicant); co-appellant is Abhay, suspended director/promoter of M/s Anand Distilleries Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Dushyant Dave (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 2 is Dera Finvest Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 3 is Punjab National Bank (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Anand Distilleries Pvt. Ltd. triggered under Section 7 by Punjab National Bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidation value of the Corporate Debtor was Rs. 22.78 crores; fair market value was Rs. 32.48 crores; Successful Resolution Plan offered Rs. 23.51 crores; Appellant offered Rs. 52.50 crores in a belated proposal; suspended director proposed an OTS of Rs. 27 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition admitted on 14.02.2018; 180-day CIRP extended by 90 days on 09.08.2018; last date for EOI/plan submission extended to 15.10.2018; CoC approved Respondent No. 2's plan via e-voting on 01.11.2018-02.11.2018; RP filed approval application MA 1363/2018 on 05.11.2018; Appellant filed MA 602/2019 on 05.11.2018 / submitted plan on 13.02.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Successful plan approved by 98.72% CoC voting share; Appellant's plan submitted months after the 15.10.2018 deadline and after CoC plan approval; promoter's objection that liquor license under the Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949 was non-transferable under Section 29A. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench approved Respondent No. 2's plan via MA 1363/2018 and rejected Appellant's MA 602/2019 and promoter's objections on 08.04.2019; both appealed to NCLAT under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses jurisdiction to direct the CoC to entertain and reconsider a late resolution plan offering higher value after the CoC has already approved a compliant resolution plan, and whether an appeal against plan approval is maintainable outside the circumscribed grounds of Section 61(3) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a resolution plan is non-justiciable; the Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction to suo motu direct the CoC to reconsider an already approved plan in favor of a belated offer, even if the latter proposes higher monetary consideration. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Scrutiny under Section 31(1) read with Section 30(2) is strictly limited to statutory compliance; appellate review under Section 61(3) read with Section 32 is circumscribed exclusively to the five enumerated grounds and does not permit equity-based inquiry into commercial feasibility. Furthermore, pendency of plan approval does not halt the statutory CIRP period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Appellants must establish specific contraventions under Section 61(3); failure to plead or substantiate any of the five statutory grounds renders an appeal against an approved resolution plan unmaintainable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC approved the plan by a 98.72% majority in accordance with law; Appellant's submission well past the deadline gave it no locus standi to disrupt the approved plan.
operative_order: The impugned common order dated 08.04.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench approving the resolution plan and rejecting the applications/objections of the Appellants is upheld; both Company Appeals are dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: An unsuccessful resolution applicant (offering Rs. 52.50 crores) and an erstwhile promoter (offering Rs. 27 crores OTS) challenged the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order approving Dera Finvest's resolution plan of Rs. 23.51 crores, which had received 98.72% CoC approval. The appellant submitted its plan after the deadline had expired and after the CoC had voted. The NCLAT, relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel, held that the commercial wisdom of the CoC is non-justiciable and the Adjudicating Authority cannot direct reconsideration of a late bid despite higher value. Absent grounds under Section 61(3), the appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Samir Agrawal vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Informant is Samir Agrawal, an independent law practitioner; Respondent No. 1 is the Competition Commission of India (CCI); Respondent No. 2 is ANI Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (Ola); Respondent Nos. 3 to 5 are Uber India Systems Pvt. Ltd., Uber B.V., and Uber Technologies Inc. (Uber Group). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: App-based on-demand taxi aggregation services provided by Ola and Uber to riders through independent driver-partners utilizing algorithmic pricing mechanisms. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; regulatory antitrust information alleging anti-competitive horizontal price fixing, hub-and-spoke cartelization under Section 3, and abuse of dominance under Section 4. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CCI closed the case under Section 26(2) on 06.11.2018 in Case No. 37 of 2018; appellate judgment delivered on 29.05.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Algorithmic fare calculation utilizing big data (time, distance, traffic, weather, supply-demand); drivers acting as independent contractors permitted to multihome and negotiate lower fares; absence of communication or price-fixing agreements between drivers inter se or between Ola and Uber; Informant suffered no personal legal injury or anti-competitive harm. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Informant filed Information under Section 19(1)(a) alleging Ola and Uber facilitated a hub-and-spoke cartel among drivers; CCI held no prima facie case existed and closed the matter under Section 26(2); Informant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an independent informant with no personal legal injury has locus standi under Section 19(1)(a) of the Competition Act, 2002, and whether the algorithmic pricing models of Ola and Uber constitute an illegal hub-and-spoke cartel under Section 3 or abuse of dominance under Section 4.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Receipt of information under Section 19(1)(a) requires the informant to be a person who has suffered an invasion of their legal rights as a consumer or beneficiary of competitive markets; further, algorithmic dynamic pricing by digital intermediaries connecting users and independent contractors without horizontal collusion between service providers does not constitute a hub-and-spoke cartel. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 19(1)(a) 'any person' must be construed as a person with affected legal rights to avoid vexatious claims; Section 3(3) requires horizontal concerted practice or meeting of minds among competitors, absent in independent dynamic pricing; Section 4 does not recognize collective dominance between separate enterprises. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To establish a hub-and-spoke conspiracy, there must be evidence of horizontal collusion or an agreement among spokes (drivers) inter se to delegate pricing power to the hub; algorithmic pricing based on big data variables without inter-driver communication fails this threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The informant lacked locus standi, and no prima facie case of cartelization or abuse of dominance was made out, justifying closure under Section 26(2).
operative_order: The appeal lacks merit and is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: An independent advocate filed information alleging that Ola and Uber operated hub-and-spoke cartels using algorithms to fix taxi prices among drivers in violation of Section 3 and abused dominance under Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002. The CCI closed the information under Section 26(2). On appeal, the NCLAT affirmed the closure, holding that the informant had no locus standi as he suffered no legal injury. On the merits, the Tribunal held that algorithmic dynamic pricing taking into account supply-demand data does not constitute a hub-and-spoke cartel absent horizontal collusion or agreement among drivers inter se, and collective dominance is not recognized under Section 4.

case_title: A. Renuga vs. Shar Theme Park Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is A. Renuga (50% shareholder and Director); Respondent No. 1 is Shar Theme Park Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 2 is N.V.S. Anandhan (Managing Director and estranged husband of Appellant); Respondent No. 3 is K. Rajendran (MD of Chennai Integrated Construction Company Pvt. Ltd., alleged Power of Attorney holder/developer); Respondents 4 to 9 are subsequent transferees/allottees. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement for Development and Sale dated 07.12.2011 concerning approximately 16.33-16.64 acres of land owned by the Company (substantially its entire asset base, valued in excess of Rs. 55 crores) executed by Respondent No. 2 with Respondent No. 3 for Rs. 6.25 crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; petition alleging oppression and mismanagement via unauthorized alienation of company assets. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Development agreement executed on 07.12.2011; disputed Board Resolution dated 04.09.2014; Power of Attorney executed on 30.10.2014; Madras High Court writ petition dismissed on 27.09.2017; civil suit O.S. 258/2018 filed; NCLT Chennai dismissed CP/281/2019 on 24.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board Resolution dated 04.09.2014 and POA dated 30.10.2014 executed without holding an EGM or obtaining shareholder approval by special resolution as required under Section 180(1)(a); Appellant denied participation in board meeting and was refused leave to file a rejoinder. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP/281/2019 under Sections 241-242 before NCLT Chennai Bench; NCLT dismissed the petition relying on High Court and civil suit proceedings, refusing rejoinder and slapping costs of Rs. 5 lakhs on Appellant; Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in dismissing an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242 and imposing exemplary costs without permitting the petitioner to file a rejoinder to contest a newly produced board resolution authorizing the sale of substantially the whole of the company's undertaking under Section 180.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority cannot shut out an oppressed shareholder from rebutting newly introduced crucial documentary evidence by refusing leave to file a rejoinder; specialized company tribunals must independently determine whether disposal of corporate undertakings violates statutory shareholder consent safeguards without being abdicated to concurrent civil litigation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 180(1)(a) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Board of Directors lacks power to sell, lease, or dispose of the whole or substantially the whole of the company's undertaking without shareholder consent by special resolution; Sections 241-242 vest wide remedial jurisdiction in NCLT to rectify prejudicial alienation of corporate property. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: When a shareholder challenges the authenticity of a pivotal board resolution produced for the first time in a counter-affidavit, principles of natural justice mandate that an opportunity be given to file a rejoinder and test its validity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT failed to follow natural justice in refusing rejoinder and wrongly imposed costs; the matter required full remand for fresh consideration.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order dated 24.07.2019 (including the imposition of Rs. 5 Lakhs costs) is set aside, and the matter is remanded back to NCLT Chennai Bench to decide afresh after giving proper opportunity to the parties to file pleadings/rejoinder, uninfluenced by earlier observations. No order as to costs.
summary: A 50% shareholder and director filed a company petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013, alleging oppression and mismanagement against her estranged husband and a developer who sold the company's entire undertaking (16.64 acres of land) based on an allegedly forged board resolution and POA without special resolution approval under Section 180(1)(a). The NCLT Chennai Bench dismissed the petition and imposed Rs. 5 Lakhs costs without permitting the appellant to file a rejoinder. The NCLAT held that statutory shareholder protection under Section 180 and principles of natural justice required affording the appellant full opportunity to contest the authenticity of the resolution. The NCLAT set aside the order and remanded the matter.

case_title: First Global Finance Pvt. Ltd. vs. IVRCL Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is First Global Finance Pvt. Ltd. (part of an unsuccessful Resolution Applicant consortium); Respondent No. 1 is IVRCL Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is State Bank of India (Lead Financial Creditor and CoC representative). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multi-crore credit facilities extended by State Bank of India consortium to IVRCL Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 604,15,36,434/- outstanding as on 22.10.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition admitted on 23.02.2018; 1st EOI published on 09.05.2018; 2nd EOI issued on 14.08.2018; Process Memorandum issued on 04.09.2018; 1st Resolution Plan submitted on 04.10.2018; revised plan submitted on 05.11.2018 and reconstituted plan on 16.11.2018; 270-day CIRP expired on 27.11.2018; liquidation orders passed on 26.07.2019 and 31.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Failure to deposit mandatory EMD of Rs. 5 Crores on time (only Rs. 2 Crores paid on 31.10.2018 and Rs. 3 Crores on 05.11.2018); unapproved changes in the consortium structure (Phoenix ARC withdrawing as resolution applicant to become financial sponsor/advisor); non-compliance with minimum net worth and turnover eligibility criteria. 6.
