PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The CoC rejected Appellant's plan on 12.11.2018 and 21.11.2018 due to eligibility deviation and commercial unacceptability; NCLT Hyderabad Bench ordered liquidation of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern on 26.07.2019 and 31.07.2019; Appellant appealed against plan rejection and liquidation.
legal_issues: Whether the rejection of a resolution plan by the CoC for deviation from EOI conditions, non-compliance with eligibility criteria, failure to timely deposit EMD, and commercial unacceptability can be interfered with by the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Adherence to the mandatory terms and conditions of an Expression of Interest and Process Memorandum, including eligibility criteria and earnest money deposit, is essential; the commercial wisdom of the CoC in rejecting a non-compliant or commercially unviable resolution plan is paramount and beyond judicial review. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 30 and 31 circumscribe judicial evaluation to statutory compliances; tribunals cannot rewrite tender conditions or force the CoC to accept unauthorized structural changes or commercial terms. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented failure to comply with EOI terms and delay in furnishing mandatory EMD constitute valid legal grounds for rejection of a bid prior to liquidation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC exercised valid commercial wisdom in rejecting the non-compliant plan; where liquidation as a going concern is already underway, eligible entities may only seek a scheme under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act subject to Section 29A/35 provisos.
operative_order: The impugned order of the NCLT Hyderabad Bench ordering liquidation is upheld; interim order dated 06.09.2019 is vacated; the appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: First Global Finance Pvt. Ltd. appealed the rejection of its resolution plan and the consequent liquidation order of IVRCL Limited passed by the NCLT Hyderabad Bench. The CoC rejected the appellant's plan due to unauthorized changes in consortium composition, non-fulfillment of EOI eligibility criteria, failure to furnish the Rs. 5 crore EMD within the prescribed deadline, and commercial unacceptability. The NCLAT reaffirmed that the commercial wisdom of the CoC is non-justiciable under the IBC and that strict compliance with EOI and Process Memorandum conditions is mandatory. Since the Corporate Debtor was already undergoing liquidation as a going concern, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Hussan Kadri vs. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Hussan Kadri (Director/Shareholder of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. (Financial Creditor / Assignee); Respondent No. 2 is M/s K.K. Kadri Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); assignor bank is Bank of Baroda. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple credit facilities (Cash Credit, Letter of Credit, and Term Loans) totaling Rs. 14.80 Crores sanctioned by Bank of Baroda on 06.01.2011, secured by loan documents; debts assigned to Edelweiss ARC via Assignment Agreement dated 26.03.2014. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total financial debt default of Rs. 44,51,74,964/- computed as on 31.07.2018; loan account declared NPA on 30.09.2012. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Sanction letter dated 06.01.2011; revival letters dated 18.01.2011 and 11.05.2012; balance acknowledgments on 09.05.2012 and 11.05.2012; account declared NPA on 30.09.2012; demand notice issued on 01.10.2012; OTS proposal dated 26.03.2014; fresh demand notice on 09.07.2015; OTS settlement letter dated 13.11.2015; OTS terms signed on 02.12.2015; part payments made on 05.12.2015, 31.03.2016, and 09.02.2017; further acknowledgment letter dated 19.03.2018; Section 7 petition filed on 16.08.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Series of written OTS proposals admitting liability (26.03.2014, 13.11.2015, 19.03.2018); signed settlement terms dated 02.12.2015; verifiable bank transfers/cheque payments of Rs. 47.50 lakhs (05.12.2015), Rs. 1 crore (31.03.2016), and Rs. 1.5 crores (09.02.2017). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Edelweiss filed CP (IB) No. 407/7/NCLT/AHM/2018 under Section 7 on 16.08.2018; admitted by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 25.07.2019; Appellant appealed challenging admission purely on grounds of limitation.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed beyond three years from the initial NPA date is barred by limitation under Article 137, or whether successive written acknowledgments of liability and part-payments under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 extend the limitation period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Successive written acknowledgments of a subsisting liability signed before the expiration of the prescribed period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and part-payments evidenced in writing under Section 19, provide fresh starting points of limitation for filing an application under Section 7 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Article 137 applies to Section 7 petitions with a three-year period commencing from default/NPA, the general bar of Section 3 is expressly subject to Sections 4 to 24; an OTS proposal or payment constitutes a valid acknowledgment of a subsisting jural relationship extending limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The creditor must prove an unbroken chain of written admissions of subsisting liability or documented part-payments where each event occurs prior to the expiry of the preceding three-year period. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor executed written OTS proposals and made part payments in 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, and 2018; the Section 7 petition filed in August 2018 fell well within three years of the February 2017 payment, making the application timely.
operative_order: The appeal is held to be frivolous and is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: A director of the Corporate Debtor appealed the admission of Edelweiss ARC's Section 7 petition, contending that the debt was time-barred as the account became an NPA in September 2012 and the petition was filed in August 2018. Edelweiss established an unbroken chain of written acknowledgments and part-payments pursuant to OTS terms in 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, and 2018. The NCLAT held that under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963, each written acknowledgment and part-payment creates a fresh period of limitation. Because the petition was filed within three years of the last part-payment on 09.02.2017 and acknowledgment on 19.03.2018, the petition was timely, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Ritu Murli Manohar Goyal vs. SVG Fashions Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ritu Murli Manohar Goyal, shareholder and Director of Arpita Filaments Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is SVG Fashions Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Regular supply of various fabrics by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor since 2013 against running invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default amount of Rs. 43,96,593/- (principal invoice debt of Rs. 21,08,821/- plus interest of Rs. 22,87,772/-) for invoices raised from 11.08.2013 to 02.09.2013; date of default specified as 07.10.2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised August-September 2013; date of default 07.10.2013; Demand Notice under Section 8 issued on 22.12.2017 / delivered 19.03.2018; Section 9 petition filed on 20.04.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Invoices covering 11.08.2013 to 02.09.2013; six cheques dated 05.12.2017 totaling Rs. 5,37,206/- issued by the Corporate Debtor and subsequently dishonoured; Corporate Debtor's plea of lost cheques and stop-payment instructions. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application CP No. (IB) 182/9/NCLT/AHM/2018 admitted by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 26.09.2019 rejecting the missing-cheques defense; Appellant appealed to NCLAT on the ground of limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the issuance of cheques towards part-payment after the expiry of the three-year limitation period prescribed under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 can constitute a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 so as to revive a time-barred operational debt for filing a Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 must be executed before the expiration of the prescribed period of limitation; an acknowledgment made after the limitation period has already expired cannot revive a time-barred claim or extend limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Article 137 of the Limitation Act governs Section 9 IBC applications, providing a three-year period from the date default occurs; Section 18 requires that written acknowledgment be made within that three-year window to start a fresh limitation period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the admitted date of default is 07.10.2013, the three-year limitation period lapsed on 07.10.2016; cheques issued subsequently on 05.12.2017 do not satisfy the timing requirement of Section 18. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The operational debt was time-barred when the Section 9 application was filed on 20.04.2018, rendering the debt legally not due and payable and the petition non-maintainable.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned admission order dated 26.09.2019 is set aside. Moratorium, appointment of IRP, and bank account freezing orders are declared illegal and set aside; the Section 9 petition is dismissed, and the Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP rigours to function independently under its Board.
summary: A director of the Corporate Debtor challenged the admission of a Section 9 IBC application filed by SVG Fashions Ltd. for unpaid fabric invoices dating from August-September 2013. The date of default was recorded as 07.10.2013, and the creditor relied on six part-payment cheques issued on 05.12.2017 to claim an extension of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. The NCLAT held that an acknowledgment under Section 18 must occur prior to the expiration of the prescribed three-year period under Article 137. Because the three-year period expired in October 2016, cheques issued in December 2017 could not revive the debt. The Section 9 application was held barred by limitation, the admission was quashed, and CIRP was set aside.

case_title: Mr. Savan Godiawala vs. Mr. G. Venkatesh Babu & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mr. Savan Godiawala, Official Liquidator of Lanco Infratech Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Mr. G. Venkatesh Babu, erstwhile Managing Director; Respondent No. 2 is Lanco Infratech Ltd. (in liquidation); Respondent Nos. 3 and 4 are Income Tax Authorities. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Infrastructure and EPC operations of the Corporate Debtor involving non-remittance of deducted Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) during the financial year 2012-13. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unremitted TDS of Rs. 37,90,87,796/- deducted during FY 2012-13 and not deposited into the government account within statutory timelines. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Default occurred during FY 2012-13; Income Tax Department filed Criminal Case No. 530366/2016 on 31.03.2016 under Sections 276B/278B; Section 7 CIRP initiated on 07.08.2017; liquidation ordered on 27.08.2018; NCLT allowed IA 97/2019 on 10.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Criminal complaint before ACMM Tis Hazari Courts, Delhi against the Corporate Debtor and MD personally; application by the ex-MD seeking that the liquidator fund the compounding fee on priority or reimburse him to avoid personal imprisonment of 3 months to 7 years. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench allowed IA No. 97/2019 filed by the ex-MD directing the Liquidator to reimburse the compounding fees incurred in the criminal complaint; Liquidator appealed to NCLAT under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the Liquidator of a Corporate Debtor in liquidation can be directed under Section 35(1)(k) or Section 53 of the IBC to pay or reimburse compounding fees on behalf of an erstwhile Managing Director facing personal criminal prosecution under Sections 276B and 278B of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for pre-CIRP defaults.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate liquidator's statutory obligation to defend proceedings on behalf of a corporate debtor under Section 35(1)(k) does not extend to assuming, funding, or reimbursing the compounding costs of personal criminal liabilities incurred by former corporate officers for pre-insolvency penal offences. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 35(1)(k) mandates the liquidator to institute or defend legal proceedings in the name of and on behalf of the Corporate Debtor, not to shield delinquent directors from personal criminal consequences; directing reimbursement of compounding fees from the liquidation estate violates the statutory waterfall priority under Section 53. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where criminal liability for non-remittance of TDS under Section 276B r/w 278B attaches personal culpability to the person in charge carrying potential imprisonment, an application for compounding is for personal benefit and cannot be saddled onto the corporate debtor in liquidation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority misconstrued Section 35(1)(k); the ex-MD must defend the prosecution in his personal capacity and cannot escape criminal consequences at the expense of the liquidation estate.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned order dated 10.06.2019 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench in IA No. 97/2019 is set aside, with no order as to costs.
summary: The Liquidator of Lanco Infratech Ltd. appealed an order of the NCLT Hyderabad Bench directing him to reimburse the compounding fees incurred by the erstwhile Managing Director in a pre-CIRP criminal prosecution initiated by the Income Tax Department under Sections 276B and 278B of the Income Tax Act for unremitted TDS of Rs. 37.90 crores. The NCLAT held that while Section 35(1)(k) of the IBC requires the liquidator to defend actions on behalf of the Corporate Debtor, it does not obligate the liquidation estate to fund or reimburse compounding expenses for criminal offences attracting personal imprisonment of former directors. Permitting such payment would violate the statutory distribution priority under Section 53. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT order.

case_title: Dinesh Pujara & Ors. vs. Madras Race Club & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 367 of 2019 & Company Appeal (AT) No. 332 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants in CA 367/2019 are Dinesh Pujara and 27 other Club Members; Appellants in CA 332/2019 are R.D. Ramasamy and Magesh Kumar M.; Respondent No. 1 is Madras Race Club (MRC, a Section 26 not-for-profit company); Respondent No. 2 is M. Muthukaruppan. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Governance and statutory AGM conduct of Madras Race Club involving voting rights and validity of membership for members admitted between 2000 and 2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in convening and conducting statutory Annual General Meetings for the financial years ending 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2019; dispute regarding unpaid entrance fees by 635 out of 924 club members admitted during 2000-2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Dispute regarding 2000-2015 admissions; special investigation audit in 2016; initial NCLT order and NCLAT remand on 03.04.2018 in CA 71 & 87 of 2018; impugned order passed on 24.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Brahmayya & Co. independent audit report (2016); inquiry report by Justice K.P. Siva Subramaniyan (Retd.) identifying only 5 out of 640 members as genuine due to non-payment of entrance fees; membership cards and payment of annual subscriptions/amenity charges for 10-15 years by appellants. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Petition CP/31/2017 filed under Section 97 to convene AGMs; NCLT Chennai Bench on 24.09.2019 directed holding AGMs for 2016-2019 under Justice R.S. Ramanathan (Retd.) as Chairman with only genuine members eligible to vote, removing 635 members; Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether members whose names appeared on the club register and who paid annual subscriptions for years can be excluded from voting in Section 97 court-convened AGMs for non-payment of entrance fees, or whether they should be permitted an opportunity to regularize membership by paying entrance fees with interest.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In court-convened general meetings under company law aimed at restoring corporate democracy, members facing disqualification solely due to historic non-payment of entrance fees may be granted an equitable opportunity to regularize their status upon payment of arrears with interest rather than suffering outright disenfranchisement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 97 of the Companies Act, 2013 empowers the Tribunal to issue ancillary and consequential directions deemed expedient to ensure proper convening and conduct of overdue AGMs. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Independent forensic and judicial inquiry reports confirming long-term non-payment of entrance fees establish defective admission, but long-standing subscription payments warrant an equitable remedy before total exclusion. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT directions appointing an independent Chairman to hold AGMs are proper, subject to modifying the order to allow the 2018-19 AGM to consider regularizing members upon payment of entrance fees plus SBI FD interest.
operative_order: The impugned order of NCLT Chennai Bench is upheld with the modification that AGMs for 2015-16, 2016-17, 2017-18, and 2018-19 shall be held within two months, and the AGM for 2018-19 shall additionally consider the issue of permitting payment of entrance fees along with interest at State Bank of India fixed deposit rates for the years of delay. No costs.
summary: Appellants challenged an order of NCLT Chennai Bench under Section 97 of the Companies Act, 2013, which directed the convening of overdue AGMs (2016-2019) for Madras Race Club under an independent retired High Court judge while excluding 635 club members whose admissions between 2000 and 2015 were found defective for non-payment of entrance fees. The NCLAT affirmed the appointment of the independent Chairman and the direction to hold the AGMs for the four pending financial years within two months based on verified rolls, but modified the order to provide that the 2018-19 AGM shall consider permitting affected members to pay their entrance fee arrears along with interest at SBI fixed deposit rates.

case_title: P. Chandra Sekhar vs. Wincere Inc. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is P. Chandra Sekhar, Director and Guarantor of Cybermate Infotek Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Wincere Inc.; Respondent No. 2 is Himanshu P. Kansara (Financial Creditors); Respondent No. 3 is the Corporate Debtor; co-lender is Wincere Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (WSPL); MD of Corporate Debtor is P.C. Pantulu. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial debt of Rs. 4.44 Crores advanced by Financial Creditors/WSPL between 06.06.2012 and 20.12.2013 for working capital and business operations of the Corporate Debtor; Loan Agreement dated 31.08.2013 followed by Settlement Deed dated 07.09.2016 settling dues at Rs. 7.37 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Settled liability of Rs. 7.37 Crores, restricted in Section 7 petition to admitted claim of Rs. 3,87,00,000/- owed directly to Respondent Nos. 1 and 2. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan advanced 2012-2013; Loan Agreement dated 31.08.2013; Settlement Deed dated 07.09.2016; confirmation/acknowledgment letter dated 01.02.2017; Section 7 petition admitted on 26.03.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreement executed by promoter for Corporate Debtor's business; Settlement Deed signed by MD as borrower representative and Appellant as guarantor; formal letter dated 01.02.2017 on Corporate Debtor letterhead acknowledging Rs. 3.87 crores liability and enclosing repayment cheques; subsequent dishonour of cheques and Section 138 NI Act proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Joint Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 215/07/HDB/2017 admitted by NCLT Hyderabad Bench on 26.03.2018; Appellant appealed arguing lack of privity, distinction between US subsidiary and parent company, and civil suit pendency.
legal_issues: Whether a corporate debtor can evade insolvency admission under Section 7 by pleading lack of privity of contract where its promoter and director executed loan and settlement deeds for corporate working capital, followed by written corporate acknowledgments and issuance of dishonoured cheques.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a company's authorized management executes financing and settlement documents for corporate working capital and reinforces them with formal written corporate debt acknowledgments and payment instruments, the corporate entity cannot repudiate privity of contract or disclaim liability for default. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 requires the Adjudicating Authority to be satisfied as to the existence of a financial debt and default; corporate disguise or separate corporate persona arguments between a parent and its alter-ego foreign subsidiary cannot defeat established financial obligations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted letters of acknowledgment on corporate letterhead coupled with the issuance of dishonoured cheques and settlement instruments establish debt and default beyond technical objections. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The loan was disbursed for the Corporate Debtor's benefit and acknowledged in writing; the plea of absence of privity was a sham defense rightly rejected by the Adjudicating Authority.
operative_order: The appeal lacks merit and is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: A director of Cybermate Infotek Limited appealed against the admission of a Section 7 IBC application filed jointly by Wincere Inc. and Himanshu Kansara for an admitted default of Rs. 3.87 crores. The appellant argued that the loan agreement was executed with the promoter in an individual capacity, that the funds went to a US subsidiary, and that there was no privity of contract. The NCLAT rejected these contentions, observing that the managing director and director had executed a settlement deed and issued a written admission on the company's letterhead along with repayment cheques that were dishonoured. Confirming the existence of financial debt and default, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. M/s. Metenere Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor); Respondent is M/s Metenere Limited (Corporate Debtor); proposed IRP is Mr. Shailesh Verma. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 7 application filed by SBI seeking initiation of CIRP against Metenere Limited, nominating its former Chief General Manager as Interim Resolution Professional. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial debt default forming the basis of the underlying Section 7 petition CP No. (IB)-639(PB)/2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Proposed IRP served SBI for 39 years until retirement in 2016; NCLT Principal Bench passed substitution order on 04.01.2020; appellate judgment delivered on 22.05.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Proposed IRP Mr. Shailesh Verma was employed by SBI for 39 years, retired as Chief General Manager in 2016, and continues to receive pension from SBI; no pending disciplinary proceedings or direct empaneled retainer relationship. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP No. (IB)-639(PB)/2018, NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench held on 04.01.2020 that there was an apprehension of bias and directed SBI to substitute its proposed IRP; SBI appealed against the substitution direction.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is justified in directing a financial creditor to substitute its proposed Interim Resolution Professional on grounds of reasonable apprehension of bias when the proposed IRP had a four-decade employment history with that creditor and draws pension from it, notwithstanding that he suffers no express statutory disqualification.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Even in the absence of express statutory disqualification, the Adjudicating Authority is fully justified in requiring substitution of a proposed IRP where circumstances create a reasonable apprehension of bias in the mind of the corporate debtor, ensuring that insolvency administration is conducted with complete fairness and perceived impartiality. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 3(1) of the IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, 2016 requires independence from the Corporate Debtor, and drawing pension does not equate to being on the active payroll under Section 17(1) of the Income Tax Act; however, the duties under Section 18 require an IRP to act fairly and uninfluenced by past employment loyalties. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The test of likelihood of bias is not whether the tribunal itself finds actual bias, but the reasonableness of the apprehension in the mind of the contesting party as laid down in Ranjit Thakur v. Union of India. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: An employee of 39 years who retired as Chief General Manager and continues to draw pension raises a legitimate apprehension of bias; substituting him does not cause prejudice to the financial creditor.
operative_order: The appeal lacks merit and is dismissed with no order as to costs; the Adjudicating Authority's order directing SBI to substitute the proposed IRP is upheld.
summary: State Bank of India appealed an order of the NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench directing it to substitute its proposed Interim Resolution Professional, Mr. Shailesh Verma, in a Section 7 proceeding against Metenere Ltd.. Metenere objected that Mr. Verma had worked for SBI for 39 years, retired as Chief General Manager, and draws pension from SBI, creating an apprehension of bias. The NCLAT held that while receiving a pension does not render an IP an 'interested person' on active payroll or violate Regulation 3(1) of the IBBI CIRP Regulations, the test for likelihood of bias depends on the reasonableness of apprehension in the mind of the corporate debtor. Upholding the NCLT's direction to ensure fairness and perceived impartiality, the NCLAT dismissed SBI's appeal.

case_title: M/s. Gradient Nirman Private Limited & Anr. vs. M/s. IFCI Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are M/s Gradient Nirman Private Limited (shareholder) and I. Karunakar Reddy (Director of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is M/s IFCI Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is M/s Indu Techzone Private Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/SPV); Respondent No. 3 is M/s Indu Projects Limited (Corporate Guarantor); Respondent No. 4 is the Directorate of Enforcement (ED). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: IFCI sanctioned a term loan of Rs. 60 Crores to develop IT sector facilities, disbursing Rs. 9.90 Crores by 21.05.2009; balance of Rs. 50.10 Crores was cancelled on 31.03.2011 due to installment defaults. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default date asserted in Part IV of the application was 15.10.2013; account declared NPA on 30.06.2014; recall notice issued on 02.07.2014 demanding outstanding loan amounts. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Term loan cancelled 31.03.2011; default date 15.10.2013; NPA declared 30.06.2014; recall notice 02.07.2014; DRT proceedings initiated 14.11.2014; SARFAESI action 2014; Section 7 petition filed on 08.11.2017; OTS letter dated 20.03.2018; Section 7 admitted on 08.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unsigned 'Default cum Outstanding Statement' for 01.04.2017 to 20.09.2017; OTS proposal letter dated 20.03.2018 issued after the 3-year limitation expired; parallel recovery actions before DRT and SARFAESI. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IFCI filed CP (IB) No. 26/7/HDB/2018 under Section 7; NCLT Hyderabad Bench admitted the petition on 08.11.2019 holding that OTS letter dated 20.03.2018 saved limitation under Section 18; Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether time spent prosecuting recovery proceedings under the SARFAESI Act or before the DRT can be excluded under Section 14(2) of the Limitation Act for computing the limitation period of a Section 7 IBC application, and whether an acknowledgment of debt made after the expiry of the three-year limitation period can revive the claim under Section 18.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Proceedings under the SARFAESI Act or DRT are recovery proceedings and not civil proceedings in a court lacking jurisdiction for the same relief, precluding the application of Section 14(2) of the Limitation Act to Section 7 IBC petitions; further, an acknowledgment under Section 18 must occur prior to the expiration of the limitation period to extend time. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 IBC applications are governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act (three-year period from the date of default/NPA); Section 14(2) requires prosecuting with due diligence another civil proceeding for the same relief in a forum lacking jurisdiction, which SARFAESI does not satisfy; Section 18 requires a signed written acknowledgment before expiration of the three-year period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where default/NPA occurred on 30.06.2014, limitation lapsed on 29.06.2017; unsigned ledger statements or an OTS offer dated 20.03.2018 made after the expiry of three years cannot extend limitation under Section 18. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application filed on 08.11.2017 was hopelessly time-barred, and neither Section 14(2) nor Section 18 came to the financial creditor's aid.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 08.11.2019 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench admitting the Section 7 application is set aside. The Section 7 application is dismissed, moratorium and appointment of IRP are quashed, and the Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP rigours to function independently through its Board.
summary: The shareholder and director of Indu Techzone Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the admission of IFCI's Section 7 IBC application, arguing that the debt was barred by limitation. The loan account was declared NPA on 30.06.2014, and the Section 7 petition was filed on 08.11.2017. The NCLT had admitted the petition relying on an OTS proposal dated 20.03.2018 and SARFAESI proceedings. The NCLAT held that Article 137 applies from the date of default/NPA, SARFAESI proceedings cannot be excluded under Section 14(2) of the Limitation Act as they are recovery actions, and an OTS proposal submitted after the expiry of the three-year limitation period cannot revive a time-barred claim under Section 18. Setting aside the admission order, the NCLAT dismissed the Section 7 application.

case_title: Shadab Khan vs. M/s. Nisus Finance and Investment Manager & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Shadab Khan, shareholder of Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Obligor-3/Corporate Guarantor); Respondent No. 1 is Nisus Finance and Investment Management LLP (Facility Agent/Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Beacon Trusteeship Limited (Debenture Trustee/Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 3 is the Corporate Debtor; Principal Borrower is Earthcon Infracon Pvt. Ltd. (EIPL); other co-guarantor is Earthcon Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (ECPL). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debenture Trust Deed dated 13.06.2017 (amended 20.12.2017 and 24.12.2018) for issuance of 3,000 secured NCDs worth up to Rs. 30 Crores by EIPL to acquire units from the Corporate Debtor, backed by corporate guarantees, hypothecation, and mortgage of 200/205 flats. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 13,12,50,000/- on NCD redemption installment due on 31.03.2019; Beacon claimed Rs. 60,90,62,274/- in EIPL's CIRP; Nisus claimed Rs. 72,59,20,489/- in the Corporate Debtor's CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: DTD executed 13.06.2017; first installment defaulted on 31.03.2019; default letter issued on 02.04.2019; reminder notices issued 24.04.2019 and 06.05.2019; CIRP initiated against principal borrower EIPL on 23.08.2019 in IB-1601/ND/2019; Supreme Court stayed EIPL CIRP on 30.09.2019 and disposed of appeal on 18.02.2020; Section 7 petition admitted against Corporate Debtor on 08.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DTD and amendments; dishonoured repayment cheques with remark 'Funds Insufficient'; identical claims filed across multiple entities; Supreme Court order remanding the Section 65 fraud/collusion issue regarding the principal borrower's CIRP to the NCLT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP (IB) No. 1348/ND/2019, NCLT New Delhi Bench-III admitted Section 7 petition against Corporate Debtor on 08.01.2020; Appellant appealed invoking the rule against simultaneous CIRPs for the same claim under Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal.
legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor can trigger and maintain CIRP against a Corporate Guarantor for the same debt when the order admitting CIRP against the Principal Borrower is under challenge, stayed by the Supreme Court, and remanded to the NCLT to determine allegations of collusive initiation under Section 65 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the doctrine established in Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal, a financial creditor cannot maintain simultaneous CIRPs against both the principal borrower and the corporate guarantor for the exact same debt and claim; where the foundational CIRP admission against the principal borrower is under eclipse and remanded for inquiry into fraudulent initiation under Section 65, the guarantor's CIRP cannot proceed independently. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 applications cannot be deployed duplicatively across principal borrowers and corporate guarantors for an identical set of claims; Section 65 inquiries into fraudulent/collusive initiation take precedence and must be resolved before consequential guarantor petitions can be sustained. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the Supreme Court stays CIRP of the principal borrower and directs investigation of collusion under Section 65, proceeding against the guarantor risks grave conflicting determinations and impermissible duplicate insolvency processes. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 admission against the corporate guarantor must be reconsidered afresh only after the disposal of the pending Section 65 application regarding the principal borrower.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of by directing the Adjudicating Authority to reconsider the Section 7 admission against the Corporate Guarantor afresh only after the pending Section 65 application regarding the principal borrower is decided; further proceedings in IB-1348/ND/2019 are stayed in the interim. The operation of this judgment was stayed for two weeks upon oral prayer.
summary: A shareholder of Corporate Guarantor Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the admission of a Section 7 application filed by Nisus Finance and Beacon Trusteeship for debenture default, arguing that simultaneous CIRP against the principal borrower (Earthcon Infracon) and guarantor for the same debt is barred under Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal. The Supreme Court had previously stayed the principal borrower's CIRP and remanded the matter to NCLT to decide an application under Section 65 alleging collusive initiation. The NCLAT held that the fate of the guarantor's insolvency is inextricably linked with the Section 65 determination. It disposed of the appeal by directing the NCLT to reconsider the guarantor's Section 7 admission only after deciding the Section 65 application, staying CIRP proceedings in the interim.

case_title: Maj. Pankaj Rai vs. Secretary, Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Informant is Maj. Pankaj Rai (franchisee in Hyderabad); Respondent No. 1 is the Secretary, Competition Commission of India; Opposite Party is NIIT Limited (computer education and training provider). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Franchise agreements for running IT and banking education centers offering courses including PGDBO and Imperia programs. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; antitrust information alleging abuse of dominance and anti-competitive practices causing revenue losses to franchisees. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CCI closure order passed on 28.11.2017; Writ Petitions before Telangana High Court dismissed; Writ Appeals dismissed on 31.12.2018; statutory appeal before NCLAT filed on 06.01.2020 (total delay of 768 days, or 708 days beyond the 60-day limitation window). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant spent 693 days pursuing writ proceedings and writ appeals before the High Court of Telangana despite the statutory appellate forum being pointed out; allegations that CCI order was obtained by fraud involving former CCI personnel. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI closed Informations under Section 26(2) on 28.11.2017 in Case Nos. 47, 48 & 49 of 2017; High Court dismissed writ petitions and writ appeals relegating appellant to statutory appeal under Section 53B; Appellant filed Competition Appeal No. 01 of 2020 with an application to condone 708 days' delay.
legal_issues: Whether the general provisions of Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 apply to appeals under Section 53B of the Competition Act, 2002, and whether pursuing writ petitions before the High Court constitutes 'sufficient cause' to condone an inordinate delay of over 700 days in filing a statutory competition appeal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Competition Act, 2002 is an exhaustive, self-contained special statute providing an expeditious appellate remedy under Section 53B, excluding the general provisions of Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 by necessary implication; persistent litigation before constitutional courts in disregard of available statutory remedies does not constitute sufficient cause for condonation of delay. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 53B(2) proviso confers discretionary power to condone delay beyond 60 days upon proof of sufficient cause, but must be interpreted strictly in harmony with Section 53B(5) mandating six-month expeditious disposal; Section 5 of the Limitation Act cannot be imported. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Deliberate choice to bypass a specialized statutory appellate forum and engage in protracted writ proceedings, maintained even after the High Court relegated the party to statutory appeal, constitutes forum shopping rather than bona fide prosecution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant failed to demonstrate sufficient cause preventing him from filing the appeal within 60 days; the appeal is hopelessly time-barred.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as barred by limitation, with no expression on the merits and no order as to costs.
summary: An informant franchisee appealed a November 2017 order of the Competition Commission of India closing allegations under Sections 3 and 4 against NIIT Limited. The appeal was filed after an inordinate delay of 708 days beyond the statutory 60-day period under Section 53B of the Competition Act, with the appellant seeking condonation on the ground that 693 days were spent pursuing writ petitions and writ appeals before the Telangana High Court. The NCLAT held that the Competition Act is a complete code whose strict timelines exclude Section 5 of the Limitation Act by necessary implication. Holding that obstinate forum shopping before writ courts does not constitute 'sufficient cause' under Section 53B(2), the Tribunal dismissed the appeal as barred by limitation.

case_title: Sumeet Maheshwari vs. Navbharat Press (Bhopal) Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sumeet Maheshwari, shareholder of Navbharat Press (Bhopal) Private Limited (Corporate Debtor / Respondent No. 1); Respondent No. 2 is Bank of Maharashtra (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities sanctioned on 23.10.2002 (Rs. 6.63 Crores) and enhanced on 23.03.2004 (Rs. 14.17 Crores) secured by demand promissory notes, hypothecation, and mortgages. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding loan as on 25.07.2009 was Rs. 24,93,08,873.73/-; DRT Jabalpur issued a Recovery Certificate on 06.05.2015 for Rs. 24,93,08,874/- plus 14.25% interest; total claim in Section 7 petition was Rs. 83,40,90,183/-; account declared NPA on 31.03.2004. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 31.03.2004; loan recall notice issued on 11.07.2007; DRT Jabalpur OA No. 135/2009 decreed on 05.08.2011; Recovery Certificate issued on 06.05.2015; Section 7 petition CP(IB) 1598/MB/C-II/2019 filed on 11.12.2018 / 16.03.2019; admitted ex-parte on 16.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Last written balance confirmation/acknowledgment letters executed by Corporate Debtor were on 05.04.2005 and 18.12.2006, with no acknowledgment thereafter; DRT decree and execution proceedings relied upon by the bank to claim a continuous cause of action. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Bank of Maharashtra filed a Section 7 petition in December 2018 / March 2019; NCLT Mumbai Bench-II admitted the petition ex-parte on 16.12.2019 based on the DRT decree and recovery certificate; Appellant appealed challenging admission on the ground of limitation.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed more than a decade after the declaration of NPA is saved by limitation on the premise that a decree or recovery certificate issued by the DRT provides a continuing cause of action or invokes the 12-year mortgage limitation under Article 62 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 7 of the IBC is governed strictly by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, requiring initiation within three years from the date of default/NPA; a decree or recovery certificate obtained from a Civil Court or DRT does not shift forward the date of default or confer a continuing cause of action for triggering insolvency. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Article 62 of the Limitation Act (12 years for mortgage recovery suits) applies strictly to suits and has no application to Section 7 IBC petitions; Section 7 is not a recovery suit or execution proceeding. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The starting point of limitation is the date of default/NPA (31.03.2004); absent any written acknowledgment under Section 18 after 18.12.2006, the claim became time-barred long before the filing of the Section 7 petition in 2018. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was barred by limitation under Article 137; the Adjudicating Authority erred in admitting the petition, which was liable to be dismissed.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned admission order dated 16.12.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-II in CP(IB) 1598/MB/C-II/2019 is set aside. The Section 7 application is dismissed, the Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP rigours, and all actions taken by the IRP/RP/CoC are declared illegal and quashed. CIRP costs are to be determined by NCLT and borne by Bank of Maharashtra.
summary: A shareholder of Navbharat Press (Bhopal) Pvt. Ltd. challenged an ex-parte order of NCLT Mumbai Bench-II admitting Bank of Maharashtra's Section 7 petition for a default of Rs. 83.40 crores. The loan had been classified as NPA on 31.03.2004, a recall notice was issued in 2007, and the bank obtained a DRT decree in 2011 and recovery certificate in 2015 before filing under Section 7 in late 2018. The NCLAT held that Section 7 applications are governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act (three years from default/NPA) and not by Article 62 (12-year mortgage limitation). Furthermore, obtaining a DRT decree or recovery certificate does not shift the date of default or renew limitation for IBC proceedings. Since no acknowledgment existed after 2006, the petition was held time-barred and dismissed.

case_title: Mr. Ujjawal Narain & Anr. vs. M/s. Goel Enclave & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants (Mr. Ujjawal Narain & Anr.) were Informants/allottees of residential flats; Respondent No. 1 (M/s. Goel Enclave, OP-1) along with OPs 2 to 4 were real estate developers; OPs 5 to 9 were other impleaded entities. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Booking of two residential flats by Informants in the housing project styled as 'Silver Line Apartments' developed by OPs 1 to 4 at Ganeshpur Rahmanpur, Chinhut, Faizabad Road, Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, under executed Agreements to Sale promising inclusive pricing. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Informants alleged extortion of Rs. 35,000/- towards car parking charges and Rs. 80,500/- towards maintenance charges beyond agreed prices, further alleging collective extortion of Rs. 5,50,00,000/- as lifetime charges and Rs. 1,75,00,000/- towards parking from allottees, alongside delayed possession. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information under Section 19(1)(a) of the Competition Act, 2002 was filed before the Competition Commission of India as Case No. 04 of 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreements to Sale, demand notes for uncontracted parking and maintenance fees, and site plans showing construction of eight additional residential blocks on earmarked common amenity areas using substandard construction materials. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: By order dated 05.05.2017, the CCI closed the Information under Section 26(2) of the Competition Act, 2002, holding that OP-1 held no dominant position in the relevant market of services for development and sale of residential flats in Lucknow given multiple prominent competing builders, thereby negating any prima facie Section 4 or Section 3 contravention.
legal_issues: Whether OP-1 held a dominant position in the relevant market of services for development and sale of residential flats in Lucknow so as to attract Section 4 contraventions under the Competition Act, 2002, and whether contractual defaults and deficiencies in construction amount to anti-competitive practices under Sections 3 or 4.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of dominance by an enterprise in the precisely defined relevant product and geographic market, allegations of unilateral exploitative conduct or abuse under Section 4 cannot be sustained, even if there is a prima facie contractual breach. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002 requires threshold proof of dominant position; breach of contractual commitments, extraction of extra-contractual charges, or construction deficiencies without market power constitute civil/contractual disputes for competent consumer or civil forums, not competition law infringements. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of market strength based on comparative size, resources, and competing presence of major real estate developers operating concurrently in the delineated geographic and product market. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because OP-1 was a smaller player facing intense competition from major real estate developers (e.g., Sahara, Eldeco, Parsvanath, Omaxe) in Lucknow, it lacked dominant market power; thus, the closure order under Section 26(2) was fully justified.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs; impugned order dated 05.05.2017 passed by the Competition Commission of India under Section 26(2) upheld, reserving liberty to Appellants to approach competent civil or consumer forums for breach of contract.
summary: Appellants/Informants appealed the CCI's Section 26(2) dismissal of their information alleging Sections 3 and 4 violations by developer M/s Goel Enclave regarding two flats in 'Silver Line Apartments', Lucknow. Informants alleged excessive demands for parking and maintenance, substandard construction, and encroachment of common areas. The NCLAT affirmed the CCI's definition of the relevant market as 'the market for the provision of services for development and sale of residential flats in Lucknow' and held that OP-1, facing competition from major developers, did not hold a dominant position. Concluding that alleged deficiencies constituted private contractual breaches rather than anti-competitive conduct, NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Sunil Sanghavi vs. State Bank of India
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant (Sunil Sanghavi, shareholder of the Corporate Debtor); Financial Creditor (State Bank of India); Corporate Debtor (Ess Dee Aluminium Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Cash credit facility and term loan disbursed by State Bank of India to the Corporate Debtor in 2005 for Rs. 21.89 Crores, incrementally increased and extended periodically up to 24.09.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount reached Rs. 424.80 Crores; loan account declared Non-Performing Asset (NPA) following recurring payment defaults; debt acknowledged on 31.03.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 followed by DRT Kolkata recovery proceedings; Section 7 CIRP application admitted on 14.02.2020 (amended on 19.02.2020). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan sanction documents, extension agreement dated 24.09.2015, balance acknowledgment dated 31.03.2017, and NCLT order sheets (01.10.2019, 28.11.2019, 02.12.2019, 10.12.2019, 03.01.2020, 03.02.2020) demonstrating failure to file reply-affidavits despite multiple opportunities. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition admitted by NCLT Kolkata Bench ex-parte on 14.02.2020 (amended 19.02.2020) upon finding debt and default established, imposing moratorium and appointing an IRP; shareholder appealed on grounds of breach of natural justice.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority violated the principles of natural justice by proceeding ex-parte and admitting the Section 7 IBC application without granting further opportunity to settle, where the Corporate Debtor repeatedly failed to file a reply-affidavit despite multiple opportunities.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority does not violate natural justice by proceeding to hear and admit an insolvency application where a party enters appearance upon notice but repeatedly defaults in filing its reply-affidavit despite multiple explicit accommodations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The summary scheme of Section 7 of the IBC mandates swift admission once financial debt and default are established; unsupported assertions of ongoing oral negotiations cannot derail statutory CIRP timelines or substitute for formal written settlement agreements. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the judicial record and interim order sheets to determine if procedural fairness was accorded, and strict requirement that any settlement claim must be evidenced by formal written terms placed before the tribunal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The record demonstrated ample opportunity was provided to file a reply-affidavit and contained no written restructuring proposal; therefore, the plea of breach of natural justice lacked merit and the debt and default justified admission.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; the order of admission passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Kolkata Bench) under Section 7 of the IBC, along with the appointment of Interim Resolution Professional and imposition of moratorium, is upheld.
summary: Appellant, a shareholder of Ess Dee Aluminium Limited (Corporate Debtor), challenged the NCLT Kolkata Bench's order admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by State Bank of India for an unpaid credit facility default of Rs. 424.80 Crores. The Appellant contended that natural justice was violated because the NCLT proceeded ex-parte without providing an opportunity to settle during alleged loan negotiation talks. The NCLAT perused the NCLT order sheets, noted that multiple opportunities to file a reply had been granted but ignored, and highlighted the absence of any written settlement terms on record. Holding that natural justice had not been violated and the default was proven, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. vs. Mr. Ashish Arjun Kumar Rathi, Liquidator of SBQ Steels Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Applicant (Indian Oil Corporation Ltd., Operational Creditor); Respondent (Mr. Ashish Arjun Kumar Rathi, Liquidator of SBQ Steels Pvt. Ltd. / Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement dated 08.02.2010 executed between Appellant and SBQ Steels Ltd. for supply of furnace oil for 15 years, requiring the company to lift a minimum of 10,000 MT per annum from years 2 to 6 or pay compensation at Rs. 2,000/- per MT, along with a 15-year lease of 1,760 sq. meters of land on annual rent of Rs. 1,000/- where Appellant installed storage tanks costing Rs. 3,09,17,932.71. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following default, Appellant initiated arbitration in 2014; after liquidation order dated 30.01.2019, Appellant filed Form-C claim totaling Rs. 15,13,00,000/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form-C submitted on 12.03.2019; Liquidator partly admitted Rs. 9,87,93,000/- and rent of Rs. 7,000/- via email dated 23.04.2019 while rejecting Rs. 2,35,00,000/- for storage facility investment and Rs. 2,90,00,000/- for interest without assigning detailed reasons. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreement dated 08.02.2010, surveyor's report verifying installed storage tanks based on October 2010 invoices, arbitration invocation records, and Liquidator's rejection email dated 23.04.2019 noting 'not admissible' and 'no provision for interest'. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant challenged the Liquidator's rejection via MA/791/2019 in CP/665/IB/2017 before NCLT Chennai; NCLT dismissed the application on 26.08.2019 holding that failure to provide detailed reasons did not invalidate the rejection since the claims lacked contractual covenants.
legal_issues: Whether the Liquidator acting as a quasi-judicial authority under Section 40 of the IBC is legally mandated to record explicit reasons for rejecting a creditor's claim, and whether unliquidated damages or interest claimed on breach of contract qualify as a 'claim' under Section 3(6)(a) requiring reasoned adjudication.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A liquidator determining claims under statutory insolvency provisions acts in a quasi-judicial capacity and is strictly obligated to record clear, speaking reasons when rejecting any portion of a submitted claim to prevent arbitrariness and enable meaningful appellate review. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 40 of the IBC, read with Section 42, requires reasons to be explicitly communicated for any rejected claim; interest sought on damages for breach of contract qualifies as an actionable right to payment under the expansive definition of 'claim' in Section 3(6)(a) that may be awarded on equitable grounds. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The requirement of reasoned adjudication entails independent evaluation of supporting documents (including surveyors' reports and billing materials) rather than cryptic, summary dismissals without rationale. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Liquidator's rejection via email without assigning detailed grounds violated Section 40, rendering both the rejection and the Adjudicating Authority's affirmation unsustainable in law, warranting remand for fresh adjudication.
operative_order: Appeal allowed without costs; impugned order dated 26.08.2019 passed by NCLT Chennai in MA/791/2019 in CP/665/IB/CB/2017 set aside; MA/791/2019 restored to file of NCLT Chennai with direction to pass a fresh reasoned order on merits after affording full opportunity of hearing to both parties.
summary: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. appealed against NCLT Chennai's order upholding the Liquidator's rejection of its claims for Rs. 2.35 Crores (storage tank investment) and Rs. 2.90 Crores (interest) against SBQ Steels Pvt. Ltd. The Liquidator had summarily rejected the claims via email without furnishing detailed reasons. Setting aside the NCLT order, the NCLAT held that under Section 40 of the IBC, a liquidator acts as a quasi-judicial authority whose decisions are appealable under Section 42, making recorded reasons the 'heart and soul' of an order. The Tribunal held that interest on damages constitutes a valid claim under Section 3(6)(a) and remanded the application to NCLT Chennai for fresh adjudication on merits.

case_title: Raj Kumar Garg & Anr. vs. Health Care At Home India Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants (Raj Kumar Garg & Anr., suspended directors and shareholders of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 (Health Care At Home India Pvt. Ltd., Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 (M/s Satyam Drugs Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Business relationship commenced in June 2017 wherein Corporate Debtor issued purchase orders for supply of paramedical staff, medical supplies, medicines, and medical equipment against which invoices were raised. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding operational debt claimed was Rs. 2,02,07,685.96 with 18% interest per annum in demand notice, computed to Rs. 80,72,422/- plus interest totaling Rs. 86,24,658/- as of 05.12.2019; 17 cheques totaling Rs. 18,50,000/- issued by Corporate Debtor were dishonored with 'Stop Payment'. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First Section 8 demand notice dated 25.02.2019 withdrawn for errors; second demand notice served on 16.04.2019; Corporate Debtor replied offering Rs. 27,08,891/- after adjusting alleged reverse sales of Rs. 1,97,06,210/-; Section 9 petition filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Purchase orders, unpaid delivery invoices, dishonored cheques leading to seven Section 138 NI Act complaints, pre-notice email admissions by Corporate Debtor dated 09.10.2018, 11.10.2018, 17.10.2018, and 26.11.2018, and absence of contemporaneous documentary proof of reverse sales. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi (Court No. IV) admitted the Section 9 petition on 19.12.2019 in IB-1177/ND/2019, holding that the conditional offer to pay Rs. 27,08,891/- was designed to evade liability against admitted supplies.
legal_issues: Whether raising a dispute regarding invoice veracity and asserting unverified reverse sales for the first time in reply to a Section 8 demand notice constitutes a valid pre-existing dispute, and whether a conditional offer to pay an admitted sum in full and final settlement satisfies Section 8(2)(b) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A conditional tender of partial payment offered as full and final settlement cannot be recognized as compliance with a statutory demand notice under Section 8(2)(b) of the IBC, nor does a belated, unsubstantiated assertion of set-off or uncommunicated invoice dispute raised post-notice constitute a genuine pre-existing dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2)(b) read with Section 9 requires unconditional payment of the unpaid operational debt evidenced by electronic bank transfer or encashed cheques; failure to remit an admitted debt exceeding the statutory threshold triggers CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Disputes must be genuine, supported by contemporaneous pre-notice documentation, and not spurious defenses concocted in reply to the demand notice where prior emails admitted liability and issued cheques were dishonored. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor failed to prove reverse sales, stopped payment on 17 cheques, and failed to unconditionally discharge even the admitted liability of Rs. 27,08,891/-, establishing an undisputed default exceeding the statutory threshold.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs; impugned order dated 19.12.2019 passed by NCLT New Delhi (Court IV) admitting the Section 9 petition and initiating CIRP against M/s Satyam Drugs Pvt. Ltd. affirmed.
summary: Suspended directors of Satyam Drugs Pvt. Ltd. appealed the NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by Health Care At Home India Pvt. Ltd. for default on medical supplies. Appellants contended that 15 invoices were unacknowledged, 17 cheques were stopped rather than bounced for lack of funds, and liability was limited to Rs. 27,08,891/- after adjusting reverse sales. NCLAT held that the reverse sales claim was unsubstantiated and raised as an afterthought in reply to the Section 8 notice. The conditional offer to pay Rs. 27,08,891/- as full and final settlement did not comply with Section 8(2)(b), and since default exceeded the statutory threshold, admission of CIRP was upheld.

case_title: Mrs. Asha Kiran & Anr. vs. Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 249-250 of 2019 & Company Appeal (AT) No. 251-252 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants (Mrs. Asha Kiran, wife of Ramesh C. Bawa, in CA 249-250/2019; Ms. Aakanksha Bawa, daughter of Ramesh C. Bawa, in CA 251-252/2019); Respondent (Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, through Regional Director, Western Region). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Investigation and oppression/mismanagement proceedings involving the financial collapse and systemic defaults of the Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services (IL&FS) Group between June and September 2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Large-scale financial defaults across public and private banks; Mr. Ramesh C. Bawa drew hefty salaries and allegedly siphoned corporate funds, transferring over Rs. 1.14 Crores and Rs. 4.84 Crores to family bank accounts. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Union of India filed CP No. 3638/2018 under Sections 241-242 of Companies Act, 2013; NCLT Mumbai passed interim freezing order on 03.12.2018 restraining erstwhile directors from creating third-party rights or alienating assets; SFIO investigation report submitted on 29.05.2019 followed by letter dated 08.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank transaction logs showing operation of joint bank lockers at Axis Bank and Standard Chartered Bank on 03.12.2018, 04.12.2018, and 10.12.2018 by Asha Kiran; electronic fund transfer of Rs. 4.84 Crores by Ramesh C. Bawa to Aakanksha Bawa on 03.12.2018; and SFIO tracing showing fund diversion to companies where Asha Kiran was a director. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai impleaded Appellants and restrained/sealed their bank accounts and lockers vide orders dated 26.04.2019 and 04.09.2019 in MA Nos. 1576/2019, 1577/2019, 2006/2019, and 2007/2019; Appellants appealed claiming to be innocent third parties.
legal_issues: Whether third-party family members who are neither directors nor employees of a mismanaged company can be impleaded and subjected to asset-freezing orders under Sections 241-242 and 339 of the Companies Act, 2013 when suspected of receiving proceeds of corporate fraud and dissipating assets post-restraint.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In corporate mismanagement and fraud proceedings, third parties and non-directors who receive suspicious monetary transfers or operate restrained joint repositories in violation of tribunal orders are proper and necessary parties whose impleadment and interim restraint are lawful to ensure effective adjudication and prevent dissipation of siphoned assets. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The equitable powers of the Tribunal under Sections 241-242, read with Section 339 of the Companies Act, 2013, extend to tracking siphoned funds into the hands of related non-directors; impleadment is not an adjudication of guilt but an essential procedural measure to facilitate complete justice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Temporal proximity between restraining orders and unauthorized bank transactions or locker operations provides sufficient prima facie justification to maintain impleadment and provisional attachment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The transfer of Rs. 4.84 Crores and operation of joint lockers on the day of and immediately following the NCLT's 03.12.2018 restraint order justified impleading Appellants to enable complete and effective adjudication.
operative_order: Both sets of appeals (Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 249-250 of 2019 and 251-252 of 2019) are dismissed without costs; the impugned orders dated 26.04.2019 and 04.09.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench are affirmed.
summary: Appellants, the wife and daughter of former IL&FS director Ramesh C. Bawa, challenged NCLT Mumbai orders impleading them and freezing their bank accounts and joint lockers in CP No. 3638/2018 filed by the Union of India under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013. Appellants argued they were non-director third parties not liable under Section 339. The NCLAT distinguished the Supreme Court ruling in Usha Ananthasubramanian, noting that large sums (Rs. 4.84 Crores) were transferred to the daughter and joint lockers were accessed immediately after NCLT's freezing order of 03.12.2018. Holding that their presence was necessary to effectively trace siphoned funds, NCLAT dismissed the appeals.

case_title: India Power Corporation Limited vs. M/s. Dynamic Cables Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant (India Power Corporation Limited, holding/contesting entity); Respondent No. 1 (M/s. Dynamic Cables Limited, Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2/Corporate Debtor (M/s. India Power Corporation (Bodhgaya) Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of industrial cables by Operational Creditor to Corporate Debtor pursuant to purchase orders and Letter of Award dated 09.04.2018, with deliveries effected across December 2017, January 2018, and May 2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of operational debt claimed at Rs. 2,32,46,235/- in Form 5; Corporate Debtor initially claimed default was only Rs. 58,000/- (below statutory threshold), but subsequently acknowledged liability of Rs. 1,74,00,775/- via letter dated 31.12.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice issued on 18.11.2018; Corporate Debtor replied on 27.11.2018; Section 9 application CP(IB) No. 30/KB/2019 admitted on 08.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Purchase orders, Letter of Award dated 09.04.2018, emails and WhatsApp communications showing requests for payment plans including email dated 27.08.2018, letter dated 31.12.2019 admitting debt of Rs. 1,74,00,775/-, and unserved/unreferenced dispute letter dated 14.05.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted the Section 9 petition on 08.11.2019, holding that quality disputes were an afterthought since goods lifted on 20.08.2018 pertained to a distinct Letter of Award, while email dated 27.08.2018 unequivocally promised a payment plan.
legal_issues: Whether a Corporate Debtor's claim of defective goods raised in reply to a demand notice constitutes a genuine pre-existing dispute under Section 9 of the IBC when contemporary correspondence contained promises to pay, and whether CIRP can be avoided on the plea that default was below Rs. 1 Lakh when liability exceeding the threshold is subsequently admitted in writing.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An uncorroborated quality dispute raised for the first time in response to a Section 8 statutory demand notice, contradicted by contemporaneous correspondence acknowledging liability, is a spurious defense that does not bar Section 9 admission. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 requires existence of a dispute prior to issuance of demand notice; belated defenses or attempts to minimize default below the Section 4 threshold (Rs. 1 Lakh) fail when contemporaneous books or subsequent written acknowledgments demonstrate default exceeding the statutory minimum. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The defense of a pre-existing dispute must be plausible, bona fide, and supported by credible contemporaneous evidence demonstrating that grievances were communicated prior to the demand notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The alleged dispute letter was never referenced in earlier communications or served, and Corporate Debtor's written acknowledgment of Rs. 1,74,00,775/- confirmed actionable default exceeding the statutory minimum, warranting admission.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs; impugned order of admission dated 08.11.2019 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench initiating CIRP, slapping moratorium, and appointing the Interim Resolution Professional affirmed.
summary: India Power Corporation Limited appealed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench order admitting a Section 9 IBC petition filed by Dynamic Cables Limited for an operational debt of Rs. 2,32,46,235/-. Appellant contended that cables supplied in Gaya DF Area failed specifications as per an unserved letter dated 14.05.2018, that goods were returned, and that outstanding default was only Rs. 58,000/- (below the Section 4 threshold). NCLAT affirmed that the quality dispute was an afterthought contradicted by an email dated 27.08.2018 promising a payment plan. Furthermore, Corporate Debtor subsequently acknowledged Rs. 1,74,00,775/- as due in its books, far exceeding the statutory threshold, justifying dismissal of the appeal.

case_title: Vasundhra Gupta, Managing Director, M/s Aesthetic Stone Arts India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mr. Sanwar Mal Tiwari, Sole Proprietor M/s. Rajasthan Steel Corporation & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant (Vasundhra Gupta, Managing Director of M/s Aesthetic Stone Arts India Pvt. Ltd. / Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 (Mr. Sanwar Mal Tiwari, Sole Proprietor of M/s Rajasthan Steel Corporation / Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 (M/s Aesthetic Stone Arts India Pvt. Ltd. / Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods/materials by Operational Creditor to Corporate Debtor under Invoice No. 52. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of principal operational debt amounting to Rs. 5,63,370/- under Invoice No. 52. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Statutory demand notice issued under Section 8 of the IBC remained unsatisfied; Section 9 application admitted by the Adjudicating Authority on 04.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unpaid Invoice No. 52 for Rs. 5,63,370/- and absence of any contemporaneous communication or record demonstrating a pre-existing dispute regarding principal liability. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT admitted the Section 9 CIRP petition against the Corporate Debtor vide order dated 04.03.2020 on finding undisputed debt and default exceeding Rs. 1,00,000/-; Managing Director appealed the admission.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in admitting an application under Section 9 of the IBC where the Corporate Debtor committed default on an undisputed principal debt exceeding the statutory minimum threshold of Rs. 1,00,000/- following service of a statutory demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for initiation of corporate insolvency resolution process under Section 9 must be admitted where an operational debt exceeding the statutory minimum threshold is established, default is demonstrated following demand notice service, and no pre-existing dispute is substantiated. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory threshold of Rs. 1,00,000/- under Section 4 of the IBC is satisfied when an admitted or undisputed principal invoice amount exceeds that sum; once default on an undisputed operational debt is established under Section 9, admission is mandatory. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the record to ascertain whether any contemporaneous dispute was raised regarding the liability or invoice amount prior to or upon receipt of the statutory demand notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because liability regarding the principal debt of Rs. 5,63,370/- was undisputed and remained unpaid despite demand notice, the order of admission suffered from no legal defect.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs; impugned order of admission dated 04.03.2020 affirmed, with the clarification that dismissal shall not preclude the Corporate Debtor from settling the claim with the Operational Creditor.
summary: Appellant, the Managing Director of Aesthetic Stone Arts India Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), appealed against the NCLT order dated 04.03.2020 admitting a Section 9 IBC petition filed by Sanwar Mal Tiwari, Sole Proprietor of Rajasthan Steel Corporation (Operational Creditor). The operational debt arose from unpaid Invoice No. 52 amounting to a principal sum of Rs. 5,63,370/-. The NCLAT observed that the Corporate Debtor raised no dispute regarding the principal debt, which exceeded the statutory threshold of Rs. 1,00,000/-, and had failed to satisfy the claim despite demand notice. Affirming the admission of CIRP, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal while clarifying that the dismissal does not preclude a settlement.

case_title: Corporation Bank vs. SJN Energy Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Corporation Bank (Financial Creditor/Appellant) and M/s SJN Energy Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 1), along with its directors/guarantors (Respondents Nos. 2 to 6). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Financial Creditor extended credit facilities consisting of a Term Loan Facility and a Cash Credit Facility to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The claimed financial debt was Rs. 31,63,29,782.20 as of 31.12.2018; the account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 23.05.2014, which was stated as the date of default in Part-IV of Form-1. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: No Section 8 demand notice was applicable; the Corporate Debtor executed two debt acknowledgement letters on 08.09.2015, extending the limitation period up to 07.09.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Core evidence included statutory Form-1, NPA classification records under RBI prudential norms dated 23.05.2014, two acknowledgement letters dated 08.09.2015, and documentation of parallel recovery proceedings, claims, and counter-claims before the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) and Civil Courts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Section 7 application was filed by the Financial Creditor on 05.02.2019; NCLT New Delhi Bench rejected the application on 25.09.2019 as barred by limitation since the default occurred on 23.05.2014 and the three-year extension from the 08.09.2015 acknowledgement letters expired on 07.09.2018.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed beyond three years from the date of NPA/default is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and whether pending proceedings before the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) or Civil Courts extend the period of limitation under the Code.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for corporate insolvency resolution is governed strictly by the residuary three-year period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act running from the date of default/NPA, and the pendency of proceedings before other recovery forums cannot extend or renew this limitation period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238A mandates the application of the Limitation Act, 1963 to Section 7 petitions; the non-obstante clause in Section 238 gives the IBC overriding effect over other laws, meaning the trigger point of limitation is not postponed or renewed by independent actions filed before DRTs or Civil Courts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict computation of the statutory 3-year period under Article 137 from the date of NPA/default (or from a valid Section 18 acknowledgement); where the claimed acknowledgement expired prior to the filing date and no Section 5 delay condonation was substantiated, the petition is legally non-maintainable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 petition was filed on 05.02.2019, whereas the date of default was 23.05.2014 and the acknowledgement dated 08.09.2015 extended limitation only until 07.09.2018; therefore, the application was barred by limitation and rightly dismissed.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as devoid of merits and the impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 25.09.2019 rejecting the Section 7 application on the ground of limitation is affirmed. No orders as to costs.
summary: Corporation Bank appealed the NCLT New Delhi Bench's order dated 25.09.2019 dismissing its Section 7 IBC application against SJN Energy Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. on limitation grounds. The Corporate Debtor was declared an NPA on 23.05.2014, and though debt acknowledgement letters were executed on 08.09.2015, the Section 7 application was initiated only on 05.02.2019. The bank contended that proceedings before the DRT and civil courts extended the period of limitation. The NCLAT held that under Section 238A read with Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the limitation expired on 07.09.2018. Overriding Section 238 prevents DRT proceedings from extending the limitation, rendering the application time-barred and resulting in the dismissal of the appeal.

case_title: Bimalkumar Manubhai Savalia vs. Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bimalkumar Manubhai Savalia (Appellant, Shareholder/Director of Corporate Debtor), Bank of India (Respondent No. 1, Financial Creditor), Chandra Prakash Jain (Respondent No. 2, Interim Resolution Professional), and M/s Radheshyam Agro Products Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Availment of loan and cash credit facilities by the Corporate Debtor secured by mortgage of property dated 18.11.2010 and a Deed of Guarantee dated 15.07.2010. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on 05.11.2014 as recorded in Part-IV of Form-1; default debt exceeded Rs. 1,00,000/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SARFAESI proceedings initiated in 2014; Section 13(2) SARFAESI notices issued; DRT proceedings initiated in 2017; Corporate Debtor submitted One Time Settlement (OTS) offers on 28.04.2016 ('without prejudice') and revised OTS offer of Rs. 14.56 Crores on 01.06.2016; guarantor transferred Rs. 1,26,619/- and Rs. 1,28,645/- into the account on 01.04.2017; Section 7 petition filed on 30.08.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-1, loan and mortgage agreements, CIBIL reports, statement of accounts, rejected OTS proposals dated 28.04.2016 and 01.06.2016, guarantor deposit slips dated 01.04.2017, and Section 17 SARFAESI appeal before DRT Ahmedabad. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed on 30.08.2018; NCLT Ahmedabad Bench admitted the application on 20.09.2019 holding that OTS proposals, DRT/SARFAESI actions, and guarantor payments on 31.03.2017 extended limitation.
legal_issues: Whether unaccepted OTS proposals, payments appropriated from a guarantor under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, or parallel SARFAESI and DRT proceedings extend the three-year period of limitation under Article 137 for initiating Section 7 IBC proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 7 IBC petitions are governed exclusively by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and the three-year limitation period is not extended by unaccepted OTS proposals, parallel SARFAESI/DRT recovery actions, or guarantor credit appropriations under Section 19. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 19 of the Limitation Act applies to suits and does not govern Section 7 applications; an unaccepted OTS offer does not constitute a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18; Section 238 of the IBC overrides separate remedies under SARFAESI or the DRT Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The creditor must produce an unequivocal acknowledgment in writing signed by the Corporate Debtor within 3 years from default/NPA; technical challenges raised in Section 17 SARFAESI pleadings do not constitute debt admissions for limitation purposes. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The date of default was 05.11.2014, and the Section 7 petition filed on 30.08.2018 was time-barred as none of the relied-upon events constituted a valid acknowledgment under law.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned admission order dated 20.09.2019 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench is quashed and set aside.
