The Corporate Debtor is released from the rigors of CIRP, the IRP is directed to hand back records and management to the promoters/directors, and the matter is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to determine CIRP costs/fees to be borne by Bank of India. No orders as to costs.
summary: A director and shareholder of M/s Radheshyam Agro Products Pvt. Ltd. appealed the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench's order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Bank of India. The default occurred on 05.11.2014, while the application was filed on 30.08.2018. The Adjudicating Authority held the petition timely based on an unaccepted OTS offer dated 01.06.2016, guarantor payments on 01.04.2017, and ongoing SARFAESI/DRT actions. The NCLAT reversed this decision, ruling that Section 19 of the Limitation Act applies only to suits, unaccepted OTS proposals do not constitute Section 18 acknowledgments, and DRT/SARFAESI proceedings do not extend the three-year limitation period under Article 137. The admission order was set aside and CIRP quashed.

case_title: Tweak The Future Innovations Pvt. Ltd. vs. Registrar Of Companies, Punjab & Chandigarh
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Tweak The Future Innovations Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Struck-off Company) and Registrar of Companies, Punjab & Chandigarh (Respondent/ROC). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Development, creation, and commercial licensing of innovative software programs, web/mobile platforms, futuristic technologies, and school management platforms. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory non-compliance due to failure to file Financial Statements and Annual Returns for three consecutive financial years (2014-15, 2015-16, and 2016-17). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Name struck off w.e.f. 11.09.2018 via Gazette notification dated 15.09.2018; pending statutory returns filed on 25.09.2018; Form ADT-1 filed on 01.10.2018; ROC issued notice on 03.11.2018 for FY 2017-18 returns. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MOUs dated 09.04.2015 (with North Atlanta Preschool, USA) and 06.05.2015 (with Achievers Technology Pvt. Ltd. for 'SoCo World'); Income Tax Returns for AY 2015-16 and 2016-17; belated ROC filing receipts totaling Rs. 73,800/- plus Rs. 3,600/-; and multiple commercial invoices issued in late 2018 and early 2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The company filed CA No. 04/CHD/2019 under Section 252 for restoration; NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed the appeal on 05.09.2019 holding that the company failed to prove it was carrying on operations at the time of strike-off.
legal_issues: Whether entering into MOUs, developing intellectual IT platforms, and incurring business expenses constitute 'carrying on business or in operation' under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, justifying the restoration of a company struck off under Section 248.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In commercial jurisprudence, the statutory requirement of 'in operation' under Section 252(3) encompasses developmental and preparatory stages of business, including IT platform development and executing MOUs, irrespective of low transaction volume. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'operation' under Section 252(3) must be construed in a broad commercial sense; active creation of software architecture and executing foreign agreements demonstrate that an enterprise is operational prior to commercial monetization. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production of subsisting bilateral MOUs, delayed statutory filings with penalty fees, and subsequent customer billing provide sufficient evidentiary proof to overcome the presumption of abandonment arising from unfiled returns. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant demonstrated continuous operational status at the time of striking off; thus, it is just and equitable to restore its name to the Register of Companies under Section 252(3), subject to compensatory costs.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 05.09.2019 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench is set aside. ROC is directed to restore the company's name to the Register of Companies. The Appellant is ordered to pay a cost of Rs. 1,00,000/- via demand draft to the Pay & Account Officer, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, for statutory defaults. No other relief granted.
summary: Tweak The Future Innovations Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh Bench order refusing to restore its name under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 after being struck off by ROC Punjab & Chandigarh for failing to file annual returns from 2014-15 to 2016-17. The Appellant demonstrated active operations via MOUs with a US school and another tech company for software development, along with late-filed returns and subsequent invoices. The NCLAT held that 'operation' in a commercial sense includes developing IT platforms. The Appellate Tribunal set aside NCLT's order, directed restoration of the company, and imposed a cost of Rs. 1,00,000/- for non-compliance.

case_title: Ramesh Kumar Chitlangia & Ors. vs. The Registrar Of Companies, Jaipur & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ramesh Kumar Chitlangia, Rajesh Chitlangia, and Ishwar Kumar Malpani (Appellants/Suspended Directors); Registrar of Companies, Jaipur (Respondent No. 1); Prabhu Dayal Chitlangia and Alka Chitlangia (Respondents Nos. 2 and 3/Shareholders); and M/s Trinity Combine Associate Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 4/Struck-off Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Internal corporate operations, shareholding interests, and real estate/commercial activities conducted since the incorporation of the Company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in statutory compliance due to non-filing of Annual Returns and Financial Statements continuously since incorporation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: ROC Jaipur issued a strike-off notice on 20.09.2018 under Section 248 of the Act; restoration was subsequently sought before the NCLT. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Records of prolonged pending litigations, including Suit No. 15/2003 decreed by Additional District Judge-1, Jaipur, with execution warrants issued under Order 21 Rule 30 CPC; an appellate order from the Rajasthan High Court regarding personal property execution; Case No. 12/1997 before the Special Court, Economic Offences, Jaipur under Section 220(3) of the 1956 Act; and execution appeals before ADJ-13, Jaipur. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents Nos. 2 and 3 filed CA No. 125/252/JPR/2019 before NCLT Jaipur; the NCLT allowed restoration on 11.10.2019 under Section 252(3) to protect ongoing litigation; the suspended directors appealed against this restoration.
legal_issues: Whether the existence of prolonged, contested litigations and execution proceedings against a company and its management constitutes an 'otherwise just' ground under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 to uphold the restoration of the company's name to the Register of Companies.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, the pendency of active and contested legal or execution proceedings involving a struck-off company satisfies the alternative statutory test of 'otherwise just', warranting restoration to protect the rights of stakeholders and litigants. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252(3) provides two disjunctive criteria: (i) carrying on business or in operation, or (ii) 'otherwise it is just'; the second condition confers broad equitable discretion on the Tribunal to maintain the legal entity for resolving pending rights and liabilities. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Admission by parties of ongoing suits, decrees, criminal complaints, or execution proceedings in competent courts establishes sufficient justification to restore the corporate shell. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly exercised its discretion to restore the company, as striking off would prejudice ongoing judicial proceedings involving the company, its directors, and its creditors.
operative_order: The appeal filed by the suspended directors is dismissed as being without merit, and the impugned order dated 11.10.2019 passed by NCLT Jaipur Bench ordering the restoration of the company's name is affirmed. No orders as to costs.
summary: Suspended directors of M/s Trinity Combine Associate Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Jaipur Bench's order restoring the company to the Register of Companies under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013. The company had been struck off by ROC Jaipur on 20.09.2018 for not filing returns since incorporation. Shareholders sought restoration due to pending litigations, including execution of a civil decree and economic offences complaints, which the Appellants claimed was done in bad faith. The NCLAT affirmed that the pendency of contested legal and execution proceedings against the company provides an 'otherwise just' ground under Section 252(3) to order restoration, dismissing the appeal without costs.

case_title: Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Ltd. & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Union of India through the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (Petitioner/Appellant), Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Ltd. (IL&FS - Corporate Entity/Holding Company Respondent No. 1), its 348 domestic and offshore subsidiaries/group companies, and institutional shareholders/creditors including LIC, SBI, IndusInd Bank, and public pension/provident funds. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multi-tier infrastructure financing, development, and group debt operations funded by banking credit lines, commercial papers, debentures, and institutional public investments. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Burgeoning external group-wide debt obligations exceeding Rs. 91,000 crores (approximately Rs. 57,000 crores borrowed from public sector banks) against consolidated equity and reserves of Rs. 6,950 crores, with defaults triggering successively across key subsidiaries (ITNL on 30.06.2018, IEDCL on 22.08.2018, IL&FS on 25.08.2018, and IFIN on 12.09.2018). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Department of Economic Affairs issued a confidential warning note on 30.09.2018; MCA filed Company Petition No. 3638/MB/2018 on 01.10.2018; NCLT Mumbai reconstituted the board on 01.10.2018 but refused an interim group moratorium under Section 14 IBC or Section 242 of the Companies Act on 12.10.2018; NCLAT granted an interim stay/moratorium on 15.10.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Credit ratings downgraded to default/junk grades by CARE and ICRA, SFIO investigation reports, RBI inspection findings documenting excessive leverage (13 times) and severe asset-liability mismatch, and cash flow classifications placing group entities into Green (22), Amber (10), and Red (38) categories. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai declined interim moratorium relief on 12.10.2018 on grounds that IBC Section 14 did not apply to financial service providers; Union of India and IL&FS appealed under Section 421 challenging the denial and seeking group-level interim protective resolution orders under Section 242(4).
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal/Appellate Tribunal under Sections 241 and 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 has the jurisdiction to issue comprehensive group-level interim moratorium and resolution orders analogous to Section 14 of the IBC, and whether asset monetization proceeds can be distributed on a fair and equitable pro-rata framework rather than strictly adhering to Section 53 of the IBC in cases involving systemic economic risk and public interest.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In proceedings initiated by the Central Government under Section 241(2) in the overarching public interest, the Company Law Tribunal possesses wide equitable powers under Section 242(4) read with Section 424 to regulate company affairs, including granting interim group-wide stays/moratoria against third-party enforcement to avoid catastrophic financial contagion and enable orderly resolution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While statutory moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC cannot be formally invoked against financial service providers, Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 empowers the Tribunal to pass any just and equitable interim directions; Section 424 permits importing IBC procedural principles without being bound by the strict rigidities of Section 53 of the IBC when public interest and preservation of public money require pro-rata distribution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Balance-of-convenience and public interest standard based on systemic macro-economic ramifications, financial interconnectedness of 300+ group entities, and risks to institutional public depositors and statutory employee benefit funds. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The interim order of 15.10.2018 was validly passed under Section 242(4), requiring no modification or recall; the asset-level resolution framework and pro-rata distribution model proposed by the Union of India are approved to safeguard overall financial stability.
operative_order: The interim stay order dated 15.10.2018 is reaffirmed and maintained under Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013. Objections raised by financial and secured lenders are rejected. The Resolution Framework and pro-rata distribution mechanism proposed by the Union of India are approved, with 15.10.2018 fixed as the cut-off date for claim crystallization. The Union of India, Board of IL&FS, and Creditors' Committees are directed to conclude resolution of all entities within 90 days under the supervision of Hon'ble Justice (Retd.) D.K. Jain.
summary: Union of India initiated proceedings under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 in public interest following massive debt defaults across IL&FS and its group companies. Challenging NCLT Mumbai's denial of an interim stay against debt enforcement, UOI and IL&FS appealed to NCLAT. Certain secured lenders objected to the NCLAT's jurisdiction to impose an IBC-style moratorium and disputed the proposed pro-rata distribution model. The NCLAT held that Section 242(4) read with Section 424 grants extensive powers to issue protective interim stay orders for group resolution in public interest, confirmed the validity of the moratorium order, approved the asset-level resolution framework, and directed completion within 90 days.

case_title: Deloitte Haskins & Sells LLP vs. Union of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Deloitte Haskins & Sells LLP (Former Statutory Auditor of IFIN / Appellant in CA 190 & 224/2019) and its audit partners/employees, BSR & Associates LLP (Joint Statutory Auditor) and its partner, various former executive/independent directors of IFIN, corporate borrower borrower entities (C. Sivasankaran/Siva Group), and Union of India through Ministry of Corporate Affairs (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory audits of the financial statements of IL&FS Financial Services Ltd. (IFIN), an NBFC-ND-SI subsidiary of IL&FS, alongside managerial decisions and intra-group loan sanctioning activities. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: IFIN defaulted on commercial paper and financial obligations starting September 2018, contributing to the parent group's Rs. 91,000 crore financial crisis. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SFIO directed to investigate on 30.09.2018; Company Petition No. 3638/2018 filed under Sections 241-242 on 01.10.2018; MCA filed Section 130 application on 04.12.2018 to recast accounts; SFIO submitted 2nd interim report on 28.05.2019; Criminal Complaint filed on 20.05.2019; impleadment applications filed via MA No. 2071/2019 and allowed on 18.07.2019; MA 2258/2019 challenging petition maintainability rejected on 09.08.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SFIO 2nd Interim Report, RBI Inspection Report under Section 45N of RBI Act, and ICAI disciplinary findings showing prima facie connivance, suppression of negative Net Owned Funds (NOF) and Capital to Risk Assets Ratio (CRAR), improper asset-classification rollover by book entries, and failure to report fraud under Section 143(12). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench allowed MCA's application MA No. 2071/2019 on 18.07.2019 impleading past statutory auditors, joint auditors, partners, and ex-directors as respondents, and dismissed the challenge to maintainability on 09.08.2019.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT possesses the statutory jurisdiction under Sections 241-242 read with Sections 246, 339, and 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 to implead former statutory auditors, audit partners, and ex-directors as proper or necessary parties in a petition filed by the Central Government alleging affairs conducted prejudicial to public interest.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In proceedings instituted by the Central Government under Section 241(2) alleging mismanagement prejudicial to public interest, the Tribunal's adjudicatory powers under Section 242 read with Sections 246, 339-341, and Rule 11 are expansive and extend beyond present management to past officers, statutory auditors, and related entities reasonably connected to the alleged fraud. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The words 'are being conducted' in Section 241(2) do not restrict the inquiry exclusively to current management; Sections 130, 212, and 241/242 operate conjointly to effectuate corporate accountability; Section 246 incorporates Sections 339-341 into Section 241/242 proceedings, permitting the Tribunal to issue inquiries and asset restraint orders against any individual party to fraudulent business conduct. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The existence of prima facie material in investigative reports (such as SFIO, RBI, or ICAI findings) demonstrating involvement or neglect of statutory reporting obligations suffices to treat an entity as a 'proper party' under natural justice standards and Section 424. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Impleading erstwhile auditors and directors does not constitute a pre-judgment of guilt or final relief under Section 140(5) or Section 447, but is a necessary exercise of power under natural justice to enable an effective, complete inquiry into affairs prejudicial to public interest.
operative_order: All appeals challenging the impleadment orders of NCLT Mumbai are dismissed as devoid of merit, upholding the order of 09.08.2019. Interim stay continued for two weeks from pronouncement to permit appellants to determine future courses of legal action. No orders as to costs.
summary: Former statutory auditors (Deloitte Haskins & Sells LLP and BSR & Associates LLP), their engagement partners, and erstwhile directors of IFIN appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order impleading them as party respondents in a Section 241(2)-242 petition filed by the Union of India concerning the collapse of the IL&FS Group. The appellants argued that as past auditors who had rotated out or resigned, they had no role in management, could not be reached under Section 241-242, and were prejudiced by unadjudicated SFIO reports. The NCLAT held that in Central Government petitions involving public interest, the Tribunal exercises broad powers under Sections 241-242 read with Sections 246 and 339 to examine all actors implicated by prima facie regulatory findings, affirming their impleadment as proper parties and dismissing the appeals.

case_title: V. Padmakumar vs. Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund (SASF) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: V. Padmakumar (Appellant, Shareholder/Director of Corporate Debtor), Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund (SASF) (Respondent No. 1, Financial Creditor/Assignee of IDBI), Interim Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2), and M/s Uthara Fashion Knitwear Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term Loan facility of Rs. 600 lakhs sanctioned by Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI) on 02.03.2000, secured by hypothecation of plant, machinery, raw materials, book debts, and equitable mortgage of immovable properties valued at Rs. 790.70 lakhs via Memorandum of Entry dated 24.08.2000. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default took place and the account of the Corporate Debtor was declared a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 29.05.2002 (also referenced as 31.10.2002). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IDBI initiated DRT recovery under Section 19 of the RDDBFI Act, 1993 in 2003 (OA No. 289/2003, re-numbered OA No. 413/2007); the DRT decreed the original application on 19.06.2009 and issued a Recovery Certificate on 31.08.2009; debt entries were reflected in the balance sheet dated 31.03.2012 and subsequent annual returns. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Term loan agreements, mortgage entries, NPA notices, DRT decree dated 19.06.2009, recovery certificate dated 31.08.2009, and Corporate Debtor's Audited Balance Sheets for FY 2011-12 onwards. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SASF filed a Section 7 IBC application in 2019; NCLT Chennai Division Bench admitted the petition on 21.11.2019; the admission order was appealed before the NCLAT, which referred the question of limitation to a five-member Larger Bench.
legal_issues: Whether a civil court or DRT decree/recovery certificate shifts forward the date of default to compute limitation under Section 7 of the IBC, and whether debt reflection in mandatory annual returns and balance sheets under Section 92 of the Companies Act constitutes an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A decree or recovery certificate issued by a civil court or DRT does not give rise to a fresh trigger point or defer the date of default for an application under Section 7 of the IBC, nor does an entry in an annual return or balance sheet mandated by statute constitute a voluntary acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 IBC petitions are governed by the 3-year limitation window under Article 137 running from the date of NPA/default; since filing annual returns and financial statements is mandatory under Section 92(4) on pain of criminal and financial penalties under Section 92(5)-(6), such statutory filings lack voluntary jural admission and cannot be treated as acknowledgments under Section 18. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An acknowledgment under Section 18 must be an express or implied conscious admission of a subsisting jural relationship made in writing before expiration of the limitation period; compulsory compliance under statutory penalty cannot serve to endlessly perpetuate limitation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor's account became NPA in 2002 and the DRT decree was passed in 2009; filing the Section 7 petition in 2019 was time-barred as neither the DRT decree nor subsequent balance sheets extended limitation.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed (by 4:1 majority; Cheema J. dissenting on balance sheet acknowledgment). The impugned admission order dated 21.11.2019 is set aside, the Section 7 application is dismissed, moratorium and appointment of IRP are vacated, and management is restored to the Board of Directors. SASF is directed to bear the costs and fees of the IRP as determined by the NCLT. No orders as to costs.
summary: In an appeal before a 5-judge Larger Bench of the NCLAT, the appellant challenged the admission of a Section 7 IBC petition filed in 2019 by SASF against Uthara Fashion Knitwear Ltd., whose loan account was declared NPA in 2002 and recovery certificate issued by the DRT in 2009. SASF contended that the DRT decree created a fresh default and that continuous reflections of debt in audited balance sheets operated as acknowledgments under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. The NCLAT majority ruled that a DRT decree does not shift forward the original date of default, and statutory filings mandated under Section 92 of the Companies Act do not constitute Section 18 acknowledgments. The petition was declared time-barred and the CIRP quashed.

case_title: Ishrat Ali vs. Cosmos Cooperative Bank Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ishrat Ali (Appellant, Director/Shareholder of Corporate Debtor), Cosmos Co-operative Bank Ltd. (Respondent No. 1, Financial Creditor), Interim Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2), and Micro Dynamics Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Banking credit facilities extended by Cosmos Co-operative Bank Ltd. to the Corporate Debtor against security interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor's loan account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 30.03.2014, marking the trigger date of default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act issued on 06.12.2014; arbitration proceedings under Section 84 of the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act initiated on 04.12.2015; physical possession of movable secured assets taken under Section 13(4) of SARFAESI on 16.01.2017; Section 7 IBC petition filed before NCLT Mumbai in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, NPA classification certificate dated 30.03.2014, Section 13(2) demand notice, Section 13(4) possession records, and arbitration filings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the Financial Creditor's Section 7 petition on 23.09.2019; the Appellant appealed on limitation grounds; a three-member bench doubted earlier precedent (Sesh Nath Singh) which had granted Section 14 limitation exclusions for SARFAESI actions, referring the issue to this 5-member Larger Bench.
legal_issues: Whether the period during which a financial creditor pursues enforcement remedies under Section 13(2) and 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 can be excluded under Section 14(2) of the Limitation Act, 1963 for computing the three-year period under Article 137 to initiate CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Enforcement steps under Section 13 of the SARFAESI Act do not constitute civil proceedings in a court of first instance for the 'same relief' as an insolvency resolution application, and therefore cannot be excluded under Section 14(2) of the Limitation Act to extend limitation for Section 7 IBC petitions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(2) requires prosecution in good faith of another civil proceeding before a court lacking jurisdiction for the identical relief; SARFAESI is an extra-judicial debt recovery mechanism, whereas Section 7 is an insolvency and resolution remedy, not an action for debt recovery; hence Section 14(2) does not apply. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To claim benefit under Section 14(2), the applicant must satisfy three conjunctive tests: (i) prosecution with due diligence in another civil proceeding, (ii) against the same party, and (iii) for the same relief before a forum lacking jurisdiction; individual security realization notices fail this legal threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Sesh Nath Singh v. Baidyabati Sheoraphuli Co-operative Bank Ltd. did not lay down correct law; the account was NPA on 30.03.2014, and the Section 7 petition filed more than 3 years later without valid acknowledgment was barred by limitation under Article 137.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned admission order dated 23.09.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench is set aside. All consequential actions taken by the IRP, including public notices and moratorium declarations, are declared illegal and quashed. The Section 7 petition is dismissed, the Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP, and the Financial Creditor is directed to pay the IRP's determined fees. No order as to costs.
summary: A director and shareholder of Micro Dynamics Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the admission of an IBC Section 7 application filed by Cosmos Co-operative Bank Ltd., arguing that the debt defaulted when the account was declared NPA on 30.03.2014 and was therefore time-barred. The bank argued under Section 14(2) of the Limitation Act that time spent pursuing remedies under Section 13 of the SARFAESI Act and arbitration should be excluded. A 5-judge Larger Bench of the NCLAT held that SARFAESI enforcement actions are not civil proceedings before a court for the same relief as corporate insolvency resolution. Overruling earlier conflicting precedent, the Bench ruled that SARFAESI proceedings do not extend the three-year limitation under Article 137, set aside the admission order, and quashed the CIRP.

case_title: Shrawan Kumar Agrawal Consortium vs. Rituraj Steel Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shrawan Kumar Agrawal Consortium (H1 Successful Resolution Applicant/Appellant in CA 1490/2019), Rituraj Steel Pvt. Ltd. (Unsuccessful Bidder/Appellant in CA 78/2020), PHIL Minerals Beneficiation & Energy Pvt. Ltd. (H2 Bidder/Appellant in CA 184/2020), Amresh Shukla (Resolution Professional), and Committee of Creditors of City Mall Vikash Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission and commercial evaluation of competing resolution plans in the CIRP of City Mall Vikash Private Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial bids evaluated on Net Present Value (NPV) metrics: H1 offered Rs. 89.86 crores, H2 offered Rs. 85.66 crores, and Rituraj Steel initially offered Rs. 57 crores (allegedly increasing to Rs. 92 crores / Rs. 102 crores at approval stage) against an assessed fair market value of Rs. 136.12 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan of H1 approved by the CoC with 84.70% voting majority within CIRP deadlines; RP submitted plan under Section 31 to NCLT; unsuccessful bidders filed applications CA No. 1577/KB/2019 and CA No. 1690/KB/2019 during approval hearings. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Voting results showing 84.70% approval by CoC, valuation reports determining fair market value at Rs. 136.12 crores, comparative bid matrix, and compliance certifications under Section 30(2). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench by order dated 10.12.2019 in CA (IB) No. 1577/KB/2019 refused to approve the plan and directed fresh re-bidding within 15 days on the ground of asset value maximization; H1 bidder appealed against the re-bidding direction, while unsuccessful bidders cross-appealed challenging evaluation transparency.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority exceeds its statutory jurisdiction under Section 31(1) of the IBC by setting aside a resolution plan approved by an 84.70% voting share of the CoC and ordering fresh re-bidding to maximize asset value.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a resolution plan by the requisite statutory majority is paramount and non-justiciable; the Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to evaluate commercial decisions or order re-bidding on grounds of asset value maximization. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The judicial review of the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31(1) is strictly circumscribed by the mandatory compliance requirements of Section 30(2); neither Section 30(4) nor general principles of value maximization permit the Tribunal to act as a court of equity to reverse a plan or direct a re-auction. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Once the statutory muster under Section 30(2) and 30(4) is certified and the plan has secured over 66% CoC approval, the inquiry ends; the existence of a higher belated offer or a plan value lower than liquidation/fair market value is legally immaterial. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction by trespassing upon the commercial wisdom of the CoC; the order directing re-bidding was illegal and void.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1490 of 2019 is allowed; appeals No. 78 of 2020 and 184 of 2020 are dismissed. The impugned order dated 10.12.2019 directing fresh bidding is set aside, and the matter is remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority to pass an order of approval for the CoC-approved resolution plan. No orders as to costs.
summary: The CoC of City Mall Vikash Pvt. Ltd. approved the resolution plan of Shrawan Kumar Agrawal Consortium (H1, Rs. 89.86 crores) with an 84.70% majority. At the Section 31 approval stage, unsuccessful bidders objected, citing higher post-voting offers and an asset fair value of Rs. 136.12 crores. The NCLT Kolkata Bench refused to approve the plan and ordered fresh bidding within 15 days for value maximization. On appeal, the NCLAT set aside the re-bidding order, ruling that the commercial wisdom of the CoC is non-justiciable and the Adjudicating Authority cannot trespass beyond Section 30(2) parameters, remitting the matter to NCLT for final plan approval.

case_title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. vs. Testtex India Laboratories Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. (Appellant/Financial Creditor) and Testtex India Laboratories Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (Respondents/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Extension of financial credit facilities by the Financial Creditor to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total financial debt due and outstanding was Rs. 1,340 lakhs; the Corporate Debtor had only paid a sum of Rs. 49 lakhs up to May 2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: No Section 8 notice was applicable; on 16.04.2019, the Financial Creditor sought admission of the Section 7 petition, but adjournment was granted for exploring settlement; on 11.06.2019, the Financial Creditor informed the NCLT that settlement efforts were exhausted; further adjournments took place on 17.07.2019 and 28.08.2019 without reaching an accord. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Statutory Form-1 Section 7 pleadings, order sheets of NCLT Mumbai dated 16.04.2019, 11.06.2019, 17.07.2019, and 28.08.2019 confirming failure of settlement negotiations, and financial records showing outstanding dues of Rs. 1,340 lakhs with a minimal payment of Rs. 49 lakhs. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed in 2018; NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected the petition on 25.11.2019 on the erroneous premise that the parties were in the process of settlement and substantial part payment had been received.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can reject a Section 7 IBC application on the grounds of ongoing settlement talks or receipt of minor part-payments, outside the statutory conditions set forth in Section 7(5)(b) of the Code.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 7 of the IBC can only be rejected on the strict statutory grounds enumerated in Section 7(5)(b), namely that default has not occurred, the application is incomplete, or disciplinary proceedings are pending against the proposed resolution professional; the Adjudicating Authority cannot reject an application based on purported or failed settlement attempts. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory scheme under Section 7(5) circumscribes the jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority; absent the specific disentitling conditions under clause (b), the Adjudicating Authority cannot invent extraneous grounds such as unfinalized settlement negotiations to dismiss a petition where default is established. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of tribunal record entries and order sheets to determine whether an enforceable settlement was concluded or whether default persisted; minimal payment (Rs. 49 lakhs against Rs. 1,340 lakhs) does not disprove default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor was an admitted defaulter and none of the statutory conditions for rejection under Section 7(5)(b) existed; the Adjudicating Authority committed a patent error in rejecting the petition.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned order dated 25.11.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai is set aside. The matter is remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority to decide the Section 7 application afresh uninfluenced by the impugned order and expeditiously in accordance with law. Parties are directed to appear before NCLT Mumbai on 23.03.2020. No orders as to costs.
summary: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 25.11.2019 rejecting its Section 7 IBC application against Testtex India Laboratories Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had rejected the petition on the premise that the parties were actively settling and substantial part payments had been made. The NCLAT examined the lower court order sheets, noting that settlement efforts had failed and only Rs. 49 lakhs of the total Rs. 1,340 lakhs default had been paid. The Appellate Tribunal held that Section 7(5)(b) strictly restricts the grounds for rejecting a petition to absence of default, defect in the application, or pending disciplinary proceedings against the IRP. Finding none of these conditions met, the NCLAT set aside the rejection and remitted the matter for fresh adjudication.

case_title: Rajive Kaul & Ors. vs. Vinod Kumar Kothari & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rajive Kaul and Pallavi Priyadarshini Kaul (Appellants/Erstwhile Promoters of Corporate Debtor), Nicco Parks and Resorts Ltd. (NPRL/Appellant in CA 224/2020), Vinod Kumar Kothari (Liquidator/Respondent No. 1), and Nicco Corporation Limited (Corporate Debtor in Liquidation). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint Sector Agreement dated 23.02.1990 executed between Government of West Bengal and Nicco Corporation Ltd. to incorporate NPRL as a joint sector company where Nicco held 25% equity (1,17,00,000 shares) with class/nomination rights under the Articles of Association (Articles 121, 140) to nominate three directors and the Managing Director. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt obligations leading to liquidation of Nicco Corporation Ltd. vide NCLT order dated 17.10.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation commenced on 17.10.2017; Liquidator issued notice on 03.11.2018 removing Kauls as nominee directors and proposing replacement nominees; NPRL rejected proposal on 03.01.2019; Kauls re-elected at 29th and 30th AGMs on 28.09.2018 and 27.09.2019; Liquidator filed CA (IB) No. 669/KB/2019 in June 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Joint Sector Agreement dated 23.02.1990, Articles of Association of NPRL (Articles 121, 140, 147), compliance intimation to Stock Exchanges dated 26.07.2019 showing replacement of State Corporation nominees, AGM notices/minutes, and emails dated 30.04.2019 and 01.05.2019 where Kauls refused to vacate board seats. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed CA (IB) No. 669/KB/2019 before NCLT Kolkata; NCLT on 18.12.2019 held that the Liquidator has the power to remove nominee directors and nominate replacements, directing the Kauls to vacate office forthwith; Appellants challenged this order.
legal_issues: Whether a Liquidator of a corporate debtor holding shares in an operating company is legally empowered under the IBC to exercise nomination rights attached to such shares, remove existing promoter nominee directors without complying with Section 169 of the Companies Act, 2013, and nominate replacement directors to facilitate beneficial liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Nomination and class rights attached to shares held by a corporate debtor form part of its 'liquidation estate' under Section 36 of the IBC, and the liquidator is legally entitled to exercise such rights, including withdrawing and replacing nominee directors, to maximize asset value and effectuate liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC has an overriding effect over inconsistent provisions of other laws, including the general procedure for director removal under Section 169 of the Companies Act, 2013; furthermore, under Section 33(7), liquidation operates as a discharge of corporate debtor personnel, and former promoters barred under Section 29A cannot retain office or derive indirect benefits from liquidation assets. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of corporate constitutional documents (Articles of Association and Joint Sector Agreement) establishing whether the right to nominate directors is a class right attached to the shareholding rather than a personal non-assignable right. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Kauls were nominees of the Corporate Debtor and could not claim an independent individual status to resist removal; the Liquidator possessed full statutory authority to replace them, and NPRL was legally bound to effectuate the Liquidator's nominations.
operative_order: All appeals are dismissed without costs. The impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 18.12.2019 directing Rajive Kaul and Pallavi Priyadarshini Kaul to forthwith vacate their seats as Nominee Directors on the Board of NPRL and directing NPRL to accept the Liquidator's nominee appointments is upheld. Connected interlocutory applications stand closed.
summary: Nicco Corporation Ltd. held 25% shares in Nicco Parks and Resorts Ltd. (NPRL) with nomination rights to appoint directors under its Articles of Association. Following Nicco's liquidation, the Liquidator sought to remove promoter nominee directors Rajive Kaul and Pallavi Kaul and appoint new nominees to assist in monetizing the shareholding. The Kauls resisted, contending they were subsequently re-appointed in individual capacities by shareholders under Section 152/169 of the Companies Act. The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's direction requiring the Kauls to vacate their directorships, holding that shareholding and attached class nomination rights constitute the liquidation estate under Section 36 IBC. Under Section 238 IBC, the Liquidator exercises these rights overriding Section 169, and ineligible promoters cannot use corporate structures to retain control.

case_title: Anil Chandanmal Singhvi & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Union of India through Ministry of Corporate Affairs (Petitioner), 63 Moons Technologies Ltd. (formerly FTIL/Respondent No. 1 Company), Jignesh Prakash Shah (Respondent No. 2/Promoter/CMD), former executive directors, subsequent non-executive directors (Anil Chandanmal Singhvi, Berjis Minoo Desai, Nisha Dutt, Sunil Hasmukhlal Shah, Devendra Kumar Agrawal, Prashant Desai, Jigish Shantilal Sonagara/Appellants), and National Spot Exchange Limited (NSEL/Respondent No. 29 subsidiary). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: FTIL provided proprietary exchange and trading technology software to its 99.99% subsidiary NSEL to run commodity spot market contracts. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: 24 trading members defaulted on payment obligations amounting to approximately Rs. 5,600 crores owed to 13,000 investors across Rs. 1,34,000 crores worth of paired contracts traded between 2009 and 2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Central Government granted Section 27 FCRA exemption on 05.06.2007; Department of Consumer Affairs issued SCN on 27.04.2012; NSEL suspended trading on 31.07.2013; FMC ordered forensic audit on 27.08.2013; FMC declared FTIL and Jignesh Shah not 'fit and proper' on 17.12.2013; UOI filed Company Petition before CLB under Sections 397-398/408/388B; transferred to NCLT Chennai. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Grant Thornton Forensic Audit Report dated 21.09.2013, SFIO Investigation Report 2018 establishing forged warehouse receipts, lack of underlying commodities, and deployment of illegal financing paired contracts (T+2 and T+25). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai by order dated 04.06.2018 disqualified past and subsequent directors (appointed before and after 31.07.2013) declaring them not 'fit and proper' under Section 388B/242, and permitted the Government to nominate up to 3 directors to FTIL's Board; various directors appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified under Sections 388B, 397-398, and 408 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013) in declaring non-executive directors who joined the Board of a holding company subsequent to the suspension of trading in its fraudulent subsidiary as not 'fit and proper' persons.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A declaration disqualifying an individual as not a 'fit and proper person' under company law requires specific proof of personal culpability, knowledge, or enabling negligence during the period when the fraudulent activities occurred; directors appointed after the cessation of the fraudulent conduct cannot be disqualified without specific adverse findings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242 read with Section 241(2) and Section 388B requires establishing that a director's conduct personally contributed to mismanagement or was prejudicial to public interest; factual verification of appointment dates is mandatory before fastening collective liability for past misfeasance. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Distinction between directors and officers in default exercising control prior to the collapse (31.07.2013) versus independent/non-executive directors inducted subsequently who had no connection to the pre-suspension operations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in relying on inaccurate tenure dates and disqualifying directors who were appointed post-31.07.2013; while disqualification of key promoters/directors managing the affairs prior to 31.07.2013 is upheld, the disqualification of subsequent directors must be set aside.
operative_order: Appeals filed by Anil Chandanmal Singhvi, Berjis Minoo Desai, Nisha Dutt, Sunil Hasmukhlal Shah, Devendra Kumar Agrawal, Prashant Desai, and Jigish Shantilal Sonagara are allowed, and their disqualifications are set aside. Appeals filed by Jignesh Prakash Shah, Dewang Sunderraj Neralla, Manjay Prakash Shah, and 63 Moons Technologies Ltd. are dismissed, affirming their disqualification and the appointment of up to three Government nominee directors. Appeal by Union of India stands disposed of.
summary: Union of India filed a company petition under Sections 397-398/408 read with Section 388B of the Companies Act, 1956 against 63 Moons Technologies Ltd. (formerly FTIL) following the Rs. 5,600 crore payment crisis at its subsidiary NSEL, which operated an illegal paired contracts scheme. NCLT Chennai disqualified both pre- and post-collapse directors and authorized the Government to nominate three directors. On appeal, the NCLAT distinguished between management managing the company prior to the trading suspension on 31.07.2013 and non-executive directors appointed thereafter. Upholding the disqualification of key executive directors including Jignesh Shah and the appointment of government nominees, the NCLAT set aside the disqualification of the directors who joined post-31.07.2013.

case_title: Adani Gas Limited vs. Competition Commission Of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Adani Gas Limited (AGL/Appellant/Dominant Supplier) and Faridabad Industries Association (FIA/Informant/Respondent No. 2), with Competition Commission of India (CCI/Respondent No. 1). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply and distribution of piped natural gas (PNG sourced from GAIL) to approximately 90 industrial unit members of FIA in Faridabad District pursuant to standard-form Gas Supply Agreements (GSAs) executed between 2009 and 2012. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Imposition of unfair contractual conditions under Section 4(2)(a)(i); CCI had imposed a penalty of Rs. 2,567.2764 Lakhs calculated at 4% of AGL's average annual turnover for FY 2009-10, 2010-11, and 2011-12. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information filed under Section 19(1)(a) by FIA in 2012; CCI order under Section 26(1) on 27.12.2012; DG report filed on 07.02.2014; CCI final order under Section 27 passed on 03.07.2014; AGL revised agreements on 01.04.2013 and tendered further modified undertakings before NCLAT in May 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DG Investigation Report, copies of executed GSAs, market share analysis showing 100% CGD exclusivity granted to AGL by the Haryana Government, and contractual clauses 11.2.1, 13.5, 13.7, 16.3, and 17.4. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI held AGL guilty under Section 4(2)(a)(i) on 03.07.2014, directing cease-and-desist, GSA modification under Section 27(d), and 4% turnover penalty under Section 27(b); AGL appealed and FIA cross-appealed before COMPAT, which were subsequently transferred to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether AGL enjoyed a dominant position in the relevant market of supply and distribution of natural gas to industrial consumers in Faridabad District, whether it abused such dominance under Section 4(2)(a)(i) by imposing unfair terms in its GSAs, and whether voluntary modification of offending clauses justifies mitigating the penalty under Section 27(b).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A sole authorized pipeline distributor in a distinct geographic market lacks gaseous substitutability and holds dominance; imposing one-sided, lopsided contractual terms constitutes abuse under Section 4(2)(a)(i), but subsequent bona fide voluntary rectification of offending clauses serves as an extenuating circumstance to reduce statutory penalties. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'any' in Section 27 empowers the Commission to issue singular, alternative, or cumulative remedies; under Section 27(b), the statutory ceiling of 10% average turnover grants judicial discretion to tailor penalties proportionately based on mitigating and aggravating factors. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of contractual clauses demonstrating unilateral asymmetries: absolving the supplier of interest on billing errors while charging interest for customer default, unilateral force majeure discretion, and disproportionate termination windows. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: AGL abused its dominant position; however, because AGL cooperatively adopted consumer-friendly modifications in its GSAs as suggested by the Appellate Tribunal, penalty reduction from 4% to 1% meets the ends of justice.
operative_order: Appeals are disposed of affirming the finding of abuse of dominant position under Section 4(2)(a)(i) and the cease-and-desist and GSA modification directions under Section 27, but modifying the penalty by reducing it from 4% to 1% of the average annual turnover of the relevant three financial years. AGL is directed to deposit the balance reduced penalty within 30 days. The revised GSA is made operational with immediate effect. No orders as to costs.
summary: Faridabad Industries Association (FIA) alleged that Adani Gas Limited (AGL) abused its dominant position in supplying piped natural gas to industrial units in Faridabad by imposing unfair conditions in its Gas Supply Agreements (GSAs). The CCI found AGL dominant with 100% market share and guilty under Section 4(2)(a)(i) for clauses concerning arbitrary interest, unilateral force majeure, and unfair termination, directing modifications and imposing a 4% turnover penalty (Rs. 2,567.28 Lakhs). On appeal, the NCLAT affirmed AGL's dominance and abusive conduct. However, observing that AGL proactively amended the offending clauses to remove disparities and complied with tribunal directions, the NCLAT reduced the penalty to 1% of average turnover while leaving other directions intact.

case_title: D & I Taxcon Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vinod Kumar Kothari
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: D & I Taxcon Services Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Tenant-Occupier claiming as Operational Creditor), Vinod Kumar Kothari (Respondent/Liquidator of Nicco Corporation Ltd.), and Nicco Corporation Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in Liquidation). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Tenancy and leasehold occupation by the Appellant of the second floor of 'Nicco House', 2, Hare Street, Kolkata, an asset owned by the Corporate Debtor forming part of its liquidation estate. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed Rs. 3.20 crores as compensation/damages arising from a fire incident that broke out in Nicco House damaging its tenanted office. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Nicco Corporation Ltd. ordered into liquidation on 17.10.2017; Liquidator issued public e-auction notices; e-auction conducted where sole selling agent M/s Narnolia Financial Advisors Pvt. Ltd. became successful bidder for Rs. 28.25 crores against reserve price of Rs. 27.50 crores; conveyance executed on 15.03.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Tenancy agreements, criminal complaint before 5th Metropolitan Magistrate Calcutta for fire compensation, successive property valuation reports justifying reserve price reduction from Rs. 55 crores to Rs. 27.45 crores, and dismissal of previous application CA No. 604/KB/2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CA (IB) No. 1335/KB/2019 before NCLT Kolkata challenging the sale of Nicco House under Section 47(1) for alleged undervaluation; NCLT on 16.10.2019 dismissed the application holding the Appellant lacked locus standi and imposed costs of Rs. 1 lakh; Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a tenant occupying a portion of a corporate debtor's property who suffered damages in a fire incident qualifies as an 'Operational Creditor' under Section 5(20) of the IBC, and whether such tenant has locus standi under Section 47(1) to challenge the liquidator's sale of liquidation assets.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A tenant occupying premises owned by a corporate debtor does not render 'goods or services' so as to qualify as an operational creditor; unliquidated tort/fire damage claims do not constitute operational debt, and a tenant lacks locus standi under Section 47(1) to challenge the liquidation sale of the premises. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(20) defines operational creditor in relation to claims arising from the provision of goods or services; occupying demised premises as a tenant cannot be treated as rendering services; Section 47(1) confines challenges against undervalued transactions during liquidation exclusively to creditors, members, or partners of the corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Incompatible claims of tortious fire damage compensation pursued in criminal proceedings negate any statutory character of an operational debt admitted in liquidation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant was a mere tenant occupier without proprietary interest or valid operational creditor status, and lacked standing under Section 47(1) to disrupt the liquidator's valuation and asset realization process.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding the NCLT Kolkata Bench order dated 16.10.2019 on merits. However, the cost of Rs. 1,00,000/- slapped on the Appellant is dispensed with and set aside, considering it was a victim of the fire incident. Interim directions vacated.
summary: D & I Taxcon Services Pvt. Ltd., a tenant occupying premises in 'Nicco House' owned by Nicco Corporation Ltd. (in liquidation), suffered damage from a fire and claimed Rs. 3.20 crores. It filed an application under Section 47(1) of the IBC before NCLT Kolkata challenging the Liquidator's sale of the building, alleging undervaluation and non-compliance with Regulation 33(2). The NCLT dismissed the application for lack of locus standi and slapped Rs. 1 lakh costs. On appeal, the NCLAT affirmed that a tenant does not render services to qualify as an operational creditor under Section 5(20) and lacks standing under Section 47(1) to challenge asset sales, while setting aside the cost penalty on humanitarian grounds.

case_title: M/s Aaj Finance & Credit Ltd. vs. M/s Keltech Infrastructure Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Aaj Finance & Credit Ltd. (Appellant/Financial Creditor) and M/s Keltech Infrastructure Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan of Rs. 50 lakhs advanced by cheque dated 01.06.2013 for 12 months at 2% monthly interest, followed by successive MoUs in 2014, 2015, and 2016, and ultimately superseded by a Builder-Buyer Agreement dated 01.10.2016 wherein the Corporate Debtor agreed to allot and transfer Flat No. K-708 in Crossing Republic, Ghaziabad for Rs. 50 lakhs with possession within 12 months plus a 180-day grace period. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default on loan principal of Rs. 50 lakhs; post-dated interest cheques were honoured until June/July 2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Builder-Buyer Agreement executed on 01.10.2016 providing a 12-month completion period plus 180 days grace period (expiring after April 2018); Appellant issued repayment demand letters on 02.05.2017 and 05.06.2017; demand notice sent on 27.10.2017; Corporate Debtor offered possession on 07.03.2018; Section 7 petition filed prematurely on 04.01.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MoUs dated 30.05.2013, 01.06.2014, 01.06.2015, and 01.06.2016; Builder-Buyer Agreement dated 01.10.2016; site photographs showing completed construction; registry records of 52 allotted flats; and possession offer letter dated 07.03.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed on 04.01.2018; NCLT New Delhi (Court No. III) by order dated 13.09.2019 in IB-28/ND/2018 dismissed the petition as premature, holding the transaction had converted to a real estate allotment under Section 5(8)(f) where the contractual completion period had not expired at filing.
legal_issues: Whether a loan transaction subsequently novated by an executed Builder-Buyer Agreement converts the creditor's status into a real estate allottee under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, rendering a Section 7 insolvency petition filed before the expiration of the agreed delivery and grace period premature and non-maintainable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Parties to a loan transaction are legally entitled to alter their contractual relationship into a builder-buyer arrangement, and in summary IBC proceedings, the Adjudicating Authority must abide by the latest admitted written agreement rather than inquire into extrinsic intentions of loan security. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Once an allotment agreement is executed, the transaction is governed as a real estate project under Section 5(8)(f); default can only occur after the expiration of the contractually agreed construction and grace periods. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of the latest admitted commercial document (Agreement dated 01.10.2016) in summary jurisdiction; since the contract lacks recital that the property was given solely as security, extrinsic oral evidence to contradict the agreement is inadmissible. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application filed on 04.01.2018 was premature because the 12-month period plus 180 days grace period had not expired, and possession was offered within the permissible timeframe.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and the impugned order dated 13.09.2019 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench III dismissing the Section 7 petition as premature is affirmed. No orders as to costs.
summary: Aaj Finance & Credit Ltd. advanced Rs. 50 lakhs as a loan to Keltech Infrastructure Ltd. in 2013, which was extended via successive MoUs until 01.10.2016, when the parties executed a Builder-Buyer Agreement for a flat in satisfaction of the principal amount with a 12-month construction timeline and 180 days grace period. The Appellant filed a Section 7 IBC petition on 04.01.2018 claiming the agreement was only security for the loan. NCLT New Delhi dismissed the petition as premature. The NCLAT affirmed, holding that in summary IBC proceedings, the latest executed contract governs the transaction, placing the applicant in the position of an allottee under Section 5(8)(f) whose petition was filed before the contractual grace period had expired.

case_title: Deepakk Kumar vs. Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Deepakk Kumar (Appellant, Promoter/Director/Shareholder and Guarantor-II/Mortgagor); M/s Sovereign Developers and Infrastructure Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Karnataka Bank Ltd. (Assignor Bank/Original Lender); M/s Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. as Trustee of Phoenix Trust FY 16-15 Scheme B (Respondent No. 1, Financial Creditor/Assignee); Guruprasad Makam (Respondent No. 2, Interim Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Karnataka Bank sanctioned a term loan facility of Rs. 25,00,00,000 on 27.04.2010 to the Corporate Debtor for constructing the 'Sovereign Unnathi' residential apartment project, repayable in monthly instalments from November 2012 to May 2014 with interest at prime lending rate plus 2% penal interest upon default. Following default, the debt was assigned to Phoenix ARC via Assignment Agreement dated 29.03.2016. On 09.06.2016, a debt restructuring Letter of Acceptance was executed acknowledging assigned dues of Rs. 28,09,60,407.22 as of 08.03.2016, alongside a New Loan Agreement sanctioning an additional credit facility of Rs. 5,00,00,000 for Phase-I works, secured by personal guarantees and mortgages. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in the original facility occurred in November 2012 (Form-1 listed default date as 01.11.2012), leading to NPA classification on 16.08.2013. The Corporate Debtor failed to clear demand notices, with dues reaching Rs. 35,33,34,286 as of 16.08.2017 and accumulating to Rs. 42,80,92,640 as of 02.09.2018 (including contractual and penal interest). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Karnataka Bank issued a SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice on 17.02.2014 demanding Rs. 19,32,25,988.22. Phoenix ARC issued a legal notice on 26.06.2017, followed by a loan recall notice on 24.08.2017 demanding Rs. 35,33,34,286. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence comprised the Loan Agreements, Assignment Agreement dated 29.03.2016, Letter of Acceptance dated 09.06.2016 containing express acknowledgment of liability signed by the Managing Director and Guarantors, repayment schedules, Certificate under Section 2A(a) of Banker's Books Evidence Act, and bank ledger records evidencing periodic part-payments by the Corporate Debtor on 17.10.2016, 11.11.2016, 29.11.2016, 29.12.2016, 31.12.2016, 10.01.2017, 23.01.2017, 25.01.2017, 28.02.2017, and 31.05.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Phoenix ARC filed O.A. No. 1083 of 2017 before DRT Bengaluru on 13.09.2017. Subsequently, it filed C.P. (IB) No. 167/BB/2018 under Section 7 of the IBC on 05.09.2018 (dated 06.09.2018 in pleadings). NCLT Bengaluru Bench admitted the application on 16.07.2019 holding that debt and default were undisputed and certified by account statements.
legal_issues: Whether the application filed under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 considering the original default occurred in November 2012 and NPA was declared on 16.08.2013, or whether limitation was extended by virtue of Section 18 and Section 19 of the Limitation Act through written debt acknowledgment and subsequent part-payments made until 31.05.2017.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 18 and Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963, an unequivocal and unqualified written acknowledgment of an existing liability or the making of part-payments towards principal/interest prior to the expiry of the limitation period creates a fresh period of limitation, renewing the right to sue for an application under Article 137 of the Limitation Act read with Section 7 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 requires an unqualified acknowledgment in writing of an existing liability and jural relationship of debtor and creditor before limitation expires, which furnishes a fresh cause of action; Section 19 read with Article 1 extends the limitation period upon evidence of part-payments entered into accounts. The pendency of debt recovery proceedings before a DRT does not operate as a bar to the initiation of CIRP under Section 7. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An unconditional written acknowledgment coupled with actual financial ledger entries reflecting continuous part-payments constitutes sufficient proof of subsisting jural debt relationship to legally extend limitation beyond the original date of default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Corporate Debtor executed the restructuring Letter of Acceptance on 09.06.2016 acknowledging debt and continuously made part-payments up to 31.05.2017 before ceasing payments, the Section 7 petition filed on 05.09.2018 was well within the three-year period under Article 137, justifying dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 848 of 2019 is dismissed without costs, affirming the order of admission passed by NCLT Bengaluru Bench dated 16.07.2019. Interlocutory Applications I.A. No. 2579 of 2019 and I.A. No. 3512 of 2019 are closed.
summary: The Appellant, a director-guarantor of Sovereign Developers and Infrastructure Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), challenged the NCLT Bengaluru order admitting Phoenix ARC's Section 7 IBC application. The Appellant contended that the petition filed on 05.09.2018 was barred by limitation since default occurred in November 2012 and the account was declared NPA on 16.08.2013. NCLAT held that the Corporate Debtor executed a debt restructuring agreement on 09.06.2016 acknowledging liability and made multiple part-payments up to 31.05.2017. Applying Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a fresh period of limitation commenced from each acknowledgment and part-payment. The Section 7 application was within the three-year period under Article 137, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Mr. Harsukbhai P. Lakkad vs. Bank of Baroda (Erstwhile Dena Bank) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Harsukbhai P. Lakkad (Appellant, Shareholder/Director); Bank of Baroda, erstwhile Dena Bank (Respondent No. 1, Financial Creditor); M/s Sunrise Ginning Private Limited (Respondent No. 2, Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dena Bank sanctioned cash credit hypothecation facilities of Rs. 9,00,00,000 vide sanction letter dated 27.09.2012 and an additional cash credit facility of Rs. 1,50,00,000 to the Corporate Debtor secured against hypothecation and equitable mortgage as collateral security. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment occurred on 31.05.2015 as per bank statements, while the bank's original DRT pleadings asserted NPA declaration as of 30.01.2014. In Form-1, the bank claimed a total default of Rs. 17,13,47,983.88 as of 30.09.2018 (comprising principal of Rs. 11,98,45,722.88, uncharged interest of Rs. 4,35,17,417.00, and penal interest of Rs. 79,84,844.00) specifying default/NPA date as 28.10.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Bank issued SARFAESI Section 13(2) notices on 03.09.2014 (as pleaded before DRT) demanding Rs. 12,57,86,554.88, followed by a subsequent notice dated 28.12.2015. The Corporate Debtor replied/objected on 24.02.2016. Section 13(4) measures were initiated on 08.03.2016. Corporate Debtor filed Securitisation Appeal No. 155 of 2016 on 26.07.2016 challenging Section 14 proceedings. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Stamped copy of Original Application No. 239 of 2016 filed on 10.03.2016 by Dena Bank before DRT-II Ahmedabad under Section 19 of the RDBA Act wherein the bank expressly pleaded that the cash credit facility was declared NPA on 30.01.2014 and Section 13(2) notice was issued on 03.09.2014. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Bank of Baroda filed Section 7 Application (C.P. (IB) No. 32 of 2020) on 19.10.2018. NCLT Ahmedabad Bench admitted the petition on 20.11.2019, accepting the 12-year limitation period under Article 62 of the Limitation Act due to mortgage security.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC is governed by the 12-year limitation period under Article 62 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for mortgage enforcement or the 3-year residuary limitation period under Article 137, and whether a financial creditor can shift the trigger date of default to a subsequent date of NPA declaration (28.10.2015) when its own prior judicial pleadings established default and NPA declaration prior to 03.09.2014.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 7 of the IBC is governed strictly by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, requiring filing within three years from the date of default; Article 62 (12-year period for mortgage enforcement) applies exclusively to suits and cannot extend limitation for insolvency proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 applications are not suits for mortgage enforcement or money recovery; hence, Article 137 applies from the date the right to apply accrues (the date of default). A creditor cannot arbitrarily alter or extend the trigger date of default by citing a subsequent classification date of NPA to bring a time-barred claim within limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Prior admissions and pleadings made by a financial creditor in judicial/statutory proceedings (such as Section 19 DRT applications) establishing an earlier NPA and default date are binding and estop the creditor from asserting a later date in Form-1. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: As the debt was declared NPA prior to 03.09.2014 (or 30.01.2014), the Section 7 petition filed on 19.10.2018 was filed well beyond three years without any legal extension, rendering the application barred by limitation and not maintainable.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 20.11.2019 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench is set aside, and the Section 7 application is dismissed. All consequential orders appointing IRP, declaring moratorium, and freezing accounts are quashed as illegal. The Corporate Debtor is released from the rigours of CIRP to function under its Board of Directors. The Adjudicating Authority shall fix IRP fees and CIRP costs to be paid exclusively by Bank of Baroda. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged the NCLT Ahmedabad order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Bank of Baroda against Sunrise Ginning Pvt. Ltd. The bank claimed default occurred on 28.10.2015 and argued that Article 62 of the Limitation Act applied due to mortgage security. NCLAT held that Section 7 applications are governed strictly by Article 137 of the Limitation Act (three-year period), and Article 62 applies only to civil suits. Furthermore, the bank's own DRT pleadings demonstrated that NPA was declared on 30.01.2014 and Section 13(2) notice issued on 03.09.2014. The petition filed on 19.10.2018 was time-barred, leading NCLAT to allow the appeal and terminate CIRP.

case_title: Digamber Bhondwe, Director Raipur Treasure Island Private Limited vs. JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Digamber Bhondwe (Appellant, Director of the suspended Board of Corporate Debtor); M/s Raipur Treasure Island Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); UCO Bank (Assignor/Original Lender); JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Limited as Trustee of JMFARCO-UCO March 2014-Trust (Respondent, Financial Creditor/Assignee). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: UCO Bank extended term loan financial assistance of Rs. 75 Crores to the Corporate Debtor for developing a shopping mall and office complex at Raipur, which was later assigned to JM Financial ARC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in loan repayment occurred leading to account classification as NPA on 30.06.2013; DRT Jabalpur subsequently adjudicated liability at Rs. 85,94,62,955 with interest pendente lite and future till realization. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: UCO Bank issued a demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act on 07.08.2013 intimating NPA classification as of 30.06.2013. The bank filed Original Application No. 225 of 2013 before DRT Jabalpur on 30.09.2013. DRT Jabalpur passed an ex-parte final judgment and Recovery Certificate under Section 19(22) of the RDBA Act on 22.10.2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 13(2) notice dated 07.08.2013 confirming NPA date of 30.06.2013; final order and Recovery Certificate dated 22.10.2016 passed by DRT Jabalpur in OA No. 225 of 2013. No written acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act was placed on record. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: JM Financial ARC filed CP No. 429 (IB)/MB/2019 under Section 7 of the IBC on 07.01.2019 (dated 17.01.2019 in pleadings) premised on the DRT Recovery Certificate dated 22.10.2016. NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the application on 22.10.2019, holding that the petition was within limitation as three years had not lapsed from the DRT order.
legal_issues: Whether the issuance of a Recovery Certificate or decree by the Debts Recovery Tribunal shifts forward the date of default to create a fresh trigger point of limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for filing a Section 7 IBC application, and whether a decree-holder is entitled to initiate CIRP under Part II of the Code to execute a DRT recovery certificate.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The period of limitation of three years under Article 137 of the Limitation Act for filing an application under Section 7 of the IBC begins to run from the original date of default/NPA; a decree or Recovery Certificate issued by a Debt Recovery Tribunal merely adjudicates that the debt is due and payable and cannot shift forward the original date of default or constitute a fresh default for insolvency purposes. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: CIRP is not a recovery proceeding or execution forum. Although Section 3(10) in Part I defines 'creditor' to include a 'decree-holder', the operative provisions of Section 7 and Section 9 in Part II restrict the initiation of CIRP exclusively to 'Financial Creditors' and 'Operational Creditors' based on financial or operational debt default. An unsatisfied decree or recovery certificate cannot be executed by invoking Section 7, which may attract Section 65. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of a valid written acknowledgment of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act within the initial three-year period, subsequent adjudication of debt by a tribunal does not arrest or reset limitation under Article 137. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The default occurred when the account became NPA on 30.06.2013, expiring the three-year limitation period on 30.06.2016. The Section 7 application filed in January 2019 was time-barred notwithstanding the DRT order dated 22.10.2016, rendering the admission unsustainable.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed and the impugned order dated 22.10.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench is set aside. The Section 7 application is dismissed. The Corporate Debtor, Raipur Treasure Island Pvt. Ltd., is released from the rigour of CIRP, and records/management are directed to be restored to the promoters/directors. The matter is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to determine CIRP costs and fees of the IRP/RP to be borne by JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Co. No costs.
summary: The Appellant, director of Raipur Treasure Island Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by JM Financial ARC. The application was filed on 07.01.2019 based on a DRT Recovery Certificate dated 22.10.2016, whereas the account had become NPA on 30.06.2013. NCLAT held that the starting point of limitation under Article 137 is the date of default/NPA and cannot be shifted forward by a DRT decree or Recovery Certificate. CIRP is not an execution mechanism, and Section 7 does not permit decree-holders to execute awards under Part II. As the three-year limitation expired in 2016, the petition was time-barred; the admission was set aside.

case_title: Mr. B. Subba Reddy vs. S.S. Organics Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 214 of 2018 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 344 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. B. Subba Reddy through GPA holder K. Pratap Reddy (Appellant, NRI Director/Promoter holding ~9% shares); S.S. Organics Ltd. (Respondent No. 1 Company); Mr. V.N. Sunanda Reddy (Respondent No. 2, Managing Director/Promoter). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: S.S. Organics Ltd. was incorporated in 1990 to manufacture life-saving bulk drugs. By 1997, its net worth was completely eroded, triggering a reference to BIFR (Case No. 91/97) under SICA. BIFR sanctioned rehabilitation scheme SS-02 on 12.02.2002 directing conversion of Rs. 200 lakhs unsecured loan brought in by Respondent No. 2 into 20 lakh equity shares. Subsequently, BIFR approved Modified Sanctioned Scheme (MSS-2004) on 27.01.2005 directing conversion of an additional Rs. 250 lakhs unsecured loan infused by Respondent No. 2 into 25 lakh equity shares of Rs. 10 each. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Complete erosion of net worth under SICA; total disputed debt converted to equity was Rs. 2,00,00,000 (SS-02) and Rs. 2,50,00,000 (MSS-2004). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: BIFR sanctioned SS-02 on 12.02.2002; company held EOGM on 27.02.2003 and allotted 20 lakh shares on 25.04.2003 (Form 2 filed on 05.11.2003). BIFR sanctioned MSS-2004 on 27.01.2005; AAIFR issued an ad-interim stay on 21.03.2005; Board allotted 25 lakh shares on 28.03.2005; AAIFR dismissed appeal on 28.12.2005; Andhra Pradesh High Court dismissed Writ Petition No. 350/2006 on 06.11.2007. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanctioned rehabilitation schemes of BIFR; board and EOGM resolutions dated 27.01.2003, 27.02.2003, and 28.03.2005; audited accounts; records proving an offer of 5,00,000 shares to the Appellant under the scheme which was expressly declined; orders of BIFR, AAIFR, and AP High Court; CLB Hyderabad order dated 14.08.2009 invalidating Appellant's unauthorized board resolution of 22.10.2006. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP No. 22/2005 and CP No. 42/2015 before CLB/NCLT alleging oppression, mismanagement, and illegal share allotment. NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissed CP No. 42/2015 on 27.02.2018 with Rs. 5 lakh costs on grounds of res judicata, issue estoppel, and laches, and dismissed CP No. 22/2005 based on the same reasoning.
legal_issues: Whether the allotment of 20 lakh and 25 lakh equity shares to Respondent No. 2 and associates upon conversion of promoter unsecured loans pursuant to BIFR sanctioned schemes under Section 18(4) of SICA constitutes acts of oppression and mismanagement under the Companies Act, and whether company petitions challenging such allotments after prior rejections by BIFR, AAIFR, and the High Court are barred by res judicata, issue estoppel, and laches.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Equity share allotments executed strictly pursuant to statutory rehabilitation schemes sanctioned by a competent authority under Section 18(4) of SICA possess statutory overriding effect and cannot be challenged as acts of oppression and mismanagement under company law, especially where the issues have attained finality in prior judicial proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18(4) of SICA carries overriding effect over the requirements of the Companies Act; hence, corporate restructuring and loan-to-equity conversions mandated by a sanctioned rehabilitation scheme are valid by operation of law without requiring separate compliance under general company provisions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a petitioner alleges discriminatory reduction to a minority but the evidentiary record demonstrates that shares were formally offered to and refused by the petitioner, while the challenging party fails to offer capital infusion, allegations of mala fide oppression cannot stand. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt conversions and allotments were carried out in compliance with binding BIFR/AAIFR orders that attained finality upon dismissal of the High Court writ petition; challenging them via subsequent company petitions is barred by res judicata and laches, fully justifying dismissal.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 214 of 2018 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 344 of 2018 are dismissed. The impugned orders dated 27.02.2018 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench in CP No. 42/2015 (including Rs. 5 lakh cost) and CP No. 22/2005 are upheld. No order as to costs in appeal.
summary: Appellant B. Subba Reddy, an NRI shareholder/director, challenged NCLT Hyderabad orders dismissing his petitions (CP No. 42/2015 and CP No. 22/2005) alleging oppression and mismanagement against S.S. Organics Ltd. and its Managing Director regarding the conversion of Rs. 4.5 crores of unsecured loans into 45 lakh equity shares under BIFR rehabilitation schemes. NCLAT held that the allotments were executed in terms of statutory schemes sanctioned under Section 18(4) of SICA, which hold overriding effect. Moreover, challenges to these schemes had already been dismissed by the AAIFR and the Andhra Pradesh High Court, attaining finality. The appeals were dismissed, upholding the NCLT orders and the Rs. 5 lakh cost.
