case_title: Laxmi Pat Surana vs. Union Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Laxmi Pat Surana (Appellant, Promoter/Director/Shareholder of Corporate Debtor and Sole Proprietor of M/s Mahaveer Construction); M/s Mahaveer Construction (Principal Borrower / Sole Proprietorship Firm); M/s Surana Metals Limited (Corporate Debtor / Corporate Guarantor); Union Bank of India (Respondent No. 1, Financial Creditor); Sunil Mohan Acharya (Respondent No. 2, Interim Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Union Bank of India extended two term loan facilities aggregating to Rs. 12,05,00,000 to M/s Mahaveer Construction (Term Loan-1 of Rs. 9,60,00,000 disbursed on 11.09.2007 and Term Loan-2 of Rs. 2,45,00,000 disbursed on 11.09.2008). Surana Metals Limited furnished Corporate Guarantees securing the facilities via Guarantee Letters dated 02.02.2007, 17.02.2007, and 30.08.2008 (also recorded as 03.08.2008). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment occurred, and the loan account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 30.10.2010 (or 03.01.2010), with outstanding liability of Rs. 12.05 Crores plus applicable interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Bank filed OA No. 310 of 2010 before DRT-III Kolkata on 14.07.2010. Demand notice under IBC was issued by the Bank on 03.12.2018, replied to by the Corporate Guarantor on 08.12.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letters of Guarantee dated 02.02.2007, 17.02.2007, and 30.08.2008; written acknowledgment letters executed by the Principal Borrower/Appellant on 16.09.2010, 03.03.2012, 27.05.2015, and 24.10.2016; and reply letter dated 08.12.2018 written by Surana Metals Limited expressly admitting the execution of guarantee agreements and liability to pay Rs. 12.05 Crores with interest. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Union Bank of India filed C.P. (IB) No. 346/KB/2019 under Section 7 of the IBC on 13.02.2019 against Surana Metals Ltd. NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted the petition on 06.12.2019, holding that debt was continuously acknowledged up to 2018 and that a corporate person guaranteeing an individual/proprietor's debt is amenable to Section 7.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC is maintainable against a corporate person acting as a corporate guarantor for a loan advanced to a sole proprietorship firm/individual (non-corporate debtor) under Section 5A and Section 3(8), and whether the Section 7 petition filed on 13.02.2019 was barred by limitation considering the account was classified as NPA in 2010.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate person who executes a guarantee securing financial credit availed by a non-corporate proprietary firm or individual owes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) and qualifies as a 'Corporate Debtor' under Section 3(8); upon default by the principal borrower and invocation, Section 7 CIRP proceedings can be validly initiated against such corporate guarantor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5A (defining corporate guarantor) is explanatory and cannot restrict Section 3(8) or Section 7. A default occurs the moment a guarantor fails to pay a demanded debt. Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a written acknowledgment of liability signed by the borrower or guarantor within the currency of limitation resets the three-year limitation period under Article 137. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Written acknowledgments in correspondence admitting subsisting liability and jural debtor-creditor relationship, even if framed as replies to demand notices or without prejudice discussions, operate as valid acknowledgments extending the limitation period. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was continuously acknowledged within successive 3-year windows (16.09.2010, 03.03.2012, 27.05.2015, 24.10.2016, and 08.12.2018); hence, the petition filed on 13.02.2019 was well within limitation and maintainable against the corporate guarantor, justifying dismissal of the appeal. (Note: On further appeal, the Supreme Court in [2021] 5 SCC 481 settled and clarified the definitive law on Section 7 maintainability against corporate guarantors of individual debts and the operation of Section 18 of the Limitation Act).
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 77 of 2020 is dismissed without costs, affirming the admission order dated 06.12.2019 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench. The Appellant is directed to furnish the certified copy of the impugned order within one week. IA No. 199/2020 and IA No. 200/2020 stand disposed/closed.
summary: Laxmi Pat Surana appealed the NCLT Kolkata order admitting Union Bank of India's Section 7 IBC application against Surana Metals Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Guarantor). The bank had financed Mahaveer Construction (a proprietorship firm of the Appellant), secured by guarantees from Surana Metals Ltd. The Appellant contended that Section 7 cannot lie against a corporate guarantor for debts of an individual/proprietorship firm and that the claim was time-barred since the account was NPA since 2010. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that a corporate guarantor is a Corporate Debtor under Section 3(8) read with Section 5(8). Furthermore, continuous written acknowledgments from 2010 to 2018 extended limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.

case_title: Association of Malayalam Movie Artists vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Informant/Respondent No. 2: Shri T.G. Vinaykumar (film director/producer, former President of MACTA Federation); Appellants/Opposite Parties: Association of Malayalam Movie Artists (AMMA/OP-1) and office bearers Shri Innocent (President) and Shri Edavela Babu (Secretary); Film Employees Federation of Kerala (FEFKA/OP-2) and office bearers Shri Sibi Malayil (President) and Shri B. Unnikrishnan (General Secretary); FEFKA Director's Union (OP-6); FEFKA Production Executive's Union (OP-7) and office bearer Shri K. Mohanan (General Secretary); Respondent No. 1: Competition Commission of India (CCI). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Engagements, contracting, and provision of creative and technical services in the Malayalam film industry (involving actors, directors, cinematographers, art directors, and technicians) across film production projects including 'Yakshiyum Njanum', 'Christian Brothers', 'Dracula', 'Little Superman', and 'DAM 999'. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary default metrics not applicable (antitrust behavioral infringement under Section 3); CCI imposed monetary penalties under Section 27 at the rate of 5% of average income for three years on AMMA, FEFKA, OP-6, and OP-7, and penalties at the rate of 3% of average income for three years on the designated individual office bearers under Section 48. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information filed under Section 19(1)(a) forming Case No. 98/2014; DG investigation report submitted on 16.11.2015; CCI final order passed under Section 27 on 24.03.2017 finding Section 3 contraventions and issuing cease-and-desist directions alongside penalties; appeals heard and decided on 13.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Executive committee minutes of AMMA dated 05.04.2010 and general meeting minutes dated 27.06.2010 showing condemnation of actors (such as Late Shri Thilakan and Captain Raju) for working with the Informant; FEFKA circulars dated 27.02.2010, 09.04.2011, and 19.04.2013; show-cause notice dated 11.10.2012 issued by OP-7 to Shri Rajan Philip; FEFKA letter dated 03.12.2009 to AIFEC instructing cinematographer Shri Rajaratnam to dissociate from the Informant's film; corroborating testimonies and cross-examinations of producers (Shri P.A. Haris, Shri Kannan Perumudiyoor, Shri Sudheer CV) and technicians/actors (Shri Salu K. George, Shri Anil Kumbazha, Shri P. Madhavan Nair/Madhu, and Shri Jayasurya/V.M. Jayan) establishing that advances were refunded and work abandoned due to threats of boycott by the Appellants. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI registered Case No. 98/2014, formed a prima facie opinion under Section 26(1) for Section 3 violations (holding Section 4 inapplicable as unions were not enterprises under Section 2(h)), directed DG investigation, and vide order dated 24.03.2017 upheld anti-competitive conduct under Section 3(1) read with Section 3(3)(b) read with Section 48, which was challenged before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether registered trade unions and film artists'/technicians' associations are exempt from the scrutiny of the Competition Act, 2002 under the MRTP Act savings clause or labor law immunities; whether an informal, tacit understanding or concerted boycott among industry associations and their office-bearers to prohibit members and non-members from working with an individual director/producer constitutes an anti-competitive agreement limiting or controlling the provision of services under Section 3(1) read with Section 3(3)(b); and whether establishing an Appreciable Adverse Effect on Competition (AAEC) under Section 19(3) is mandatory when evaluating horizontal agreements governed by the statutory presumption under Section 3(3).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Trade unions, professional trade guilds, and employee associations enjoy no blanket immunity from competition law when their collective decisions, bans, boycotts, or concerted practices transgress statutory contours by artificially restricting, foreclosing, or dictating the supply or provision of services in a market. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'agreement' under Section 2(b)/2(l) includes informal, tacit, unwritten understandings not intended to be enforceable by legal process; horizontal concerted practices covered by Section 3(3)(b) that limit or control the provision of services carry a statutory presumption of an Appreciable Adverse Effect on Competition (AAEC) under Section 3(3)(d), dispensing with any statutory requirement to delineate a relevant market or prove actual market harm under Section 19(3). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In concerted boycott cases, anti-competitive understanding can be established through minutes of internal association meetings, show-cause notices issued to members who breach the boycott, letters directing affiliates to force professionals to abandon projects, and consistent testimonial depositions of affected producers and artists confirming commercial cancellation and advance refunds following coercive communications. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The collective enforcement of an informal ban and issuance of diktats against the Informant directly restricted and controlled the supply of film making services in the Malayalam cinema market in violation of Section 3(1) read with Section 3(3)(b), and the participating office-bearers are liable under Section 48, justifying dismissal of all appeals and affirmation of penalties and cease-and-desist directions.
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) Nos. 05, 08, 09, and 10 of 2017 are dismissed on the merits. The order of the Competition Commission of India dated 24.03.2017 in Case No. 98 of 2014 imposing cease-and-desist directions and penalties under Sections 27 and 48 of the Competition Act, 2002 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Shri T.G. Vinaykumar, a film director, filed an information alleging that AMMA, FEFKA, and affiliated unions boycotted him, issued show-cause notices to technicians/actors working with him, and pressured producers to cancel projects. CCI found the associations and office-bearers guilty of anti-competitive practices under Section 3(1) read with Section 3(3)(b) and Section 48, issuing cease-and-desist orders and monetary penalties. On appeal, NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that trade unions are not exempt from the Competition Act. NCLAT held that the concerted informal ban and coercive diktats limited the supply of film services in the market, attracting the statutory presumption of an Appreciable Adverse Effect on Competition without requiring proof of actual harm.

case_title: Jai Mahal Hotels Pvt. Ltd. vs. Rajkumar Devraj & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 270 of 2018 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 271 of 2018 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 329 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants: M/s Jai Mahal Hotels (Pvt) Ltd (Company Appeal No. 270/2018), Rajkumar Vijit Singh & Maharaj Prithvi Raj (Company Appeal No. 271/2018), Rambagh Palace Hotel Pvt Ltd (Company Appeal No. 329/2018); Respondents/Petitioners: Rajkumar Devraj and Rajkumari Lalitya (children of Late Maharaj Jagat Singh); Proforma Party: Late Maharani Gayatri Devi (mother of Late Maharaj Jagat Singh). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Governance, capital structure, and shareholding of M/s Jai Mahal Hotels Pvt Ltd (incorporated on 05.08.1981 taking over the partnership firm operating the Jai Mahal Palace Hotel), involving 5,050 equity shares originally held by Late Maharaj Jagat Singh (99% equity), and subsequent capital expansion in 2001. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement action; disputed dilution occurred on 27.03.2001 and 28.04.2001 when authorized capital was expanded tenfold (from Rs. 10 Lakhs to Rs. 1 Crore) and 60,882 additional equity shares of Rs. 100 each were allotted to Maharaj Prithvi Raj (58,794 shares) and Rajkumar Vijit Singh (10,000 shares), reducing the 5,050 shares holding from 99% to ~6%. NCLT had imposed costs of Rs. 10 Lakhs on the appellants. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Maharaj Jagat Singh executed a Will on 23.06.1996 and died on 05.05.1997. Board and EOGM resolutions increasing share capital passed on 27.03.2001; letter from Maharani Gayatri Devi declining additional shares dated 10.04.2001; allotment of 60,882 shares on 28.04.2001. Contesting respondents filed CP No. 30(ND)/2006 before CLB on 30.03.2006. Settlement/compromise deed between Maharani Gayatri Devi and the respondents executed on 14.11.2008; Succession Certificate issued jointly on 19.02.2009; Maharani Gayatri Devi executed Will on 10.05.2009 and died on 29.09.2009. Supreme Court affirmed title/transmission in (2016) 1 SCC 423 on 23.09.2015. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Undisputed Will of Late Maharaj Jagat Singh dated 23.06.1996 bequeathing his entire estate solely to Maharani Gayatri Devi; letter dated 10.04.2001 by Maharani Gayatri Devi declining further share subscription and approving corporate actions; absence on record of any affidavit by Maharani Gayatri Devi's secretary (improperly referenced by NCLT); share transfer deeds executed by Maharani Gayatri Devi in 2008; and binding Supreme Court judgment dated 23.09.2015 settling succession in favor of the Devraj Group derived from Maharani Gayatri Devi. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents filed CP No. 30(ND)/2006 under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956 alleging oppression/mismanagement regarding the 2001 capital increase and director appointments. NCLT New Delhi Bench-III vide judgment dated 01.08.2018 allowed the petition, nullified board appointments and the 2001 capital increase/allotment, ordered board reconstitution, ordered a special audit from 1997 to 2018, and imposed Rs. 10 Lakhs cost.
legal_issues: Whether legal heirs who were disinherited by a probated/undisputed will of a deceased shareholder and who only acquired rights in the company's shares in 2008-2009 through transfer/bequest from the sole legatee have locus standi under Section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956 to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition challenging concluded corporate actions executed in 2001; and whether CP No. 30/2006 filed in 2006 challenging 2001 corporate resolutions was barred by delay, laches, and limitation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Locus standi to invoke the equitable jurisdiction against oppression and mismanagement under Section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956 (Section 244 of the 2013 Act) must exist at the date of the impugned corporate actions; persons who were not members or holders of beneficial interest in shares at the time past, concluded transactions occurred cannot retroactively challenge those transactions upon subsequently acquiring shares. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A succession certificate under Section 381 of the Indian Succession Act facilitates debt collection and affords protection to debtors but does not confer general title or administrative heirship over an estate. Where an undisputed Will bequeaths entire shares to a sole legatee, other Class-I legal heirs cannot invoke Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act to claim instantaneous devolution as members from the date of death. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where binding determinations of the High Court and Supreme Court establish that rights were derived solely from a legatee under a 2008 settlement and 2009 Will, lower tribunals cannot record contrary findings that legal heirs inherited share title upon death in 1997. Furthermore, relying on non-existent affidavits not found in pleadings to discard written corporate disclaimers vitiates findings of fact as perverse. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Respondents possessed no right, title, or interest in the 5,050 shares in 2001, at which time Maharani Gayatri Devi was the sole legatee who specifically approved the corporate actions and declined subscription; hence, the respondents lacked standing to challenge 2001 allotments under Section 399, and the petition filed in 2006 suffered from fatal delay and laches.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 270 of 2018 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 271 of 2018 are allowed. The impugned judgment dated 01.08.2018 passed by NCLT New Delhi (Bench-III) in CP No. 30(ND)/2006 is set aside in its entirety, and the company petition is dismissed. Company Appeal (AT) No. 329 of 2018 (relating to Rambagh Palace Hotel Pvt Ltd) is disposed of with the observation that the legal findings herein shall govern the rights in CP No. 59(ND)/2008. No order as to costs.
summary: Rajkumar Devraj and Rajkumari Lalitya filed an oppression and mismanagement petition in 2006 challenging the 2001 tenfold increase in share capital and allotment of 60,882 shares in Jai Mahal Hotels Pvt. Ltd. to the Prithvi Raj group, which diluted their late father's 99% holding to 6%. NCLT set aside the allotments and appointments. NCLAT reversed the judgment and allowed the appeals, holding that under Late Maharaj Jagat Singh's 1996 Will, Maharani Gayatri Devi was the sole legatee in 2001 who had consented to the capital changes and declined shares. Because the respondents only acquired rights through a 2008 compromise and 2009 Will, they had no title in 2001 and lacked locus standi under Section 399, and their petition was barred by laches.

case_title: Verifone India Sales Pvt. Ltd. vs. Competition Commission of India & Anr.
appeal_number: TA (AT) (Competition) No. 01 of 2017 and TA (AT) (Competition) No. 02 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Opposite Party No. 1: M/s Verifone India Sales Pvt. Ltd. (wholly owned subsidiary of Verifone Systems Inc., dominant manufacturer/supplier of POS terminals and ETMs); Respondent No. 1: Competition Commission of India (CCI); Respondent No. 2 (in TA No. 01/2017): M/s Atos Worldline India Pvt. Ltd. (Third Party Processor/TPP and Value Added Service/VAS provider); Respondent No. 2 (in TA No. 02/2017): M/s Three D Integrated Solutions Ltd. (contractor for Jaipur City Transport Services automated bus fare ticketing project). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of Point of Sale (POS) Terminals and mobile Electronic Ticketing Machines (ETMs) along with associated core Operating System software, Kernels, and Software Development Kits (SDKs) and File Signing Tools (FST) needed to develop and integrate independent third-party VAS and payment application software. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Antitrust abuse of dominance; CCI imposed a monetary penalty under Section 27 at the rate of 5% of average turnover for the preceding three financial years amounting to Rs. 4,48,40,236 on Verifone India in Case No. 56/2012, and issued cease-and-desist directions without cumulative financial penalty in Case No. 13/2013 in light of the prior penalty. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Atos filed information in Case No. 56/2012; Three D filed information in Case No. 13/2013; DG submitted investigation reports on 20.03.2014 and 30.05.2014; CCI issued common final orders under Section 27 on 10.04.2015; appeals decided by NCLAT on 13.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Restrictive clauses in Verifone's 2012 draft SDK License Agreement prohibiting customers/VAS providers from developing payment software interacting directly or indirectly with acquiring banks, barring licensing or transfer of developed software to third parties, and mandating disclosure of all proprietary VAS activities and pipeline development; internal emails dated 18.01.2012, 03.02.2012, 05.03.2012, and 20.04.2012 demonstrating intent to exploit the VAS market; comparable industry agreements from competitors (Ingenico and Pax); purchase order dated 05.04.2012 by Three D for 275 Vx680 devices; proof of withholding of the mandatory File Signing Tool (FST) security keys and supply of incompatible SDKs; market share records proving Verifone controlled 70% to 80% of the Indian POS terminal market. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI found a prima facie case under Section 26(1), directed DG investigations, and vide order dated 10.04.2015 held Verifone guilty of abusing its dominant position under Section 4(2)(a)(i), 4(2)(b)(i), 4(2)(b)(ii), and 4(2)(e), imposing cease-and-desist orders and Rs. 4.48 crore penalty, which Verifone challenged before COMPAT/NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the relevant product market is broad (all electronic payment devices/systems) or narrow (hardware POS/ETM terminals in India under Sections 2(r) and 2(t)); whether Verifone held a dominant position in the relevant market; and whether imposing non-negotiable restrictive clauses in SDK licensing agreements, withholding necessary cryptographic signing tools (FST), and requiring disclosure of sensitive commercial VAS software pipelines constitute abuse of dominance under Section 4(2)(a)(i), 4(2)(b)(i), 4(2)(b)(ii), and 4(2)(e) of the Competition Act, 2002.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An enterprise holding a dominant position in an upstream hardware equipment market abuses its dominance under Section 4 when it leverages its control over essential proprietary software integration tools (such as SDKs and cryptographic signing keys) to impose unfair restrictions, access confidential downstream data, stifle independent technological development, and restrict competition in the downstream value-added software services market. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The relevant product market under Section 2(t) is defined by the underlying instrument/hardware device rather than secondary application modifications; because POS terminals and mobile ETMs utilize identical underlying EMV/PCI-certified hardware architectures, they constitute the relevant market in India under Section 2(r). Forcing counterparties to 'sign on the dotted line' of take-it-or-leave-it agreements containing restrictive conditions constitutes the imposition of unfair trading conditions under Section 4(2)(a)(i). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Market share dominance (70-80%) evaluated alongside high switching barriers and consumer dependence establishes a position of strength; exclusionary intent is substantiated by emails and contractual clauses requiring competitors to reveal proprietary application architecture and restraining bank integration. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Verifone abused its dominant position in POS terminals by imposing restrictive SDK terms, withholding FST security keys, and seeking sensitive business data to leverage itself into the downstream VAS market in violation of Sections 4(2)(a)(i), 4(2)(b)(i), 4(2)(b)(ii), and 4(2)(e), justifying dismissal of the appeals and confirmation of CCI's orders and penalties.
operative_order: TA (AT) (Competition) No. 01 of 2017 (Old Appeal No. 82 of 2015) and TA (AT) (Competition) No. 02 of 2017 (Old Appeal No. 83 of 2015) are dismissed. The orders of the Competition Commission of India dated 10.04.2015 in Case Nos. 56/2012 and 13/2013, including the cease-and-desist directions and penalty of Rs. 4,48,40,236, are affirmed in their entirety. No order as to costs.
summary: Informants Atos Worldline and Three D Integrated Solutions filed informations alleging that Verifone abused its dominant position in the Indian POS terminal market (holding 70-80% market share) by forcing non-negotiable SDK agreements that barred third parties from developing payment solutions for acquiring banks, withholding critical security signing keys (FST), and demanding disclosure of commercially sensitive VAS innovation plans. CCI found Verifone guilty of abusing dominance under Section 4(2)(a)(i), 4(2)(b)(i), 4(2)(b)(ii), and 4(2)(e), imposing cease-and-desist directions and a penalty of Rs. 4.48 crores. On appeal, NCLAT dismissed both appeals, affirming that Verifone leveraged upstream terminal dominance to stifle downstream software development and protect its VAS offerings.

case_title: M/s. Eli Lilly and Company vs. Competition Commission of India
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: M/s Eli Lilly and Company (innovation-driven pharmaceutical company based in USA, acquirer); Target Business: Novartis Animal Health in India (NAH India), an unincorporated division of Novartis India Limited (seller/transferor); Respondent: Competition Commission of India (CCI). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Global acquisition of the animal health business of Novartis AG (Switzerland) by Eli Lilly pursuant to a global Stock and Asset Purchase Agreement (SAPA) dated 22.04.2014, and subsequent transfer of the Indian animal health division via Slump Sale Agreement dated 03.12.2014 between the parties' Indian subsidiaries. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory filing non-compliance; CCI had imposed a monetary penalty under Section 43A of Rs. 1,00,00,000 (INR 1 Crore) on Eli Lilly for failure to give pre-merger notification under Section 6(2) of the Act and closing the global transaction outside India prior to CCI approval. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Global SAPA executed on 22.04.2014; Slump Sale Agreement executed on 03.12.2014; transaction notified to Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) on 10.11.2014; global transaction closed on 01.01.2015; CCI inquiry letter issued on 08.04.2015; voluntary Form-I filing submitted under reservation of rights; CCI cleared combination under Section 31 on 03.12.2015; Indian transaction closed on 31.12.2015; CCI issued show cause notice under Section 43A on 14.12.2015; CCI penalty order passed on 14.07.2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Slump Sale Agreement dated 03.12.2014 isolating only the animal health business; financial statements of NAH India certifying turnover of Rs. 93.9 Crores and asset book value of Rs. 36.2 Crores; Central Government De Minimis Exemption Notifications S.O. 482(E) dated 04.03.2011, S.O. 674(E) dated 04.03.2016, and clarifying Notification S.O. 988(E) dated 27.03.2017 with Press Release dated 30.03.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI issued an order dated 14.07.2016 holding that the De Minimis Exemption applied only to incorporated target entities and not to unincorporated business divisions, calculating thresholds against Novartis India Limited's total assets/turnover (including its human health business), and imposing a Rs. 1 Crore penalty under Section 43A. Eli Lilly appealed under Section 53B.
legal_issues: Whether the De Minimis Exemption Notification dated 04.03.2011 issued under Section 54(a) of the Competition Act, 2002 applies to the specific assets/business division being acquired (in an asset or slump sale) or to the entire parent seller company (transferor) merely because the target division is not separately incorporated, and whether an acquirer is liable for Section 43A penalties for failing to notify a combination under Section 6(2) when the target asset falls below the prescribed statutory exemption thresholds.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For the purpose of assessing thresholds under the De Minimis Exemption and Section 5 of the Competition Act in an asset or division acquisition, only the value of assets and turnover attributable to the specific business/division being acquired is relevant, not the total aggregate assets or turnover of the transferor company. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 54(a) exemption notifications exempt combinations below threshold values from the requirements of Section 5 and Section 6(2). The term 'enterprise' cannot be artificially limited to incorporated corporate entities to exclude unincorporated business divisions or asset purchases; if a transaction falls within the de minimis monetary thresholds, neither party is required to give notice under Section 6(2), and Section 43A penal proceedings are without jurisdiction. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The applicability of statutory exemption must be evaluated based on the audited financial metrics and certified book value of the specific target assets and business transferred under the transaction documents (e.g., Slump Sale Agreement). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the turnover (Rs. 93.9 Crores) and asset value (Rs. 36.2 Crores) of NAH India were well below the statutory thresholds of Rs. 750 Crores and Rs. 250 Crores respectively under Notification S.O. 482(E), the transaction was completely exempt from Section 5 and did not require notice under Section 6(2), rendering the CCI's Section 43A penalty illegal.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order of the Competition Commission of India dated 14.07.2016 passed in Combination Registration No. C-2015/07/289 imposing a penalty of INR 1 Crore under Section 43A is set aside in its entirety. No order as to costs.
summary: Eli Lilly acquired the animal health business of Novartis AG globally and acquired its Indian counterpart, NAH India, via a slump sale agreement. NAH India had Indian assets of Rs. 36.2 crores and sales of Rs. 93.9 crores, below the De Minimis threshold (Rs. 250 crores assets / Rs. 750 crores turnover). CCI imposed a Rs. 1 crore penalty under Section 43A for non-notification, holding that the exemption only applied to incorporated target entities, measuring thresholds against the entire parent seller (Novartis India Ltd). NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the penalty, ruling that the De Minimis exemption applies to the specific business/assets being acquired and is not restricted to incorporated entities; since the acquired business was below the thresholds, no Section 6(2) filing was required.

case_title: T. Johnson vs. St. John Freight Systems Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: T. Johnson (suspended Managing Director, Promoter, and majority shareholder of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1: St. John Freight Systems Ltd. represented through Resolution Professional/Liquidator R. Venkatakrishnan; Respondent No. 2: Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor and petitioner in original Section 7 petition). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency resolution and proposed resolution plans for St. John Freight Systems Limited (an international logistic and freight forwarding company incorporated in 1991) undergoing CIRP initiated by Phoenix ARC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt repayments owed to Phoenix ARC Private Limited (as Trustee of Phoenix Trust FY-16-26); Corporate Debtor entered CIRP on 10.12.2018; liquidation value determined at Rs. 161.25 Crores; Appellant submitted a resolution plan offering a resolution value of Rs. 242 Crores (including Rs. 222.5 Crores to Financial Creditors) with an Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) requirement of Rs. 5 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 10.12.2018; appeal against admission dismissed by NCLAT on 07.05.2019; 90-day extension granted by NCLT on 07.06.2019; maximum 270-day CIRP period expired on 06.09.2019; initial resolution plan rejected by CoC on 04.09.2019; RP filed Section 33 liquidation application MA No. 989/2019 (MA No. 536/2019) on 06.09.2019; Appellant filed MA No. 995/2019 on 14.09.2019; revised resolution plan rejected by CoC on 28.09.2019; NCLT passed liquidation order on 21.11.2019 (issued 26.11.2019). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Voting results of the 12th CoC meeting dated 04.09.2019 rejecting the initial plan (55.49% voted in favor, failing to achieve the statutory 66% threshold under Section 30(4)); voting results of the 14th CoC meeting dated 28.09.2019 rejecting the revised plan (only 20.54% voted in favor, 63.02% voted against, and 12.74% abstained); evidence that Appellant failed to deposit the mandatory Rs. 5 Crore EMD in cash/DD/Bank Guarantee, instead transferring only Rs. 50 Lakhs via RTGS and tendering property title deeds valued at Rs. 6.6 Crores; and evidence that suspended management fraudulently obtained an MSME registration on 23.01.2019 post-commencement of CIRP without RP knowledge to circumvent Section 29A disqualifications. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed an application under Section 33(1) for liquidation upon expiry of the CIRP statutory period on 06.09.2019. NCLT Chennai Bench dismissed Appellant's reconsideration plea (MA No. 995/2019) and ordered liquidation of the Corporate Debtor on 21.11.2019 appointing the RP as Liquidator, which was appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is statutorily mandated to order liquidation under Section 33(1) of the IBC when the CIRP period has expired and the Committee of Creditors has rejected the resolution plan by failing to secure the mandatory 66% majority voting share under Section 30(4); and whether an ex-promoter can circumvent Section 29A ineligibility by procuring an MSME registration certificate during the CIRP without the knowledge of the Resolution Professional.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 33(1) of the IBC, where no resolution plan is approved by the Committee of Creditors with the requisite statutory majority of 66% under Section 30(4) before the expiry of the maximum permissible CIRP period under Section 12, the Adjudicating Authority has no residual equitable discretion and is statutorily bound to order the liquidation of the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 timelines are strict to ensure value maximization and prevent indefinite insolvency proceedings; Section 33(1)(a) provides exhaustive, non-discretionary grounds for ordering liquidation. Section 240A exemptions intended for genuine preexisting MSMEs cannot be claimed through a back-door entry by obtaining an MSME certificate post-commencement of CIRP to bypass Section 29A disqualifications. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors is non-justiciable; where certified voting sheets show that a resolution plan failed to attain the 66% affirmative vote and the applicant failed to comply with mandatory process requirements (e.g., full cash/bank guarantee EMD deposit), the rejection is conclusive. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC twice rejected the resolution plan on commercial merits (receiving only 55.49% and 20.54% votes), the statutory CIRP period had expired, and the EMD conditions were not fulfilled; therefore, the Adjudicating Authority was legally bound to pass the order of liquidation, justifying dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (INS) No. 1402 of 2019 is dismissed without costs, affirming the liquidation order dated 21.11.2019 passed by NCLT Chennai Bench in MA No. 989/2019 in CP No. 759/IB/2018. Interim Applications I.A. No. 3973/2019 and I.A. No. 3974/2019 are closed.
summary: The Appellant, suspended Managing Director of St. John Freight Systems Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Chennai order directing liquidation under Section 33(1) of the IBC. The Appellant contended that the CoC should have accepted his resolution plan (offering Rs. 242 crores against a liquidation value of Rs. 161.25 crores) and granted an extension of time, relying on an MSME certificate obtained during CIRP. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the statutory CIRP period had expired and the CoC had twice rejected the resolution plan for failing to attain the mandatory 66% voting threshold under Section 30(4) and failing to provide the required Rs. 5 crore EMD. In the absence of an approved plan, the Adjudicating Authority had no option but to order liquidation.

case_title: Mr. Soumitra Banerjee & Anr. vs. Mr. Asher Ebrahim Melamed & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants: Mr. Soumitra Banerjee and Mrs. Shampa Banerjee (Directors and minority shareholders holding 49% equity); Respondent No. 1: Mr. Asher Ebrahim Melamed (Iranian national, majority shareholder holding 51% equity, original Petitioner before CLB); Respondent No. 2: Touranto Company (India) Private Limited (closely-held Private Limited Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Incorporation and joint operation of Touranto Company (India) Pvt. Ltd. (having only 3 shareholders/directors) engaged in the business of exporting chemicals and pharmaceuticals from Indian manufacturers to Iranian buyers on commission basis, alongside procurement of a corporate office premises at Acme Plaza, Andheri, Mumbai financed through USD 100,000 (approx. Rs. 41 Lakhs) remitted by Respondent No. 1 and matching contributions from Appellants. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Complete operational and management deadlock; financial accounts from 31.03.2009 to 31.03.2012 revealed conduct prejudicial to the company; failure to maintain statutory books of accounts outside 2009-2012; total cessation of export business; office property leased out from 15.02.2012 with rental income being the sole surviving revenue. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respondent No. 1 appointed Director on 14.03.2000; removed from directorship by Appellants via MCA portal deletion in 2009; criminal complaint filed by Appellant No. 1 on 03.12.2011; company petition CP No. 106/397-398/CLB/MB/MAH/2013 filed before CLB Mumbai on 30.09.2013; transferred to NCLT Mumbai and decided on 09.02.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deutsche Bank foreign remittance records of USD 100,000 for acquiring corporate premises; profit and loss statements (2009-2012); absence of statutory books of accounts, board minutes books, and attendance registers under Appellants' custody; correspondence demonstrating irrevocable friction and bilateral cheating allegations (over-invoicing of commissions vs. non-accounting of profits). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed CP No. 106/397-398/CLB/MB/MAH/2013 alleging oppression, illegal removal from directorship, and misappropriation. NCLT Mumbai Bench vide order dated 09.02.2018 found complete deadlock and oppression, directing sale of the immovable office property via independent valuation, distribution of proceeds strictly per 51:49 shareholding ratio, and winding up with the ROC.
legal_issues: Whether the Company Law Tribunal/Adjudicating Authority exercising equitable jurisdiction under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 (corresponding to Sections 397-398 and 402 of the 1956 Act) has jurisdiction to order the winding up, sale of capital assets, and distribution of proceeds of a deadlocked closely-held private company, and whether the petition was barred by delay, laches, or failure to establish oppression.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a quasi-partnership or closely held private company with a binary shareholding structure, an irremediable functional deadlock between shareholder-directors accompanied by the unlawful exclusion of a majority shareholder from management, failure to maintain statutory records, and cessation of primary corporate objects justifies an order directing asset liquidation and winding up under just and equitable grounds to end oppression. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The equitable remedial jurisdiction under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 (and Sections 397/402 of the 1956 Act) is sufficiently wide to empower the Tribunal to direct a vertical split, sale of sole immovable assets, and winding up of a non-functional company where continuation would cause continuing prejudice and reconciliation is impossible. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Systemic governance failure is proved where directors in exclusive day-to-day control fail to maintain statutory books of accounts, disregard corporate registers, unilaterally remove a 51% shareholder from directorship on corporate records, and divert the sole commercial asset to tenancy. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the company ceased core export operations, reached complete deadlock between the 51% and 49% factions, and the Appellants committed oppression by removing Respondent No. 1 and failing to maintain statutory records, the NCLT's direction to sell the property and wind up the company was just, equitable, and legally valid.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 100 of 2018 is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 09.02.2018 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench directing the valuation, sale of immovable property, pro-rata distribution of proceeds (51:49), and dissolution of Touranto Company (India) Pvt. Ltd.
summary: Appellants Soumitra and Shampa Banerjee (49% shareholders) appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order directing the winding up and asset sale of Touranto Company (India) Pvt. Ltd. on a petition filed by Asher Ebrahim Melamed (51% shareholder). The parties reached an irreconcilable deadlock following disputes over export commissions, the Appellants' unilateral removal of Respondent No. 1 from directorship in 2009, complete stoppage of commercial business, and failure to maintain statutory books. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal is fully empowered to order the sale of corporate assets and winding up on just and equitable grounds where a quasi-partnership company is deadlocked and non-functional.

case_title: Rai Bahadur Shree Ram and Company Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Bhuvan Madan, Resolution Professional of Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants: Rai Bahadur Shree Ram and Company Pvt. Ltd. and Ram Kishan Saraf (Promoters/Shareholders of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1: Bhuvan Madan (Resolution Professional of Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 & 3: Committee of Creditors of Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd. through Rural Electrification Corporation Ltd. (REC Ltd., Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 4: Sterlite Power Transmission Ltd. (SPTL, Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 5: Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd. arising out of default in debt repayments owed to REC Ltd. and other financial creditors, culminating in competitive resolution plans and a promoter-backed settlement proposal. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit facilities leading to admission under CP(IB) No. 251/KB/2017; resolution plan submitted by Sterlite Power Transmission Ltd. (SPTL) approved by 95.15% voting share of the CoC; rival promoter settlement proposal submitted under IA No. 175/CTB/2019 rejected by CoC with requisite majority. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP(IB) No. 251/KB/2017 transferred to NCLT Cuttack Bench as TP No. 42/CTB/2019; RP filed IA No. 157/CTB/2019 for plan approval; Appellants filed IA No. 175/CTB/2019 for settlement reconsideration; NCLT Cuttack passed simultaneous orders approving SPTL's plan and rejecting the settlement application on 30.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certified voting records of the Committee of Creditors establishing that SPTL's resolution plan obtained 95.15% approval based on expert technical and feasibility evaluations, and that the Appellants' settlement proposal was formally considered and rejected by the CoC with the requisite majority. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Cuttack Bench vide order dated 30.01.2020 in IA No. 157/CTB/2019 approved SPTL's resolution plan, and vide separate order dated 30.01.2020 in IA No. 175/CTB/2019 dismissed Appellants' application seeking direction to reconsider their settlement proposal. Appellants filed appeals under Section 61 challenging both orders on grounds of non-application of mind and undervaluation.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) or the Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) has the jurisdiction to review, question, or overturn the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a resolution plan with a 95.15% majority and rejecting an ex-promoter's settlement proposal, and whether the tribunal can direct the CoC to reconsider a rejected settlement proposal on grounds of value maximization.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors exercised through its statutory voting majority in approving a resolution plan or rejecting a settlement proposal is non-justiciable and completely outside the purview of judicial review by the Adjudicating Authority and the Appellate Tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Judicial review under Section 31(1) read with Section 30(2) by the NCLT and under Section 61(3) read with Section 32 by the NCLAT is strictly circumscribed to examining compliance with the statutory parameters specified in Section 30(2) and verifying that no material irregularity occurred during the CIRP; it does not extend to an inquiry into the commercial soundness, business justification, or quantitative assessment of the plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of demonstrable material irregularity or legal infraction of Section 30(2), an approved resolution plan supported by the requisite voting share (95.15%) cannot be challenged on subjective assertions regarding asset valuation or alternative settlement feasibility. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC duly deliberated and rejected the Appellants' settlement proposal while approving SPTL's plan with a 95.15% majority; neither the NCLT nor the NCLAT has the statutory power to direct the CoC to reconsider a rejected settlement proposal or substitute its own judgment for the commercial decision of the creditors.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 207-208 of 2020 are dismissed without costs, affirming the orders dated 30.01.2020 passed by NCLT Cuttack Bench in IA No. 157/CTB/2019 (approving SPTL's resolution plan) and IA No. 175/CTB/2019.
summary: Appellants Rai Bahadur Shree Ram and Co. Pvt. Ltd. and Ram Kishan Saraf (promoters of Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd.) challenged the NCLT Cuttack order approving the resolution plan of Sterlite Power Transmission Ltd. (SPTL) with 95.15% CoC voting share and rejecting the Appellants' application for reconsideration of their settlement proposal. NCLAT dismissed the appeals, reaffirming the Supreme Court precedent in K. Sashidhar and Essar Steel. NCLAT ruled that the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors is non-justiciable, and the Adjudicating Authority possesses no statutory power under Section 31 to evaluate business decisions, assess quantitative metrics, or force the CoC to reconsider a rejected settlement proposal.

case_title: Late Mona Aggarwal through her Legal heir Mr. Vijay Kumar Aggarwal & Anr. vs. Ghaziabad Engineering Company Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants: Late Mona Aggarwal (deceased shareholder) through sole legal heir/husband Vijay Kumar Aggarwal and other shareholders; Respondent No. 1: Ghaziabad Engineering Company Ltd. (Company sought to be wound up); Respondent Nos. 2 & 3: Management/Opposing Directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate winding-up petition under just and equitable grounds concerning the affairs, assets, and liabilities of Ghaziabad Engineering Company Ltd., whose name was subsequently struck off from the register of companies by the Registrar of Companies (ROC). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate dissolution/winding up; petition filed under Section 433(c), (f), and (g) of the Companies Act, 1956 (amended to Section 271 of the Companies Act, 2013). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Winding up petition filed before Delhi High Court on 22.11.2016; transferred to NCLT New Delhi on 12.04.2017; amended to Section 271 on 28.07.2017; ROC struck off company name under Section 248(5) on 30.06.2017 effective from 07.06.2017; Respondent No. 2 filed revival appeal under Section 252 (Appeal No. 632-252-ND-2018); NCLT dismissed winding-up petition on 07.08.2019 granting liberty to refile upon revival; NCLT review application withdrawn on 25.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Will of Late Mona Aggarwal dated 07.09.2015 bequeathing all assets exclusively to Vijay Kumar Aggarwal (with children Vikas and Sohini succeeding only if husband predeceased); ROC Gazette Notification and strike-off order dated 30.06.2017; order sheet in Section 252 revival proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants originally petitioned Delhi High Court on 22.11.2016 for winding up. Following transfer to NCLT New Delhi (CP No. 1176/2016), NCLT rejected the petition on 07.08.2019 holding that the company had been struck off by the ROC and granted liberty to refile if restored under Section 252. Appellants appealed to NCLAT under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether the striking off of a company's name from the register of companies by the Registrar of Companies under Section 248(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 divests or deprives the National Company Law Tribunal of its statutory jurisdiction under Section 248(8) to hear, adjudicate, and order the winding up of the company under Section 271 during the pendency of a restoration appeal under Section 252; and whether a legal heir who is the sole universal legatee under a probated Will has standing to maintain the appeal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: By virtue of the express non-obstante savings clause in Section 248(8) of the Companies Act, 2013, the administrative striking off and dissolution of a company by the Registrar of Companies does not impair, eclipse, or extinguish the statutory power and jurisdiction of the Tribunal to proceed with and adjudicate a winding-up petition against the struck-off company under Section 271. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 248(8) explicitly provides that nothing in Section 248 shall affect the power of the Tribunal to wind up a company whose name has been struck off; consequently, NCLT is not required to dismiss a pending winding-up petition or defer proceedings until an administrative restoration appeal under Section 252 is determined. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Locus standi of a legal representative to continue company proceedings on behalf of a deceased shareholder is conclusively established where testamentary documents (Will) demonstrate sole legatee status in favor of the applicant. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed a clear legal error in dismissing the winding-up petition merely because the ROC struck off the company's name; Section 248(8) preserved full adjudicatory jurisdiction, mandating reversal and remand.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order of NCLT New Delhi dated 07.08.2019 in CP No. 1176/2016 is set aside. The company petition is remitted back to NCLT New Delhi for fresh adjudication on the merits in accordance with law. Parties are directed to appear before NCLT New Delhi on 07.04.2020. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellants (shareholders of Ghaziabad Engineering Company Ltd.) appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing their winding-up petition (CP No. 1176/2016) with liberty to file afresh if the company was revived, following the ROC's administrative action striking off the company's name under Section 248(5). NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the dismissal, holding that under Section 248(8) of the Companies Act, 2013, the power of the Tribunal to wind up a company is entirely unaffected by its name being struck off. NCLAT held that NCLT was not required to await Section 252 revival proceedings and remitted the matter to NCLT New Delhi to decide the winding-up petition on its merits.

case_title: C.P. Yogeshwara & Ors. vs. Union of India through Assistant Director SFIO & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants: Shri C.P. Yogeshwara (Managing Director/Promoter), Shri P. Mahadevaiah, Shri C.P. Gangadhreshwara, Shri Ramesh H.P. (Directors/Shareholders); Respondent No. 1: Union of India through Assistant Director, Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO), Ministry of Corporate Affairs; Respondent No. 2: Registrar of Companies, Karnataka; Respondent No. 3: M/s Megacity Bangalore Developers and Builders Limited (MBDBL, Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development scheme known as the 'Vajragiri Township Project' on Bangalore-Mysore Highway launched by MBDBL in 1994-1995, soliciting site membership applications from 9,600 public members across 60-66 instalment payment schemes, alongside land acquisitions from village farmers. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Widespread corporate fraud and financial irregularities involving approximately 9,300 enrolled public members where 3,100 paid in full and 6,200 paid partial instalments without delivery of sites; Rs. 10 Crores given as loans/advances to directors/relatives on a meager paid-up capital base of Rs. 6,00,000; undisclosed land purchase of Rs. 46,72,500 omitted from the balance sheet of 31.03.2006. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Vajragiri project operated between 1994 and 2002; non-filing of statutory returns noted for 2006-2007; SFIO investigated affairs and filed comprehensive fraud report; Union of India filed CP No. 02 of 2014 before CLB (transferred to NCLT as TP No. 300 of 2017); NCLT Bengaluru Bench passed final order on 14.03.2019 removing directors and allowing UOI to nominate a new board. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SFIO Investigation Report documenting systemic financial fraud, lack of Bangalore Metropolitan Region Development Authority (BMRDA) approvals while falsely advertising government sponsorship in promotional brochures, siphoning of Rs. 10 crores to promoter family members, falsification of the 31.03.2006 balance sheet, non-filing of annual returns, and proof that C.P. Yogeshwara fraudulently obtained three Director Identification Numbers (DINs) using manipulated names. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Union of India filed a petition under Sections 388B, 397, 398, 401, and 408 of the Companies Act, 1956 alleging affairs conducted prejudicial to public interest. NCLT Bengaluru Bench vide order dated 14.03.2019 declared that Appellants ceased to be directors, debarred them from managing company affairs, and authorized Union of India to appoint government-nominated directors.
legal_issues: Whether, following the repeal of the Companies Act, 1956 and the absence of a direct textual replica of Section 388B in the Companies Act, 2013, the National Company Law Tribunal retains statutory jurisdiction under Sections 241(2) and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 to remove an entire board of directors for fraud prejudicial to public interest and authorize the Central Government to appoint nominee directors to manage the company.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 241(2) read with Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, when the affairs of a company are conducted in a manner gravely prejudicial to public interest, the Tribunal possesses plenary equitable powers to terminate, supersede, and remove the existing management and authorize the Central Government to appoint new directors, notwithstanding the repeal of Section 388B of the Companies Act, 1956. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 465 (repeal and savings) read with Section 434(1) seamlessly transfers pending proceedings; Sections 241(2) and 242 encompass comprehensive remedial authority permitting the Tribunal to make 'such order as it thinks fit' to terminate oppressive or fraudulent conduct, empowering it to grant the same management-replacement remedies formerly provided under Section 388B and Section 408 of the 1956 Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted findings in an SFIO statutory investigation establishing large-scale public deception, unapproved land projects, falsified financial statements, illicit diversion of company funds to promoter relatives, and multiple fraudulent DIN acquisitions provide conclusive factual basis demonstrating prejudice to public interest. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The management conducted company affairs in a manner gravely injurious to public investors and statutory compliance, fully justifying the NCLT's order debarring the directors and permitting the Union of India to appoint nominee directors.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 111 of 2019 is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 14.03.2019 passed by NCLT Bengaluru Bench in C.P. No. 02 of 2014 (T.P. No. 300 of 2017) removing Appellants as directors and authorizing the Union of India to appoint nominee directors.
summary: Appellants, former directors of Megacity Bangalore Developers and Builders Ltd., challenged the NCLT Bengaluru order removing them from the board and authorizing the Union of India to appoint government-nominated directors following an SFIO investigation revealing financial fraud in the Vajragiri Township project (where 9,300 members were enrolled and Rs. 10 crores diverted). Appellants contended that NCLT could not grant relief under Section 388B of the repealed 1956 Act. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under Sections 241(2) and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal retains full statutory power to remove fraudulent management and empower the Central Government to appoint new directors when corporate affairs are conducted prejudicial to public interest.

case_title: Focus Energy Limited vs. Reebok India Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Focus Energy Limited (minority shareholder holding 6.85% equity, originally 20%); Respondent No. 1: Reebok India Limited (joint venture company with Reebok Mauritius Ltd., selling apparels/footwear); Respondent Nos. 2-3 & 7-9: Controlling management and directors; Respondent No. 11: BSR and Co. (Statutory Auditors); Proposed Respondent No. 12: BSR and Company. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Equity participation and investment in Reebok India Ltd. where Appellant's original 20% equity stake was diluted to 6.85% in 2003 through the issuance of Compulsorily Convertible Debentures (CCDs), alongside statutory and component auditing services provided by BSR entities between financial years 2007 and 2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Allegations of oppression, mismanagement, and financial fraud of Rs. 1,500 Crores to Rs. 8,700 Crores in siphoning of corporate funds; contested CCD conversions scheduled for February 2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Equity dilution occurred in 2003; CCDs issued on 01.02.2013 and 02.08.2013; Company Petition No. 126(ND)/2015 filed by Appellant before CLB in 2015 (transferred to NCLT New Delhi); CA No. 97 of 2016 filed seeking amendment; NCLT New Delhi Bench dismissed CA No. 97 of 2016 on 22.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Balance sheets of Reebok India Ltd. for FY 2012-13 and FY 2013-14 reflecting CCD disclosures; SFIO investigation report relating to FY 2011-12 under Section 212 of the Companies Act, 2013; absence of new, unpleaded factual evidence linking auditors to active management. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In pending CP No. 126(ND)/2015, Appellant filed CA No. 97 of 2016 seeking to amend the petition to alter the name of Respondent No. 11 to 'BSR and Co. LLP', implead 'BSR and Company' as Respondent No. 12, and insert Para 3.8 specifying professional misconduct and connivance in siphoning funds. NCLT New Delhi Bench dismissed the application on 22.10.2019, which was appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether a petitioner in an oppression and mismanagement proceeding under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 can amend the petition to define explicit fraud roles and implead external statutory auditors/affiliates as necessary parties merely because an ongoing SFIO investigation under Section 212 highlights auditing lapses.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Allegations of oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 pertain exclusively to internal affairs, governance, and proprietary conduct of the company and its management; third-party statutory auditors acting in an external professional capacity cannot be impleaded or joined as necessary parties to an oppression petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 241 and 242 are directed against members and directors conducting company affairs in a prejudicial manner; professional negligence, misconduct, or auditing failures fall under distinct regulatory provisions (such as Section 212 investigations by SFIO or professional disciplinary proceedings) and cannot be incorporated by belated amendments to sustain an oppression action against an auditor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An amendment application filed with substantial delay after having full prior knowledge of corporate filings, based merely on an interim SFIO report without establishing direct participation of auditors in corporate governance, is liable to be rejected as an attempt to cause procedural delay. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant had full knowledge of the facts when filing the 2015 petition, and an ongoing SFIO investigation under Section 212 cannot justify amending the petition to implead another auditing entity or expand oppression claims against statutory auditors, justifying dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 356 of 2019 is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 22.10.2019 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench in Company Application No. 97 of 2016 in CP No. 126(ND)/2015.
summary: Appellant Focus Energy Ltd. (6.85% shareholder of Reebok India Ltd.) challenged an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its application (CA No. 97/2016) to amend its oppression and mismanagement petition (CP No. 126(ND)/2015). The amendment sought to define the role of statutory auditors in an alleged Rs. 1,500-8,700 crore siphoning fraud, change Respondent No. 11 to BSR and Co. LLP, and implead BSR and Company as Respondent No. 12, relying on an SFIO report. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, following the Bochapathar Tea Estate precedent. It held that statutory auditors are not necessary parties in oppression and mismanagement proceedings under Sections 241-242, and an SFIO probe does not furnish grounds to belatedly implead auditing firms.

case_title: Manoj K. Daga vs. ISGEC Heavy Engineering Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Manoj K. Daga (suspended Director of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1: ISGEC Heavy Engineering Limited (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2: Shikhar Jain (Interim Resolution Professional/Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 3: Deepak Kumar Daga (suspended Director/authorized cheque signatory of Corporate Debtor); Corporate Debtor: M/s Shree Vishnu Power & Energy Pvt. Ltd.; Financial Creditor: State Bank of India (sole CoC member having ~Rs. 45 Crores claim). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational debts arising from contracts/supplies between ISGEC Heavy Engineering Limited and Shree Vishnu Power & Energy Pvt. Ltd.. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admission under Section 9 on operational debt default; post-admission unauthorized bank withdrawals/transfers by suspended directors totaled Rs. 6,72,12,146 from the Corporate Debtor's Vijaya Bank account, leaving a balance of only Rs. 6,315.27, of which merely Rs. 8,95,412.22 qualified as permissible CIRP costs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Cuttack admitted Section 9 petition and declared moratorium on 27.09.2019; NCLAT passed conditional interim order regarding bank operations on 23.10.2019; IRP filed IA No. 3878/2019 highlighting violations on 25.11.2019; NCLAT modified interim directions on 05.12.2019; directors tendered affidavits/undertakings to redeposit funds within 4 weeks on 05.02.2020; Supreme Court issued directions in Civil Appeal No. 2001/2020 on 06.03.2020; NCLAT dismissed appeal on 12.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements of Vijaya Bank establishing transfers of Rs. 4,54,73,285 between 25.10.2019 and 15.11.2019 (including transfers to Deepak Kumar Daga, Pooja Trading Co., Chhattisgarh State Power, and self-cheques), Appendix A transfers of Rs. 2,04,70,000 (27.09.2019 to 23.10.2019), and Appendix C transfers of Rs. 12,68,861.34 (25.11.2019 to 17.12.2019); formal undertakings and affidavits dated 04/05.02.2020 given by Manoj K. Daga and Deepak Daga undertaking to return the remaining Rs. 5,50,12,146 within four weeks which were breached. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Cuttack Bench admitted ISGEC's Section 9 petition in TP No. 105/CTB/2019 [CP (IB) No. 646/MB/2019] on 27.09.2019. Appellant appealed to NCLAT. During appeal pendency, IRP reported massive unauthorized fund siphoning in breach of the Section 14 moratorium and NCLAT orders.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal challenging the admission of a Section 9 application deserves to be dismissed in default/for abuse of process where suspended directors flout statutory moratorium under Section 14, withdraw corporate funds without IRP approval, and breach solemn undertakings given to the Appellate Tribunal to redeposit siphoned monies; and whether such actions justify initiation of contempt proceedings under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013 and criminal proceedings under Sections 70 and 74 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellant who willfully violates statutory moratorium provisions, obstructs the insolvency resolution process, and deliberately breaches formal undertakings given on affidavit to the appellate court to restitute siphoned corporate debtor funds forfeits the right to equitable audience on merits, warranting dismissal of the appeal in default and contempt action. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14, Section 17, and Section 19 mandate the complete transfer of management and control of corporate assets and bank accounts to the IRP/RP upon initiation of CIRP; ex-directors have no legal authority to withdraw corporate funds or issue self-cheques without express IRP sanction. Under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal possesses plenary powers to initiate contempt for willful disobedience of its orders and breach of undertakings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where certified banking ledgers confirm substantial unauthorized dissipation of corporate funds during CIRP and respondents fail to comply with time-bound solemn undertakings tendered on affidavit, deliberate contumacious conduct is established prima facie. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The suspended directors engaged in willful disobedience and criminal breach of trust by siphoning Rs. 6.72 Crores and failing to honor undertakings to restitute the monies; hence, the appeal is dismissed in default, contempt proceedings are initiated, and IRP is empowered to pursue criminal recovery.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1113 of 2019 is dismissed in default. IA No. 1075 of 2020 seeking extension of time is rejected. Contempt case is registered as 'State vs. Manoj K. Daga and Deepak Daga' under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013 to be listed on 07.04.2020. The IRP is granted liberty to initiate proceedings before the Adjudicating Authority or police authorities for criminal breach of trust and misappropriation, and to pursue actions under Sections 70 and 74 of the IBC.
summary: Manoj K. Daga appealed the NCLT Cuttack order admitting ISGEC Heavy Engineering's Section 9 IBC application against Shree Vishnu Power & Energy Pvt. Ltd. During the pendency of the appeal, the IRP discovered that the suspended directors had siphoned Rs. 6.72 crores from the corporate debtor's bank accounts without approval, in violation of the Section 14 moratorium and interim court orders. Although the directors gave solemn undertakings on affidavit to redeposit the funds within four weeks, they failed to do so. NCLAT dismissed the appeal in default, initiated suo motu criminal contempt proceedings against the directors under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013, and directed police and statutory prosecution under Sections 70 and 74 of the IBC.

case_title: Indiana Conveyors Pvt. Ltd. vs. Ducon Technologies (I) Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Indiana Conveyors Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent: Ducon Technologies (I) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Non-Party Client: M/s Hindalco Industries Limited (Project Client for Aditya Aluminium Project 1 and Mahan Aluminium Project 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor issued purchase orders/letters of intent between 2010 and 2013 for designing, engineering, manufacturing, supply, and supervision of erection/commissioning of bulk material handling belt conveyors for Hindalco's units. Operational Creditor performed the supplies and raised corresponding commercial invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed unpaid operational debt was Rs. 1,15,50,712 (principal amount of Rs. 56,58,764 plus interest of Rs. 58,91,948), adjusted to Rs. 56,21,572 principal after reconciling an excess past credit of Rs. 37,501; Corporate Debtor's own statement of accounts admitted at least Rs. 35,10,600.68 net outstanding after adjusting all unilateral debit notes. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised during 2011-2013; reconciliation meetings held on 21.02.2014, 01.03.2014, and 17.01.2015; statutory notice under Sections 433/434 of Companies Act issued on 05.02.2016; Form 3 Section 8 demand notice issued on 03.02.2018; Corporate Debtor replied on 14.02.2018 claiming dispute. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's statement of accounts dated 26.07.2013 admitting Rs. 56,48,671 payable; minutes of meeting dated 21.02.2014 admitting Rs. 52,87,267 and revised minutes dated 08.03.2014 confirming Rs. 57,42,410; email dated 28.01.2015 confirming Rs. 30,01,985.21 due for Project 1; email dated 03.07.2015 and accounts statement confirming Rs. 5,08,615.47 due for Project 2 even after debit notes; PBG submitted on 23.03.2015; lack of any contractual novation agreement executed with Hindalco. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP (IB) No. 2825/(IB)/MB/2018 under Section 9 of the IBC. NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed the application on 02.04.2019 holding that pre-existing disputes existed regarding damaged conveyor belts and that payment liability was novated to Hindalco. Operational Creditor appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether an informal understanding to facilitate direct payment from a third-party principal client (Hindalco) constitutes a legal novation of contract discharging the Corporate Debtor's primary liability, and whether raising debit notes for damages occurring outside the contractual scope of work constitutes a genuine pre-existing dispute under the Mobilox Innovations standard to warrant rejection of a Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Corporate Debtor cannot evade insolvency proceedings under Section 9 by contriving spurious, after-thought disputes or relying on informal tripartite payment arrangements that do not legally novate the underlying contract or extinguish the debtor's primary liability for accepted goods and services. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 9 read with the Mobilox test, the Adjudicating Authority must determine whether the dispute is a real, bona fide dispute and not a sham or frivolous defense. An arrangement permitting direct disbursement from a client does not constitute novation in the absence of a binding contract extinguishing the debtor's liability. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the Corporate Debtor's own signed reconciliations, emails, and ledgers unequivocally admit substantial unpaid debt (exceeding statutory thresholds) even after accounting for contested debit notes, assertions of belt damages and quality issues outside the operational creditor's contractual scope cannot constitute a plausible pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liability remained that of the Corporate Debtor and was repeatedly acknowledged; the alleged dispute was an afterthought to evade payment, rendering NCLT's dismissal erroneous and requiring admission of the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 508 of 2019 is allowed. The impugned order dated 02.04.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in CP (IB) No. 2825/(IB)/MB/2018 is set aside, and the matter is remitted to NCLT Mumbai Bench to admit the Section 9 application without further hearing, subject to any settlement reached prior to formal admission. No order as to costs.
summary: Indiana Conveyors Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dismissing its Section 9 IBC application against Ducon Technologies (I) Pvt. Ltd. on grounds of a pre-existing dispute regarding damaged conveyor belts and alleged novation of payment obligations to Hindalco. NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that under Mobilox Innovations, the dispute must be real and substantiated. The record demonstrated that the Corporate Debtor repeatedly admitted net liability exceeding Rs. 35 Lakhs after debit notes and attempted to shift liability to Hindalco without legal novation. Finding the defense to be a sham after-thought, NCLAT remitted the matter to NCLT Mumbai with directions to admit the Section 9 petition.

case_title: Confederation of All India Traders vs. Competition Commission of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Confederation of All India Traders (CAIT, trade association representing domestic retailers/wholesalers); Respondent No. 1: Competition Commission of India (CCI); Respondent No. 2: Wal-Mart International Holdings, Inc. (Walmart, acquirer); Target Entity: Flipkart Private Limited (Flipkart, e-commerce marketplace operator, non-impleaded entity). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Proposed combination involving the acquisition of between 51% and 77% of the outstanding share capital of Flipkart Private Limited by Walmart International Holdings, Inc. pursuant to a Share Purchase Agreement (SPA) and Share Issuance and Acquisition Agreement (SIAA) dated 09.05.2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Merger review regulation; statutory combination approval under Section 31(1) challenged by third-party trade associations alleging potential market distortion and search bias. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form-I notice of combination filed by Walmart under Section 6(2) on 18.05.2018; CAIT and trade associations filed representations opposing the merger; CCI granted approval under Section 31(1) on 08.08.2018; NCLAT heard and dismissed the appeal on 12.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Walmart's notice under Section 6(2); market data showing overlapping horizontal activities restricted strictly to pan-India B2B wholesale cash-and-carry trading with a combined market share of less than 5%; regulatory covenants under FDI Policy 2017 barring foreign-invested marketplace entities from engaging in B2C inventory sales; and lack of documentary evidence establishing elimination of competitors or foreclosure of non-preferred sellers. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI evaluated the notice under Section 6(2), considered third-party representations, and approved the transaction vide order dated 08.08.2018 under Section 31(1) upon finding no likelihood of AAEC. CAIT filed an appeal under Section 53B before NCLAT challenging the approval.
legal_issues: Whether third-party competitors or trade associations possess a statutory right to an oral hearing during pre-merger combination reviews under Section 29 and Section 31 of the Competition Act, 2002, and whether CCI is obligated to initiate detailed Phase-II investigations under Section 29 when it forms an opinion that no prima facie case of Appreciable Adverse Effect on Competition (AAEC) exists in the pan-India B2B wholesale market.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 29 read with Section 31 of the Competition Act, 2002, the Commission is required to initiate detailed public notice and inquiry procedures under Section 29 only if it forms a prima facie opinion that a proposed combination causes or is likely to cause an Appreciable Adverse Effect on Competition (AAEC); in the absence of such a prima facie opinion, the Commission is legally mandated to approve the combination under Section 31(1). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Unlike antitrust prohibitions against anti-competitive agreements (Section 3) and abuse of dominance (Section 4), combinations under Section 6 are regulated through ex-ante review. Third parties have no statutory entitlement to an oral hearing during merger evaluation, and their interests are sufficiently protected through written representations. Allegations regarding FDI policy infractions pertain to distinct regulatory regimes and cannot determine AAEC under the Competition Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where empirical market share data demonstrates an insignificant horizontal overlap (under 5% combined share in wholesale B2B) and no elimination of any major player in the relevant market, speculative assertions of vertical foreclosure and preferential listing cannot displace the finding of no AAEC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CCI properly assessed horizontal and vertical market effects and rightly formed an opinion that no prima facie case of AAEC existed; hence, approval without formal Section 29 proceedings was legally sound, justifying dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 62 of 2018 is dismissed without costs, affirming the combination approval order dated 08.08.2018 passed by the Competition Commission of India under Section 31(1) of the Competition Act, 2002.
summary: CAIT appealed against the CCI's order approving Walmart's acquisition of a 51% to 77% stake in Flipkart under Section 31(1) of the Competition Act, 2002, contending that the merger would accentuate preferential seller bias, predatory pricing, and market foreclosure. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that third parties do not possess an absolute right to an oral hearing in merger clearance proceedings. Furthermore, because the horizontal overlap was limited to wholesale B2B trade where the combined market share remained below 5%, and FDI rules barred B2C retail inventory operations, the CCI properly formed an opinion that no prima facie AAEC existed, obviating the need for detailed Section 29 inquiry procedures.

case_title: Uttarakhand Agricultural Produce Marketing Board vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Opposite Party No. 1: Uttarakhand Agricultural Produce Marketing Board (sole wholesale procurer of IMFL in Uttarakhand); Respondent No. 1: Competition Commission of India (CCI); Respondent No. 2/Informant: International Spirits and Wines Association of India (ISWAI); Respondent Nos. 3 & 4/Opposite Party Nos. 2 & 3: Garhwal Mandal Vikas Nigam Ltd. (GMVN) and Kumaon Mandal Vikas Nigam Ltd. (KMVN) (exclusive regional distributors). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Wholesale procurement, distribution, and supply of branded Indian Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL) in the State of Uttarakhand pursuant to the Liquor Wholesale Order valid between 27.04.2015 and 19.04.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Antitrust abuse of dominance; Informant alleged arbitrary and discriminatory procurement favoring select manufacturers over major suppliers (USL and Pernod); no financial penalty was adjudicated in the impugned interlocutory order. 4.
