STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information filed under Section 19(1)(a) forming Case No. 02/2016; prima facie investigation ordered under Section 26(1) on 19.07.2016; DG report submitted concluding Section 4 violations against OP-1; CCI heard objections and passed impugned order on 30.08.2018 issuing show-cause notices to OP-2 and OP-3; appeal dismissed by NCLAT on 12.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DG Investigation Report establishing 100% procurement monopoly of OP-1; sales volume records proving sharp declines for USL/Pernod during 2015-16 alongside anomalous increases for rival suppliers; impugned order dated 30.08.2018 expressly recording that observations were tentative. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI issued an order on 30.08.2018 issuing show-cause notices to GMVN and KMVN to show cause why they should not be held to have contravened Sections 4(2)(b)(i) and 4(2)(c) read with Section 4(1). OP-1 appealed under Section 53B contending the order operated as a final Section 27 finding.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal under Section 53B read with Section 53A of the Competition Act, 2002 is maintainable against an interlocutory order of the Competition Commission of India that issues show-cause notices to co-respondents and records tentative observations without passing a final order of contravention or penalty under Section 27.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal before the Appellate Tribunal under Section 53B lies strictly against definitive, appealable directions, decisions, or orders enumerated under Section 53A; an interlocutory show-cause notice recording prima facie tentative observations does not constitute an order under Section 27 and is non-appealable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 27 empowers the Commission to pass final remedial and penal orders only upon the conclusion of an inquiry; where the Commission explicitly clarifies that its findings are tentative and invites replies, the order does not conclude the inquiry under Section 27. Section 53A and Section 53B cannot be invoked prematurely to stifle ongoing administrative inquiries. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The character of an order is determined by its operative terms and reservation of final adjudication; an express caveat stating 'nothing stated herein shall tantamount to a final expression of opinion' establishes that the order is purely interlocutory. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The impugned order did not determine liability or impose penalties under Section 27 against the Appellant, rendering the statutory appeal premature and not maintainable under Section 53B.
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 84 of 2018 is dismissed as not maintainable, with liberty granted to the Competition Commission of India to hear the parties and pass appropriate final orders in accordance with law. No order as to costs.
summary: Uttarakhand Agricultural Produce Marketing Board appealed under Section 53B against a CCI order dated 30.08.2018 in Case No. 02/2016 which issued show-cause notices to co-distributors GMVN and KMVN regarding alleged abuse of dominance under Section 4 in IMFL procurement and distribution. NCLAT dismissed the appeal as not maintainable, holding that the impugned order was merely an interlocutory show-cause notice containing tentative observations rather than a final determination under Section 27 of the Competition Act, 2002. As Section 53A does not permit appeals against interlocutory show-cause notices, the appeal was dismissed, leaving the CCI free to finalize proceedings on the merits.

case_title: Central Transmission Utility (Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd.) vs. Korba West Power Company Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Central Transmission Utility / Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. (Operational Creditor, CTU under Section 38 Electricity Act); Respondent No. 1: Korba West Power Company Limited / Raigarh Energy Generation Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2: Abhijit Guhathakurta (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 3: Adani Power Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 4: Committee of Creditors of Korba West Power Company Ltd.. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bulk Power Transmission Agreement (BPTA) dated 24.02.2010 for Long Term Access (LTA) executed between PGCIL and Corporate Debtor under the Electricity Act, 2003 and CERC Regulations, 2009. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid transmission charges and relinquishment liabilities due from 01.10.2017; Appellant submitted operational debt claim of Rs. 3,19,36,312 to the RP, out of which Rs. 2,78,81,825 was admitted on 08.04.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 10 CIRP petition admitted on 26.07.2018; NCLT Ahmedabad approved Adani Power's resolution plan on 24.06.2019; Appellant appeared and acknowledged the approval order before CERC on 04.07.2019; CERC proceedings terminated on 25.09.2019; Section 61 appeal filed before NCLAT on 11.11.2019 (~150 days after impugned order). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certified record of proceedings before CERC in Petition No. 269/MP/2017 dated 04.07.2019 where Appellant's counsel explicitly stated that NCLT had approved the resolution plan on 24.06.2019; IA No. 3811 of 2019 seeking condonation of delay. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench approved Adani Power's resolution plan for Korba West Power Company Ltd. on 24.06.2019. Operational Creditor PGCIL filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1334 of 2019 along with IA No. 3811 of 2019 on 11.11.2019 challenging the resolution plan.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal has the statutory jurisdiction or discretion under Section 61(2) proviso of the IBC to condone a delay beyond the maximum condonable period of 15 days (total 45 days) where an appellant claims lack of operational debt quantification due to pending regulatory proceedings before the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The period of limitation for filing an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC is 30 days, extendable by a maximum of 15 days only upon showing sufficient cause; the Appellate Tribunal possesses no statutory power or jurisdiction to condone any delay beyond the strict outer ceiling of 45 days. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) is an exhaustive, mandatory code for limitation; collateral proceedings pending before regulatory authorities (such as CERC) or alleged difficulty in quantifying operational claims do not constitute a legal bar or ground to defer or suspend the running of limitation against an approved resolution plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where certified court records establish that an appellant's advocate had explicit, documented knowledge of the impugned approval order in another legal proceeding (CERC on 04.07.2019), assertions of delayed knowledge until the formal disposal of regulatory proceedings are false and contradicted by the record. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was filed ~150 days after the impugned order and more than 45 days after verified knowledge, placing it beyond the non-extendable statutory jurisdiction of the Tribunal, mandating dismissal as time-barred.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1334 of 2019 and IA No. 3811 of 2019 are dismissed as barred by limitation without entering into the merits of the challenge.
summary: Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. (Central Transmission Utility) appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 24.06.2019 approving Adani Power's resolution plan for Korba West Power Company Ltd. The appeal was filed on 11.11.2019, approximately 150 days after the order. Appellant contended that limitation should be computed from 25.09.2019 when CERC proceedings terminated, allowing quantification of debt. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that CERC order sheets showed Appellant had knowledge of the approval order as early as 04.07.2019. Because Section 61(2) of the IBC limits condonable delay strictly to 15 days beyond the initial 30 days, NCLAT lacked jurisdiction to condone delay beyond 45 days.

case_title: Shri Venkatesh Koravadi vs. Viney Kaushal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Shri Venkatesh Koravadi (Director/Shareholder of Respondent Company); Respondent Nos. 1, 2 & 3: Viney Kaushal, minority shareholders holding 52,530, 39,420, and 12,269 equity shares respectively (original Petitioners); Respondent No. 4: M/s World Schools Pvt. Ltd. (Company incorporated on 24.01.2005 to establish and run educational institutions); Respondent Nos. 5-9: Co-shareholders/Directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management, governance, and share capital of M/s World Schools Pvt. Ltd. having an authorized share capital of Rs. 1,00,00,000 and paid-up capital of Rs. 95,58,060. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate governance and oppression dispute; allegations of arbitrary share allotments at differing premiums without notice, convening meetings without statutory notice, exclusion from management via removal resolution dated 07.03.2016, and diversion/misuse of company funds through an external educational Trust. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respondent Nos. 1-3 removed from directorship on 07.03.2016; Company Petition CP No. 07/2016 filed in September 2016; NCLT Bengaluru Bench passed disposal order on 22.03.2019; NCLAT heard and decided the appeal on 05.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Auditor reports reflecting financial irregularities; complaints lodged before the Registrar of Companies (ROC), Principal Director of Income Tax (Investigation), and Prime Minister's Office (PMOPG portal); absence in NCLT order of any defined terms of reference, scope of enquiry, or reporting timelines for investigating agencies. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent Nos. 1-3 filed CP No. 07/2016 under Sections 210, 213, 241, 242, and 246 of the Companies Act, 2013. NCLT Bengaluru Bench disposed of the petition on 22.03.2019 by appointing an independent Chairman (Prof. Dr. O.V. Nandimath at Rs. 75,000/month) as an interim arrangement pending indefinite investigations by the ROC and Income Tax authorities, granting liberty to file a fresh petition thereafter. Appellant appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal exercising jurisdiction under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 can dispose of an oppression and mismanagement petition by appointing an interim independent Chairman for an indefinite duration while delegating unresolved allegations to external statutory authorities (ROC and Income Tax) without defining the scope, terms, or timeline of inquiry.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority exercising equitable company jurisdiction cannot abdicate its statutory duty to adjudicate core allegations of oppression and mismanagement on merits by disposing of a company petition through an open-ended interim arrangement that delegates fact-finding to external statutory bodies without defining the scope of enquiry, reporting timelines, or receiving forums. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 241 and 242 mandate the Tribunal to examine rival contentions, determine whether corporate affairs are being conducted in an oppressive manner, and pass definitive, effective orders to bring an end to the matters complained of; vague, non-speaking disposal orders that neither evaluate evidence nor set definite investigation parameters are legally unsustainable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Judicial orders directing regulatory investigations or divesting managerial control must be grounded in specific findings of fact and reasoned analysis of the submissions and defenses raised by the contesting parties rather than speculative interim delegation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's order was vague and non-speaking, failing to set timelines or delineate the scope of enquiry while leaving the company under an indefinite interim administration; hence, the order is set aside and remitted for fresh, expeditious adjudication on merits.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 101 of 2019 is allowed. The impugned order dated 22.03.2019 passed by NCLT Bengaluru Bench in C.P. No. 07 of 2016 is set aside, and the matter is remitted back to NCLT Bengaluru Bench to pass a fresh reasoned order after hearing all parties on merits without being influenced by previous observations. Parties are directed to appear before NCLT Bengaluru Bench on 25.03.2020. No costs.
summary: Venkatesh Koravadi appealed against an NCLT Bengaluru order disposing of an oppression and mismanagement petition regarding World Schools Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had disposed of the petition by appointing an independent Chairman at Rs. 75,000 per month as an interim arrangement pending completion of investigations by the ROC and Income Tax authorities. NCLAT set aside the order and remitted the matter back to NCLT Bengaluru for fresh adjudication on the merits, holding that the impugned order was vague and non-speaking, as it failed to evaluate the appellant's defenses and omitted essential parameters such as the scope, timeline, and reporting procedure for the external investigations.

case_title: Rajesh Kumar Agarwal & Ors. vs. M/s Srivani Merchants Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants: Rajesh Kumar Agarwal, Kavita Agarwal, and Chayank Agarwal (minor through guardian), third-party occupants of corporate residential property (non-shareholders/non-directors); Respondent No. 1: M/s Srivani Merchants Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2: M/s RLA Holdings Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities advanced by Financial Creditor to Corporate Debtor, where the Corporate Debtor's balance sheets for successive years carried ownership of Flat No. 3E, 3 Lower Rowdon Street, Ballygunge, Kolkata as its core corporate asset. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default under Section 7 IBC leading to initiation of CIRP in CP (IB) No. 616/KB/2017; CIRP period of 180/270 days expired without receipt of any compliant resolution plan, culminating in liquidation order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Oral family arrangement alleged in 2013; Title Suit No. 85 of 2015 filed before Civil Court Alipore; Section 7 petition admitted and public notice issued by IRP; CIRP statutory period lapsed; NCLT passed liquidation order on 16.05.2019 and appointed substitute liquidator on 17.05.2019; NCLAT dismissed appeals on 18.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Plaint in Title Suit No. 85 of 2015 wherein Appellants explicitly conceded in paragraph 9(c) that the title of Flat No. 3E stood in the name of Defendant No. 10 (Corporate Debtor); audited balance sheets of the Corporate Debtor recording the flat as company property; common chartered accountant (Uttam Chand Choudhary) acting professionally for both Corporate Debtor and Financial Creditor without shareholding or directorship interest; failure of Appellants to submit Form G Expression of Interest or tender a resolution plan during CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following admission of Section 7 application, Appellants filed applications before NCLT Kolkata Bench for impleadment, claiming fraud under Section 65, and seeking consideration as resolution applicants. NCLT Kolkata Bench ordered liquidation under Section 33 on 16.05.2019 and replaced the liquidator on 17.05.2019 as CIRP expired without a resolution plan. Appellants appealed both orders.
legal_issues: Whether a liquidation order passed under Section 33 of the IBC upon expiry of the statutory CIRP period can be challenged by non-shareholder third parties asserting property rights under an unadjudicated family arrangement, and whether prospective resolution applicants can circumvent mandatory CIRP expression of interest mechanisms by directly petitioning the Adjudicating Authority after the statutory period has expired.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A person seeking to act as a resolution applicant must strictly comply with the statutory procedures, timelines, and Form-G expressions of interest through the Resolution Professional and Committee of Creditors; an uninvited, belated offer made directly before the Adjudicating Authority after the statutory CIRP period has expired lacks bona fides and cannot stall liquidation under Section 33. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33 mandates an order of liquidation where no approved resolution plan is submitted before the expiry of the maximum CIRP period. Allegations of collusive initiation under Section 65 cannot be entertained on mere suspicion or because a common chartered accountant acted professionally for both entities, absent evidence of shareholding or managerial control. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an appellant's own civil court plaint admits that the disputed property stands in the legal name of the corporate debtor, the Resolution Professional and Liquidator have the statutory duty and power to take possession of the corporate asset. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor owned the property, no resolution plan was submitted within statutory timelines, and collusion was unproven; hence, the NCLT's liquidation order was valid, justifying dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 669 & 689 of 2019 are dismissed without costs, affirming the liquidation and liquidator-appointment orders dated 16.05.2019 and 17.05.2019 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench in CP (IB) No. 616/KB/2017.
summary: Appellants, occupants of a residential flat belonging to Corporate Debtor RLA Holdings Pvt. Ltd., appealed NCLT Kolkata's liquidation orders. Appellants claimed ownership under an oral family arrangement, alleged collusion under Section 65 because the applicant and debtor shared a common chartered accountant, and requested consideration as resolution applicants. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Appellants' own civil pleadings admitted the company held legal title to the flat, giving the Liquidator full right to custody. Furthermore, common professional services did not prove fraud, and the Appellants failed to submit an EOI during the statutory CIRP period, making their belated proposal non-bona fide.

case_title: U.V. Hari Prasada Raju & Ors. vs. Achala Gold Agritech Investment Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 311 of 2018 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 273 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants in CA 311/2018 / Respondents in CA 273/2018: Om Prakash Avulla and associates (Founders/Core Promoters holding 38.46% equity); Appellants in CA 273/2018 / Respondents in CA 311/2018: U.V. Hari Prasada Raju and associates (controlling shareholders holding 61.54% equity); Company: M/s Achala Gold Agritech Investment Ltd.. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Share capital split, director appointments, and proposed public/private auction of immovable agricultural/corporate lands owned by M/s Achala Gold Agritech Investment Ltd., which were originally acquired using funds of Rs. 1,12,00,000 infused by Respondent No. 2 and associates (Rs. 52 Lakhs towards share capital and Rs. 60 Lakhs towards land purchase). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate governance dispute regarding the transfer and split of 2,000 shares of Respondent No. 2 to Respondents 6-15 to constitute a quorum, appointment of additional directors without unanimous consent under Section 162, and authorization to sell company landed properties to fund day-to-day operational expenses. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Purported Board Meeting held on 06.06.2014; EGM convened on 30.06.2014; Form MGT-14 filed on 22.07.2014; AGM held on 08.08.2015; EGM notice issued on 21.10.2015 for meeting on 12.11.2015; NCLT Hyderabad passed impugned order on 13.07.2018; NCLAT decided cross-appeals on 03.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Postal courier receipts and tracking reports establishing service and refusal of meeting notices by the minority faction; share transfer and splitting instruments executed under Section 56 and the Articles of Association; ROC complaint disposal orders treating the row as an internal management dispute. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Om Prakash Avulla filed CP No. 82 of 2015 before NCLT Hyderabad alleging oppression and mismanagement. NCLT upheld the validity of corporate meetings and share splitting, found no oppression, but directed in paras 47-48 that an EOGM be held to sell assets where one of the minority Appellants must be a mandatory joint signatory to sale agreements, creating a de facto veto. Both factions appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT, having found that no acts of oppression and mismanagement were committed and that share transfers were valid, can legally confer a veto power upon a minority shareholder by requiring them to be an indispensable joint signatory to corporate land sale deeds; and how shareholder voting regarding corporate asset sales must be conducted in closely disputed entities.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a company tribunal finds that allegations of oppression and mismanagement are unsubstantiated and that shareholding structures are legally valid, it cannot interfere with democratic corporate governance by granting extraordinary veto rights or mandatory co-signatory powers to a minority shareholder over corporate asset dispositions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under the Companies Act, 2013, voting power in general meetings is governed by shareholding percentage rather than head count; asset sales must comply with Section 102 requirements via an explanatory statement and open transparent auction mechanisms rather than conferral of non-statutory individual veto powers. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Shareholder resolutions concerning the liquidation of immovable corporate property must be verified through independent oversight ensuring transparent notice, comprehensive disclosure of valuation, and formal poll voting rather than informal show of hands. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in conferring veto power on the minority faction by requiring them to be joint signatories to sale documents; that condition is deleted, and the matter is remanded to conduct an EOGM under the supervision of an Independent Administrator with voting by poll.
operative_order: Both appeals are disposed of by modifying the NCLT order: the requirement that an Appellant must be a joint signatory to sale agreements or deeds is removed. The matter is remanded to NCLT Hyderabad to appoint an Independent Administrator to convene a fresh Board meeting and EOGM with proper Section 102 notices, conduct a transparent public/newspaper/online auction for corporate properties, and supervise voting by poll, with final orders to follow review of the Administrator's report. No costs.
summary: Om Prakash Avulla (38.46% shareholder) and U.V. Hari Prasada Raju (61.54% shareholder) filed cross-appeals against an NCLT Hyderabad order in CP No. 82/2015. NCLT held that Raju's group did not commit oppression, validated the splitting of 2,000 shares, but ordered an EOGM to sell properties on condition that an Avulla group member be a mandatory signatory to sale deeds. NCLAT held that granting such veto power to a minority faction was improper after rejecting oppression claims. NCLAT removed the joint-signatory requirement and remanded the matter to NCLT Hyderabad to appoint an Independent Administrator to supervise a transparent property auction and conduct EOGM voting strictly by poll.

case_title: Mooldhan Advisory System (P) Ltd. & Ors. vs. Yashdeep Trexim Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 266 of 2019 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 294 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant 1: Mooldhan Advisory System (P) Ltd. & Ors. (Appellants in CA 266/2019); Appellant 2: Juggilal Kamlapat Jute Mills Company Ltd. (Appellant in CA 294/2019); Respondent No. 1: Yashdeep Trexim Pvt. Ltd. (Petitioner in original company petition); Respondent No. 2: Co-respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Transfer, purchase, and alienation of fixed assets and corporate shareholding of the subject company, governed by an interim status quo injunction operating over the company's properties and shareholding structure. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Pending oppression and mismanagement petition CP No. 942/2012; regulatory compliance conflicts with SEBI orders; contested alienation of properties to third-party subsequent purchasers. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP No. 942/2012 filed before CLB Kolkata (transferred to NCLT Kolkata); Respondent No. 1 filed IA No. 222/2017 to implead subsequent purchasers; Appellant 1 filed IA No. 352/2017 to modify the interim status quo injunction to comply with SEBI directions; NCLT passed common disposal order on 24.07.2019; NCLAT decided appeals on 16.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Binding directions issued by SEBI requiring compliance by Mooldhan Advisory Systems; interim injunction orders restraining alterations to fixed assets and share capital; earlier dismissal order in IA No. 223/2017 regarding identical impleadment prayers; absence of any judicial reasoning in the NCLT order addressing the merits of IA No. 352/2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In pending CP No. 942/2012, NCLT Kolkata Bench heard IA No. 222/2017 (impleadment) and IA No. 352/2017 (modification of injunction). Vide order dated 24.07.2019, NCLT disposed of IA No. 222/2017 holding that lis pendens under Sections 52/55 of the Transfer of Property Act applied to subsequent purchasers without impleading them, and simultaneously disposed of IA No. 352/2017 without recording separate reasons. Both appeals followed.
legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal can mechanically dispose of an independent application seeking modification of an interim injunction (to comply with SEBI statutory directives) by merely referencing the disposal of an unrelated impleadment application without recording separate judicial reasons; and whether the doctrine of lis pendens obviates the necessity of impleading subsequent property purchasers in an oppression proceeding.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicatory authority must assign clear, reasoned findings when determining distinct interlocutory prayers; disposing of an independent application for injunction modification sub silentio, merely as a consequence of disposing of an unrelated impleadment plea, constitutes an error of law necessitating remand. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applications seeking modification of status quo orders to enable compliance with regulatory mandates (such as SEBI directives) raise distinct substantive legal questions that cannot be subsumed under general property lis pendens principles governing transfer of assets under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Orders affecting statutory compliance obligations must demonstrate judicial application of mind on the record; where an order disposes of two distinct applications but only provides reasoning applicable to one, the unreasoned portion is legally unsustainable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT assigned zero reasons for dismissing IA No. 352/2017 while correctly applying lis pendens to IA No. 222/2017, justifying setting aside the order regarding IA No. 352/2017 and remanding it for reasoned adjudication.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 266 of 2019 is allowed, the impugned order dated 24.07.2019 to the extent of IA No. 352/2017 is set aside, and the application is remitted to NCLT Kolkata Bench for fresh, reasoned adjudication after hearing parties. Company Appeal (AT) No. 294 of 2019 is dismissed, maintaining the impugned order regarding IA No. 222/2017. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellants appealed against an NCLT Kolkata common order disposing of IA No. 222/2017 (filed by Yashdeep Trexim to implead subsequent purchasers) and IA No. 352/2017 (filed by Mooldhan Advisory to modify an interim injunction to comply with SEBI orders). NCLT held that lis pendens applied to subsequent purchasers and disposed of both applications simultaneously without assigning any reasons for IA No. 352/2017. NCLAT held that the reliefs were entirely distinct and unreasoned dismissal of IA No. 352/2017 was unsustainable. NCLAT set aside the order qua IA No. 352/2017, remitted it to NCLT Kolkata for fresh reasoned adjudication, and dismissed the appeal challenging the impleadment order.

case_title: Sarada Prasad Rath vs. Registrar of Companies, Odisha
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Sarada Prasad Rath (Promoter/Director of struck-off company); Subject Company: Infrastructure/Real Estate Company incorporated on 20.04.2012; Respondent: Registrar of Companies, Odisha (ROC). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development and infrastructure business operated by the struck-off company through a registered partnership firm named 'AML Homes' formed under a Deed of Partnership dated 11.04.2013 entered into with M/s Laxmi Real Infra Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Complete failure to file statutory annual returns and balance sheets with the ROC since incorporation on 20.04.2012; striking off effected under Section 248(1)(c) with dissolution published on 21.06.2017/22.07.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company incorporated on 20.04.2012; partnership deed executed on 11.04.2013; Form STK-1 notice issued under Section 248(1)(c); Form STK-5/5A gazette notification published; name struck off and company dissolved via Form STK-7 gazette notification on 21.06.2017 (published 22.07.2017); NCLT Cuttack Bench dismissed restoration appeal TP No. 68/CTB/2019 on 23.10.2019; NCLAT allowed appeal on 03.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deed of Partnership dated 11.04.2013 between the company and M/s Laxmi Real Infra Pvt. Ltd.; audited financial statements and Auditor's Report of partnership firm 'AML Homes' for the year ending 31.03.2016 showing active ongoing real estate operations; ROC administrative records and Form STK-7 gazette publication. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following striking off, Appellant filed an appeal under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 before NCLT Cuttack Bench (CP No. 02/KB/2018 / TP No. 68/CTB/2019). NCLT rejected the appeal on 23.10.2019 citing failure to file returns, absence of direct employees/stock, and non-filing of income tax returns. Appellant appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether a company whose name has been struck off by the Registrar of Companies under Section 248 for failure to file statutory returns since incorporation is entitled to restoration under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 upon proving that it was carrying on business and in active commercial operation through a partnership firm at the time of strike-off.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, where a company demonstrates that it was actively carrying on business or in operation at the time of its name being struck off—including commercial operations conducted through a valid partnership with another entity—it is just and equitable to order restoration of its name to the register, subject to compliance with statutory filings and payment of compensatory costs. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252 is a remedial provision aimed at affording defaulting companies an opportunity to regularize their legal standing; conducting active business operations via an established partnership firm satisfies the statutory criterion of 'carrying on business or in operation', notwithstanding direct administrative omissions in filing company annual returns. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Partnership deeds and contemporaneous audited financial statements of the operating partnership firm showing active business turnover provide cogent, admissible evidence of ongoing operations sufficient to rebut the presumption of dormancy under Section 248. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The company established active operations through 'AML Homes' as corroborated by the 2016 audit report, rendering NCLT's refusal to restore unjustified; restoration is directed subject to filing overdue returns and paying Rs. 2,50,000 costs.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 355 of 2019 is allowed and the order of NCLT Cuttack Bench dated 23.10.2019 is quashed and set aside. ROC Odisha is directed to restore the company's name to the Register of Companies subject to: (1) payment of Rs. 2,50,000 costs to Union of India through ROC; (2) filing of all overdue annual returns and balance sheets; and (3) payment of statutory fines and penalties, without prejudice to ROC's right to initiate permissible penal actions. No costs in appeal.
summary: Sarada Prasad Rath appealed against an NCLT Cuttack order rejecting an application under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 to restore his real estate company, which was struck off by ROC Odisha on 21.06.2017 under Section 248 for failing to file annual returns since incorporation in 2012. The Appellant established that the company was actively carrying on business in partnership with another company under the firm name 'AML Homes', substantiated by partnership deeds and a 2016 audit report. NCLAT allowed the appeal and directed restoration of the company's name, holding that active operations through a partnership satisfied Section 252, subject to filing all overdue returns, paying applicable fines, and depositing Rs. 2.5 lakhs in costs.

case_title: All India Online Vendors Association vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Informant: All India Online Vendors Association (AIOVA, an association of online marketplace sellers); Respondent No. 1: Competition Commission of India (CCI); Respondent No. 2/OP-1: Flipkart India Private Limited (wholesale B2B trading and distribution entity); Respondent No. 3/OP-2: Flipkart Internet Private Limited (operator of e-commerce marketplace platform 'Flipkart.com'). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Wholesale procurement and sale of books, mobiles, computers, and accessories by OP-1 to selected preferred retail sellers (principally WS Retail Services Pvt. Ltd., formerly owned by founders of OP-2) at deep discounts below cost price, which were then resold at discounted rates on OP-2's marketplace platform Flipkart.com. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Antitrust abuse of dominant position; Assessing Officer's findings recorded in ITAT proceedings established purchases of Rs. 10,335,73,05,882 against discounted sales of Rs. 9,351,75,05,319, yielding a gross trading loss of Rs. 242,14,93,727 (2.52% below cost) aimed at predatory market penetration. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information filed under Section 19(1)(a) forming Case No. 20 of 2018; ITAT Bangalore Bench delivered order in ITA No. 202/Bang/2018 on 25.04.2018; CCI closed proceedings under Section 26(2) on 06.11.2018; NCLAT decided appeal on 04.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Assessment order and findings of fact recorded by the Assessing Officer in ITAT proceedings (ITA No. 202/Bang/2018) documenting deliberate selling at below cost price to create enduring intangible marketing assets and establish market power; sworn statements of Flipkart Senior VP and Finance Controller admitting below-cost discounting strategies; platform listing preferences and preferential inventory sourcing benefiting related entities. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: AIOVA filed information alleging abuse of dominance under Section 4. CCI vide order dated 06.11.2018 closed the case under Section 26(2), defining the relevant market as 'services provided by online marketplace platforms for selling goods in India' and concluding Flipkart lacked dominance and treated sellers objectively. AIOVA appealed under Section 53B.
legal_issues: Whether the Competition Commission of India erred in closing the information under Section 26(2) by restricting its inquiry to Flipkart Internet (OP-2) and ignoring the structural nexus and below-cost wholesale discounting practices between Flipkart India (OP-1) and preferred retailers like WS Retail, and whether the factual findings of predatory pricing recorded by tax authorities establish a prima facie case under Section 4 to direct a Director General investigation under Section 26(1).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: At the stage of forming a prima facie opinion under Section 26(1) of the Competition Act, 2002, the Commission is not required to render a final conclusive finding on liability; if uncontroverted official regulatory records demonstrate a structural nexus between affiliated wholesale and platform entities engaging in below-cost predatory discounting to favor select marketplace sellers, a prima facie case is established warranting a Director General investigation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 19(1)(a) read with Section 26(1) establishes a low evidentiary threshold of 'prima facie opinion' to initiate an investigation; Section 4(2)(a)(ii) expressly covers predatory pricing mechanisms, and the adjudicatory body cannot bifurcate intertwined group entities to disregard wholesale practices that directly distort marketplace competition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Facts and figures documented by statutory assessment authorities illustrating systematic below-cost sales (generating hundreds of crores in gross losses to build market control) constitute credible material to warrant inquiry under the Competition Act, irrespective of whether the tax penalty was subsequently set aside on distinct taxation principles. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Informant successfully demonstrated a prima facie case of abuse of dominance and predatory pricing through the coordinated operations of OP-1 and OP-2, rendering the CCI's summary closure under Section 26(2) erroneous and necessitating remand for a DG investigation.
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 16 of 2019 is allowed. The impugned order of the Competition Commission of India dated 06.11.2018 passed in Case No. 20 of 2018 is set aside, and the matter is remitted back to the CCI with a direction to order the Director General to cause an investigation into the matter under Section 26(1) of the Competition Act, 2002. No costs.
summary: All India Online Vendors Association appealed against a CCI order closing its Section 4 information under Section 26(2) against Flipkart India (OP-1) and Flipkart Internet (OP-2). The Appellant alleged that OP-1 purchased wholesale goods and sold them at deep discounts to select preferred retailers (such as WS Retail) to be resold at predatory rates on OP-2's marketplace, foreclosing independent sellers. NCLAT set aside the closure, holding that tax assessment records and ITAT proceedings documented substantial below-cost pricing designed to capture market share. Holding that a prima facie case was made out, NCLAT remitted the matter to CCI to direct a Director General investigation.

case_title: Peoples International & Services Private Limited & Anr. vs. Alliance Industries Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants: Peoples International & Services Pvt. Ltd., PHG International Pvt. Ltd., Peoples General Hospital Pvt. Ltd., and Suresh Narayan Vijay (Directors/Shareholders of Bhopal-based companies); Respondent No. 1: Alliance Industries Limited (represented by Director Ashok Kumar Khosla, UAE/USA, original Petitioner in CP alleging oppression); Respondent Nos. 2 & 3: Registrar NCLT Ahmedabad Bench and Registrar NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company petitions initiated under the Companies Act, 1956 alleging oppression and mismanagement, rectification of register, and investigation into the affairs of three closely-held companies having their registered offices in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Territorial jurisdiction challenge; no monetary debt metric (procedural contest regarding the competent NCLT Bench to adjudicate pending company petitions originating from the State of Madhya Pradesh). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petitions filed before CLB Mumbai in 2015/2016; transferred to NCLT Ahmedabad under Notification S.O. 1935(E) dated 01.06.2016; Ministry of Corporate Affairs issued Notification S.O. 1216(E) on 08.08.2019/08.03.2019 constituting the Indore Bench and omitting Madhya Pradesh from Ahmedabad; NCLAT stayed proceedings on 20.08.2019; MCA issued clarificatory Notification S.O. 484(E) on 31.01.2020; MP High Court dismissed WP No. 4479-2020 on 24.02.2020; NCLAT disposed of appeals on 17.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MCA Notifications dated 01.06.2016, 08.03.2019, and 31.01.2020 published in the Gazette of India; High Court of Madhya Pradesh judgment dated 24.02.2020 in WP No. 4479-2020 upholding the legal validity of Notification dated 31.01.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants objected before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench against hearing company petitions pertaining to Madhya Pradesh following the 08.03.2019 notification constituting the Indore Bench. When NCLT Ahmedabad scheduled final hearings, Appellants filed appeals under Section 421. During appeal pendency, MCA notified on 31.01.2020 that Ahmedabad Bench shall continue exercising jurisdiction over MP until Indore is operationalized.
legal_issues: Whether, upon the publication of the Central Government Notification dated 08.03.2019 constituting the NCLT Indore Bench, the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench was completely divested of territorial jurisdiction over pending company matters pertaining to the State of Madhya Pradesh, and whether the subsequent Notification dated 31.01.2020 rendered the challenge infructuous.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal challenging the territorial jurisdiction of a judicial bench premised on an earlier government notification becomes entirely infructuous once the competent executive authority issues a subsequent valid statutory notification conferring interim territorial jurisdiction pending the operationalization of a newly constituted bench. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 419(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Central Government possesses the power to constitute benches and define or adjust territorial jurisdictions through official gazette notifications; a notification specifying that jurisdiction over a state shall continue with an existing bench until a new bench is operationalized governs the forum's competence. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a jurisdictional notification has been challenged and upheld by a competent Constitutional Court (High Court), the Appellate Tribunal will not question its validity and must give full legal effect to the gazetted mandate. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: By virtue of Notification S.O. 484(E) dated 31.01.2020, NCLT Ahmedabad Bench retains legal jurisdiction over Madhya Pradesh matters until Indore is functional; hence, the appeals are rendered infructuous and dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) Nos. 227, 228, and 229 of 2019 are dismissed as having become infructuous in view of the Central Government Notification dated 31.01.2020. The interim stay on proceedings before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench is vacated. No costs.
summary: Appellants, involved in oppression disputes regarding Bhopal-based companies, challenged the territorial jurisdiction of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench, arguing that following MCA Notification dated 08.03.2019 constituting the Indore Bench, Ahmedabad lost jurisdiction over Madhya Pradesh matters. During the pendency of the appeal, the MCA issued a fresh Gazette Notification on 31.01.2020 clarifying that the Ahmedabad Bench will continue to exercise jurisdiction over Madhya Pradesh until the Indore Bench is formally operationalized, which was upheld by the MP High Court. NCLAT held that the foundation of the appeals was extinguished, dismissed the appeals as infructuous, and vacated the stay on NCLT Ahmedabad.

case_title: Gourav Kishor Shinde vs. Uday Yashwant Nayak & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Gourav Kishor Shinde (Service Manager Operations, authorized representative of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1: Uday Yashwant Nayak (former Head of Sales & Marketing - Rice Division, Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2: Godawat Consumer Product LLP (Corporate Debtor, represented through IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment contract dated 11.04.2016 appointing Respondent No. 1 as Head of Sales and Marketing on an annual remuneration of Rs. 36,00,000, containing clauses requiring a 60-day resignation notice period or payment of 3 months' basic pay as liquidated damages, alongside compliance with Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) dated 11.01.2017 mandating field NOCs from distributors prior to full and final settlement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed total outstanding employment dues of Rs. 9,05,000 (salary for March 2017 of Rs. 2,50,000, salary for April 2017 of Rs. 1,25,000, annual performance incentive of Rs. 6,00,000, minus short notice period deduction of Rs. 70,000). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resignation tendered by email on 11.03.2017; conditional acceptance email issued by Corporate Debtor on 14.03.2017; employee stopped working on 15.04.2017 after serving 1 month 5 days; first Section 8 demand notice issued on 26.03.2018 (replied with dispute on 24.04.2018 and abandoned); second Section 8 demand notice issued on 12.11.2018; Corporate Debtor replied raising disputes on 23.11.2018; Section 9 petition filed in 2018; NCLT passed oral admission on 10.10.2019 (reasoned order uploaded 18.10.2019); NCLAT decided appeal on 16.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appointment letter dated 11.04.2016; SOP email dated 11.01.2017; resignation email and prompt reply dated 11.03.2017 and 14.03.2017 conditioning relief upon clearing distributor outstandings and handovers; trail emails dated 15.04.2017 insisting on full 60-day service and client NOCs; Leave Policy barring adjustment of leave against notice period; Reply to Section 8 notice dated 24.04.2018 and 23.11.2018 detailing financial losses and failure to hand over charge. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP 4538 (IB)/MB/2018 under Section 9 of the IBC. NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the application vide a two-line order on 10.10.2019 (reasoned judgment on 18.10.2019) rejecting the Corporate Debtor's defense as spurious under Mobilox Innovations. Corporate Debtor appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether unresolved employment disputes regarding failure to complete a mandatory 60-day notice period, failure to obtain client/distributor clearances under company SOP, and entitlement to unassessed annual performance incentives constitute a bona fide 'pre-existing dispute' under the Mobilox Innovations standard to warrant rejection of a Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Genuine, substantiated employer-employee service disputes concerning contractual notice period shortfalls, handover of operational charge, and non-satisfaction of conditions precedent for incentive pay constitute pre-existing disputes that bar the admission of a Section 9 IBC application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 proceedings are summary in nature and cannot be utilized as a debt recovery mechanism to adjudicate contentious service and employment contract disputes; where contemporaneous pre-notice correspondence establishes genuine friction regarding breach of service conditions, the defense is not a sham or spurious claim under Mobilox. Furthermore, Adjudicating Authorities must refrain from issuing cryptic admission orders without simultaneous reasoned determinations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Email exchanges occurring contemporaneous with the employee's resignation establishing that relieving was expressly conditional upon departmental clearances, along with earlier dispute replies under Section 8, demonstrate a plausible, bona fide controversy. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The record proved substantial pre-existing service disputes existing long before the Section 8 notice was issued, rendering the Section 9 admission improper and mandating dismissal of the insolvency petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1107 of 2019 is allowed. The impugned order dated 10.10.2019 (and 18.10.2019) is quashed and set aside, and the Section 9 application is dismissed. All actions taken by the IRP are quashed, and the Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP to function under its Board. The Adjudicating Authority shall determine CIRP costs/fees to be paid by the Operational Creditor. No costs.
summary: Corporate Debtor Godawat Consumer Product LLP appealed an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 9 IBC petition filed by its former Head of Sales, Uday Yashwant Nayak, for alleged salary and incentive arrears of Rs. 9.05 lakhs. The Corporate Debtor demonstrated that the employee resigned abruptly, served only 35 days of a mandatory 60-day notice period, failed to obtain distributor NOCs required under company SOP, and claimed unverified incentives. NCLAT allowed the appeal and quashed CIRP, holding that these issues represented genuine, pre-existing service disputes under the Mobilox doctrine, precluding insolvency resolution under Section 9.

case_title: Elaine Info Solutions Pvt. Ltd. vs. J & A Avenues India Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 210 of 2019 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 246 of 2019 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 258 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant in CA 210/2019: Elaine Info Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (Purchaser of subject property); Appellant in CA 246/2019: V. Lakshmi Chenchu Venkata Satya Siva Prasad Satya (Director/50% shareholder of Corporate Debtor); Appellants in CA 258/2019: M/s J&A Avenues India Pvt. Ltd. (Company) and Mrs. Vishnumolaka Govardhanamma (82-year-old mother, Director/50% shareholder); Respondent No. 4: Sub-Registrar Sangareddy. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purported sale and transfer of corporate agricultural land measuring Acres 9-18 Guntas (correctly Acres 9-28 Guntas) owned by J&A Avenues India Pvt. Ltd. to Elaine Info Solutions Pvt. Ltd. vide Registered Sale Deed No. 15747/2015 dated 04.09.2015 for a stated consideration of Rs. 4,36,50,000, alongside an alleged receipt of Rs. 7,91,00,000 by Prasad Satya from one Y. Naga Satish. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression, mismanagement, and fraudulent alienation of corporate immovable property; NCLT directed cancellation of the registered sale deed, restoration of land title, refund of Rs. 4,36,50,000 with 8% interest by the company to Elaine Info Solutions, refund of Rs. 7,91,00,000 with 8% interest to Y. Naga Satish, and debarred Prasad Satya from directorship for 5 years. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Purported Board Resolution fabricated on 01.08.2015; registered sale deed executed on 04.09.2015; Annual Return filed on 02.09.2016; CP No. 574/241/HDB/2018 filed under Section 241 in 2018 within one month of discovering fraud; NCLT Hyderabad passed final order on 02.08.2019; NCLAT decided appeals on 18.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Annual return of the company filed on 02.09.2016 proving no Board Meeting ever took place on 01.08.2015; balance sheet and profit & loss account for FY 2015-16 containing no entry of land sale or proceeds; lack of due diligence by purchaser who acted solely on a certified copy without inspecting original board minutes; testimony of the 82-year-old co-director establishing complete lack of notice or knowledge of the transaction. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Co-director Govardhanamma filed CP No. 574/241/HDB/2018 before NCLT Hyderabad under Section 241 alleging fraud and oppression. NCLT declared the Board Resolution dated 01.08.2015 and Sale Deed dated 04.09.2015 null and void, ordered debarment of Prasad Satya for 5 years, ordered refunds of consideration with 8% interest, and directed restoration of land title. Three separate appeals were preferred under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether the alienation of corporate immovable property executed by a director on the strength of a forged board resolution without board convening, consideration accounting, or shareholder approval constitutes an act of oppression and mismanagement warranting cancellation of the registered sale deed and debarment under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013; and whether the petition is saved from the bar of limitation under Section 17(1)(b) of the Limitation Act, 1963 due to fraudulent concealment.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A conveyance of corporate immovable property executed pursuant to a fabricated board resolution without the authority of the board of directors is void ab initio; where the fraud is concealed through falsification of statutory financial statements, the limitation period to challenge the fraudulent transaction commences only from the date of actual discovery of the fraud under Section 17(1)(b) of the Limitation Act, 1963. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 241 and 242 empower the Tribunal to grant comprehensive relief against fraudulent property alienation, including setting aside void conveyances, directing rectification with registration authorities, and disqualifying delinquent directors; a third-party purchaser who relies on a certified board resolution copy without conducting due diligence cannot claim bona fide purchaser protection against corporate fraud. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Statutory filings with the Registrar of Companies (Annual Returns) proving that no board meeting was held on the purported date, coupled with the absence of transaction entries in audited financial statements, conclusively establish fraud and lack of corporate authorization. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The sale was unauthorized and fraudulent, discovered within limitation under Section 17, justifying the cancellation of the deed, debarment of the delinquent director, and restoration of corporate ownership.
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) Nos. 210, 246, and 258 of 2019 are dismissed, and the impugned order dated 02.08.2019 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench in CP No. 574/241/HDB/2018 is upheld in its entirety. No order as to costs.
summary: Three cross-appeals were filed challenging an NCLT Hyderabad order in an oppression and mismanagement petition regarding J&A Avenues India Pvt. Ltd. Director Prasad Satya sold 9+ acres of corporate land to Elaine Info Solutions for Rs. 4.36 crores using a forged board resolution dated 01.08.2015, omitting the sale from corporate financial records. NCLT declared the sale deed void, cancelled the registration, ordered refund of monies, and debarred the director for 5 years. NCLAT affirmed the order, holding that under Section 17(1)(b) of the Limitation Act, limitation ran from the discovery of the concealed fraud. As statutory annual returns confirmed no board meeting ever occurred and the buyer failed to exercise due diligence, the alienation was void ab initio.

case_title: Living Consumer Products Private Limited vs. Play Games 24x7 Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Applicant: Living Consumer Products Private Limited (Operational Creditor, digital marketing and advertising service provider); Respondent: Play Games 24x7 Private Limited (Corporate Debtor, online gaming portal operator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Advertising Agreement dated 09.07.2018 for digital marketing campaigns via SMS, Facebook, and Google to generate user marketing leads for the Corporate Debtor's gaming platform, under representations and warranties in Clause 4(a) to diligently protect the Corporate Debtor's interests. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed unpaid operational debt of Rs. 6,35,13,977 under an invoice dated 28.12.2018 for advertising services rendered between 01.12.2018 and 15.12.2018 (after 54 earlier invoices had been cleared). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Advertising Agreement executed on 09.07.2018; Corporate Debtor issued campaign pause instruction on 15.12.2018; disputed invoice issued on 28.12.2018; Deloitte forensic investigation report completed in March 2019; Corporate Debtor issued legal notice on 23.03.2019 suspending services and payments; Operational Creditor replied to legal notice; Operational Creditor issued Section 8 demand notice on 05.04.2019; Corporate Debtor replied within 10 days on 15.04.2019; NCLT rejected Section 9 petition on 14.10.2019; NCLAT dismissed appeal on 02.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's legal notice dated 23.03.2019 alleging bribery (INR 6,04,346 paid in October 2017 to Chief Marketing Officer Sachin Uppal) and unauthorized use of brand keywords; forensic investigation report by Deloitte Touche (March 2019) revealing improper keyword use and geo-location data manipulation to inflate lead charges; email dated 15.12.2018 ordering immediate suspension of campaigns. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP (IB) No. 1775/NCLT/MB/2019 under Section 9 of the IBC. NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected the petition on 14.10.2019 holding that the legal notice dated 23.03.2019 and forensic audit disclosed a genuine pre-existing dispute under the Mobilox Innovations doctrine. Operational Creditor appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether a formal legal notice served prior to the Section 8 demand notice, which suspends contractual payments based on an independent forensic investigation report revealing employee collusion, commercial bribery, and fraudulent data inflation, establishes a genuine pre-existing dispute under Section 8 and Section 9 of the IBC to preclude insolvency admission.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Section 9 petition under the IBC cannot be admitted where the Corporate Debtor, prior to the receipt of the Section 8 statutory demand notice, has issued a substantiated legal notice suspending payments based on an independent forensic investigation detailing contractual breach, fraud, and commercial malpractice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under the Mobilox Innovations doctrine, the Adjudicating Authority in Section 9 proceedings is confined to examining whether a plausible, non-spurious dispute existed prior to the demand notice; the summary jurisdiction under the IBC does not extend to conducting an in-depth evidentiary trial to evaluate contested allegations of data manipulation and bribery. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A pre-demand legal notice supported by a comprehensive forensic investigation report prepared by an independent auditing firm proves that the dispute is not a spurious afterthought contrived merely to evade debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the legal notice dated 23.03.2019 was issued prior to the Section 8 demand notice of 05.04.2019 and documented serious breaches of warranty and inflated invoicing, a valid pre-existing dispute existed, requiring dismissal of the Section 9 application and appeal.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1436 of 2019 is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 14.10.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in CP (IB) No. 1775/NCLT/MB/2019.
summary: Living Consumer Products Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting its Section 9 IBC application against online gaming operator Play Games 24x7 Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid advertising invoices of Rs. 6.35 crores. The Corporate Debtor demonstrated that prior to the Section 8 demand notice, it had issued a legal notice suspending payments based on a Deloitte forensic investigation that uncovered payments/bribery to its Chief Marketing Officer, unauthorized keyword usage, and geo-location data manipulation to inflate fees. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the pre-demand notice and forensic findings established a bona fide pre-existing dispute under the Mobilox standard that could not be adjudicated in summary IBC proceedings.

case_title: George Vinci Thomas vs. Capedge Consulting Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is M/s Capedge Consulting Pvt. Ltd.; Corporate Debtor is M/s India Techs Private Limited; Appellant is George Vinci Thomas, Managing Director of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor engaged Operational Creditor in November 2015 to render consultancy services to improve productivity by restructuring financial, administrative, and operational systems across four consultancy agreements, with professional fees structured under an MOU dated 15.11.2015 as a combination of a fixed monthly retainer of Rs. 2 Lakhs and success-based fees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 1,71,74,366/- arising from services rendered between 01.03.2013 and 03.02.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice under Section 8 of IBC was issued on 11.02.2019, to which no reply was delivered by the Corporate Debtor. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor relied on email correspondences, specifically an email dated 04.06.2018 proposing amicable settlement and return of bounced cheques, an email dated 21.01.2018 seeking reports on project progress and asset sales, and Section 138 NI Act criminal proceedings involving sister concerns (M/s Telsa Marketing Pvt. Ltd., M/s Capedge Energy Pvt. Ltd., and M/s Capedge Metals & Minerals Pvt. Ltd.). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP (TIBA/14/KOB/19) before NCLT Kochi Bench under Section 9; the Adjudicating Authority admitted the application on 25.10.2019 holding that communications merely requested information and did not demonstrate a pre-existing dispute regarding debt or quality of services.
legal_issues: Whether internal inquiries or requests for further information/reports on services rendered constitute a valid 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 9 of the IBC, and whether collateral disputes/litigation involving sister concerns can serve as a ground to establish a dispute between the primary operational parties.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Mere demands for operational reports, requests for informational clarification regarding invoices, or collateral disputes among affiliated corporate entities do not constitute a bona fide pre-existing dispute regarding operational debt or service deficiency under the Code. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 requires a demonstrable dispute touching upon the existence of the debt or the quality of goods/services; vague references to settlement overtures or unrelated commercial disputes between directors' sister entities fail to fulfill the statutory threshold of a 'dispute'. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority must evaluate whether the documentary record reveals an actual challenge to the quality of services or enforceability of debt prior to the demand notice, rather than vague queries or spurious, hypothetical controversies. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor failed to show any dispute concerning the quality of consultancy services rendered, particularly regarding the unpaid monthly retainer components which independently crossed the statutory threshold, warranting admission under Section 9.
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal, upholding the order dated 25.10.2019 passed by NCLT Kochi Bench admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP. No order as to costs.
summary: George Vinci Thomas, Managing Director of Corporate Debtor M/s India Techs Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Kochi Bench order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Operational Creditor M/s Capedge Consulting Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid consultancy dues of Rs. 1,71,74,366/-. The Appellant contended that a pre-existing dispute existed, citing an email requesting progress reports and separate Section 138 NI Act proceedings involving sister companies. The NCLAT held that merely requesting progress reports or clarification of services does not equate to a dispute regarding debt or service quality. Holding that undisputed fixed retainer fees remained in default, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal without costs.

case_title: Geopetrol International Inc. vs. JEKPL Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 410 of 2020 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 411 of 2020
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Geopetrol International Inc. (consortium partner/participating interest holder); Corporate Debtor is JEKPL Private Limited (formerly Enpro India Limited); Respondent No. 1 is JEKPL Pvt. Ltd. and Successful Resolution Applicant is Atyant Capital India Fund-I. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Participating interest in a Production Sharing Contract and Joint Operating Agreement dated 16.06.1995 for exploration of Kharsang Oil Field with Oil India Ltd (40%), Appellant (25%), Corporate Debtor (25%), and Geoenpro Petroleum Ltd (10%), under which Appellant claimed a first charge and pre-emptive right under Article 12.3 over Corporate Debtor's 25% share. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; CIRP had been initiated in 2017 against the Corporate Debtor, and the appeal arose from resolution plan approval. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan originally approved on 15.12.2017, re-approved after litigation on 17.01.2020, and modified via corrective order on 04.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Production Sharing Contract, Joint Operating Agreement dated 16.06.1995, and regulatory framework under the Oil Fields (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948 and Petroleum and Natural Gas Rules, 1959. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench approved the resolution plan submitted by Atyant Capital India Fund-I on 17.01.2020, followed by a corrigendum and exclusion order on 04.02.2020; Appellant filed appeals challenging the approval orders on the premise of its contractual pre-emptive rights.
legal_issues: Whether a non-creditor third-party participating interest holder under a production sharing contract has standing to challenge the approval of a resolution plan under Section 61(3) of the IBC without establishing any of the statutorily enumerated grounds.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal challenging an order approving a resolution plan under Section 31 can strictly be maintained only within the explicit, exhaustive grounds prescribed under Section 61(3) of the Code, and an entity that is not a creditor under Section 3(10) cannot derail an approved plan on collateral contractual claims. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(3) sets out an exhaustive threshold for challenging an approved plan; a contractual claim of pre-emptive right or priority charge not submitted as a creditor claim under Section 3(10) does not satisfy any condition under Section 61(3)(i) to (v). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To sustain an appeal under Section 61(3), the record must substantiate a material irregularity by the Resolution Professional, a contravention of law, non-compliance with IBBI criteria, or statutory payment priority violations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant failed to establish any violation falling under Section 61(3), rendering the appeals devoid of merit.
operative_order: Both appeals (Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 410 and 411 of 2020) were dismissed for lack of merit. Plan approval upheld.
summary: Appellant Geopetrol International Inc. challenged the NCLT Allahabad Bench order dated 04.02.2020 approving the resolution plan of Atyant Capital India Fund-I for Corporate Debtor JEKPL Pvt. Ltd. Appellant argued that it held a 25% participating interest and pre-emptive rights over the Corporate Debtor's asset under a Joint Operating Agreement. The NCLAT observed that the Appellant had never filed a claim as a financial, operational, secured, or unsecured creditor during the CIRP and did not qualify as a creditor under Section 3(10). Concluding that the challenge failed to meet any of the exhaustive grounds set out under Section 61(3) of the IBC, the NCLAT dismissed both appeals.

case_title: Prokash Datta & Ors. vs. Ikramul Majid & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Prokash Datta, Rishikesh Datta, and Krishna Datta (promoters, directors, and 66.90% majority shareholders); Respondents No. 1 and 2 are Ikramul Majid and Richard Andrew Willian Leitch (petitioning shareholders); Respondent No. 3 is Allahabad Bank; Respondent No. 4 is M/s Cleanopolis Energy System India Pvt. Ltd. (the Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants acted as promoters and full-time executive directors for over seven years, extending unsecured interest-free loans of approximately Rs. 2.4 Crores to Respondent No. 4. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Allegations of total operational shutdown of plant and machinery and siphoning of corporate funds for personal use by the Appellants. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition filed under Sections 241, 242, and 244 in October 2019; interim order passed by NCLT on 03.02.2020; matter listed for final hearing before NCLT on 26.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT order sheets dated 08.11.2019, 18.11.2019, 03.12.2019, 06.12.2019, and 17.12.2019 establishing deliberate non-appearance and dismissal of the Appellants' recall applications for non-prosecution. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents No. 1 and 2 filed CP No. 15/241/242/GB/2019 before NCLT Guwahati Bench; on 03.02.2020, NCLT appointed a Special Officer to take over possession of company records and run the company with the help of Respondents and Allahabad Bank, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT acted within its jurisdiction under Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 by appointing an independent Special Officer to take custody of corporate records and manage company operations where promoters/directors failed to defend proceedings diligently.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal possesses wide statutory discretion under Section 242(4) to make any interim order it deems just and equitable for regulating the conduct of a company's affairs to prevent prejudice to the company and its stakeholders. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(4) empowers the Adjudicating Authority to impose interim regulatory frameworks; appointing a Special Officer to oversee operations with guidance from stakeholders does not constitute an unlawful transfer of corporate ownership or control to the rival shareholders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where procedural order sheets reveal a systematic failure by the management to defend allegations of oppression and mismanagement with due diligence, interim intervention is justified to preserve assets. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The impugned order of the NCLT was well within its equitable jurisdiction under Section 242(4) to protect the company from standing idle and deteriorating prior to final adjudication.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed without costs, leaving the interim order intact and directing the NCLT to make all endeavors to decide the petition on merits expeditiously. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellants, holding a 66.90% majority shareholding in M/s Cleanopolis Energy System India Pvt. Ltd., challenged an interim order of NCLT Guwahati Bench appointing a Special Officer to take possession of records and operate the company in an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242. Appellants argued they were ousted without a prima facie finding. The NCLAT reviewed the order sheets revealing that Appellants repeatedly failed to appear and neglected the proceedings while plant operations remained shuttered. Concluding that the NCLT's interim order was just, equitable, and properly exercised under Section 242(4) to regulate corporate affairs, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Prayag Polytech Private Limited vs. Iworld Digital Solution Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor/Appellant is Prayag Polytech Private Limited; Corporate Debtor/Respondent is Iworld Digital Solution Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant claimed disbursements of Rs. 3,51,00,000/- made between 20.08.2015 and 01.03.2016 under an alleged oral loan agreement with interest payments and TDS deductions; Respondent relied upon a written Loan Agreement dated 19.12.2014 and a subsequent tripartite MOU dated 03.04.2017 treating the lender as an investor for Compulsorily Convertible Debentures (CCDs) requiring further investment of Rs. 3,25,00,000/- within 18 months. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan recall notice claimed default of Rs. 3,51,00,000/- principal plus Rs. 1,85,12,378/- interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial Creditor issued loan recall notice on 02.01.2019; Corporate Debtor replied on 18.01.2019 invoking dispute resolution and referral to arbitration under the MOU. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements reflecting disbursement and TDS deductions produced by Appellant; written Loan Agreement dated 19.12.2014, MOU dated 03.04.2017 containing a forfeiture clause (Clause 1.4) for failure to complete debenture investments, and pending inter-director disputes under the Companies Act between Appellant's promoters. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application (C.P. No. IB-189/(ND)/2019) filed by Appellant was rejected by NCLT New Delhi Bench-III on 16.05.2019, finding that debt was not clearly admitted and subject to contractual forfeiture/arbitration.
legal_issues: Whether an applicant under Section 7 of the IBC can establish an admitted and enforceable financial debt in default when disbursals are asserted under an oral agreement but contradicted by written agreements providing for debenture conversion, damages, and forfeiture.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In summary proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC, the applicant must establish the existence of a clear, legally admitted, and presently enforceable financial debt that has fallen into default; complex disputed oral claims unsupported by board resolutions or security cannot override contradictory written contracts. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 requires the Adjudicating Authority to be satisfied that a default has occurred on an undisputed or clearly enforceable financial debt; where documents assert forfeiture rights and subject the funding to debenture agreements referred to arbitration, default cannot be summarily determined. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Merely claiming a document executed by an authorized director is forged or unconscionable without prima facie proof is insufficient to discard written contracts in summary insolvency proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Financial Creditor failed to prove that the claimed sum was an admitted and enforceable debt in default, justifying dismissal of the Section 7 petition.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed without prejudice to the rights of the parties to pursue claims before an Arbitrator or other appropriate forum. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Prayag Polytech Pvt. Ltd. challenged the NCLT New Delhi Bench-III order rejecting its Section 7 IBC application against Respondent Iworld Digital Solution Pvt. Ltd. for default of Rs. 3.51 Crores. Appellant asserted the amounts were lent under an oral arrangement evidenced by bank disbursements and TDS deductions. The Respondent contended the funds were governed by a Loan Agreement and subsequent MOU converting the debt into Compulsorily Convertible Debentures, which provided for forfeiture due to breach and referral to arbitration. The NCLAT held that substantial corporate loans without security or board resolutions were improbable, that written contracts could not be discarded as forged without evidence, and that no admitted, enforceable debt in default was proven. Appeal dismissed.

case_title: Chandralekha Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (through Gajendra Parihar) vs. Devi Industrial Engineers & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is M/s Devi Industrial Engineers; Corporate Debtor is M/s Chandralekha Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (represented by Director Gajendra Parihar); Respondent No. 2 is the Interim Resolution Professional Deepak Kumar Agarwal. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor issued a work order dated 09.09.2017 for hiring a 36-meter Boom Pump with accessories at Rs. 4,00,000/- per month with a minimum guaranteed 280 flexi working hours per month (27 working days) along with an operator and helper for its project at Godrej Golf Link, Greater Noida. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed an outstanding operational debt of Rs. 11,93,375/- along with interest, based on invoices dated 01.10.2017, 31.10.2017, and 29.09.2018 (after accounting for an advance payment of Rs. 1,96,000/-), while Corporate Debtor argued that a revised settlement invoice of Rs. 1,56,076/- had been issued on 05.03.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice under Section 8 of the IBC was issued on 01.11.2018 claiming Rs. 11,93,375/-; Corporate Debtor responded via WhatsApp on 30.11.2018 disputing aspects of the claim while mentioning Rs. 6,35,000/-; the Section 9 petition was filed in February 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor produced emails dated 31.10.2017, 25.12.2017, 26.12.2017, and 07.01.2018 complaining about frequent pump breakdowns, unilateral removal of machinery for a week, and deficient service causing project delays; notice of termination dated 07.01.2018; rejected/returned third invoice dated 29.09.2018 bearing endorsement 'rejected as service was not provided'; and Operational Creditor's conciliation request to the Construction Equipment Rental Forum (CERA) dated 09.01.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP No. IB-285/ND/2019 before NCLT New Delhi (Court No. IV); the Adjudicating Authority admitted the application on 08.11.2019 holding that CERA had decided against the debtor and WhatsApp messages admitted partial debt.
legal_issues: Whether pre-existing contemporaneous communications demonstrating persistent machine breakdowns, deficient services, contract termination, and bilateral billing disputes establish a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 8 and 9 of the IBC to preclude admission of an insolvency petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where documentary evidence demonstrates that genuine complaints regarding deficiency of goods/services and correctness of invoices were raised contemporaneously prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice, a pre-existing dispute exists and an application under Section 9 cannot be admitted. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the test of Mobilox Innovations, Section 9(5)(ii)(d) mandates rejection of an application if a dispute exists in fact and is not spurious, hypothetical, or illusory; disputes over equipment breakdowns and non-performance prior to statutory notice constitute such a pre-existing dispute. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal must review whether email and message exchanges prior to the Section 8 demand notice reveal active contestation of invoice amounts and service quality, without determining the final merits or likelihood of success of the underlying commercial claims. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in admitting the Section 9 application because contemporaneous emails dated October 2017 to January 2018 and recourse to industry mediation clearly proved an active pre-existing dispute regarding service deficiency and billing.
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal, set aside the NCLT order dated 08.11.2019, and released the Corporate Debtor from the rigors of CIRP. The IRP was directed to restore management and records to the promoters, and the matter was remitted to the NCLT to determine IRP fees and costs to be borne exclusively by the Operational Creditor. No order as to costs.
summary: Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Chandralekha Constructions Pvt. Ltd. appealed the NCLT New Delhi Bench order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Operational Creditor M/s Devi Industrial Engineers for Rs. 11,93,375/- concerning boom pump rental services.
