The Appellant proved that right from the inception of work in late 2017, multiple emails were exchanged documenting equipment breakdowns, unannounced removal of machinery, deficient services, invoice rejections, and contract termination, culminating in an approach to CERA for conciliation. The NCLAT held that the record clearly substantiated a bona fide pre-existing dispute under the principles of Mobilox Innovations, rendering the Section 9 application inadmissible. The impugned admission order was set aside and CIRP was terminated.

case_title: Vishal Vijay Kalantri vs. DBM Geotechnics & Constructions Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 139 of 2018, 697 of 2019, 698 of 2019 and 722 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is DBM Geotechnics and Constructions Pvt. Ltd.; Corporate Debtor is Dighi Port Limited; Appellant is Vishal Vijay Kalantri (Promoter/Director/Shareholder); Resolution Applicants are Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited (APSEZL), Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT), and Veritas Consortium. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Construction and geotechnical operational contracts relating to port development works executed by the Operational Creditor for Corporate Debtor's Dighi Port project. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 9 application admitted on operational debt default, with total creditor claims during CIRP subsequently accumulating to approximately Rs. 3,000 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 25.03.2018; JNPT plan initially approved on 08.05.2019 but delayed due to modification queries; Section 12A withdrawal settlement proposal put to vote and rejected by 99.68% voting share of CoC on 17.09.2019; revised APSEZL plan approved by 99.68% voting share of CoC on 19.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Voting sheets of the 22nd CoC meeting confirming 99.68% rejection of the Section 12A promoter settlement proposal and 99.68% approval of APSEZL's resolution plan; failure of promoter to furnish requisite 20% EMD, Form FA, and bank guarantee under Regulation 30A. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted Section 9 application on 25.03.2018; Appellant challenged admission claiming pre-existing dispute but repeatedly sought adjournments for settlement/Section 12A exit; subsequent appeals arose from JNPT plan approval extensions, during which CoC voted to approve APSEZL's plan.
legal_issues: Whether an Appellate Tribunal should reopen and adjudicate an initial Section 9 admission order on the ground of an alleged pre-existing dispute after nearly two years of CIRP have elapsed, multiple Section 12A promoter settlement proposals have been rejected, and the Committee of Creditors has approved a compliant resolution plan by an overwhelming majority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not overturn a CIRP admission order on the ground of an alleged pre-existing dispute where significant time has elapsed, admitted defaults exist across creditors, Section 12A proposals have failed, and the CoC has approved a resolution plan in exercise of its commercial wisdom. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12A mandates a 90% voting threshold by the CoC, and courts cannot compel acceptance of an unapproved promoter proposal; once the CoC exercises its commercial wisdom under Section 30(4) to approve a resolution plan, adjudicating authorities are bound by the principles of Essar Steel not to interfere in business determinations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Quashing an admission order when admitted debt default of massive scale (Rs. 3000 Crores) exists would only trigger immediate fresh insolvency petitions and jeopardize public concession agreements; commercial finality governs. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 12A proposal having been decisively rejected and APSEZL's compliant resolution plan having been approved by 99.68% voting share, reopening the Section 9 admission order on a pre-existing dispute plea is unwarranted.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 139 of 2018 and 722 of 2019 were dismissed; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 697 and 698 of 2019 were declared infructuous. The matter was remitted to the NCLT Mumbai Bench to pass appropriate orders under Section 31 in accordance with law.
summary: Vishal Vijay Kalantri, promoter of Dighi Port Ltd., appealed the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order dated 25.03.2018 admitting a Section 9 application filed by DBM Geotechnics, alleging a pre-existing dispute while repeatedly seeking time to negotiate a settlement under Section 12A. Over two years, total claims reached Rs. 3,000 Crores. The CoC rejected Kalantri's Section 12A settlement proposal by a 99.68% voting share due to non-compliance and lack of EMD, and subsequently approved the resolution plan of APSEZL by 99.68%. Refusing to reopen the pre-existing dispute plea, the NCLAT held that setting aside the process would merely prompt fresh proceedings, jeopardize port concessions, and infringe upon the CoC's commercial wisdom under Essar Steel. The admission order was upheld and the appeals were dismissed/disposed of.

case_title: Pramod Kumar vs. Pawan Hans Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Pramod Kumar (Aircraft Technician and employee); Respondent No. 1 is Pawan Hans Ltd. (a Government Company/PSU); Respondent No. 2 is Krishan Kumar (Foreman/Painter); Respondents No. 3 to 15 are senior officers, joint general managers, and retired executives of Pawan Hans Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment relationship and internal corporate administration regarding standard operating procedures for the maintenance and repair of helicopters and sea planes, including the allocation of overtime compensation, travel allowances, and daily allowances to ground personnel. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant alleged an estimated loss of Rs. 50 Lakhs to the company and highlighted overtime disbursements of Rs. 19,20,000/- paid to Respondent No. 2 between October 2009 and May 2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition filed under Section 213(b)(ii) in 2018; dismissed by NCLT New Delhi Bench on 08.05.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Pay slips of Respondent No. 2 from 2009 to 2018 showing overtime payments; inquiry report conducted under the direction of the Ministry of Civil Aviation by Sh. B.C. Behra; internal and external audit reports of Respondent No. 1 showing no audit objections or unauthorized payments. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP No. 210/213(b)(ii)/ND/2018 before NCLT New Delhi Bench alleging fraudulent mismanagement and seeking investigation by an Inspector; NCLT dismissed the petition with Rs. 50,000/- costs payable to the Prime Minister's Relief Fund, finding the petition to be a mala fide vendetta by a disgruntled employee.
legal_issues: Whether an individual employee can maintain an application under Section 213(b)(ii) of the Companies Act, 2013 to order an investigation into a government company's affairs based on administrative decisions regarding overtime payments and deployment of maintenance staff.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An investigation under Section 213(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be initiated on the speculative allegations of a disgruntled employee challenging routine managerial, personnel, or administrative decisions, in the absence of objective material establishing prima facie fraud, misfeasance, or misconduct. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 213(b) conditions the exercise of power on the subjective 'satisfaction' of the Tribunal that circumstances suggest fraudulent formation, management, or misconduct towards the company or its members; internal operational decisions in compliance with service rules do not constitute such circumstances. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To trigger a statutory corporate investigation, the petitioner must place cogent, unimpeachable evidence demonstrating fraudulent loss or siphoning; unchallenged audited financial statements and internal approvals negate allegations of financial misfeasance. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Inclusion of qualified helpers in maintenance teams and payment of overtime in the normal course of corporate administration does not amount to defrauding creditors, members, or siphoning funds.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed at the admission stage. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Pramod Kumar, an aircraft technician employed with PSU Pawan Hans Ltd., challenged the NCLT New Delhi Bench's order dismissing his application under Section 213(b)(ii) of the Companies Act, 2013, which sought an investigation into alleged fraudulent payments of Rs. 19.20 Lakhs in overtime and travel allowances to a foreman painter (Respondent No. 2). The NCLT had dismissed the petition with Rs. 50,000/- costs, deeming it a frivolous vendetta. The NCLAT affirmed that deployment of personnel and overtime payments in normal corporate operations, verified by clean audit reports, are purely administrative decisions and do not satisfy the statutory threshold of fraud or misfeasance required under Section 213. Appeal dismissed at admission.

case_title: Sangeeta Goel vs. Roidec India Chemicals Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Sangeeta Goel; Corporate Debtor is Roidec India Chemicals Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Rendering of professional patent and legal consulting services by the Operational Creditor (through M/s Sim and San) to the Corporate Debtor between 09.09.2013 and 03.01.2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 63,29,169/- (with an alleged ledger acknowledgment on 10.03.2017 of Rs. 53,83,299/- after TDS). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form 4 Demand Notice issued on 20.03.2019 and served on 23.03.2019; Corporate Debtor replied via email on 22.03.2019 and issued an additional detailed reply on 17.04.2019; Section 9 petition filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated 22.03.2019 alleging extensive delays by the creditor causing cancellation/rejection of international patent filings; emails dated 19.01.2018 and 09.04.2018 demonstrating that nearly a year prior to the demand notice, the Corporate Debtor contested invoices for FY 2016-17 and 2017-18 stating accounts were settled with a director and no further services were authorized or required; lack of Section 9(3)(b) affidavit. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI dismissed the Section 9 application (CP (IB)-1078(ND)/2019) on 19.11.2019 on grounds of pre-existing dispute and failure to furnish a Section 9(3)(b) affidavit.
legal_issues: Whether prior email communications contesting the validity of invoices and repudiating the requirement of services establish a pre-existing dispute under Section 9, and whether the omission of a Section 9(3)(b) affidavit is fatal where the Corporate Debtor has issued a timely reply notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Section 9 IBC application must be dismissed where the corporate debtor establishes that it raised genuine objections regarding service entitlement, invoice legitimacy, or service quality prior to the receipt of the statutory demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(3)(b) requiring an affidavit stating no notice of dispute has been received is inapplicable where the debtor has actively delivered a reply to the demand notice raising a dispute, in accordance with Macquarie Bank. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Mobilox Innovations, the adjudicating authority must verify whether the corporate debtor's defense presents a plausible contention of dispute supported by contemporaneous pre-notice communications, rather than a moonshine or afterthought defense. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The emails dated January and April 2018, sent approximately one year prior to the demand notice, established an undisputed, genuine pre-existing dispute regarding the rendering of services and validity of invoices, justifying dismissal under Section 9(5)(ii)(d).
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal upheld the order of NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI dated 19.11.2019 and dismissed the appeal. No order as to costs.
summary: Operational Creditor Sangeeta Goel appealed the dismissal of her Section 9 application against Roidec India Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. for claimed professional fees of Rs. 63,29,169/- relating to patent services. The NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI had dismissed the petition due to a pre-existing dispute and non-filing of a Section 9(3)(b) affidavit. The NCLAT held that while the Section 9(3)(b) affidavit was not mandatory since the debtor responded to the Section 8 notice (applying Macquarie Bank), emails from January and April 2018 showed that the debtor had contested the invoices and terminated services nearly a year before the demand notice was served. Applying Mobilox Innovations, the pre-existing dispute warranted dismissal. Appeal dismissed.

case_title: Asmi Metal Products Pvt. Ltd. vs. SKF India Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Informant/Appellant is Asmi Metal Products Pvt. Ltd. (supplier/machining unit); Opposite Party/Respondent is SKF India Limited (multinational manufacturer of bearing and mechanical products). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Machining and forging of bearing rings and fabricated metal products by Appellant for supply to Respondent to be processed and sold in open automobile and electrical markets; governed by various MoUs and arrangements between 2004 and 2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant alleged uncompensated capital expenditures including Rs. 1.15 Crores for establishing a dedicated forging plant in 2004, unpaid VAT of Rs. 57,56,028/- for 2005-2009, import duty burdens of Rs. 20,00,000/- per order from Chinese steel imports, and financial losses resulting in closure of its plant in October 2009. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information filed under Section 19(1)(a) before CCI in 2017; MoU containing liability-exclusion clause executed on 28.04.2017; CCI dismissed information on 24.01.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of meetings, emails from 2004-2016, bilateral MoU dated 28.04.2017 (Clause 12 exculpating liability), third-party market analyst reports (ICICI Direct, ICRA, Nirmal Bang showing 25-41% market share), and CMIE Industrial Outlook market data for FY 2013-14 to 2015-16. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 19(1)(a) information alleging abuse of dominance under Section 4; CCI dismissed the information holding that pre-May 2009 actions were outside its jurisdiction and that the market for industrial bearings was fragmented, where Respondent was not dominant; Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether conduct occurring prior to the enforcement of Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002 (May 2009) can be examined for abuse of dominance, and whether SKF India Ltd enjoyed a position of dominance in the relevant market for industrial bearings in India.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The provisions of Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002 are prospective from the date of their enforcement in May 2009 and cannot be applied retroactively to alleged anti-competitive conduct occurring prior thereto; furthermore, abuse of dominance cannot be sustained without establishing that the enterprise operates independently of competitive forces in the relevant geographic and product market. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 4 requires establishing dominance as a condition precedent; an enterprise operating in a market with fluctuating market shares (10-17%) alongside significant domestic competitors and heavy imports (approx. 44.8%) does not possess the requisite economic strength to dictate market conditions independently. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comprehensive industry database metrics (CMIE) showing dynamic, fluctuating market shares across multiple competitors and high import penetration outweigh isolated analyst reports in assessing dominance under the Act. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Most allegations predated May 2009, and for the post-2009 period, SKF India Ltd was not in a dominant position in the relevant market across India, precluding any violation of Section 4.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed. The order dated 24.01.2018 passed by the Competition Commission of India was affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Asmi Metal Products Pvt. Ltd., a component supplier, appealed against the CCI's dismissal of its information under Section 19(1)(a) alleging abuse of dominant position under Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002 against SKF India Ltd. Appellant claimed SKF coerced it into heavy capital investments, altered machining requirements, imposed Chinese import duties, and introduced an onerous liability waiver in an MoU dated 28.04.2017. The NCLAT affirmed the CCI's ruling, holding that allegations prior to May 2009 fell outside the statutory purview of the Act. Relying on CMIE data, the Tribunal found that the market for industrial bearings across India was fragmented with competitive constraints from domestic manufacturers and imports, proving SKF was not in a dominant position. Appeal dismissed.

case_title: Varsha Jain vs. ISEO Chemdis Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor/Appellant is Varsha Jain; Corporate Debtor/Respondent is ISEO Chemdis Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purported investment of Rs. 100 Lakhs by Appellant in Respondent under an unexecuted Draft Agreement dated 18.06.2018, whereby Rs. 50 Lakhs was infused as equity and the remaining Rs. 50 Lakhs was to be treated as a shareholder loan carrying interest at 33.33% per annum, subject to an express lock-in period of 60 months. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed on the Rs. 50 Lakhs loan component alongside accrued interest under Section 7. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Draft Agreement signed inter-se on 18.06.2018; Section 7 application filed prior to the expiry of the mandatory 60-month lock-in period. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: An unformalized Draft Agreement dated 18.06.2018 not followed by the execution of any formal contract or enforceable legal instrument. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT rejected Appellant's application under Section 7 of the IBC on the ground that the applicant failed to establish the existence of a legally enforceable financial debt; Appellant challenged the rejection order before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an unformalized draft agreement without an executed enforceable instrument can substantiate a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and whether a Section 7 petition is maintainable when the underlying transaction is subject to an active contractual lock-in period that has not matured.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An applicant cannot maintain an insolvency petition under Section 7 based solely on a draft agreement that was never culminated into an enforceable legal contract, nor can a default be declared on an investment when a binding lock-in period has not yet expired. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) requiring disbursal against time value of money cannot be established absent an enforceable instrument; furthermore, 'default' under Section 3(12) does not arise when the principal repayment is not yet legally due or payable owing to a subsisting lock-in clause. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority must examine whether the underlying debt instrument is legally enforceable and whether the claimed amount is due and payable in praesenti, rather than premature under the agreed investment terms. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Draft Agreement lacked enforceable legal status, and even if assumed valid, the active 60-month lock-in period barred repayment of the principal, confirming that no default occurred.
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal, affirming the NCLT's rejection of the Section 7 application. No costs.
summary: Appellant Varsha Jain appealed against the NCLT's rejection of her Section 7 IBC application against ISEO Chemdis Pvt. Ltd. seeking recovery of an alleged shareholder loan of Rs. 50 Lakhs with 33.33% interest out of an overall Rs. 100 Lakhs infusion. The claim was based on a Draft Agreement dated 18.06.2018 containing a 60-month lock-in period. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that an unfinalized draft agreement without an executed enforceable contract cannot establish a 'financial debt'. The Tribunal further held that since the 60-month lock-in period was still running, the principal was not yet due and payable, meaning no default had occurred. Appeal dismissed.

case_title: Duggal Associates Private Limited (through Anil Duggal) vs. Roofs & Ceilings Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Roofs & Ceilings Pvt. Ltd.; Corporate Debtor is Duggal Associates Private Limited; Appellant is Anil Duggal, Director representing the suspended management of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor issued Purchase Order No. 37 dated 18.10.2016 to Operational Creditor for the supply of roofing materials for a project at Carpet Export Mart, BIDA Carpet City, Bhadohi, Uttar Pradesh. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total invoices amounted to Rs. 1,66,57,721.95, against which part-payments totaling Rs. 1,38,30,182/- were made, leaving an unpaid operational debt of Rs. 28,26,817.95 (principal) plus Rs. 14,03,853.95 (interest), aggregating to Rs. 42,30,671.90. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8(1) dated 28.05.2018 was delivered via speed post on 02.06.2018 and MCA email on 14.06.2018; no notice of dispute or payment was delivered within 10 days; Section 9 petition filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor issued a completion certificate dated 05.01.2018 certifying good quality execution of work; emails dated 27.02.2018 admitting delay/default and promising clearance of dues; email dated 20.06.2018 confirming the balance outstanding sum of Rs. 28,26,818/-; Section 9(3)(b) affidavit of no dispute; postal tracking proof establishing court notice service on active employee Ashish Gupta on 17.08.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP (IB) No. 1581/ND/2019 before NCLT New Delhi Bench; the Corporate Debtor was set ex-parte following served notice, and NCLT admitted the Section 9 application on 11.12.2019 finding operational default established beyond doubt.
legal_issues: Whether an ex-parte Section 9 CIRP admission order is valid where tribunal process was received by an employee in active service of the Corporate Debtor, and whether retrospective assertions of material quality defects and a debit note can establish a pre-existing dispute in the presence of an unconditional completion certificate and written balance confirmations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Service of judicial process upon an employee in active corporate employment constitutes valid and effective service upon the company, and subsequent pleas of pre-existing quality disputes cannot survive summary scrutiny when contradicted by prior contemporaneous completion certificates and written balance acknowledgments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5) obligates the Adjudicating Authority to admit a complete application where operational debt exceeding the statutory threshold is unpaid and no notice of dispute under Section 8(2) exists on record; post-notice assertions of cash flow difficulties constitute an admission of default rather than a dispute. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unconditional work completion certificates and written balance confirmation emails negate subsequent uncorroborated allegations of defective supplies or unilateral debit notes concocted to evade insolvency proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The ex-parte procedure was justified due to valid receipt of notice by an active employee, and the debt and default were conclusively demonstrated without any bona fide pre-existing dispute.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed without costs, affirming the order of the NCLT New Delhi Bench dated 11.12.2019 admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP.
summary: Appellant Anil Duggal, Director of Duggal Associates Pvt. Ltd., appealed against the NCLT New Delhi Bench order admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by Roofs & Ceilings Pvt. Ltd. for default on an operational debt of Rs. 28,26,817.95 (plus interest) relating to roofing supplies. The Appellant challenged the ex-parte nature of the order and alleged pre-existing quality disputes supported by a debit note. The NCLAT held that receipt of court notice by an employee in active service constituted valid service. Furthermore, the debt and default were undisputed as evidenced by a completion certificate of good quality, written emails confirming balance dues, and an admission of a cash crunch. The admission of CIRP was upheld and the appeal dismissed.

case_title: Heavy Metal & Tubes Ltd. vs. Bank of Baroda
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Heavy Metal & Tubes Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Respondent Bank of Baroda (amalgamated with erstwhile Dena Bank) is the Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying credit facilities/loans availed by the Corporate Debtor from erstwhile Dena Bank (now Bank of Baroda). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount and specific date of default are not specified in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Dates of Section 8 or loan recall notices are not detailed in the order. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 7 application Form-1, cause title, and supporting affidavit which mistakenly bore the heading 'Affidavit in support of initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process by Operational Creditor under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016'. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent filed an application under Section 7 of the Code before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench; prior to admission, Respondent sought amendment to rectify typographical error in the affidavit title where petitioner was typed as 'Operational Creditor' instead of 'Financial Creditor'; NCLT allowed the correction; Corporate Debtor appealed arguing the rectification improperly changed the nature of the proceeding.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in permitting the Financial Creditor to rectify an inadvertent typographical error in the title of its supporting affidavit in an unadmitted Section 7 petition from 'Operational Creditor' to 'Financial Creditor'.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Inadvertent clerical or typographical errors in pleadings and supporting affidavits do not alter the fundamental legal nature of an action when the substantive form and petition whole make the statutory invocation manifest. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC by definition cannot be filed by an Operational Creditor; therefore, describing the applicant as an 'Operational Creditor' within the affidavit title of a Section 7 Form-1 petition is a patent, curable typographical error. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Holistic assessment of pleadings where the contents of the Form-1 and the cause title take precedence over an obvious inadvertent misnomer in the title of an accompanying affidavit. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: An inadvertent typographical error in designating a creditor in an affidavit in support of a Section 7 petition can be validly permitted to be rectified, causing no prejudice to the debtor's substantive rights prior to admission.
operative_order: The impugned order permitting correction of the typographical error is upheld, and the appeal is dismissed with no orders as to costs.
summary: Heavy Metal & Tubes Ltd. challenged an order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench allowing Bank of Baroda to rectify a clerical error in the affidavit title of its Section 7 petition, where the bank had inadvertently been typed as 'Operational Creditor' instead of 'Financial Creditor'. The Corporate Debtor contended this changed the character of the proceeding. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that a Section 7 application can only be filed by a Financial Creditor and a holistic reading of Form-1 demonstrates the misdescription was an obvious typing error properly rectifiable without causing prejudice before admission.

case_title: Akriti Agnihotri & Anr. vs. Blackberry Realcon Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Akriti Agnihotri & Anr. are original allottees claiming status as Financial Creditors; Respondent M/s Blackberry Realcon Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (a real estate company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of real estate units coupled with a subsequent agreement of refund. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default quantum and default dates under the refund agreement are not specified in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Precise dates of statutory notices are not detailed in the order. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Independent agreement of refund executed between the allottees and the Corporate Debtor upon which the claim was founded. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed an application under Section 7 of the IBC; NCLT New Delhi Court V adjourned the proceedings on 27.01.2020 awaiting the outcome of Supreme Court Writ Petition (Civil) No. 26/2020 challenging the IBC Amendment Ordinance dated 28.12.2019; Appellants appealed the mechanical stay/adjournment.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 grounded on an independent agreement for refund must be stayed pending Supreme Court scrutiny of real estate allottee threshold amendments, or whether the Adjudicating Authority must determine the applicant's creditor status before deferring proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority must ascertain the precise legal capacity under which a petition is maintained before mechanically subjecting it to general interim status quo orders applicable solely to real estate allottee classes. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8) differentiates an applicant invoking remedies purely as an allottee seeking possession/allotment from one proceeding independently upon an agreement of refund creating an actionable financial debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Direct scrutiny of the underlying prayer and founding agreement to identify whether the cause of action is for flat/shop allotment or debt enforcement under a refund agreement. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: If an application is premised on an independent debt arising from an agreement of refund rather than an allottee seeking unit delivery, the Section 7 petition proceeds on its own merits without awaiting the Supreme Court decision on the allottee-specific ordinance.
operative_order: The impugned adjournment order is set aside; matter is remitted to NCLT New Delhi Court V to determine whether the Appellants filed as independent Financial Creditors under Section 5(7) & (8) pursuant to the refund agreement or as allottees; if as independent creditors, proceed forthwith; if as allottees, await the Supreme Court ruling.
summary: Allottees Akriti Agnihotri & Anr. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order that adjourned their Section 7 application sine die pending Supreme Court proceedings in WP (Civil) No. 26/2020 challenging the threshold ordinance for allottees. The Appellants contended their petition was grounded on an independent refund agreement under Section 5(7) and 5(8). NCLAT remitted the matter, directing the Adjudicating Authority to first determine whether the application was filed in the capacity of an independent Financial Creditor on the refund agreement or as an allottee, ordering that only the latter would remain subject to the Supreme Court's status quo order.

case_title: Punjab National Bank vs. State Bank Of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Punjab National Bank is a dissenting minority Financial Creditor (2.84% voting share); Respondent No. 1 State Bank of India is the majority Financial Creditor in consortium (97.16% voting share); Respondent No. 2 Mr. Anil Kohli is the Resolution Professional of Kannu Aditya (India) Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Working capital/credit facilities extended to the Corporate Debtor by both banks. Corporate Debtor executed a Joint Deed of Hypothecation and a Working Capital Consortium Agreement dated 04.05.2013 hypothecating stock in favour of the consortium including SBI; subsequently executed a document of pledge dated 29.09.2015 over rice stock lying in its godowns in favour of PNB. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amounts and exact date of default are not stated in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: No statutory notices are cited in the order. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Joint Deed of Hypothecation dated 04.05.2013 in favour of SBI consortium, Document of Pledge dated 29.09.2015 in favour of PNB, and CoC minutes approving sale of perishable rice stock despite PNB's objections. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: During CIRP, the RP filed CA No. 1692(PB)/2019 before NCLT Principal Bench pursuant to CoC approval to sell perishable rice stock and utilize proceeds for CIRP costs and day-to-day operations; NCLT allowed the application; PNB appealed alleging its sole security was being dissipated.
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional and the Committee of Creditors can sell pledged/hypothecated perishable stock belonging to the Corporate Debtor and utilize the proceeds toward CIRP costs and going-concern operational expenses over the objection of a minority secured creditor holding an alleged pledge.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Resolution Professional is statutorily authorized under commercial guidance of the CoC to liquidate perishable assets of a Corporate Debtor and deploy the realized proceeds toward CIRP costs and maintaining going-concern operations, while reserving the priority security rights of affected creditors for consideration at the stage of resolution plan or liquidation distribution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Utilizing sale proceeds of perishable inventory for day-to-day operations, including wages, supplier bills, and insolvency costs, falls squarely within the statutory mandate of maintaining the Corporate Debtor as a going concern, without extinguishing the underlying proprietary security interest in the ultimate financial distribution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Commercial wisdom of the CoC exercised by statutory supermajority (97.16%) deciding on the perishable nature of agricultural inventory overrides minority dissent, provided the claim to underlying security value is preserved. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: There is no illegality in the RP using sale proceeds of perishable stock for CIRP expenditures; the priority rights and security value asserted by the minority creditor are deferred and kept open to be addressed in the resolution plan or under liquidation waterfall distribution.
operative_order: The impugned order permitting the RP to utilize the sale proceeds and operate the bank accounts of the Corporate Debtor for operational expenses and CIRP costs is upheld; Appellant's security claim by way of pledge and the value thereof are directed to be kept open and considered by the RP, CoC, and Adjudicating Authority at the stage of Resolution Plan approval or liquidation; the appeal is disposed of without costs.
summary: Punjab National Bank appealed against an NCLT order permitting the Resolution Professional of Kannu Aditya (India) Ltd., pursuant to a 97.16% majority CoC vote led by State Bank of India, to sell perishable rice stock and utilize the proceeds for CIRP costs and day-to-day operations. PNB argued that the rice stock was pledged exclusively to it as sole security. NCLAT held that there is no illegality in utilizing sale proceeds of perishable goods for maintaining the corporate debtor as a going concern and funding CIRP, ruling that PNB's security interest and valuation claims are to be addressed during resolution plan approval or liquidation.

case_title: JSW Steel Ltd. vs. Mahender Kumar Khandelwal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant JSW Steel Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant; Bhushan Power & Steel Ltd. (BPSL) is the Corporate Debtor; Mahender Kumar Khandelwal is the Resolution Professional; Sanjay Singal is the erstwhile Promoter/Guarantor; other parties include the Committee of Creditors (CoC), Directorate of Enforcement (ED), Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), and various Operational Creditors (Jaldhi Overseas Pte. Ltd., Medi Carrier Pvt. Ltd., Kalyani Transco, CJ Darcl Logistics Ltd., and State of Odisha). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of BPSL culminating in the approval of JSW Steel Ltd.'s resolution plan by the CoC and subsequent conditional approval by NCLT New Delhi on 05.09.2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Massive corporate insolvency default by BPSL leading to CIRP initiation; exact original default figure and default dates are not quantified in the judgment text. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan approved by NCLT on 05.09.2019; provisional attachment order issued by ED under Section 5 PMLA on 10.10.2019; Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Ordinance, 2019 promulgated on 28.12.2019 inserting Section 32A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Annual returns of Rohne Coal Company Pvt. Ltd. showing JSW holding 49% and BPSL holding 24.09% equity pursuant to a compulsory joint allocation mandated by the Ministry of Coal via LOI dated 09.04.2007; lack of investigative findings or charge sheets by ED/CBI alleging abetment or conspiracy against JSW's management under Section 32A(1)(b). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench approved JSW's plan on 05.09.2019 subject to several conditions in para 128; ED attached BPSL's assets on 10.10.2019 under PMLA; JSW appealed challenging conditions and ED's jurisdiction; multiple cross-appeals were preferred by Promoters and Operational Creditors challenging plan approval, pre-CIRP adjustments, and treatment of contingent claims.
legal_issues: Whether the Directorate of Enforcement possesses statutory authority to attach the assets of a Corporate Debtor post-approval of a Resolution Plan under Section 31 of the IBC in respect of offences committed prior to CIRP commencement; whether Section 32A of the IBC applies retrospectively to plans approved prior to the 28.12.2019 Ordinance; whether common investment in a government-mandated joint venture renders the Resolution Applicant a 'related party' under Section 5(24) disentitling it to Section 32A immunity; and whether an Adjudicating Authority can modify commercial terms regarding CIRP EBITDA distribution, avoidance transaction recoveries, or grant liberty to pursue undecided claims under Section 60(6).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon approval of a resolution plan by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31, the corporate debtor and its assets acquire complete statutory immunity under Section 32A from attachment, seizure, or prosecution by enforcement agencies for pre-CIRP offences, provided the incoming resolution applicant is a bona fide third party not controlled by or related to erstwhile promoters. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 32A is clarificatory and applies retrospectively to protect bona fide acquirers whose plans were approved prior to the Ordinance; Section 5(24) and Section 32A(1)(a) do not treat two independent corporate entities as 'related parties' of each other solely because both hold shares in an unrelated downstream joint venture created under statutory compulsion. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To defeat immunity under Section 32A(1)(b), the investigating authority must demonstrate existing 'reason to believe' based on objective material already in its possession as of the confirmation date showing actual abetment or conspiracy, rather than relying on future indeterminate inquiries. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The attachment order dated 10.10.2019 by ED is illegal and without jurisdiction; the Adjudicating Authority possesses no jurisdiction to rewrite commercial terms regarding CIRP EBITDA distribution or avoidance proceeds, nor can it revive undecided pre-CIRP claims under Section 60(6) contrary to the clean slate doctrine.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 957 of 2019 filed by JSW Steel Ltd. is allowed; the provisional attachment order dated 10.10.2019 passed by ED is declared illegal and set aside; the conditions imposed under para 128(e), (f), (g), (i), (j), and (k) of NCLT's order dated 05.09.2019 are modified/substituted in alignment with the approved plan and clean slate doctrine; all connected appeals preferred by Sanjay Singal, Jaldhi Overseas, Medi Carrier, Kalyani Transco, CJ Darcl, and State of Odisha are dismissed without costs.
summary: JSW Steel Ltd. challenged NCLT New Delhi's conditional approval of its resolution plan for Bhushan Power & Steel Ltd. and the ED's subsequent attachment of BPSL's assets under the PMLA for alleged offenses of erstwhile promoters. Promoter Sanjay Singal and various operational creditors filed appeals challenging plan eligibility and claim allocations. NCLAT held that Section 32A is clarificatory and operates retrospectively, immunizing corporate debtors and approved resolution applicants from pre-CIRP criminal liabilities and asset attachments. Co-investing in a government-mandated JV did not make JSW a related party. Modifying the NCLT conditions, NCLAT upheld the resolution plan, dismissed all objections, and quashed the ED's attachment.

case_title: Neeraj Jain vs. Cloudwalker Streaming Technologies Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Neeraj Jain is a Director of Flipkart India Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 Cloudwalker Streaming Technologies Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor; Respondent No. 2 is Flipkart India Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply Agreement dated 29.12.2016 for importing and supplying LED TVs by Cloudwalker to Flipkart based on purchase orders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 26,95,00,000/- (comprising Rs. 13.95 crores for value of goods, Rs. 5.25 crores custom charges, and Rs. 7.75 crores interest @ 12.65%) with default date alleged as 31.03.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice issued under Form 3 dated 08.06.2019, received by Flipkart on 13.06.2019; no formal Section 8(2) reply filed within 10 days; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 260/BB/2019 filed thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor failed to produce purchase orders, corresponding invoices, or mandatory bank statements under Form 5 Part V; it relied solely on projection emails; pre-existing dispute demonstrated by Respondent's prior legal notice dated 26.03.2018 invoking arbitration under Clause 18 of the Supply Agreement for damages due to uncollected stock of 21,808 TVs (which was later withdrawn to negotiate). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru admitted the Section 9 petition on 24.10.2019 holding there was no pre-existing dispute and the application was complete; Neeraj Jain appealed against the admission order.
legal_issues: Whether an Operational Creditor has unfettered discretion under Section 8(1) of the IBC to issue a demand notice in Form 3 without invoices when the underlying commercial transaction generates invoices; whether an uncrystallized claim for damages on uncollected goods constitutes an 'operational debt'; and whether the prior issuance and unilateral withdrawal of an arbitration notice erases a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 9(5)(ii)(d).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The choice between issuing a demand notice under Form 3 or Form 4 is governed by the objective nature of the debt rather than creditor discretion; where transactions inherently generate invoices, failure to furnish purchase orders, invoices, and mandatory bank statements renders a Section 9 application defective and legally untenable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Operational debt under Section 5(6) and Section 8(1) requires actual provision and delivery of goods or services; uncrystallized claims for damages, lost profits, custom duties, or inventory holding losses cannot be adjudicated as liquidated operational debt in summary insolvency proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Plausible contention standard under Mobilox Innovations; a prior legal notice invoking arbitration alleging breach of contract constitutes incontrovertible evidence of a pre-existing dispute which is not obliterated by its subsequent tactical withdrawal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was fundamentally defective for lack of proof of debt/default, involved an unliquidated claim for damages, and was barred by a bona fide pre-existing dispute.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 24.10.2019 admitting the Section 9 petition is set aside; CP (IB) No. 260/BB/2019 is rejected; Flipkart India Pvt. Ltd. is released from CIRP; IRP directed to hand over control to the Promoters immediately; NCLT directed to pass orders for CIRP costs.
summary: Neeraj Jain, Director of Flipkart India Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Bengaluru order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Cloudwalker Streaming Technologies claiming Rs. 26.95 crores for uncollected imported LED TVs. NCLAT set aside the admission order and rejected the insolvency petition. The Tribunal ruled that Cloudwalker failed to produce purchase orders, invoices, or bank statements, and that an unliquidated claim for damages arising from unpicked goods cannot constitute an operational debt. Furthermore, a prior notice invoking arbitration sent by Cloudwalker in 2018 established a genuine pre-existing dispute that was not wiped out by subsequent withdrawal.

case_title: K.L. Jute Products Pvt. Ltd. vs. Tirupati Jute Industries Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant K.L. Jute Products Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant; Respondent No. 1 Tirupati Jute Industries Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (in Liquidation); Respondent No. 2 Daaksh Jute LLP is the lessee; Respondent No. 3 Pinaki Sircar is the erstwhile RP; Respondents 4-7 are Financial Creditors (SIDBI, Federal Bank, Abinandan Holdings, Everbright Vinimay); Respondents 8-9 are unsuccessful resolution applicants; Respondents 10-11 are workers' unions. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor executed an unregistered lease deed dated 01.08.2016 leasing its jute mill to Daaksh Jute LLP for 9 years at Rs. 11 Lakhs/month following SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice dated 01.04.2016 by Federal Bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 7,18,21,128/- owed to SIDBI; date of NPA was 31.10.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition admitted on 12.01.2018; CoC approved K.L. Jute's plan with 97.20% voting on 03.10.2018; 270-day CIRP period expired prior to NCLT adjudication. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unregistered 9-year lease deed dated 01.08.2016; EOI published on 06.05.2018 calling for bids on 'AS IS WHERE IS AND AS IS WHAT IS BASIS'; Appellant's email dated 03.10.2018 asserting absolute right to withdraw its bid if conditional terms regarding lease cancellation and eviction were modified. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench by order dated 13.02.2019 rejected Appellant's approved resolution plan under Section 30(2)(e) because it made implementation conditional upon NCLT evicting Daaksh Jute LLP and terminating the lease, ordered liquidation of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern, and appointed Chhedi Rajbhar as Liquidator replacing the RP; Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under the IBC to order summary eviction of a third-party tenant/lessee in possession of the corporate debtor's premises under an approved resolution plan; whether a conditional resolution plan containing unilateral withdrawal stipulations violates Section 30(2)(e); and whether preferential transaction claims under Section 43 can be pursued during liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority lacks summary jurisdiction under the IBC to evict a third-party tenant or cancel a subsisting lease deed; any resolution plan that conditions its viability on obtaining summary eviction orders from the NCLT is unexecutable and contravenes Section 30(2)(e). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(e) mandates that a resolution plan must not contravene any provision of law for the time being in force; an applicant who bids on 'as is where is' terms cannot impose conditional prerequisites requiring tribunals to bypass ordinary civil property remedies. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective facial validity of plan terms; when a resolution applicant stipulates an unreserved entitlement to withdraw upon non-fulfilment of conditions outside the tribunal's jurisdiction, the plan lacks legal feasibility and certainty. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT rightly rejected the conditional resolution plan and properly ordered liquidation under Section 33 upon expiry of the CIRP period, while leaving Section 43 avoidance actions open for the Liquidator to pursue.
operative_order: The impugned order of NCLT Kolkata dated 13.02.2019 rejecting the resolution plan, directing liquidation of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern, and appointing a new Liquidator is affirmed; the appeal is dismissed without costs.
summary: K.L. Jute Products Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT Kolkata order rejecting its CoC-approved resolution plan for Tirupati Jute Industries Ltd. and ordering liquidation. The NCLT rejected the plan because the Appellant made implementation conditional on the Tribunal evicting a long-term lessee (Daaksh Jute LLP) and cancelling an unregistered lease deed, despite bidding on an 'as is where is' basis. NCLAT affirmed the rejection, holding that NCLT lacks summary jurisdiction to order eviction of tenants or nullify leases as a condition precedent in a resolution plan. As 270 days had elapsed, the order of liquidation as a going concern was upheld.

case_title: Sagar Sharma & Anr. vs. Phoenix ARC Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Sagar Sharma and Vishal Sharma are Directors/Shareholders of Hotel Horizon Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. is the Assignee/Financial Creditor; IDFC Ltd. is the Assignor Bank. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Rupee Term Loan Agreement dated 20.11.2009 for Rs. 22 Crores (Loan 2) and Secured Facility Agreement dated 24.05.2012 for Rs. 46 Crores (Loan 3) executed between IDFC and Hotel Horizon. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Aggregate default exceeding Rs. 53,91,20,000/-; defaults occurred between 14.02.2014 and 14.06.2014; accounts classified as SMA-2 on 14.08.2014; declared NPA on 15.03.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Debt assigned by IDFC to Phoenix ARC on 11.09.2014; Section 7 application filed on 29.09.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-1 default matrix showing default dates between 14.02.2014 and 14.06.2014; Form No. CHG-1 dated 11.09.2014 establishing cut-off date of outstanding debt; complete lack of any written acknowledgment signed by Corporate Debtor under Section 18 within the 3-year limitation window. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted Section 7 application on 29.01.2019; NCLAT dismissed appeal on 05.09.2019 applying Article 62 (12 years); Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 7673/2019 reversed and remanded on 30.09.2019 holding Article 137 applies exclusively; matter heard afresh on remand.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed beyond three years from the date of default/classification as SMA-2 is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, and whether entries in books of account or Section 22 tort principles can extend limitation in the absence of a signed Section 18 acknowledgment.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Applications under Section 7 of the IBC are governed exclusively by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, requiring filing within three years from the date default occurs; the limitation period cannot be expanded by invoking Article 62 mortgage periods or Section 22 continuing wrong concepts. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The 'right to apply' under Article 137 accrues on the date default occurs, and time cannot be extended under Section 18 without an explicit acknowledgment of liability in writing duly signed by the debtor or its authorized representative prior to the expiration of the 3-year period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Books of account and balance sheet disclosures do not ipso facto constitute signed acknowledgments under Section 18 of the Limitation Act to establish a revived limitation timeline. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Default occurred prior to 09.09.2014, and three years expired prior to 09.09.2017; the Section 7 application filed on 29.09.2017 was time-barred.
operative_order: The impugned order of admission dated 29.01.2019 is set aside; Hotel Horizon Pvt. Ltd. is released from CIRP; IRP directed to restore assets to the Board of Directors; NCLT to determine IRP fees/costs to be borne by Phoenix ARC; appeal allowed without costs.
summary: Appellants appealed the admission of a Section 7 application filed by Phoenix ARC against Hotel Horizon Pvt. Ltd., following a remand from the Supreme Court directing NCLAT to decide limitation strictly under Article 137 of the Limitation Act. Phoenix claimed debt assigned from IDFC Ltd. where defaults took place between February and June 2014. NCLAT held that the default date occurred prior to 09.09.2014, making the three-year limitation period expire before 09.09.2017. In the absence of any signed written acknowledgment under Section 18, the petition filed on 29.09.2017 was time-barred. Admission was set aside and the corporate debtor released.

case_title: Vijay Pal Garg & Ors. vs. Pooja Bahry (Liquidator)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Vijay Pal Garg & Ors. are Suspended Directors of Gee Ispat Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent Pooja Bahry is the Liquidator (former Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP initiated against Gee Ispat Pvt. Ltd. under Section 9, which subsequently entered liquidation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidator alleged financial fraud, Rs. 191 Crores in non-existent trade receivables/fake debtors, and outstanding unrecovered debt of approx. Rs. 512 Crores owed to financial creditors. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP and liquidation ongoing; CA-64/C-II/2018 filed by RP during proceedings; impugned order passed on 19.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audit qualifications in FY 2013-14 regarding unsupported receivables exceeding Rs. 187 Crores; field visits revealing 90% of debtor firm addresses were fake/non-existent; excise show cause notice for CENVAT evasion on bogus invoices; suspicious fire incident on 12.02.2018 (FIR No. 0138/2018) destroying records, followed by physical assault on security guards on 15.03.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed CA-64/C-II/2018 under Sections 60(5), 66, 67, 70-73, and 235A of the IBC; NCLT New Delhi Bench-II held that summary proceedings precluded in-depth inquiry and directly ordered Central Government investigation under Section 210(2) of the Companies Act, 2013; Directors appealed challenging NCLT's jurisdiction.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT acting as the Adjudicating Authority under the IBC possesses statutory jurisdiction to straightaway direct the Central Government to conduct an investigation under Section 210(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 without adhering to the procedural prerequisites of Section 213 of the Companies Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) is not empowered in law to issue direct, mandatory directions to the Central Government under Section 210(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 without issuing show cause notice and establishing a prima facie case pursuant to Section 213 of the Companies Act, adhering to principles of natural justice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Although NCLT possesses dual jurisdiction under the IBC and Companies Act, Section 210(2) cannot be invoked as a shortcut to bypass the mandatory procedures under Section 213(b) of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Investigation into corporate affairs cannot rest on mere surmises or summary convenience; it requires the tribunal to provide reasonable opportunity of hearing, form a prima facie opinion under Section 213, and refer the matter to the Central Government to appoint Inspectors. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT exceeded its statutory bounds by directly ordering an investigation under Section 210(2); the proper course is to refer allegations to the Central Government under Section 213 for inspection, which may thereafter refer fraud findings to SFIO or Special Courts.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 19.07.2019 is varied; the matter is referred to the Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Government of India to investigate through Inspectors following due procedure under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013, with liberty to refer to SFIO or Special Court if fraud is established; appeal disposed of without costs.
summary: Suspended Directors of Gee Ispat Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT New Delhi order which directly commanded the Central Government under Section 210(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 to investigate the corporate debtor's affairs following allegations of Rs. 191 Crores in fake receivables and record destruction by fire. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction to straightaway order a Section 210(2) Central Government investigation. Instead, the Tribunal must follow Section 213(b), afford reasonable opportunity of being heard, and refer the matter to the Central Government for appointment of Inspectors, who may then recommend SFIO or Special Court action. The order was varied accordingly.

case_title: Sh G Eswara Rao vs. Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Sh G Eswara Rao is Shareholder/Director of M/s Saritha Synthetics & Industries Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund (SASF) is the Financial Creditor; Respondent No. 2 is the Corporate Debtor through IRP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple Rupee Term Loans and Foreign Currency Term Loans disbursed between 30.11.1994 and 31.05.2001 aggregating to principal debt of Rs. 43,32,00,000/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred in 2004; SASF filed O.A. No. 193 of 2004 before DRT-I Hyderabad; DRT passed a recovery decree on 17.08.2018 for Rs. 158,16,18,256/- with 12% interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original debt classified as NPA in 2004; DRT decree passed on 17.08.2018; Section 7 petition TCP (IB) No. 87/7/AMR/2019 filed in 2019 citing 17.08.2018 as date of default. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-1 Section 7 petition where SASF listed 17.08.2018 (DRT decree date) as the date of default; balance sheets/annual returns for FYs 2014-15, 2015-16, and 2016-17 relied upon as debt acknowledgments. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Amaravathi Bench admitted Section 7 application on 01.10.2019 holding that the DRT decree dated 17.08.2018 brought the petition within 3 years under Article 137; Director appealed on limitation grounds.
legal_issues: Whether the date of a recovery decree passed by the Debts Recovery Tribunal constitutes a fresh 'date of default' for computing the three-year limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act for a Section 7 IBC application; and whether mandatory filing of annual balance sheets under Section 92 of the Companies Act, 2013 serves as an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A money decree or recovery certificate issued by a Debts Recovery Tribunal does not shift forward or renew the date of default for the purposes of Section 7 of the IBC; the limitation period must be reckoned strictly from the original date of default/NPA. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC is not an execution forum for enforcing civil decrees; utilizing insolvency proceedings to execute time-barred decrees violates the object of the Code and attracts Section 65. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mandatory balance sheets and annual returns filed under the statutory compulsion and penal sanctions of Section 92 of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be treated as voluntary acknowledgments in writing under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Default occurred in 2004 and the limitation period expired in 2007; as the DRT decree does not constitute a fresh default, the Section 7 application was barred by limitation under Article 137.
operative_order: Impugned order of admission dated 01.10.2019 is set aside; Section 7 application dismissed as time-barred; Corporate Debtor released from CIRP; IRP to restore assets to the Board of Directors; NCLT to determine IRP expenses/fees to be borne by SASF; appeal allowed without costs.
summary: Director G Eswara Rao challenged the admission of SASF's Section 7 application against Saritha Synthetics & Industries Ltd.. SASF disbursed loans between 1994 and 2001, declared the account NPA in 2004, and obtained a DRT recovery decree on 17.08.2018. SASF argued that the decree date was the date of default and relied on balance sheets under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. NCLAT reversed the admission, ruling that a DRT decree does not shift forward the original date of default and IBC cannot serve as an execution forum. Additionally, statutory balance sheets mandated by penal law do not constitute Section 18 acknowledgments. The petition was dismissed as time-barred.

case_title: M/s Reliance Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. vs. M/s Hotel Poonja International Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Reliance Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. is the Assignee/Financial Creditor; Respondent M/s Hotel Poonja International Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Vijaya Bank is the Assignor Bank. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term Loan facility of Rs. 40 Lakhs sanctioned by Vijaya Bank on 20.05.1986 secured by mortgage of immovable properties in Mangalore. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account classified as Non-Performing Asset on 01.04.1993; total claimed outstanding of Rs. 145,44,46,651.32 (Principal Rs. 40,00,000 + Interest Rs. 145,04,46,651.32). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Vijaya Bank filed O.A. No. 547 of 1998 before DRT Bengaluru; joint compromise recorded on 27.03.2003 and Recovery Certificate issued; debt assigned to Reliance ARC on 03.05.2011; Recovery Certificate amended on 13.12.2012; Section 7 petition filed on 27.07.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form 1 Section 7 petition omitting default date and recording NPA date as 01.04.1993; statement of accounts dated 18.07.2018; lack of any written acknowledgment executed and signed by the Corporate Debtor within 3 years of default. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru rejected Section 7 application on 20.08.2019 holding IBC cannot be invoked as a recovery forum for disputed debts pending execution; Reliance ARC appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 application filed 25 years after the date of NPA classification and 15 years after issuance of a DRT recovery certificate is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, and whether statements of accounts or pending DRT recovery proceedings save limitation under Section 14 or 18.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 7 of the IBC is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 and must be initiated within three years from the date of default/NPA; pending debt recovery certificate execution does not grant an ongoing extension of limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of the Limitation Act applies only to prior proceedings prosecuted bona fide in a court lacking jurisdiction, not to distinct recovery or execution actions; IBC is not an alternative debt recovery mechanism. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To constitute an acknowledgment of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, there must be an unequivocal, signed writing made prior to the expiration of the three-year limitation period; creditor bank statements do not suffice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Default and NPA occurred on 01.04.1993, well over three years prior to filing the Section 7 petition on 27.07.2018; the application was hopelessly time-barred.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 20.08.2019 of NCLT Bengaluru rejecting the Section 7 application is affirmed, and the appeal is dismissed without costs, without prejudice to other lawful remedies.
summary: Reliance ARC appealed against the rejection of its Section 7 application by NCLT Bengaluru against Hotel Poonja International Pvt. Ltd.. The loan was sanctioned by Vijaya Bank in 1986, became NPA on 01.04.1993, and led to a DRT recovery certificate in 2003, subsequently assigned to Reliance ARC in 2011. Appellant filed under Section 7 on 27.07.2018 claiming over Rs. 145 Crores. NCLAT held that the petition was governed by Article 137 and barred by limitation since default took place decades earlier, and neither pending DRT execution nor unilateral account statements constituted valid acknowledgment under Section 18. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Mr. Savan Godiwala (Liquidator of Lanco Infratech Ltd.) vs. Apalla Siva Kumar
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Mr. Savan Godiwala is the Liquidator of Lanco Infratech Limited; Respondent Apalla Siva Kumar represents 66 ex-employees of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory employment dues claimed by former employees toward gratuity under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Aggregate accrued employee dues of Rs. 33,91,22,120/- uploaded as proposed CIRP costs; specific gratuity entitlement of 66 ex-employees left unpaid. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation order passed against Lanco Infratech under Section 33 on 27.08.2018; public announcement issued under Regulation 12; claims submitted in Form E. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Annual Report 2016-17 of Lanco Infratech showing proposed gratuity provisions of Rs. 9.77 crores for FY 2017 and Rs. 11.53 crores for FY 2016, but disclosing that the gratuity plan was entirely unfunded with no separate dedicated gratuity fund or insurance policy established. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Ex-employees filed I.A. No. 96 of 2019 in CP (IB) No. 111/7/HDB/2017 before NCLT Hyderabad seeking priority gratuity release; NCLT directed Liquidator to create sufficient provision and pay gratuity despite absence of a separate fund; Liquidator appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a Liquidator can be directed to create a reserve or make payment of employee gratuity dues where the Corporate Debtor failed to maintain a separate statutory gratuity fund prior to liquidation commencement, given the exclusion in Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC, only sums due from an actually established and existing gratuity fund are excluded from the liquidation estate; where a corporate debtor fails to create a dedicated gratuity fund, the liquidator cannot be mandated to carve out payments from general liquidation assets. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 36(2) confines the Liquidator's fiduciary management strictly to the 'liquidation estate'; if no separate trust or gratuity fund was maintained under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, the Liquidator has no legal domain to manufacture an artificial fund out of liquidation assets to pay gratuity outside the Section 53 waterfall. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documentary verification of balance sheet and cash flow statements; an 'unfunded' accounting provision in an annual report does not equate to the creation or existence of a statutory fund under Section 36(4)(a)(iii). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in directing the Liquidator to create provisions and pay gratuity when no separate fund existed prior to liquidation.
operative_order: The impugned order of NCLT Hyderabad in I.A. No. 96 of 2019 directing the Liquidator to make provision and pay gratuity in the absence of a separate fund is set aside; the appeal is allowed.
summary: The Liquidator of Lanco Infratech Ltd. appealed an NCLT Hyderabad order directing him to make provision for and pay gratuity dues of 66 ex-employees on top priority. Although Lanco had recognized unfunded gratuity provisions in its balance sheet, it had failed to create a separate dedicated gratuity fund under the Payment of Gratuity Act. NCLAT set aside the direction, ruling that while Section 36(4)(a)(iii) excludes existing gratuity funds from the liquidation estate, where no dedicated fund was established by the debtor, the Liquidator cannot be ordered to create provisions or make direct disbursements outside the Section 53 priority waterfall.

case_title: Flat Buyers Association Winter Hills 77, Gurgaon vs. Umang Realtech Pvt. Ltd. through IRP & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Flat Buyers Association Winter Hills 77, Gurgaon (and original Section 7 applicants Rachna Singh and Ajay Singh); Respondent No. 1 is Umang Realtech Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) through IRP; Uppal Housing Pvt. Ltd. is the Promoter/Intervenor; JM Financial Credit Solutions Ltd. is a secured Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development and construction of 706 flats/apartments in the Winter Hills - 77 project in Gurgaon. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in delivery of possession to allottees leading to Section 7 application; individual default figures of allottees not quantified in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted by NCLT Principal Bench on 20.08.2019 directing allottees to deposit Rs. 2 Lakhs with IRP; completion deadlines established by NCLAT up to 30.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Project status showing 624 of 706 flats booked, 453 allottees in possession, 26 fully paid awaiting possession, 142 defaulting allottees, and 92 sale deeds registered; promoter's undertaking to inject funds from outside as a lender to achieve completion. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT admitted Section 7 application on 20.08.2019; allottees appealed seeking completion of the project without bringing in third-party resolution applicants, proposing a project-specific 'Reverse CIRP' model.
legal_issues: Whether Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against a multi-project real estate developer must encompass the entire corporate entity or be confined strictly to the specific distressed project; and whether a 'Reverse CIRP' can be conducted by allowing promoters to fund completion as outside lenders without inducting a third-party resolution applicant.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In corporate insolvencies concerning real estate infrastructure companies, CIRP is confined exclusively to the specific project in default to prevent asset contagion across separate viable projects; resolution may be achieved through a 'Reverse CIRP' wherein promoters act as outside lenders cooperating with the IRP to complete construction without third-party takeover. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 20 requires keeping the debtor a going concern, which in real estate necessitates completing physical housing units; allottees under Section 5(8)(f) are unsecured financial creditors whose claims cannot be haircut and whose entitlement to physical possession supersedes secured creditors' monetary priority over the project land. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Feasibility and viability analysis demonstrating substantial completion (70-75%) and availability of promoter funding and receivables sufficient to achieve project completion without third-party resolution applicants. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A project-specific Reverse CIRP is permissible in economic public interest to safeguard homebuyers and workmen, directing construction completion by 30.08.2020 under IRP supervision.
operative_order: The CIRP is confined strictly to Winter Hills - 77 Gurgaon; Promoter Uppal Housing directed to inject capital from outside as an external lender; bank account to be operated under joint signatures of Corporate Debtor and IRP; construction and fit-outs to be completed by 30.08.2020; IRP authorized to sell unsold units via tripartite agreements; upon completion, IRP to report to NCLT for closure of Section 7 proceedings; appeal disposed of.
summary: Flat buyers and allottees appealed an NCLT order admitting a Section 7 application against real estate developer Umang Realtech Pvt. Ltd., seeking to complete their project without handing the company over to third-party bidders. NCLAT established the landmark doctrine of 'Reverse CIRP' and 'Project-Wise Insolvency'. The Tribunal held that insolvency against a developer must be confined strictly to the specific project in default. Promoter Uppal Housing was permitted to inject funds as an outside lender to complete construction alongside the IRP, ensuring allottees receive possession rather than haircuts, with CIRP closure upon completion.

case_title: Bank of India vs. Multi Arc Coating and Straps Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Bank of India is the Financial Creditor (consortium lead); Respondent Multi Arc Coating and Straps Limited is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities sanctioned by consortium of Bank of India and Punjab National Bank in 2006, secured by joint loan documents dated 10.08.2007 and 23.11.2009. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding financial debt of Rs. 22,01,85,312/-; account declared NPA on 30.06.2009. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 30.06.2009; Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice issued on 10.04.2012; O.A. No. 334/2015 filed before DRT-II Ahmedabad in 2015; Section 7 petition C.P.(I.B.) No. 349/7/NCLT/AHM/2018 filed on 11.07.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Acknowledgement and balance confirmation letters dated 24.04.2012; OTS proposal letter dated 12.03.2014; and formal OTS letter dated 09.06.2016 offering Rs. 12.30 Crores referencing sale of mortgaged Bharuch plots 'without prejudice' to pending litigation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed the Section 7 application holding that limitation computed from the 24.04.2012 letter expired in April 2015 and that subsequent letters did not save limitation; Bank of India appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a written One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal issued by a corporate debtor bearing the words 'without prejudice' constitutes a valid acknowledgment of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 so as to reset the limitation period for an application under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An offer of One Time Settlement (OTS) constitutes an unequivocal acknowledgment of debt liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963; appending the phrase 'without prejudice' to an OTS proposal does not destroy its legal character as an acknowledgment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, successive acknowledgments made before the expiration of each preceding three-year period create renewed starting points of limitation, keeping the right to apply under Section 7 alive. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Blue Coast Hotel test; admissions made during settlement negotiations are acknowledgments of the debt itself, and the 'without prejudice' reservation merely protects contentions in collateral court proceedings without negating debt existence. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Successive written acknowledgments on 24.04.2012, 12.03.2014, and 09.06.2016 each occurred within three years of the preceding event, extending limitation up to June 2019; the Section 7 petition filed on 11.07.2018 was well within limitation.
operative_order: The impugned order of NCLT Ahmedabad rejecting the Section 7 petition is quashed and set aside; the matter is remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority with a direction to admit the Section 7 application and proceed in accordance with law; appeal allowed without costs.
summary: Bank of India appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing its Section 7 application against Multi Arc Coating and Straps Ltd. as time-barred. The corporate debtor's account became NPA on 30.06.2009, but the debtor executed written balance confirmations and OTS proposals on 24.04.2012, 12.03.2014, and 09.06.2016. NCLAT set aside the dismissal, ruling that successive OTS letters constitute valid acknowledgments of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. The insertion of the phrase 'without prejudice' in an OTS letter does not vitiate its effect as an acknowledgment. The Section 7 application filed on 11.07.2018 was held within limitation and remitted for admission.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Maithan Alloys Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Lead Financial Creditor/Appellant); Impex Metal & Ferro Alloys Limited (Corporate Debtor in Liquidation); Samir Kumar Bhattacharya (Liquidator/Respondent No. 5); Maithan Alloys Limited (Highest Successful Bidder in E-Auction/Respondent No. 1); Sova Electrocasting Limited, Typhoon Financial Services Limited, and Sonar Bangla Career Academy Pvt. Ltd. (Unqualified Intervener Consortium/Respondent Nos. 2 to 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities/loans extended by SBI to the Corporate Debtor amounting to approximately Rs. 469.29 Crores outstanding as on 31.12.2017. Following CIRP failure, liquidation was ordered on 12.02.2019 to sell the Corporate Debtor as a going concern. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 469.29 Crores outstanding as of 31.12.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 09.03.2018; liquidation order passed on 12.02.2019; second e-auction notice issued on 27.05.2019 fixing reserve price at Rs. 68 Crores. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: R-1 declared successful bidder on 10.06.2019 after depositing 10% EMD (Rs. 6.84 Cr) and subsequently 15% (Rs. 10.26 Cr) on 19.06.2019, satisfying the mandatory 25% deposit. R-2 to R-4 failed to submit required consortium credentials/net-worth documents to the Liquidator, yet intervened before the NCLT offering Rs. 70 Crores across the bar without participating in the auction. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench vide orders dated 25.09.2019, 23.10.2019, and 06.11.2019 entertained R-2 to R-4's oral bid, allowed R-1 to withdraw from the auction, directed refund of R-1's Rs. 17,06,25,000/- deposit, and accepted R-2 to R-4's Rs. 70 Cr offer. SBI appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to interfere with a concluded public auction sale conducted by a liquidator under the IBC and Liquidation Process Regulations by entertaining a belated, higher oral offer made across the bar by non-participants, and whether a declared successful auction purchaser can be permitted to unilaterally withdraw from a concluded bid.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of established fraud or material irregularity, a concluded public auction conducted under statutory liquidation cannot be reopened or set aside simply because a subsequent higher offer is made after the close of bidding by third parties who did not participate in the auction, nor can a successful bidder unilaterally rescind its bid. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 35(1)(f) read with Regulation 33 mandates sales by public auction; the Adjudicating Authority's supervisory jurisdiction under Section 60(5) does not extend to disrupting concluded auction processes to accept belated private offers under the guise of asset maximization. 3.
