EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict threshold where interference in public auction requires proof of fraud or material procedural irregularity; mere oral assertions or affidavits of higher value without timely participation and credential verification do not warrant judicial disruption. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT acted without jurisdiction in allowing R-1 to withdraw and entertaining the oral offer of R-2 to R-4, thereby undermining the sanctity and finality of statutory e-auctions.
operative_order: Appeal allowed. Impugned orders dated 25.09.2019, 23.10.2019, and 06.11.2019 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench are set aside. Respondent No. 1 (Maithan Alloys Limited) is directed to complete the sale transaction by paying the balance sale consideration. A penalty of Rs. 10 Lakhs each is imposed on Respondent Nos. 2, 3, and 4 to be paid to the Corporate Debtor (in liquidation) within 30 days.
summary: SBI appealed against NCLT Kolkata orders setting aside a concluded e-auction sale of Corporate Debtor Impex Metal & Ferro Alloys Ltd. R-1 had been declared the successful bidder at Rs. 68 Crores and deposited 25% consideration. R-2 to R-4, having failed to meet qualification criteria during the auction, made an oral offer of Rs. 70 Crores before NCLT, which prompted NCLT to permit R-1's withdrawal, refund R-1's deposit, and accept the intervener's offer. NCLAT held that absent fraud or irregularity, NCLT cannot disrupt a concluded public auction for subsequent higher offers. Setting aside the NCLT orders, NCLAT directed R-1 to complete the purchase and penalized R-2 to R-4 Rs. 10 Lakhs each.

case_title: Ashish Kumar vs. Vinod Kumar Pukhraj Ambavat & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ashish Kumar, Shareholder/Director of R.K. Jain Construction (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Corporate Debtor); Vinod Kumar Pukhraj Ambavat (Respondent No. 1/Resolution Professional); M/s ASREC (India) Limited (Respondent No. 2/Financial Creditor/Assignee of Allahabad Bank). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility granted by Allahabad Bank to the Corporate Debtor in 2008 and enhanced until 2010. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account declared NPA on 29.08.2012; recovery claim of Rs. 28,64,67,561/- filed before DRT Jabalpur. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 29.08.2012; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice issued on 03.10.2012; Section 13(4) notice on 05.12.2012; Section 7 petition admitted by NCLT Cuttack on 03.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor issued multiple written One-Time Settlement (OTS) letters and acknowledgment proposals admitting debt on 26.11.2012, 01.08.2013, 25.10.2013 (offering Rs. 13.75 Cr), settlement cheques on 25.05.2014, 05.06.2014, 20.06.2014, admissions in SA No. 263/2016 before DRT Jabalpur on 13.09.2016, and OTS letters on 22.09.2016, 25.01.2018, 04.03.2018, 15.10.2018, 30.10.2019, and 01.11.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed in CP (IB) No. 54/CTB/2019; Corporate Debtor failed to appear despite paper publication and was set ex-parte on 04.09.2019; NCLT Cuttack admitted petition on 03.10.2019.
legal_issues: Whether written One Time Settlement (OTS) offers and admissions in DRT pleadings submitted by a corporate debtor within the statutory three-year period from the date of NPA classification constitute a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, thereby resetting the limitation period for an application under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While Article 137 of the Limitation Act governs Section 7 IBC applications and begins running from the date of default/NPA, the limitation period is continuously refreshed under Section 18 of the Limitation Act where the debtor makes written, signed acknowledgments of subsisting jural liability prior to the expiration of each successive three-year window. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18(1) requires an admission of an existing debtor-creditor relationship; an OTS proposal offering compromised payment amounts to a conscious admission of subsisting liability and extends the right to apply under Section 7. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Liberal construction of written statements indicating a subsisting jural relationship of debtor and creditor, verified via contemporaneous OTS letters, post-dated settlement cheques, and sworn pleadings before legal tribunals. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because successive written OTS proposals were submitted prior to the expiration of each three-year period following the NPA date, the Section 7 petition was within limitation.
operative_order: Appeal rejected. The admission order dated 03.10.2019 initiating CIRP against R.K. Jain Construction (India) Pvt. Ltd. is upheld. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged the NCLT Cuttack Bench's admission of a Section 7 IBC petition filed by M/s ASREC (India) Ltd against R.K. Jain Construction (India) Pvt. Ltd., contending the action was time-barred since the loan account was classified as NPA on 29.08.2012. NCLAT held that the Corporate Debtor repeatedly acknowledged its subsisting jural debtor-creditor relationship by submitting multiple written OTS proposals and settlement cheques between 2012 and 2019. Applying Section 18 of the Limitation Act, each acknowledgment triggered a fresh three-year limitation period. Consequently, the petition was held to be within limitation, and the appeal was rejected.

case_title: Committee of Creditors of Metalyst Forgings Ltd. vs. Deccan Value Investors LP & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Committee of Creditors of Metalyst Forgings Ltd. through State Bank of India (Appellant in CA 1276/2019); Deccan Value Investors LP and DVI PE (Mauritius) Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant / Appellant in CA 1281/2019); Dinkar Venkatasubramanian (Resolution Professional); Metalyst Forgings Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of Metalyst Forgings Ltd. Deccan submitted a resolution plan on 13.04.2018, approved by the CoC on 28.08.2018 and placed before NCLT for approval under Section 31. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial defaults by Metalyst Forgings Ltd. leading to admission in CP No. (IB) 1555 (IB)/MB/2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan approved by CoC on 28.08.2018; RP demanded performance guarantee on 15.10.2018; Deccan sought withdrawal via letter dated 17.10.2018 and MA No. 1272/2018 under Section 60(5). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: VDR data and Mott MacDonald Report (2016 MM Report) represented realistic production capacity as 210,747 MTPA, whereas actual production capacity was only ~45,000 to 66,000 MTPA; 70% of historical revenue was trading rather than manufacturing; a crucial 12,500-ton forging press required by the plan could not be installed on the debtor's land but belonged to Clover (sister concern in CIRP). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench vide order dated 27.09.2019 rejected Deccan's resolution plan, allowed withdrawal due to unfeasibility and misinformation, ordered re-bidding within 21 days, and clarified bid bond forfeiture would occur if Deccan did not participate/win fresh bidding. Both CoC and Deccan appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the power under Section 60(5) and Section 31(2) to reject an approved resolution plan and permit the successful resolution applicant to withdraw where the information memorandum contained material factual misrepresentations and the plan was fundamentally unfeasible, and whether the bidder's bid bond guarantee can be forfeited.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority cannot compel specific performance of an unfeasible resolution plan against an unwilling resolution applicant when the basis of the plan was contaminated by material misrepresentations in the Information Memorandum provided during CIRP, rendering the plan non-compliant under Section 30(2)(e). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5)(c) confers wide residuary jurisdiction to determine questions of fact and law arising in CIRP, while Section 31(2) empowers the Adjudicating Authority to reject a plan that fails the criteria of Section 30(2). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective discrepancy analysis comparing the representations made in the Information Memorandum/VDR against actual operational and technical capacity, establishing reliance on materially flawed and misleading data. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Rejection of the resolution plan by NCLT was justified due to unviability and lack of statutory power to compel specific performance; Deccan remained disentitled to refund of the bid bond guarantee under the tender terms.
operative_order: Both appeals (CA 1276 of 2019 and CA 1281 of 2019) are dismissed. NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 27.09.2019 is upheld. CoC permitted to evaluate other resolution plans without extension of time. No order as to costs.
summary: Deccan Value Investors LP submitted a resolution plan for Metalyst Forgings Ltd., approved by CoC in August 2018. Before NCLT approval, Deccan discovered that the Corporate Debtor's actual production capacity was ~45,000 MTPA compared to 210,747 MTPA represented in the Information Memorandum, that 70% of revenue came from undisclosed trading, and that land for essential equipment was unavailable. Deccan sought withdrawal under Section 60(5), which NCLT Mumbai allowed while rejecting the plan under Section 31(2) and withholding bid bond refund. CoC appealed the rejection, while Deccan appealed the bid bond clarification. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, affirming NCLT's refusal to force specific performance of an unworkable plan.

case_title: Rajesh Goyal vs. Babita Gupta & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rajesh Goyal, Promoter/Director of Corporate Debtor (Appellant); Babita Gupta, Manoj Kumar Gupta, and Sweta Gupta (Homebuyer Allottees / Financial Creditors / Respondents); Rajesh Projects (India) Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Gaurav Katiyar (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development of residential project comprising 1,920 flats in 9 towers (Towers A to H & M) in Phase-1; 1,650 units booked with collections of Rs. 595.75 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Delay in completion and delivery of residential flats; alleged institutional financial creditor debt of ~Rs. 81.48 Crores (Allahabad Bank, PNB, Indiabulls, IIFL). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed by allottees; NCLT Principal Bench admitted CIRP on 19.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Physical project structure reached 75% completion; superstructures of 9 towers completed; unaudited accounts established over Rs. 617 Crores spent directly on construction and project costs in line with RERA 70:30 norms; 95.74% of allottees voted in favor of project completion by promoter infusion outside CIRP without third-party resolution applicant. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted Section 7 application on 19.09.2019; promoter appealed challenging CIRP admission and offering 'Reverse CIRP'.
legal_issues: Whether in real estate corporate insolvency proceedings where a project is near completion, a 'Reverse Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process' can be invoked under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules, 2016, allowing the promoter to infuse funds as an outside lender to complete construction and deliver flats without handing over the entity to third-party resolution applicants.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In corporate insolvency proceedings involving real estate infrastructure companies, CIRP should be project-specific, and the Adjudicating Authority/Appellate Tribunal may permit a 'Reverse CIRP' allowing promoters to act as external financial lenders to complete construction and deliver units to allottees, obviating the necessity of third-party resolution applicants or liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) recognizes allottees as financial creditors whose primary interest is delivery of homes rather than liquidation haircuts; Rule 11 inherent powers can be invoked to fashion customized resolution mechanisms balancing stakeholder interests without liquidating viable infrastructure. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Supermajority consent of allottees (95.74%), advanced stage of physical project completion (75%), and concrete proof of external fund infusion capability by the promoter. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The project should be resolved through supervised promoter infusion under IRP control rather than conventional third-party plan bidding.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of with directions. Promoter directed to infuse Rs. 5.88 Crores immediately and approx. Rs. 70 Crores over scheduled timelines as an outside lender. Construction and internal fit-outs ordered for completion by 30.07.2020, common areas by 30.08.2020. Dues of financial institutions and refunds to dissenting allottees (at 6% p.a. interest) to be discharged within 180 days. IRP to supervise bank accounts and project completion, following which CIRP shall be closed.
summary: NCLT admitted a Section 7 CIRP application filed by homebuyer allottees against Rajesh Projects (India) Pvt. Ltd. Promoter Rajesh Goyal appealed, establishing that the project was 75% complete and proposing to infuse ~Rs. 70 Crores as an external lender to finish construction. Over 95% of allottees supported the proposal. Following the precedent in Umang Realtech, NCLAT applied the doctrine of 'Reverse CIRP' under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules, 2016, holding that real estate insolvencies should remain project-specific to deliver homes to allottees rather than forcing haircuts or liquidation. NCLAT directed supervised completion by August 2020 under IRP oversight, leading to CIRP closure upon completion.

case_title: Anubhav Anilkumar Agarwal vs. Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anubhav Anilkumar Agarwal, Director/Shareholder (Appellant); Bank of India (Respondent No. 1/Financial Creditor); RNA Corp. Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Guarantor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Term Loan facility of Rs. 75,00,00,000/- sanctioned vide letter dated 24.10.2013, secured by Deeds of Guarantee dated 29.10.2013 and 09.12.2013 and registered mortgage deeds. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account declared NPA on 31.12.2014; total default amount claimed as of 10.02.2019 was Rs. 80,73,76,364.84 (Principal: Rs. 40,58,23,360.83, Interest: Rs. 34,81,43,071.74, Penal Interest: Rs. 5,30,37,157.27, Legal Expenses: Rs. 3,72,775.00). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan sanctioned 24.10.2013; NPA declared 31.12.2014; SARFAESI notice under Section 13(2) issued 29.07.2015; Section 7 petition filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor sent a letter dated 18.03.2016 admitting borrowals, asserting absence of willful default, citing real estate slump, detailing prior payments of Rs. 5 Crores made between Dec 2015 and Jan 2016, and submitting an express repayment proposal to regularize dues. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted Bank of India's Section 7 petition on 26.11.2019. Appellant appealed on grounds of limitation and parallel proceedings against co-guarantor Chamber Constructions Pvt. Ltd.
legal_issues: Whether a signed written communication containing a proposal to repay outstanding bank dues and seeking regularization of an NPA account constitutes a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, sufficient to extend the period of limitation for filing an application under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The three-year limitation period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act for filing an application under Section 7 of the IBC is extended from the date of a written acknowledgment signed by the corporate debtor admitting its subsisting debt and expressing an intent to repay. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 applies to Section 7 proceedings; an unequivocal written communication acknowledging debt and offering repayment terms resets the starting point of limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of debtor's direct correspondence to determine conscious admission of liability; debtor's letter acknowledging loan liability and seeking restructuring satisfies Section 18. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the debtor submitted a signed letter on 18.03.2016 acknowledging liability and promising payment, a fresh three-year limitation period commenced, rendering the 2019 Section 7 filing well within limitation.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Order of NCLT Mumbai Bench dated 26.11.2019 initiating CIRP against RNA Corp. Pvt. Ltd. is upheld. No costs.
summary: Appellant challenged the NCLT Mumbai Bench's admission of Bank of India's Section 7 petition against RNA Corp. Pvt. Ltd., contending that the account had been declared NPA on 31.12.2014 and the three-year limitation expired on 31.12.2017. NCLAT held that the Corporate Debtor's signed letter dated 18.03.2016, which admitted indebtedness, referred to payments made in January 2016, and submitted a repayment proposal to regularize the account, constituted a valid acknowledgment of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. This created a fresh limitation period running up to March 2019, rendering the petition filed in 2019 timely. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Manesh Agarwal vs. Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Manesh Agarwal, Shareholder/Director (Appellant); Bank of India (Respondent No. 1/Financial Creditor); M/s B.B. Foods Private Limited (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities sanctioned to the Corporate Debtor by Bank of India aggregating Rs. 28,00,00,000/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account declared NPA on 29.01.2013; total claimed default amount of Rs. 40,33,04,620/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NPA classified 29.01.2013; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice issued 06.03.2013; Section 19 DRT recovery filed 04.07.2015; Section 7 petition filed 29.09.2018; NCLT admitted CIRP on 22.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor executed written debt acknowledgment on 13.04.2015; submitted written OTS offer on 01.06.2016; further submitted OTS proposal on 05.10.2018 with Rs. 1.60 Crores payment via Demand Draft; Bank also recovered Rs. 4,93,10,000/- through SARFAESI sale. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Bank filed CP (IB) No. 349/ALD/2018 before NCLT Allahabad; debtor opposed solely on grounds of limitation; NCLT admitted CIRP on 22.10.2019.
legal_issues: Whether written acknowledgments and One Time Settlement proposals executed consecutively within successive three-year windows from the date of NPA classification extend the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for filing a Section 7 IBC application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a written acknowledgment of liability executed before the expiration of the prescribed three-year period under Article 137 resets the limitation clock, allowing successive timely acknowledgments to continuously maintain an enforceable debt under Section 7 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 applies to Section 7 IBC petitions via Section 238A; an OTS offer constitutes an unequivocal admission of a subsisting debtor-creditor relationship and renews the period of limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented verification of executed acknowledgment letters and OTS proposals accompanied by part-payments to establish unbroken continuity within successive three-year limitation windows. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Fresh three-year limitation periods commenced on 13.04.2015 and 01.06.2016, making the Section 7 petition filed on 29.09.2018 fully timely.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Impugned admission order dated 22.10.2019 passed by NCLT Allahabad Bench is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant challenged the NCLT Allahabad Bench's admission of Bank of India's Section 7 petition against M/s B.B. Foods Pvt. Ltd., asserting that since the account became NPA on 29.01.2013, the claim was barred after 29.01.2016 under Article 137 of the Limitation Act. The NCLAT held that the Corporate Debtor executed a written acknowledgment on 13.04.2015 and submitted an OTS proposal on 01.06.2016, both within the three-year limitation periods. Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, each acknowledgment reset the three-year clock. The Section 7 application filed on 29.09.2018 was therefore within limitation, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Hammond Power Solutions Private Limited vs. Sanjit Kumar Nayak & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Hammond Power Solutions Private Limited (Operational Creditor/Appellant); Sanjit Kumar Nayak (Resolution Professional/Respondent No. 1); Committee of Creditors of Marsons Limited through Allahabad Bank (Respondent No. 2); Marsons Limited (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 3); Yashoda Inn Pvt. Ltd. & Uneecops Solar Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicants/Respondent Nos. 4 & 5). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods/operational services to Marsons Limited resulting in unpaid operational debt admitted during CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Average liquidation value of the Corporate Debtor was determined to be Rs. 34,02,78,000/-; admitted claims of secured financial creditors and workmen totaled Rs. 100.816 Crores; resolution amount offered was Rs. 40.8490 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Revised resolution plan submitted and approved by CoC on 14.03.2019; approved by NCLT Kolkata on 09.05.2019 in CP (IB) No. 628/KB/2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Earlier resolution plan dated 06.02.2019 proposed paying Operational Creditors Rs. 2.668 Crores out of Rs. 35.641 Crores; following negotiations, revised plan reduced overall payout to Rs. 34.95 Crores and reduced operational creditors' distribution to NIL, recording no reasons for the total denial. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata approved the resolution plan on 09.05.2019; Operational Creditor appealed on grounds that allocating NIL violated Section 30(2) and Supreme Court principles in Essar Steel.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan approved by the CoC that reduces payments to operational creditors from Rs. 2.668 Crores to NIL without providing any cogent reasons in the CoC minutes satisfies the requirements of Section 30(2) of the IBC and the legal principles laid down in Essar Steel regarding balancing the interests of all stakeholders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors governs distribution of funds, its decision must be supported by reasons showing that it considered the objective of maximizing asset value and balancing the interests of all stakeholders, including operational creditors; allocating NIL to operational creditors without reasoned deliberation violates Section 30(2)(e). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) and Section 30(2)(e) read with Regulation 38 require that the resolution plan protect operational creditors to keep the corporate debtor a going concern; allocating NIL solely because liquidation value is deemed insufficient, while negotiating down previous provisions, does not satisfy statutory scrutiny. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of CoC minutes to verify whether the CoC recorded objective reasoning demonstrating active consideration of stakeholder balancing. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan failed to comply with Section 30(2) because the CoC minutes contained no reasons justifying the reduction of operational creditors' dues to NIL, requiring remand to the CoC.
operative_order: Appeal allowed. Impugned order dated 09.05.2019 approving the Resolution Plan is set aside. The matter is remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority with directions to send the Resolution Plan back to the Committee of Creditors for resubmission in accordance with the parameters laid down in Essar Steel and the IBC within a specified time period. No order as to costs.
summary: An operational creditor appealed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench's approval of a resolution plan for Marsons Ltd submitted by a consortium of Yashoda Inn and Uneecops Solar. The initial resolution plan allocated Rs. 2.668 Crores to operational creditors, but following negotiations, the revised plan reduced this allocation to NIL without any rationale recorded in the CoC minutes. The NCLAT held that under the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel, the commercial wisdom of the CoC must reflect deliberate balancing of all stakeholders' interests and preservation of going-concern status. Finding no justifiable reasons on record for allotting NIL to operational creditors, NCLAT set aside the approval order and remanded the plan to the CoC for reconsideration.

case_title: Rakesh Kumar Gupta vs. Mahesh Bansal & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rakesh Kumar Gupta, Director of Corporate Debtor (Appellant); Mahesh Bansal (IRP/Respondent No. 1); Punjab National Bank (Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 2); Gupta Marriage Halls Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by Punjab National Bank to Gupta Marriage Halls Pvt. Ltd. secured by mortgaged immovable properties. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan account classified as NPA on 28.10.2016; debt remained unpaid and in default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 28.10.2016; Section 7 application filed on 23.03.2019; admitted by NCLT New Delhi on 03.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Postal department delivery confirmations establishing delivery of notice at the registered office of the Corporate Debtor on 01.05.2019; affidavits of service dated 14.05.2019, 18.07.2019, and 07.08.2019; appellant failed to establish that the financial debt was not due or payable. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: PNB initiated SARFAESI measures and filed DRT recovery proceedings in Lucknow; subsequently filed Section 7 IBC application (IB-979/ND/2019); NCLT New Delhi admitted petition on 03.09.2019 after Corporate Debtor failed to appear despite service.
legal_issues: Whether parallel pending recovery proceedings under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 and before the Debt Recovery Tribunal under the RDDBFI Act, 1993 preclude a financial creditor from initiating CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC, and whether service of notice on the corporate debtor's registered office satisfies the principles of natural justice without separate service on individual directors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The pendency of recovery proceedings under the SARFAESI Act or before the DRT does not bar a financial creditor from initiating Section 7 CIRP against a corporate debtor, as IBC proceedings aim at insolvency resolution rather than debt recovery, and the Code overrides inconsistent enactments by virtue of Section 238. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of IBC explicitly gives the Code overriding effect over other laws including the SARFAESI Act, 2002 and RDDBFI Act, 1993; Section 7 remedies operate independently of civil recovery suits. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Postal verification and delivery certificates establishing valid dispatch and receipt of notice at the corporate debtor's registered office suffice to demonstrate proper statutory service. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Admission under Section 7 was lawful because the debt and default were unrefuted, service was legally completed at the registered office, and SARFAESI/DRT actions create no legal impediment to IBC initiation.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Order of NCLT New Delhi Court No. III dated 03.09.2019 admitting Section 7 application is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: The Director of Gupta Marriage Halls Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT New Delhi order admitting Punjab National Bank's Section 7 IBC application. The Appellant argued lack of personal service on directors and contended that PNB's parallel proceedings under the SARFAESI Act and DRT barred it from invoking the IBC. The NCLAT rejected both contentions, holding that postal tracking proved valid service at the debtor's registered address and that, under Section 238 of the IBC, the Code has overriding effect over other enactments. Pending SARFAESI or DRT proceedings do not prevent a creditor from seeking resolution under Section 7. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: M/s Steel India vs. Theme Developers Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Steel India, a registered partnership firm (Appellant/Operational Creditor); Theme Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and delivery of steel bars for construction activities under four invoices dated 30.07.2015 (Invoice Nos. S1/086, S1/100, S1/101, S1/102). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal claim of Rs. 13,35,952/- plus interest of Rs. 22,64,054/- calculated @ 2% per month on delayed payments; principal amount of Rs. 13,35,952/- was paid in full on 28.01.2019, leaving only the interest claim of Rs. 22,64,054/- in dispute. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First demand notice in Form-3 issued on 28.12.2018; dispute raised by debtor on 10.01.2019; principal paid via RTGS on 28.01.2019; second demand notice issued on 15.01.2019; Section 9 petition filed in 2019 in CP (IB) No. 843/MB/2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant relied solely on a unilateral quotation email dated 05.09.2015 containing a clause for 2% interest per month if payment delayed beyond 60 days; invoices and supply orders contained no agreed stipulation for interest; Corporate Debtor explicitly disputed interest liability upon receiving the first notice. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected the Section 9 petition on 23.07.2019 on grounds that the application pursued solely interest after principal was paid, demonstrating a pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6)(a). Operational Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a petition under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable solely for the recovery of disputed delayed-payment interest when the entire principal operational debt has already been paid, and whether a unilateral interest condition in a quotation constitutes an agreed operational debt.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC cannot be maintained solely for the recovery of disputed interest after the principal debt has been paid; pursuing insolvency proceedings exclusively as a tool for interest recovery constitutes an impermissible debt collection mechanism under Section 65. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(6)(a) and Section 9 bar admission when a pre-existing dispute regarding interest liability is documented prior to statutory demand notices; interest does not constitute an operational debt unless unequivocally agreed upon between the parties. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unilateral terms in quotation emails unsupported by mutual acceptance or stipulations in purchase orders/invoices fail to prove an enforceable contractual obligation for interest. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debtor having cleared the principal debt and disputed the interest liability prior to the Section 8 notice, the petition involved a pre-existing dispute and was properly rejected.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Order dated 23.07.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench rejecting the Section 9 application is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: M/s Steel India supplied steel bars to Theme Developers Pvt. Ltd. under invoices raised in 2015. After receiving a demand notice in December 2018, the Corporate Debtor paid the principal debt of Rs. 13,35,952/- via RTGS and formally disputed the claim of Rs. 22,64,054/- towards delayed payment interest. The Operational Creditor issued a second demand notice and filed a Section 9 IBC petition solely for interest based on a quotation email. NCLAT held that pursuing insolvency purely for interest recovery after the principal debt is cleared is contrary to the object of the IBC and barred under Section 65. Furthermore, since interest was not agreed in the contract and was disputed prior to the demand notice, the rejection by NCLT was affirmed.

case_title: Bank of India vs. Shrenuj & Company Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bank of India (Financial Creditor / Appellant); Shrenuj & Company Limited (Corporate Debtor / Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Extension of multiple fund-based and non-fund-based credit facilities to the tune of Rs. 205.00 Crores from 2005 onwards against hypothecation/pledge of diamond stocks. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of the loan facility of Rs. 205 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed on 06.01.2018; admission order passed by NCLT Mumbai on 12.03.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor did not deny financial debt and default, but alleged in reply that diamond stock hypothecated/seized by ICICI Bank's Court Receiver (initially valued by debtor at Rs. 1561.87 Crores) was replaced with fake/inferior stones valued at only Rs. 199.51 Crores, and filed an EOW police complaint. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 7 petition on 12.03.2019 but made adverse disparaging remarks in paragraphs 31–33 against the bank authorities for being 'blinded by the shine of fake diamonds' and directed IRP to report the order to ED, EOW, IT, and SFIO. Bank appealed against these observations.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority while adjudicating a Section 7 IBC application has jurisdiction to make adverse, disparaging remarks against the Financial Creditor regarding the valuation and veracity of pledged securities under active criminal/regulatory investigation, and whether such remarks must be expunged.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While adjudicating an application under Section 7 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority's jurisdiction is confined to ascertaining the existence of financial debt and default; it must not record disparaging observations on collateral allegations of fraud or security valuation that are extraneous to the lis and pending investigation by independent authorities. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 read with Section 3(10), (11), and (12) requires satisfaction strictly of debt and default; peripheral disputes regarding security misappropriation do not impact CIRP admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The three-prong test from State of U.P. v. Mohammad Naim: (a) opportunity of explanation, (b) justification by record, and (c) necessity for deciding the lis. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The adverse remarks made against the Appellant-Bank were avoidable, beyond the scope of Section 7 adjudication, and must not prejudice independent ongoing investigations.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of. Adverse remarks made against the Appellant Bank in paragraphs 31, 32, and 33 of the NCLT order are held avoidable and clarified not to affect ongoing investigations or form the basis of holding adversely against the Bank or its officials. No costs.
summary: Bank of India appealed against adverse remarks made by the NCLT Mumbai Bench while admitting its Section 7 petition against Shrenuj & Co. Ltd. Although debt and default were established, the NCLT incorporated severe remarks against bank officials concerning hypothecated diamonds alleged by the Corporate Debtor to be fake or switched, directing copies to investigative agencies (EOW, SFIO, ED). NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority's scope under Section 7 is strictly confined to ascertaining debt and default. Applying the Mohammad Naim doctrine, NCLAT held that such remarks were extraneous, avoidable, and shall not prejudice ongoing investigations.

case_title: K.B. Polychem (India) Ltd. vs. Kaygee Shoetech Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: K.B. Polychem (India) Ltd. (Operational Creditor / Appellant); Kaygee Shoetech Private Limited (Corporate Debtor / Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods under invoices raised between 03.03.2017 and 27.03.2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid operational debt in excess of Rs. 1,00,000/-; last partial payment of Rs. 4,08,205/- was made on 20.06.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 sent on 30.07.2018/01.08.2018; last payment on 20.06.2017; Section 9 application filed on 15.09.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Speed post to registered office returned marked 'not available', but notice sent to Director's residential address was not returned; Corporate Debtor in its reply affidavit before NCLT acknowledged receiving the demand notice and claimed it had replied to it, though it filed no pre-existing dispute documentation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the Section 9 petition on 27.08.2019 holding delivery of Section 8 demand notice was not established, reasoning IBC is a complete code excluding General Clauses Act and Evidence Act presumptions. Operational Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the presumption of valid service under Section 26 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 and Section 114 of the Evidence Act, 1872 applies to Section 8 demand notices under the IBC, and whether admission of receipt of demand notice in the debtor's reply cures an postal endorsement of 'not available'.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Delivery of a Section 8 demand notice is sufficiently established when sent by registered/speed post and reinforced by the corporate debtor's implicit or explicit admissions of receipt in its pleadings, satisfying statutory service requirements. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 and Section 9(5) mandate delivery of notice; where postal records show delivery to director addresses and the debtor responds to the contents without specific denial of receipt, delivery is legally complete. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluation of postal tracking reports and admissions in the corporate debtor's reply affidavit; absence of specific denial combined with admissions of sending a reply confirms service. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The operational debt exceeded Rs. 1 Lakh, default was within limitation (post 20.06.2017 payment), no pre-existing dispute existed, and notice was duly served; hence the rejection was erroneous.
operative_order: Appeal allowed. Impugned order dated 27.08.2019 is set aside. Adjudicating Authority directed to pass the order of admission under Section 9. Parties directed to appear before NCLT on 24.02.2020.
summary: K.B. Polychem appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order dismissing its Section 9 application on the ground that service of the Section 8 demand notice was not established since speed post to the registered office was returned 'not available'. NCLAT found that notice sent to the director's residence was not returned, and the debtor admitted in its reply that it had received and responded to the demand notice. With operational debt exceeding statutory threshold, no documented pre-existing dispute, and the application filed within three years of the last partial payment, NCLAT set aside the dismissal and directed NCLT to admit the Section 9 petition.

case_title: Gautam Sinha vs. UV Asset Reconstruction Company Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gautam Sinha, Ex-Director/Promoter of Kalpataru Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant); UV Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (Assignee Financial Creditor / Respondent No. 1); United Bank of India (Assignor Bank / Respondent No. 2); Anup Kumar Sinha (IRP / Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sanction of seasonal cash credit, working capital loan, and bank guarantee facilities by United Bank of India in 2006, assigned to UV ARCL on 29.03.2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged debt and default of Rs. 21,61,12,013/-; date of default stated as 31.12.2013; account declared NPA on 30.03.2014. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Default on 31.12.2013; NPA on 30.03.2014; SARFAESI 13(2) notice on 03.04.2014; OA 530/2015 filed in DRT; Section 7 application filed on 31.10.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Financial Creditor relied on balance sheet for year ending 31.03.2016. Auditor's report Note 29 explicitly stated that the company denied default, received no balance confirmations from the bank, did not provide for interest, and noted the bank's NPA declaration was sub-judice before DRT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted Section 7 application on 30.09.2019 relying on the 2016 balance sheet as an acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. Promoter appealed on limitation.
legal_issues: Whether a statement in an auditor's report attached to a company's balance sheet qualifying that the company has not defaulted in borrowings and noting that the lender's NPA classification is sub-judice before DRT amounts to an acknowledgment of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entry in a company's balance sheet cannot be construed as an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act unless read alongside the accompanying Directors' Report and Auditors' notes, which must reflect an unequivocal, conscious admission of subsisting liability and jural relationship. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 requires an intentional admission of a subsisting debtor-creditor relationship; a conditional notation highlighting dispute and asserting that no default was committed negates any admission of liability. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Holistic construction of balance sheet entries together with qualifying notes and directors' reports without relying on isolated liability entries. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The 2016 balance sheet contained a disclaimer rather than an admission; consequently, the Section 7 petition filed in 2018 for an NPA declared in 2014 was barred by limitation under Article 137.
operative_order: Appeal allowed. Impugned order dated 30.09.2019 admitting Section 7 application is quashed and set aside. Application under Section 7 dismissed. Corporate Debtor released from CIRP rigours and management restored to Board of Directors. IRP fees/costs to be paid by Financial Creditor.
summary: Promoter Gautam Sinha appealed against NCLT Kolkata's admission of UV Asset Reconstruction Co.'s Section 7 petition regarding Kalpataru Cold Storage. The account was classified as NPA on 30.03.2014, while the Section 7 petition was filed on 31.10.2018. NCLT held the claim was saved from limitation by debt acknowledgment in the debtor's 2016 balance sheet. NCLAT reviewed the balance sheet notes and discovered that the auditor specifically reported that the company claimed no default and stated that bank recovery was sub-judice before DRT. Holding that a qualified entry disputing default does not constitute an acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, NCLAT set aside the admission order as time-barred.

case_title: Ravinder Kumar Magoo vs. AMA India Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ravinder Kumar Magoo, 25% Shareholder/Petitioner (Appellant in CA 95/2019 / Respondent No. 1 in CA 103/2019); AMA India Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. (Company / Respondent No. 1 / Appellant in CA 103/2019); Alessandro Malavolti, 75% Shareholder/CEO (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint venture entity incorporated on 26.02.1999 with 5,613,632 equity shares of Rs. 10 each. Appellant filed an oppression/mismanagement petition under Sections 397/398 of Companies Act, 1956. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Valuation and exit pricing of petitioner's 25% equity holding pursuant to CLB order dated 02.01.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CLB order directing valuation as of 31.03.2014 passed on 02.01.2015; initial valuer report submitted 16.04.2015; revised valuation report submitted 12.10.2015; NCLT order passed 21.01.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuer determined adjusted fair value per share at Rs. 21.725 and added 20% control premium arriving at Rs. 26.07; NCLT reduced valuation adjustment by 8% based on Cost Inflation Index to Rs. 21.483, removed 20% control premium, and granted 12% interest from 05.02.2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench modified valuer report on 21.01.2019; both shareholder and company cross-appealed regarding control premium, cost inflation adjustment, and interest rate.
legal_issues: Whether a 20% control premium can be added to the fair valuation of a minority (25%) shareholder's exit when the acquiring majority shareholder already holds 75% controlling interest, and what is the reasonable rate of interest payable on delayed exit consideration.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A control premium is payable exclusively to acquire a controlling stake in a company; where the majority shareholder already holds effective control (75%), acquiring an outgoing minority 25% stake confers no new controlling interest, disentitling the minority shareholder to a control premium. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Fair valuation for exiting minority members under oppression and mismanagement orders must reflect actual economic value without inflating minority exit costs via inapplicable control premiums. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of capital structure and shareholding percentages under ICAI valuation standards CAS-1; expert valuation adjustments based on the Cost Inflation Index are legally tenable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT correctly excised the 20% control premium and applied the 8% Cost Inflation Index adjustment; however, given prevailing economic conditions, the 12% interest awarded is excessive and reduced to 9% simple interest p.a.
operative_order: Appeals disposed of. Impugned order of NCLT Chandigarh Bench dated 21.01.2019 is upheld regarding valuation and removal of control premium, but modified reducing the rate of interest from 12% to 9% simple interest per annum. Respondent company directed to pay consideration with interest within 30 days. No costs.
summary: In an oppression and mismanagement exit proceeding, the independent valuer fixed fair value at Rs. 21.725 per share and added a 20% control premium (Rs. 26.07) for Ravinder Kumar Magoo's 25% stake. NCLT Chandigarh removed the 20% control premium, adjusted the valuation by 8% using the Cost Inflation Index (Rs. 21.483), and awarded 12% interest. On appeal, NCLAT affirmed the removal of the control premium, holding that since the majority shareholder already held 75%, acquiring the minority stake did not confer control. Factoring prevailing market conditions, NCLAT modified the interest rate from 12% to 9% per annum and directed payment within 30 days.

case_title: Meena V. Kothari vs. M/s Maberest Hotels Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Meena V. Kothari through SPA holder Dilip V. Kothari (Appellant / Financial Creditor); M/s Maberest Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Temporary financial assistance loan of Rs. 10 Lakhs advanced on 12.08.2002 at 18% per annum repayable within 6 to 12 months. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 10 Lakhs plus 18% interest per annum; date of default determined as 25.11.2007. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Last balance confirmation letter dated 01.04.2007; demand letter dated 17.09.2007; legal notice served on 04.11.2007 giving 3 weeks to pay (expiry 25.11.2007); Section 7 petition filed on 17.04.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Winding-up Petition No. 25/2009 was disposed of directing appellant to file a civil suit; Civil Suit No. 165/2010 was rejected under Order VII Rule 11(d) CPC on 05.10.2018 as barred by limitation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai rejected Section 7 application on 29.03.2019 holding the debt was contingent upon civil court outcome. Financial Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the limitation period of three years under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for filing a Section 7 IBC application is suspended or extended by the pendency of a civil suit or appeal arising from a rejected plaint.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For an application under Section 7 of the IBC, the right to sue accrues on the date default occurs; the pendency of independent civil suits, recovery proceedings, or appellate challenges thereto neither suspends nor revives the three-year limitation period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5) requires the Adjudicating Authority to determine if a debt is due and payable in law and fact; where the default occurred over three years prior to filing and was not saved by timely acknowledgment under Section 18, the debt is not legally enforceable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Computation of statutory time elapsed from the expiry of the cure period stipulated in the creditor's legal demand notice (25.11.2007) to the filing date of the petition (17.04.2018). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Default occurred on 25.11.2007 upon non-compliance with the legal notice; the Section 7 petition filed more than a decade later on 17.04.2018 was hopelessly barred by limitation under Article 137.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Order dated 29.03.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench rejecting the Section 7 application is affirmed, modified to the extent that the petition is dismissed as barred by limitation. No order as to costs.
summary: Meena V. Kothari advanced a loan of Rs. 10 Lakhs to Maberest Hotels Pvt. Ltd. in 2002. Following balance confirmations up to 01.04.2007, she issued a legal notice giving the debtor three weeks to repay, which expired on 25.11.2007. Parallel civil proceedings ended with the rejection of the plaint under Order VII Rule 11(d) CPC as time-barred. The creditor filed a Section 7 IBC application on 17.04.2018, which NCLT Mumbai rejected as contingent on civil proceedings. NCLAT clarified that while NCLT erred regarding contingency, the application was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, as default occurred on 25.11.2007 and was filed over ten years later.

case_title: Vishal Doshi vs. Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vishal Doshi, Shareholder/Promoter/Director (Appellant); Bank of India (Financial Creditor / Respondent No. 1); Shrenuj & Company Limited (Corporate Debtor / Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple loan facilities extended by Bank of India Consortium (including ICICI Bank, SBI, UBI, PNB) amounting to Rs. 205 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment exceeding Rs. 226 Crores; ICICI Bank recalled loans claiming Rs. 1,65,71,12,358.13; loan declared NPA on 31.03.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account NPA 31.03.2016; loan recall notice 02.05.2016; reply admitting difficulty 09.05.2016; DRT OA 406/2016 filed June 2016; Section 7 petition admitted 12.03.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor admitted financial distress in reply letter dated 09.05.2016; debtor raised counter-claim of Rs. 1561.87 Crores for alleged missing/swapped pledged diamond stock seized by DRT Receiver and filed EOW police complaint. Official valuation was Rs. 199.51 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted Bank of India's Section 7 petition on 12.03.2019; promoter appealed alleging debt was extinguished via set-off against seized stock damages.
legal_issues: Whether unadjudicated counter-claims or claims for set-off in the nature of damages regarding pledged assets can be adjudicated by the Adjudicating Authority to bar or defeat admission of an application under Section 7 of the IBC where financial debt and default are established.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority is strictly mandated to admit an application under Section 7 of the IBC once financial debt and default are established; claims for set-off or unliquidated counter-claims for damages cannot be adjudicated at the threshold stage of admission to resist CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Unlike Section 9, Section 7 does not permit raising pre-existing disputes; by virtue of Section 238, pending DRT proceedings or cross-claims provide no impediment to triggering CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unrefuted documentary proof of sanction, disbursement, and admitted failure to pay; unsubstantiated damage claims unsupported by official valuation cannot set off admitted financial debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Financial debt and default were conclusively established from the record; set-off and counter-claims are preserved for claim verification during CIRP and cannot defeat Section 7 admission.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Order dated 12.03.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench admitting Section 7 application is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Vishal Doshi, promoter of Shrenuj & Co. Ltd., appealed the admission of Bank of India's Section 7 petition for default exceeding Rs. 226 Crores. The Appellant argued that the financial debt was extinguished by equitable set-off, alleging that pledged diamond stocks worth Rs. 1,561.87 Crores seized by a DRT receiver were misappropriated and undervalued at Rs. 199.51 Crores. The NCLAT held that under Section 7 of the IBC, once financial debt and default are established, the Adjudicating Authority must admit the application. Following Swiss Ribbons, claims of set-off or damage counter-claims cannot be determined at admission and must be relegated to claim collation during CIRP. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Punjab National Bank vs. M/s Vindhya Cereals Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Punjab National Bank (Financial Creditor / Appellant); M/s Vindhya Cereals Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lending facilities granted by PNB to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of loan facilities exceeding statutory threshold. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice issued on 03.01.2017; Section 7 petition filed in March–April 2018 in CP (IB) No. 20/7/NCLT/AHM/2018; impugned order passed on 19.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor sent OTS proposal during pendency; PNB had ongoing SARFAESI auction measures disclosed transparently in Section 7 application; no suppression of facts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 19.07.2019 held that pursuing SARFAESI auction while filing under Section 7 amounted to forum shopping and issued a show cause notice under Section 65 IBC to PNB's Chief Manager. PNB appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor is precluded from initiating an application under Section 7 of the IBC due to ongoing parallel proceedings and auction measures under the SARFAESI Act, 2002, and whether pursuing such parallel statutory remedies amounts to fraudulent or malicious initiation under Section 65 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A financial creditor is fully entitled to pursue simultaneous proceedings under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 and under Section 7 of the IBC; initiating CIRP alongside SARFAESI recovery does not constitute forum shopping or fraudulent/malicious initiation under Section 65. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 provides that IBC overrides all inconsistent laws, and Section 60(4) vests powers of DRT in NCLT; the Code enables filing irrespective of pending SARFAESI proceedings, which automatically become subject to moratorium under Section 14 once admitted. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Clear disclosure of pending SARFAESI actions in the Section 7 petition refutes any allegation of bad faith or factual suppression. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in treating legitimate multi-track enforcement as forum shopping and penalizing bank officials under Section 65.
operative_order: Appeal allowed. Impugned show cause order dated 19.07.2019 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench is set aside. Adjudicating Authority directed to decide the Section 7 application expeditiously in accordance with law. No order as to costs.
summary: Punjab National Bank appealed an order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench which held that PNB engaged in forum shopping by pursuing SARFAESI auction measures alongside a Section 7 IBC application, and directed PNB's Chief Manager to show cause why penalties under Section 65 should not be imposed. NCLAT set aside the impugned order, ruling that the IBC does not preclude a financial creditor from proceeding simultaneously under SARFAESI and the Code. By virtue of the non-obstante clause in Section 238, IBC proceedings operate independently. The transparent disclosure of parallel proceedings negated any finding of malicious intent under Section 65.

case_title: IFCI Ltd. vs. M/s ACCIL Hospitality Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: IFCI Ltd. (Financial Creditor / Appellant); Asian Colour Coated Ispat Limited (Principal Borrower); M/s ACCIL Hospitality Ltd. (Corporate Guarantor / Corporate Debtor / Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Loan Agreement for Rs. 150 Crores disbursed in two tranches (Rs. 35.07 Cr on 28.08.2014 and Rs. 114.93 Cr on 20.09.2014) secured by Corporate Guarantee executed by ACCIL Hospitality Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal Borrower account classified as NPA on 30.09.2016; total claim of Rs. 227,48,91,019.15. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NPA on 30.09.2016; loan recalled and guarantees invoked 16.02.2016; SARFAESI notice 03.05.2017; CIRP against Principal Borrower admitted on 20.07.2018 in CP (IB) No. 562/2018; claim filed and admitted in full on 20.07.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: IFCI submitted its entire claim of Rs. 227.48 Crores before the Resolution Professional in the ongoing CIRP of Principal Borrower (Asian Colour Coated Ispat Ltd.), where it was collated and admitted in full, and a resolution plan approved by 79.3% CoC was pending NCLT approval. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IFCI subsequently filed Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 1167(PB)/2019 against the Corporate Guarantor; NCLT Principal Bench dismissed it on 21.10.2019 based on the bar against duplicate claims under the Piramal doctrine.
legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor can trigger a fresh Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 7 of the IBC against a Corporate Guarantor for the identical claim and default that has already been submitted, collated, and admitted in its entirety in an ongoing CIRP against the Principal Borrower.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a financial creditor's claim has been filed, collated, and admitted in its entirety by the Resolution Professional in an ongoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against the principal borrower, a second application under Section 7 for the identical claim and default cannot be admitted against the corporate guarantor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While surety liability is coextensive under Section 128 of the Contract Act, the IBC scheme bars concurrent duplicate CIRP admissions by the same creditor for the identical debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Complete identity of the default amount, underlying credit contract, and full collation of the claim by the Resolution Professional in the principal borrower's CIRP. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Applying the binding precedent in Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal v. Piramal Enterprises Ltd., initiating a second CIRP against the guarantor constitutes impermissible duplicity of claims.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Impugned order dated 21.10.2019 passed by NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi rejecting the Section 7 application is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: IFCI Ltd. granted a loan of Rs. 150 Crores to Asian Colour Coated Ispat Ltd. guaranteed by ACCIL Hospitality Ltd. Following default, SBI initiated CIRP against the principal borrower, wherein IFCI filed its entire claim of Rs. 227.48 Crores, which was collated and admitted in full by the RP. Pending resolution plan approval, IFCI filed a Section 7 petition against the corporate guarantor for the same debt. NCLT dismissed the petition, and NCLAT affirmed, ruling under the Piramal doctrine that a financial creditor cannot trigger a second CIRP against a corporate guarantor for the identical set of claims already fully admitted in the principal borrower's CIRP.

case_title: Action Barter Private Limited vs. SREI Equipment Finance Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Action Barter Private Limited (Shareholder / Appellant); SREI Equipment Finance Limited (Financial Creditor / Respondent No. 1); Shree Ram Urban Infrastructure Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Respondent No. 2); Srigopal Choudhary (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit financing facility extended by SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. to Shree Ram Urban Infrastructure Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of financial facilities. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court of Bombay admitted winding-up petition against the debtor on 05.10.2016; Official Liquidator appointed as Provisional Liquidator on 15.11.2017; Official Liquidator took over debtor's assets on 17.04.2018; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 494/NCLT/MB/2019 admitted by NCLT Mumbai on 06.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Shareholder contested admission pointing to prior admission of winding-up proceedings, appointment of provisional liquidator, and physical takeover of debtor's assets. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted SREI's Section 7 application on 06.11.2019. Appellant shareholder appealed on the ground that CIRP cannot be triggered once a provisional liquidator is appointed in High Court winding-up proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether the admission of a winding-up petition and appointment of a Provisional Liquidator by a High Court bars a Financial Creditor from initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The admission of a winding-up petition or appointment of a provisional liquidator by a High Court under the Companies Act does not preclude an independent financial creditor from initiating CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC against the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the Supreme Court ruling in Forech India Ltd., Section 11(d) of the IBC only bars a corporate debtor from initiating voluntary insolvency under Section 10 after a liquidation order has been passed; it does not restrict financial creditors under Section 7, whose application constitutes an independent statutory remedy. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessing whether the proceeding under challenge is an independent Section 7 application by a financial creditor as distinct from an ineligible voluntary corporate debtor application. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: SREI's Section 7 application was maintainable notwithstanding pending winding-up proceedings before the High Court; parties have liberty to apply under the proviso to Section 434 of the Companies Act, 2013 to transfer winding-up petitions to the NCLT.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Order dated 06.11.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench admitting the Section 7 petition is upheld. Liberty granted to appellant to move the Bombay High Court for transfer of winding-up proceedings to NCLT. No order as to costs.
summary: Action Barter Pvt. Ltd., a shareholder of Shree Ram Urban Infrastructure Ltd., appealed against NCLT Mumbai's admission of SREI Equipment Finance Ltd.'s Section 7 IBC petition. The Appellant contended the petition was barred because the Bombay High Court had already admitted a winding-up petition in 2016 and appointed a Provisional Liquidator who took custody of the debtor's properties. Following the Supreme Court's ruling in Forech India Ltd. v. Edelweiss ARC, NCLAT held that Section 11(d) applies only to corporate debtor applications under Section 10 and does not bar financial creditors from invoking Section 7, which operates as an independent proceeding. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Goodwill Tracon Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Oriental Bank of Commerce & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 940 of 2019 and 941 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Oriental Bank of Commerce is the Financial Creditor; RDH Technologies Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Saurav Mukherjee (Erstwhile Director) and M/s Goodwill Tracon Private Limited are the Appellants. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Financial Creditor sanctioned a term loan facility of Rs. 23,00,000,000/- on 17.04.2007 against an equitable mortgage of 0.34 acres of leasehold land and construction thereon at Plot No. F1, Block GP, Electronics Complex, Sector V, Salt Lake City, Kolkata, and pledge of shares. The Corporate Debtor also stood as Corporate Guarantor for five group entities (M/s Bahubali Commercial Pvt. Ltd., M/s Safal Dealers Pvt. Ltd., M/s Gandhyanya Properties Pvt. Ltd., M/s Purushotam Trade Promotion Pvt. Ltd., and M/s Rameshwaram Trexim Pvt. Ltd.). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor availed Rs. 6.70 crore approx without commensurate work, leading to a recall letter on 06.03.2010. The account was classified as NPA on 15.12.2012 with default date cited as 16.09.2012. Total claimed default was Rs. 7,54,68,438/- as on 30.09.2018 for the direct loan, and Rs. 19,04,12,812.21 across the 5 corporate guarantees. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Recall notice was issued on 06.03.2010; a liquidation-of-claims modification agreement was executed on 04.03.2015; balance and security confirmation letter was signed on 01.08.2017; demand notice issued on 26.09.2018; Section 7 petition filed on 08.12.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered RoC modification of charge dated 02.11.2015; agreement stipulating liquidation of claims dated 04.03.2015 acknowledging Rs. 7,38,61,086/- utilization; signed balance confirmation dated 01.08.2017 acknowledging debit balance of Rs. 6,63,31,700.00 as of 30.06.2017; certified bank statements under the Bankers Books Evidence Act showing continuous part payments from 28.12.2013 up to 29.07.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application CP (IB) No. 1671/KB/2018 was filed before NCLT Kolkata Bench, which admitted the CIRP application on 28.08.2019 rejecting the defense of limitation on ground of continuous part payments till 29.07.2017.
legal_issues: Whether the application under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and whether Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to extend the limitation period for initiating CIRP based on written acknowledgments of debt.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 7 of the Code is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act (three-year period), but Section 18 of the Limitation Act operates to renew the limitation period upon a valid, signed acknowledgment of subsisting liability made prior to the expiration of the initial or running limitation period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to proceedings under the Code by virtue of Section 238A. A signed written acknowledgment of liability does not create a fresh cause of action but renews the debt and triggers the computation of a fresh three-year limitation period from the date of execution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the test from J.C. Budhraja and Shapoor Freedom Mazda, the writing must consciously admit a subsisting jural debtor-creditor relationship before the expiration of the prescribed period; continuous part-payments reflected in certified bank ledgers coupled with written agreements and balance confirmations satisfy this standard. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Default occurred in 2012 with a 3-year limitation ending in December 2015; however, the modification agreement of 04.03.2015 extended limitation to 03.03.2018, and subsequent balance confirmation of 01.08.2017 (and payments up to 29.07.2017) validly extended the period by three years up to August 2020, making the Section 7 petition filed on 08.12.2018 timely.
operative_order: The appeals are rejected without costs. The interim stay on the constitution of the Committee of Creditors granted on 11.09.2019 is vacated, and the Interim Resolution Professional is directed to proceed with the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process forthwith.
summary: Oriental Bank of Commerce filed an application under Section 7 of the IBC against corporate debtor RDH Technologies Pvt. Ltd., which had defaulted on a term loan and corporate guarantee obligations, with its account declared NPA on 15.12.2012. Appellants challenged the NCLT Kolkata Bench's admission order solely on the ground of limitation. The NCLAT held that Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to Section 7 petitions; the execution of an agreement on 04.03.2015 and subsequent balance confirmation on 01.08.2017, alongside verified part-payments up to 29.07.2017, each triggered fresh 3-year limitation periods. Consequently, the petition filed on 08.12.2018 was well within limitation. The appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Manoj Kunwar vs. Oriental Bank of Commerce & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Manoj Kunwar (Promoter and Ex-Director of M/s SSMP Industries Ltd.) is the Appellant; Oriental Bank of Commerce (holding 99.4% debt) is Respondent No. 1; M/s Impex Services India Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 2; Yogesh Sethi (Liquidator) is Respondent No. 3; M/s SSMP Industries Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (an MSME). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit/lending facilities extended by Oriental Bank of Commerce to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dues of Oriental Bank of Commerce amounted to approximately Rs. 16 Crores; liquidation value of the company was assessed at Rs. 1.5 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority passed an order of liquidation on 31.07.2019; OTS proposal submitted by the promoter offering Rs. 8.5 Crores with 5% upfront deposit was formally rejected by Respondent No. 1 via letter dated 03.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Rejection letter of OTS dated 03.02.2020 marked as Exhibit X; verification that Oriental Bank of Commerce held 99.4% voting/debt share and held securities against the loans. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bench-III, New Delhi ordered liquidation of the Corporate Debtor under the IBC on 31.07.2019, which was assailed by the promoter on appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an order of liquidation under the IBC should be set aside due to a rejected OTS offer from an MSME promoter, and whether a liquidator is mandated to pursue a compromise or arrangement scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 before proceeding to sell the corporate debtor's assets in liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order of liquidation will not be interfered with merely because a creditor rejected an OTS proposal; however, liquidation remains a measure of last resort, and the liquidator is legally obligated to explore compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 and going-concern sale before piecemeal asset dissolution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with IBBI Liquidation Process Regulations (Regulation 32) applies to liquidation proceedings under IBC, requiring the liquidator to take steps for revival and preservation of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Commercial wisdom of secured creditors holding 99.4% debt to reject an OTS in favor of realization from security assets is upheld, but subject to the statutory procedural priority of examining revival under Section 230. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: There was no legal ground to interfere with the NCLT's liquidation order, but the liquidation must proceed strictly in terms of the revival mechanism delineated in Y. Shivram Prasad vs. S. Dhanapal.
operative_order: Interference with the Impugned Order is declined and the appeal is disposed of with directions in terms of Y. Shivram Prasad vs. S. Dhanapal: Liquidator directed to first invite schemes of compromise/arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013, failing which the business must be offered for sale as a going concern, before proceeding with the piecemeal asset liquidation.
summary: The promoter of MSME corporate debtor M/s SSMP Industries Ltd. appealed against NCLT New Delhi's liquidation order dated 31.07.2019, arguing that an OTS offer of Rs. 8.5 Crores against a liquidation value of Rs. 1.5 Crores was arbitrarily rejected by Oriental Bank of Commerce (holding 99.4% debt). Oriental Bank opposed on grounds that total dues were Rs. 16 Crores and recovery through securities was preferred. The NCLAT refused to set aside the liquidation order but disposed of the appeal by directing the liquidator to follow the protocol in Y. Shivram Prasad: first explore compromise/arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013, then sale as a going concern, and resort to asset dissolution only upon failure of revival.

case_title: Duke Sponge and Iron Pvt. Ltd. vs. Laxmi Foils Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Duke Sponge and Iron Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor/Appellant; Laxmi Foils Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 1; Respondents 2 to 4 are Directors of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Running account business relationship since 2012 involving sale and supply of aluminium foils/goods by the Appellant to the Respondent on continuous invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed in Section 9 application was Rs. 84,85,505/- for FY 2015-16, arising out of Invoices 0243 & 0244 dated 10.01.2015 and Invoices 0337 & 0338 dated 30.03.2015. Last payment received was Rs. 1,14,882/- on 02.01.2016. Additional claim arose from non-supply of 'C' Forms valued at Rs. 7,59,72,649/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice issued on 12.12.2018; Corporate Debtor replied on 28.12.2018; Section 9 application filed in early 2019; 'C' Forms provided on 14.01.2019 during pendency. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor produced two debit notes—dated 31.03.2015 for Rs. 24,54,000/- (rate difference) and 15.04.2016 for Rs. 60,00,000/- (short supply)—bearing stamps and signatures of Appellant, extinguishing the balance; email dated 03.09.2015 requesting account reconciliation; email dated 28.12.2015 requesting only 'C' Forms with no reference to unpaid operational debt. Operational Creditor claimed debit notes were forged/fabricated. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP No. (IB)-87(PB)/2019 before NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi, which dismissed the petition on 06.08.2019 holding that signed and stamped debit notes and non-pursuance of claims from 2015 to 2018 constituted a plausible pre-existing dispute requiring trial.
legal_issues: Whether an allegation of forgery and fabrication regarding duly stamped and signed debit notes produced by the corporate debtor can be adjudicated in a summary Section 9 IBC proceeding, and whether the existence of such contemporaneous debit notes and reconciliation correspondence establishes a pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6) of the Code.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In summary insolvency proceedings under Section 9, the Adjudicating Authority does not conduct a roving enquiry or mini-trial into disputed assertions of document forgery; if documents evidencing a pre-existing dispute bear prima facie marks of receipt (such as company seal/signature), the dispute is plausible and excludes IBC admission. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A 'dispute' under Section 5(6) read with Section 9 requires only a plausible contention requiring further investigation; it is not necessary that the defense must ultimately succeed at trial. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Ordinarily, acknowledgments bearing the signature and seal of a company are sufficient prima facie evidence of receipt. The absence of contemporaneous police complaints or FIRs regarding unauthorized stamp usage at the time of transaction leaves the dispute plausible and genuine, requiring plenary trial in a civil court. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was bona fide disputed through stamped debit notes and reconciliation emails long prior to the Section 8 demand notice, justifying the rejection of the Section 9 application while reserving the parties' right to pursue civil/criminal remedies.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's rejection order. Liberty is granted to the Appellant to pursue appropriate civil or criminal remedies regarding allegations of forgery, and if forgery is established, to invoke Part II Chapter VII of the IBC.
summary: Duke Sponge and Iron Pvt. Ltd. filed an appeal against the NCLT Principal Bench's dismissal of its Section 9 IBC petition against Laxmi Foils Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid invoices from 2015 amounting to Rs. 84,85,505/-. The Corporate Debtor resisted on the grounds that two debit notes dated 31.03.2015 and 15.04.2016 bearing the Operational Creditor's seal and signature had completely extinguished the dues, alongside lack of any demand between 2015 and 2018. The Appellant claimed the debit notes were forged. The NCLAT held that Section 9 proceedings are summary and cannot adjudicate allegations of forgery requiring trial. As stamped debit notes prima facie evidenced a genuine pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6), the dismissal was upheld.

case_title: Neeta Saha vs. Ram Niwas Gupta & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Neeta Saha (Member of Suspended Board of Palm Developers Pvt. Ltd.) is the Appellant; Ram Niwas Gupta (Proprietor of Ram Niwas Gupta & Sons) is Respondent No. 1/Operational Creditor; Palm Developers Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 2/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of materials/goods by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose upon dishonor of cheque No. 218403 dated 31.08.2019 for Rs. 78,000/- out of settlement post-dated cheques totalling Rs. 1,18,00,554/-; principal default exceeded the statutory threshold of Rs. 1,00,000/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original Section 9 petition disposed of as withdrawn on 04.06.2019 with liberty to restore upon cheque dishonor; settlement agreement executed on 01.08.2019; cheque dishonored on 31.08.2019; restoration application filed under Rule 11 of NCLT Rules, 2016; reply filed on 25.11.2019; amended memo of parties filed on 22.01.2020; admission order passed by NCLT admitting CIRP. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement Agreement dated 01.08.2019 admitting debt including interest up to 04.06.2018; dishonored cheque dated 31.08.2019; admission of liability in Corporate Debtor's reply dated 25.11.2019 stating intent to clear outstanding amounts from April 2020 onwards; absence of any contemporaneous pre-existing dispute. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After settlement cheque was dishonored, NCLT restored the Section 9 application under Rule 11. Overruling the Corporate Debtor's objection that a sole proprietorship is not a 'person', NCLT permitted amendment of memo of parties and admitted the Section 9 petition.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable when initially filed in the name of a sole proprietorship firm rather than the individual proprietor, and whether default arising out of a dishonored settlement cheque constitutes operational debt default under Section 9.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Filing an insolvency petition under the business style of a sole proprietorship is a curable procedural defect, as Section 2 applies the Code to proprietorship firms and the definition of 'person' under Section 3(23) is inclusive; once cured by substituting or naming the proprietor, the application is fully maintainable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 2 expressly extends the application of IBC to proprietorship firms, and the definition of 'person' under Section 3(23) is inclusive, not exhaustive. Therefore, technical misdescriptions in title can be rectified under inherent powers without vitiating jurisdiction. 3.
