EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A signed settlement agreement acknowledging unpaid operational liability coupled with the subsequent dishonor of a settlement cheque provides irrefutable proof of default; admissions in written pleadings expressing future intent to pay corroborate default and negative any assertion of a pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The cure of memo of parties was lawful, default above Rs. 1,00,000/- was undisputed, and there was no pre-existing dispute, warranting admission under Section 9(5).
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, upholding the admission order and initiation of CIRP against Palm Developers Pvt. Ltd. The constitution of the CoC stands and settlement can only be pursued strictly under Section 12A of the Code.
summary: Ram Niwas Gupta, proprietor of Ram Niwas Gupta & Sons, initiated Section 9 proceedings against Palm Developers Pvt. Ltd. The petition was earlier withdrawn on settlement terms, but restored under Rule 11 of NCLT Rules after a post-dated settlement cheque was dishonored. The Corporate Debtor challenged the admission on grounds that a sole proprietorship firm is not a legal 'person' under Section 3(23) of IBC and that interest was wrongly claimed. NCLAT affirmed the admission, holding that Section 2 of IBC covers proprietorships, Section 3(23) is inclusive, and curing the party description via an amended memo of parties is legally valid. Given the undisputed debt and cheque dishonor, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Indo Alusys Industries Limited vs. SMW Metal Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Indo Alusys Industries Limited is the Appellant/Operational Creditor; SMW Metal Private Limited is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Long-standing business dealings involving the supply and sale of aluminium extrusions, ingots, billets, wire rods, and scrap between the parties. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed outstanding dues of Rs. 13,76,36,931.50/-. Corporate Debtor claimed a counter-liability of Rs. 2,46,34,100/- (principal) exceeding Rs. 4 Crores with interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Commercial MoU and Indemnity Bond executed on 25.01.2016; Corporate Debtor issued termination letter rescinding MoU on 17.04.2017; Appellant replied on 02.05.2017; Section 8 demand notice issued on 15.09.2017; Section 8 reply disputing debt sent on 25.09.2017; Section 9 petition filed in late 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MoU and Indemnity Bond dated 25.01.2016 under which Respondent issued 3 Credit Notes aggregating Rs. 24,86,67,626/-; termination letter dated 17.04.2017 stating credit notes were conditional discounts/concessions for future bulk purchases that were breached by Indo Alusys; cross Section 9 application (IB No. 553(ND)/2017) filed by Respondent claiming Rs. 2,46,34,100/-. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench heard cross-petitions (IB-552(ND)/2017 and IB-553(ND)/2017) and by common order dated 12.02.2019 dismissed both Section 9 petitions, holding that claims and cross-claims rooted in terminated agreements required trial.
legal_issues: Whether a claim based on credit notes issued under a Memorandum of Understanding that was unilaterally terminated prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice constitutes an undisputed operational debt or a pre-existing dispute requiring plenary trial.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the foundation of an operational debt depends on disputed interpretations and termination of a settlement agreement/MoU that preceded the Section 8 demand notice, the dispute is pre-existing and cannot be determined within the summary jurisdiction of Section 9. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 summary proceedings are confined to determining the existence of default of an undisputed operational debt; they do not extend to interpreting whether a commercial contract was lawfully terminated or quantifying complex cross-claims. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: If documentary evidence shows that the Corporate Debtor contested and formally repudiated the liability and terms of an MoU prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice under Section 8, the dispute is genuine and substantiated, not a subsequent afterthought. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The adjudication of whether credit notes were issued towards subsisting liabilities or conditional discounts, and the validity of MoU termination, require full-fledged trial before a civil court, thereby barring Section 9 admission.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's dismissal of the Section 9 petition.
summary: Indo Alusys Industries Ltd. appealed against the dismissal of its Section 9 petition against SMW Metal Pvt. Ltd., wherein it claimed operational debt of Rs. 13,76,36,931.50/- based on credit notes issued under an MoU and Indemnity Bond dated 25.01.2016. The Corporate Debtor had unilaterally terminated the MoU via letter dated 17.04.2017, asserting that the credit notes were conditional discounts for future orders that were never placed, and filed a cross-petition claiming Rs. 2.46 crores. NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that the repudiation and termination of the MoU occurred prior to the Section 8 demand notice dated 15.09.2017, proving a genuine pre-existing dispute that cannot be resolved in summary insolvency proceedings.

case_title: The Deputy Commissioner Commercial Taxes (Audit), Raichur vs. Surana Industries Ltd. (In Liquidation) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Deputy Commissioner Commercial Taxes (Audit), Raichur is the Appellant; Surana Industries Ltd. (In Liquidation) is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 1. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory commercial tax assessment and claim submitted by the tax authority during the liquidation process of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Assessment claim submitted to and rejected by the Liquidator during the liquidation period. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidator rejected the Appellant's claim; Appellant filed an appeal against the rejection with a delay of 7 days beyond the statutorily prescribed 14-day period under Section 42 of the IBC; no separate formal application for condonation of delay was filed. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator's rejection order; absence of an application for condonation of delay; plea of internal miscommunication regarding the transmission of the rejection order. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Division Bench I Chennai declined to entertain the appeal filed against the Liquidator's decision due to the absence of a condonation of delay application for the 7-day delay beyond the 14-day statutory limit. The tax department appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory appeal under Section 42 of the IBC against a Liquidator's claim rejection can be entertained after the expiry of the mandatory 14-day limitation period without an application showing sufficient cause for condonation of delay, having regard to the time-bound nature of the liquidation process.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appeals against a Liquidator's decision under Section 42 of the IBC must strictly adhere to the prescribed statutory limitation period of 14 days, and delay cannot be condoned without a formal application demonstrating cogent reasons and sufficient cause. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 42 prescribes a strict 14-day timeline to challenge a liquidator's decision on claims. Given that the IBC liquidation process is strictly time-bound to be completed within statutory parameters, timelines must be rigorously enforced. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Vague administrative assertions of departmental confusion or communication delays do not constitute 'sufficient cause' or cogent legal grounds to condone delay in IBC liquidation proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: In the absence of an application for condonation and sufficient cause, the NCLT rightly refused to entertain the time-barred appeal against the Liquidator.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the order of NCLT Chennai Bench declining to entertain the delayed appeal against the Liquidator's rejection.
summary: The Deputy Commissioner Commercial Taxes (Audit), Raichur challenged an order of NCLT Chennai Division Bench I which declined to entertain its appeal against the rejection of its claim by the Liquidator of Surana Industries Ltd. The appeal before NCLT was filed with a delay of 7 days beyond the 14-day period prescribed under Section 42 of the IBC, and without any application for condonation of delay. The Appellant cited departmental communication confusion as the reason for delay. The NCLAT held that liquidation under the IBC is a time-bound process and administrative confusion does not constitute sufficient cause. The dismissal of the appeal was affirmed.

case_title: Triveni Turbine Ltd. vs. GE Triveni Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Triveni Turbine Ltd. is the Appellant/50% joint venture shareholder; GE Triveni Ltd. is Respondent No. 1 (the JV entity); DI Netherlands BV is Respondent No. 2; Nuovo Pignone Spa is Respondent No. 3; Baker Hughes LLC is Respondent No. 4; General Electric Company is Respondent No. 5. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint venture established to manufacture steam turbines (30-100 MW range) governed by a Joint Venture Agreement, Articles of Association, and ancillary Technology License and Marketing Services Agreements where GE supplied technology/global marketing and Triveni provided domestic manufacturing. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement alleged involving wrongful diversion of business enquiries, failure to supply technology, board-level breach of fiduciary duty by nominee directors, suppression of operational enquiries, and deletion of corporate data from June 2017 to September 2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP No. 102 of 2019 filed under Sections 241-242; NCLT granted ad-interim injunction on 12.06.2019; NCLT vacated injunction on 23.08.2019; NCLAT granted interim conditional order on 27.08.2019; Section 45 arbitration application moved on 25.09.2019; NCLT issued notice on Section 45 on 27.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Joint undertaking affidavit dated August 2019 submitted by R-4 and R-5; one whole year of missing emails (June 2017 to September 2018) recovered from the CTO's repaired laptop; Board minutes dated 30.10.2019 proposing third-party forensic audit. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru vacated its ad-interim injunction on 23.08.2019 holding it lacked jurisdiction over foreign entities R-4 and R-5, and subsequently issued notice on 27.09.2019 to hear R-2 and R-3's Section 45 arbitration application before deciding Appellant's investigation applications (IA Nos. 494 and 495 of 2019).
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT possesses jurisdiction under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 to restrain foreign share transfers executed outside India that impact an Indian joint venture company, and whether an application under Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 must be heard and determined prior to considering applications for company ownership investigation under Section 216.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal possesses the jurisdiction to substitute interim arrangements with conditional safeguards over foreign share transfers to ensure performance of subsisting commercial agreements and access to corporate data, while statutory applications under Section 45 of the Arbitration Act must be prioritized at the threshold by the judicial authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 mandates that whenever a judicial authority is seized of an action concerning an international commercial arbitration agreement, it must prioritize determining whether the agreement is null, void, inoperative, or incapable of being performed; Section 216 ownership investigation remains discretionary at an appropriate future stage. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the threshold standard in Chloro Controls, fundamental issues regarding jurisdiction and reference to arbitration must be addressed at the very first instance before directing roving enquiries into corporate affairs. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's order vacating interim relief was substituted with NCLAT's interim directions preserving JV contracts and data access during the pendency of the petition, and the NCLT's order issuing notice on Section 45 was upheld with a direction to decide it within two months.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 23.08.2019 stands substituted by NCLAT's interim order dated 27.08.2019 permitting share transfer subject to non-interference with JV agreements and mandatory provision of operational data; interference with the impugned order dated 27.09.2019 is declined, and NCLT is directed to decide the Section 45 application within two months. All appeals disposed of without costs.
summary: Triveni Turbine Ltd. approached NCLAT challenging two orders of NCLT Bengaluru Bench arising from an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013. NCLT had vacated an interim injunction restraining General Electric and Baker Hughes from transferring offshore shares affecting the joint venture GE Triveni Ltd., and subsequently issued notice on an application under Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The NCLAT substituted NCLT’s order with its own interim directions, permitting share transfers only on strict condition that all five joint venture agreements remain fully enforceable and operational data is provided. NCLAT upheld the issuance of notice under Section 45, directing NCLT to determine arbitrability within two months.

case_title: Aashish Mohan Gupta vs. Hind Inn and Hotels Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Aashish Mohan Gupta is the Appellant/Promoter; Hind Inn and Hotels Ltd. is Respondent No. 1/Corporate Debtor; CTC Projects Private Limited is Respondent No. 2/Operational Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Work order dated 19.08.2011 awarded by Corporate Debtor to Operational Creditor for civil construction of Ginger Hotel at Plot No. 15, Industrial Area, Phase No. 1, Chandigarh, containing Clause 4 and Clause 8 providing for 5% retention money deduction from each running account bill to be released after completion of a one-year defect liability period. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed unpaid operational debt was Rs. 24,74,085/- as retention money plus interest at 18% per annum (total claim Rs. 37,72,979/-), falling due on 27.07.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Virtual Completion Certificate issued on 04.04.2014 establishing defect liability period from 31.03.2014 to 01.04.2015; request letters issued on 10.04.2015, 27.09.2016, 02.03.2017, and 24.10.2017; Form 3 Demand Notice issued on 01.03.2018 (received 09.03.2018); reply sent on 17.03.2018; Section 9 petition filed on 27.04.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Work order dated 19.08.2011; Virtual Completion Certificate dated 04.04.2014; email dated 13.07.2015 alleging basement water accumulation; reply email dated 14.07.2015 stating works were completed in 2013 and defect period expired; Corporate Debtor's email dated 21.07.2015 appreciating rectification and requesting assistance as a special case request. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh admitted CTC Projects Pvt. Ltd.'s Section 9 petition in CP(IB) No. 168/CHD/2018 on 31.10.2019, holding that the operational debt was established, notice was duly served, and no pre-existing dispute was raised.
legal_issues: Whether retention money deducted from running account bills under a civil construction contract constitutes an operational debt under Section 5(21) of the IBC, and whether the Section 9 petition was time-barred under Article 137 of the Limitation Act or precluded by a pre-existing dispute.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Retention money withheld from running bills of a contractor forms an integral part of the total consideration for services rendered and constitutes an operational debt under Section 5(21) of the IBC, which becomes due and payable upon expiration of the defect liability period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Operational debt under Section 5(21) includes claims arising out of provision of goods or services; non-release of retention money constitutes a default under Section 3(2) and Section 3(11), entitling the contractor to status as an operational creditor under Section 5(20). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Mobilox Innovations standard, a dispute must be genuine, substantial, and raised prior to the Section 8 demand notice; an employer's email acknowledging that all concerns were rectified and soliciting subsequent assistance as a 'special case request' proves that the issue was merely maintenance and not a pre-existing contractual dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The defect liability period concluded on 01.04.2015 and the debt fell due upon Corporate Debtor's acknowledgment email on 21.07.2015/27.07.2015; therefore, the application filed on 27.04.2018 was within the three-year limitation period under Article 137, with no pre-existing dispute.
operative_order: The appeal is devoid of merits and is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 31.10.2019 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP.
summary: Aashish Mohan Gupta, promoter of corporate debtor Hind Inn and Hotels Ltd., appealed against NCLT Chandigarh Bench’s order admitting a Section 9 application filed by operational creditor CTC Projects Pvt. Ltd. The operational creditor claimed unpaid retention money of Rs. 24,74,085/- withheld under a hotel construction contract following expiry of the one-year defect liability period. The Appellant contended that retention money is not an operational debt, that the claim was time-barred, and that basement water accumulation constituted a pre-existing dispute. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that retention money is part of the main construction bill falling squarely within Section 5(21), the claim was within limitation, and subsequent requests for repairs did not constitute a pre-existing dispute.

case_title: G. Shivramkrishna vs. M/s Isgec Covema Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: G. Shivramkrishna (Director of Corporate Debtor) is the Appellant; M/s Isgec Covema Limited is Respondent No. 1/Operational Creditor; M/s Om Shakti Renergies Limited is Respondent No. 2/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Work order placed on 05.12.2002 for Rs. 24,60,000/- leading to arbitration before a Sole Arbitrator appointed by the High Court of Andhra Pradesh on 26.04.2010. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Arbitral award passed on 30.05.2013 granting Rs. 65,18,000/- with interest at 24% per annum, accumulating to Rs. 1,89,02,200/- as of 22.01.2019; date of default specified as 02.02.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Arbitral award passed 30.05.2013; demand notice under award issued 06.11.2013; Section 34 petition OP No. 739 of 2014 dismissed on 27.01.2016 by XXIV Additional Chief Judge, City Court Hyderabad; Section 8 IBC Demand Notice dispatched 22.01.2019 (delivered 24.01.2019); Section 9 petition filed on 03.04.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Arbitral Award dated 30.05.2013; court dismissal order dated 27.01.2016; courier POD dated 24.01.2019 establishing delivery of Section 8 notice to Corporate Debtor's registered office prior to address change notified on 16.04.2019; memo of postal track reports. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad admitted the Section 9 petition CP(IB) No. 277/9/HDB/2019 on 16.09.2019 ex-parte as Corporate Debtor remained absent despite notice, holding that the operational debt was established and filed within limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the holder of an arbitral award qualifies as a creditor entitled to maintain a Section 9 application under the IBC, whether delivery of demand notice at the existing registered office is valid, and whether the limitation period under Article 137 commences after the expiry of the appeal period under Section 37 following dismissal of Section 34 proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An arbitral award crystalizes an operational debt, making the award-holder a decree-holder creditor under Section 3(10) of the IBC; the limitation period under Article 137 begins to run upon final culmination of arbitral challenge proceedings and the expiry of the statutory appeal period under Section 37 of the Arbitration Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(10) defines 'creditor' to include a decree-holder. Under K. Kishan vs. Vijay Nirman Co., the pendency of a Section 34 petition constitutes a continuation of a pre-existing dispute, which ceases upon its dismissal; computing the 90-day appeal limitation under Article 116 of the Limitation Act excludes that period from the start of limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Service of statutory demand notice under Section 8(1) is legally complete and valid if dispatched and delivered to the Corporate Debtor at its registered office on record as of the date of delivery, regardless of subsequent ROC office changes. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 34 challenge was dismissed on 27.01.2016, and the 90-day limitation to file a Section 37 appeal expired on 27.04.2016; hence the three-year period under Article 137 expired on 27.04.2019, rendering the application filed on 03.04.2019 fully timely.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, sustaining the order of admission dated 16.09.2019 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench initiating CIRP against M/s Om Shakti Renergies Limited.
summary: G. Shivramkrishna, director of corporate debtor Om Shakti Renergies Ltd., appealed against NCLT Hyderabad Bench's order admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by Isgec Covema Ltd. The claim for Rs. 1,89,02,200/- was based on an unpaid arbitral award passed on 30.05.2013. The Corporate Debtor’s challenge under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 was dismissed on 27.01.2016. The Appellant argued that IBC cannot execute arbitral awards, demand notice was not served, and the application was time-barred. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that an award holder is a decree-holder creditor under Section 3(10), service at the registered office was valid, and limitation under Article 137 commenced after the expiry of the Section 37 appeal window.

case_title: Ashish Chaturvedi vs. Inox Leisure Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ashish Chaturvedi (Ex-Director of A to Z Barter Pvt. Ltd.) is the Appellant; Inox Leisure Ltd. is Respondent No. 1/Operational Creditor; Anoop Kumar Goyal is Respondent No. 2/IRP; A to Z Barter Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 3/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial operational debt claim under Section 9 of the IBC leading to initiation of CIRP against A to Z Barter Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default admitted leading to admission of insolvency application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Insolvency application filed 01.06.2018; admission order passed by NCLT on 05.12.2018; NCLT Registry failed to communicate admission order to IRP or Corporate Debtor; Operational Creditor informed IRP via email on 12.11.2019; IRP filed CA 862/C-III/ND/2019 seeking exclusion of period; NCLT passed impugned order on 10.12.2019 excluding 370 days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Admission order dated 05.12.2018 mandating under Para 11 that Registry communicate the order to IRP and Corporate Debtor; email dated 12.11.2019 from Operational Creditor informing IRP of his appointment and requesting revival; confirmation letter and eligibility declaration from IRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-III on 10.12.2019 found that its Registry inadvertently failed to communicate the admission order of 05.12.2018 to the IRP, and excluded 370 days from the maximum CIRP timeline, granting 180 days fresh period from 10.12.2019. Ex-Director appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC to exclude time from the statutory CIRP period where the commencement of CIRP was stalled due to the Tribunal Registry's failure to communicate the admission order to the IRP, notwithstanding the 330-day outer limit under Section 12(3).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the legal maxim actus curiae neminem gravabit (an act of the court shall prejudice no one), institutional failure or administrative omission by a tribunal's registry in communicating an admission order to the interim resolution professional justifies the exclusion of the lost period from the calculation of the CIRP timeline. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Section 12 mandates strict CIRP timelines, Section 60(5) read with the principles established in Quinn Logistics empowers the Adjudicating Authority to exclude unforeseen intervening periods during which the resolution professional was wholly unable to function due to lack of notice of appointment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the tribunal's own records confirm that the Registry failed to execute the express direction in the admission order to communicate the order to the IRP, neither the operational creditor nor the resolution professional can be penalized for the elapsed time. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no legal error in excluding 370 days and extending 180 days with effect from the date of the exclusion order to enable the IRP to take charge and conduct CIRP.
operative_order: The appeal fails and is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 10.12.2019 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-III excluding 370 days from the CIRP duration.
summary: Ashish Chaturvedi, ex-director of A to Z Barter Pvt. Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi Court-III which excluded 370 days from the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process and granted 180 days to complete CIRP. Due to an inadvertent administrative failure by the NCLT Registry, the initial admission order dated 05.12.2018 was never communicated to the Interim Resolution Professional, who remained unaware of his appointment until contacted by the operational creditor in November 2019. The Appellant argued that Section 12(3) strictly prohibits extension beyond 330 days. Applying the maxim actus curiae neminem gravabit, NCLAT dismissed the appeal, affirming that judicial delays and registry omissions cannot prejudice parties and justify time exclusion under Section 60(5).

case_title: Parvesh Magoo vs. IREO Grace Realtech Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Parvesh Magoo is the Appellant/Financial Creditor-Allottee; IREO Grace Realtech Private Limited is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Booking of Unit No. 203, Tower A6, in residential project 'The Corridors' at Sector 67A, Gurgaon, Haryana, followed by Allotment Letter dated 07.08.2013 and Apartment Buyer's Agreement dated 03.06.2014. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Allottee paid Rs. 1,59,29,016/- and claimed default of Rs. 2,07,57,385/- (principal + interest) upon issuing unilateral termination on 08.12.2018 for alleged delay in handing over possession due in July 2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Building plan approved 23.07.2013 subject to preconditions; Environmental approval granted 12.12.2013; Fire safety approval under Section 15 of Haryana Fire Safety Act granted 27.11.2014; Occupation Certificate applied for on 05.07.2018 and received 31.05.2019; termination email sent 08.12.2018; notice of possession issued 14.06.2019; Section 7 application CP No. IB-10/(ND)/2019 filed in early 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clauses 13.3-13.5 of Apartment Buyer's Agreement defining delivery within 60 months (42 months commitment + 6 months grace + 12 months extended delay) from approval of plans and fulfillment of pre-conditions; Fire Safety Approval dated 27.11.2014; Occupation Certificate dated 31.05.2019 covering 700 units; letter offering possession dated 14.06.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi rejected the Section 7 petition on 26.09.2019, holding that the 60-month commitment ran from the date of Fire Safety approval (27.11.2014) and expired on 27.11.2019, so possession offered in June 2019 precluded any finding of default.
legal_issues: Whether the possession delivery deadline under a real estate contract is computed from the initial building approval date or from the date of fulfillment of mandatory statutory pre-conditions (Fire Safety Approval), and whether an allottee seeking solely refund rather than project resolution can trigger Section 7 when possession has been offered within the contractually adjusted period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a builder-buyer contract expressly conditions the commencement of construction and possession timelines upon the fulfillment of statutory preconditions, the commitment period runs from the date the final mandatory statutory clearance is granted, and an offer of possession within that computed window negates any default under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A default under Section 3(12) requires non-payment of an operational or financial debt that has become legally 'due and payable' under Section 3(11); where the contractual delivery date has not expired due to legitimate statutory approval timelines, no financial debt is due and payable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Pioneer Urban Land and Navin Raheja, the Adjudicating Authority must determine whether the construction delay was caused by force majeure or statutory dependencies outside developer control and verify whether the allottee is abusing insolvency provisions as a recovery tool for refund rather than seeking resolution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor had 60 months from the Fire Safety approval of 27.11.2014 (expiring 27.11.2019) to deliver possession; having obtained the Occupation Certificate on 31.05.2019 and offered possession on 14.06.2019, no default occurred.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the order dated 26.09.2019 passed by NCLT New Delhi rejecting the Section 7 application.
summary: Parvesh Magoo, a homebuyer in 'The Corridors' project, appealed against the NCLT New Delhi Bench order rejecting her Section 7 IBC application against IREO Grace Realtech Pvt. Ltd. claiming default of Rs. 2,07,57,385/- for delayed possession. The Appellant argued that possession was due in July 2017 based on the building plan approval date. The Corporate Debtor demonstrated that statutory fire safety approval was obtained only on 27.11.2014, making the contractually agreed 60-month delivery deadline expire on 27.11.2019. As the developer obtained an Occupation Certificate and offered possession in June 2019, NCLAT affirmed that no default occurred under Section 3(12) and reiterated that speculative refund applications by allottees are impermissible under Section 7.

case_title: Mrs. R. Mangalam vs. M/s SPML Infra Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mrs. R. Mangalam is the Appellant/Financial Creditor; M/s SPML Infra Ltd. is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Letter of Offer dated 19.09.1995 issued by Respondent offering shares and debentures of face value Rs. 150/-; Appellant applied for and was allotted 66,530 debentures paying Rs. 20/- per debenture on application (Rs. 13,30,600/-) with balance Rs. 130/- due on allotment. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed as Rs. 3,20,46,117/- (principal Rs. 13,30,600/- plus 15% interest per annum from 05.01.1996) based on condition that subscription proceeds must be refunded if 90% minimum subscription was not received within 60 days of closure. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Refund due date stated as 05.01.1996; Respondent issued call notices on 01.02.1996 and 19.09.1998, and final letter on 09.10.2000; debentures forfeited on 12.12.2000; SEBI passed restraint order on 28.01.2004 holding minimum subscription was not achieved; SAT affirmed finding on 01.06.2006; Section 7 petition CP No. IB-1576/(ND)/2018 filed in 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letter of Offer dated 19.09.1995; Debenture Certificate providing for redemption in instalments by 12.12.2000 or forfeiture; Annual Report dated 31.03.2001 recording forfeiture of partly paid debentures on 12.12.2000; SEBI order dated 28.01.2004; SAT order dated 01.06.2006. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-III dismissed the Section 7 petition on 19.07.2019 as hopelessly time-barred under Article 137, rejecting the argument that alleged knowledge of SEBI/SAT orders in 2015 extended limitation under Section 17 of the Limitation Act.
legal_issues: Whether a claim for refund of debenture application money arising out of an alleged fraudulent public issue in 1995 can be saved from the bar of limitation under Section 17 of the Limitation Act, 1963 based on SEBI and SAT regulatory orders passed in 2004 and 2006, for the purpose of initiating CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9 of the Limitation Act, once limitation begins to run from the date of default, no subsequent disability or lack of knowledge stops it; to claim extension under Section 17(1) for fraud, the applicant must demonstrate that the fraud could not have been discovered earlier with reasonable diligence. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 17(1) of the Limitation Act requires establishing that the applicant was kept from the knowledge of their right by fraud and could not, with reasonable diligence, have discovered it; public regulatory orders passed by SEBI and SAT do not constitute concealed fraud. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Inordinate inaction from 1996 to 2018 and bald assertions of obtaining knowledge of public regulatory orders over a decade after their pronouncement fail the evidentiary test of reasonable diligence. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Default occurred on 05.01.1996 and debentures were forfeited on 12.12.2000; SEBI and SAT orders passed in 2004 and 2006 were matter of public record. The Section 7 application filed in 2018 was hopelessly barred by limitation under Article 137.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of without costs, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order dismissing the Section 7 petition as time-barred, with liberty to pursue remedies under the Companies Act, 2013 if available.
summary: Mrs. R. Mangalam appealed against NCLT New Delhi Bench-III’s dismissal of her Section 7 IBC petition against SPML Infra Ltd. as time-barred. The Appellant had subscribed to debentures in 1995 under a Letter of Offer stipulating refund if 90% subscription was not reached. Following non-payment of allotment calls, the company forfeited the debentures in 2000. In 2004, SEBI found the issue fraudulent, which SAT affirmed in 2006. The Appellant claimed Section 17 of the Limitation Act extended limitation until her alleged discovery of fraud in 2015. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that default commenced in 1996, forfeiture occurred in 2000, and public regulatory orders could have been discovered with reasonable diligence, making the 2018 petition hopelessly time-barred.

case_title: Harish Jain vs. Haveli Restaurant & Resorts Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Harish Jain is the Appellant; Haveli Restaurant & Resorts Ltd. (formerly Asha Builders) is Respondent No. 1; Satish Jain (Managing Director) is Respondent No. 2; Mrs. Bhavna Jain and Ajit Prasad Jain are Respondents 3 & 4 (Directors); M/s Surinder Mahajan and Associates is Respondent No. 5 (CA); Gautam Goyal is Respondent No. 6 (CS). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Asha Builders incorporated on 03.09.1997 with Appellant and R-2 holding 1,000 equity shares each (50% each); share capital was subsequently expanded from Rs. 20,000/- to Rs. 4,54,20,000/-; family arrangement allocated complete control of Asha Shoppers Pvt. Ltd. to Appellant and R-1 Company to R-2. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement alleged regarding transfer of Appellant's 1,000 shares on 24.08.2007 reducing holding to nil, and removal from Directorship via allegedly forged resignation letter dated 31.10.2011. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Share transfer registered 24.08.2007; Board meeting and Form 32 filing on 31.10.2011; alleged discovery of fraud in family meeting in September 2015; MCA records inspected on 08.09.2015; police complaint dated 12.09.2015; civil suit filed 28.03.2016; CP No. 138/CHD/PB/2018 filed on 08.06.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Annual returns of 1999, 2001, and 2003 signed by Appellant showing capital expansion; Form MGT-14 filed by Appellant for Asha Shoppers omitting interest in R-1; Board meeting notice dated 20.10.2011; Form 32 dated 31.10.2011; private handwriting expert report dated 30.12.2015 based on a photocopy of resignation letter. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh dismissed CP No. 138/CHD/PB/2018 in limine with cost of Rs. 50,000/-, holding Appellant lacked locus under Section 244 and that the petition was barred by limitation.
legal_issues: Whether an erstwhile shareholder whose shares were transferred 11 years prior and directorship ceased 7 years prior satisfies the eligibility criteria under Section 244 of the Companies Act, 2013, and whether an expert opinion based on a photocopy of a resignation letter is sufficient to establish fraud to extend limitation under Section 17 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An applicant who has transferred their entire shareholding and exited directorship pursuant to a family arrangement lacks standing to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 244; belated allegations of fraud unsupported by primary evidence cannot extend limitation under Section 17 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 244 of the Companies Act, 2013, qualification to maintain a petition is determined based on subsisting shareholding; under Section 433, the Limitation Act applies to proceedings before the NCLT, barring stale claims instituted 11 years after cessation of membership. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A handwriting expert report prepared on the basis of a photocopy carries no legal or evidentiary value to prove document forgery; signing annual returns and statutory corporate filings precludes a director from pleading ignorant faith or fraud. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appellant voluntarily transferred his shares in 2007 and resigned in 2011; the petition filed in 2018 was not maintainable under Section 244 and was hopelessly barred by limitation.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT Chandigarh Bench judgment dismissing the company petition in limine.
summary: Harish Jain appealed against NCLT Chandigarh Bench’s in limine dismissal of his petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 against Haveli Restaurant & Resorts Ltd. The Appellant alleged that his 50% shareholding was fraudulently reduced to nil and that his 31.10.2011 directorship resignation letter was forged. The Respondents demonstrated that share transfers in 2007 and directorship resignations were part of an agreed family partition between brothers, reflected in signed annual returns. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that a private handwriting expert opinion on a photocopy cannot establish forgery, the Appellant ceased to be a member in 2007 lacking standing under Section 244, and the claim filed in 2018 was hopelessly barred by limitation under Section 433.

case_title: Ateet Bansal & Ors. vs. Unitech Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ateet Bansal (Appeal 216), Sunita Bansal (Appeal 218), and Shweta Bansal (Appeal 219) are Appellants/Fixed Deposit Holders; Unitech Ltd. is Respondent/Defaulting Company. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Fixed Deposit Receipts issued by Respondent: FDR No. 1220500 dated 01.06.2013 for Rs. 1,00,000/- maturing at Rs. 1,45,217/- on 01.06.2016; FDRs No. 1220015 & 1246693 for Rs. 3,50,000/- maturing at Rs. 4,35,652/- and Rs. 72,609/- in 2016; FDR No. 1222585 for Rs. 50,000/- maturing at Rs. 72,609/- on 20.06.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of maturity proceeds on respective three-year due dates in May, June, and November 2016; agreed interest rate was 12.5% per annum. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Deposits matured in 2016; company petitions filed in March 2019 under Section 73(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Section 45Q of RBI Act; NCLT passed orders on 30.05.2019; Supreme Court reconstituted Board on 20.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Fixed Deposit Receipts showing matured amounts; non-appearance and failure of Respondent to file reply before NCLT despite service on 25.04.2019; Supreme Court orders in SLP (Crl) No. 5978-79 of 2017 and Bhupinder Singh vs. Unitech Ltd. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench allowed the Section 73(4) petitions on 30.05.2019 but arbitrarily reduced the interest rate to 10% per annum and granted interest only pendente lite from date of filing instead of the date of maturity. Depositors appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has the statutory authority under Section 73(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 to arbitrarily reduce the contracted interest rate payable on matured fixed deposits and deny pre-litigation interest from the date of maturity to the date of filing.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Corporate deposit protection provisions under company law are enacted to protect public depositors, and tribunals cannot reward a defaulting corporate debtor by arbitrarily reducing contracted interest rates or refusing interest for the period between maturity and the filing of the petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 73(4) read with penal provisions under Section 76A of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates that a company failing to repay deposits must pay the deposit amount along with all interest due thereon in accordance with the terms of acceptance. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: General Supreme Court protective orders restraining coercive bail-related execution against directors do not bar statutory adjudication or modify the substantive contractual liabilities of a defaulting company to its depositors. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT erred in reducing the agreed interest rate from 12.5% to 10% without justification and in failing to award interest from the maturity date; depositors are entitled to full contracted maturity amounts with 12.5% interest from maturity until actual realization.
operative_order: The impugned orders are set aside and the appeals are allowed. A decree is granted in favor of each Appellant for the matured FDR amount together with pendente lite and future interest at 12.5% per annum from the date of maturity of the respective FDR until receipt thereof. Respondent is directed to pay Rs. 50,000/- to each Appellant towards litigation costs.
summary: Ateet Bansal and other fixed deposit holders appealed under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 against NCLT New Delhi Bench orders under Section 73(4). The NCLT had directed Unitech Ltd. to repay matured fixed deposits but reduced the agreed interest rate from 12.5% to 10% per annum and granted interest only from the petition filing date. The NCLAT set aside the orders and allowed the appeals, ruling that deposit rules under Section 73 and Section 76A protect honest depositors and do not permit tribunals to arbitrarily lower contracted interest rates or deny interest between maturity and filing. The NCLAT decreed the full matured sums with 12.5% interest from maturity alongside Rs. 50,000/- litigation costs per appellant.

case_title: Surinder Mehta & Ors. vs. Prime Meiden Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Surinder Mehta & Ors. are Appellants/Applicants; Prime Meiden Ltd. & Ors. are Respondents in proceedings under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial corporate joint venture and shareholder arrangements subject to an international arbitration clause. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Impugned refusal by the NCLT to refer dispute to arbitration in a pending oppression and mismanagement petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Application under Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 filed before NCLT; NCLT New Delhi Bench passed impugned order on 10.09.2018 refusing to refer the matter to arbitration; appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 preferred before NCLAT. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT New Delhi Bench order dated 10.09.2018 refusing arbitration reference under Section 45; arbitration agreements between parties. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench refused to refer the parties to arbitration under Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996; Appellants preferred an appeal before NCLAT under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013.
legal_issues: Whether an order of refusal passed by the NCLT acting in the capacity of a 'judicial authority' under Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is appealable before the NCLAT under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When the NCLT adjudicates an application under Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, it acts as a 'judicial authority' and not as a company tribunal, and appeals against such orders lie exclusively to the court authorized under Section 50 of the Arbitration Act, not under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 provides for appeals only against orders passed by NCLT in its capacity as a 'Tribunal' under Section 420; where the Tribunal acts as a judicial authority under Section 45 of the Arbitration Act, the appeal forum is strictly circumscribed by Section 50 read with Explanation to Section 47 of the Arbitration Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying Thota Gurunath Reddy and Sumitomo Corporation vs. CDC Financial Services, the statutory capacity in which the judicial authority renders an order determines the maintainability of the appeal; in the absence of power delegated under the Arbitration Act, company appellate jurisdiction cannot be invoked. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The impugned order having been passed under Section 45 of the Arbitration Act, the appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act is not maintainable before NCLAT.
operative_order: The appeal is held not maintainable and is dismissed without costs, leaving it open to the Appellants to seek remedies before the appropriate court authorized under Section 50 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
summary: Surinder Mehta and others filed an appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 challenging an order of NCLT New Delhi Bench refusing to refer an ongoing oppression and mismanagement dispute to international arbitration under Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The NCLAT held that while the NCLT is established under Section 408 of the Companies Act, when adjudicating an application under Section 45 of the Arbitration Act, it functions as a 'judicial authority'. Consequently, appeals against such orders do not lie under Section 421 of the Companies Act before NCLAT, but must be pursued under Section 50 of the Arbitration Act before the appropriate civil court. The appeal was dismissed as not maintainable.

case_title: S. Shivaswamy vs. Concentrix Daksh Services India Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: S. Shivaswamy (RP and Liquidator of Le Ecosystem Technology India Pvt. Ltd.) is the Appellant; Concentrix Daksh Services India Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 1/Operational Creditor; NCLT Bengaluru is Respondent No. 2; Le Ecosystem Technology India Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP initiated under Section 9 on 09.11.2018 culminating in liquidation approved by CoC on 23.05.2019; Corporate Debtor had no tangible assets except an assessed Income Tax refund of Rs. 2.20 crores for AY 2017-18. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidation process initiated due to lack of viable resolution plan; IT Department determined refund of Rs. 2.20 crores vide intimation dated 26.02.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted 09.11.2018; CoC resolved for liquidation on 23.05.2019; NCLT passed liquidation order in IA Nos. 267 & 268 of 2019 on 28.06.2019; IT refund communication issued 26.02.2019; CIT directed to expedite refund on 22.03.2019 in IA 141/2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Income Tax Department refund communication Ref. No. CPC/1718/G14/201902220457881 dated 26.02.2019; NCLT order dated 28.06.2019 directing under Para 12(vi) that liquidator's fees shall not be recovered from the IT refund or FDRs. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru on 28.06.2019 ordered liquidation and appointed Appellant as Liquidator, but ruled in Para 12(vi) that liquidator fees shall not be recovered from the Rs. 2.20 crore IT refund on the ground that virtually no effort was required to convert it to cash. Liquidator appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses statutory jurisdiction to exclude certain assets of the Corporate Debtor, such as an Income Tax refund, from the liquidation estate or from the calculation of the liquidator's statutory fee contrary to Section 34(8) and Section 36(3)(h) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 36(3)(h) and Section 34(8) of the IBC read with IBBI Liquidation Regulations, all assets and receivables belonging to the corporate debtor form part of the liquidation estate, and the liquidator is legally entitled to remuneration on the realization and distribution thereof without arbitrary judicial exclusions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 36(3)(h) includes any asset belonging to or vested in the corporate debtor on the insolvency commencement date; Section 34(8) mandates that the liquidator's fee be determined in proportion to the value of the liquidation estate assets as specified by IBBI Regulations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: While tribunals possess supervisory authority to disallow unjustified or non-ancillary expenses, they cannot exclude statutory assets from the fee calculation matrix simply because realization involves ministerial or administrative follow-up. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Liquidator is entitled to claim remuneration for services rendered in realizing the IT refund and converting it to cash in conformity with the IBC and IBBI Liquidation Process Regulations.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of without costs and the impugned order dated 28.06.2019 is modified, setting aside the restriction in Para 12(vi) and holding that the Liquidator is entitled to claim fees and remuneration on the IT refund realization in accordance with the IBC and IBBI Regulations.
summary: S. Shivaswamy, Liquidator of Le Ecosystem Technology India Pvt. Ltd., appealed against Para 12(vi) of NCLT Bengaluru Bench's liquidation order, which prohibited him from recovering liquidator fees from an admitted Income Tax refund of Rs. 2.20 crores and fixed deposit receipts on grounds that virtually no effort was required to convert them into cash. The NCLAT set aside the restriction and modified the order, holding that under Section 36(3)(h) and Section 34(8) of the IBC, tax refunds constitute part of the liquidation estate assets, and the Adjudicating Authority cannot arbitrarily restrict the liquidator's statutory remuneration contrary to the Code and IBBI Liquidation Process Regulations. The Liquidator is entitled to fee on the realization.

case_title: Western Electric & Trading Company & Anr vs Competition Commission Of India & Ors
appeal_number: TA (AT) Competition No. 37 of 2017 (Old Appeal No.07 of 2017) & TA (AT) Competition No. 38 of 2017 (Old Appeal No.15 of 2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Western Electric & Trading Co. with partner Ramesh Parchani (OP-3) and R. Kanwar Electricals with partner Ashish Jain (OP-2); Respondent No. 1 is Competition Commission of India (CCI); co-cartel participant was Pyramid Electronics with partner Sandeep Goyal (OP-1, leniency applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bidding and supply of RDSO-approved Brushless DC (BLDC) fans (400 mm sweep, 110 Volts) under four public tenders issued by North Eastern Railway, South Central Railway, Northern Railway, and Bharat Earth Movers Ltd (BEML). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Anti-competitive cartelization and bid-rigging under an agreed price formula allocating L-1, L-2, and L-3 positions (benchmarking tender rates around Rs. 3,481 to Rs. 3,520 per fan) during February-March 2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CBI forwarded preliminary enquiry findings via letter dated 01.04.2014; CCI registered Suo Motu Case No. 03/2014 and directed DG investigation under Section 26(1) on 23.06.2014; DG investigation report filed on 27.03.2015; cross-examination completed on 09.09.2015; supplementary DG report submitted on 19.10.2015; CCI penal order passed on 18.01.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated 17.03.2013 sent from Sandeep Goyal to Ashish Jain and forwarded to Ramesh Parchani containing an exact tender bid distribution chart; Call Data Records (CDRs) showing over 50 calls between Sandeep Goyal and Ashish Jain and 26-30 calls between Ashish Jain and Ramesh Parchani clustered around tender dates; confessional and leniency statements of Sandeep Goyal corroborated by matching identical tender prices in bids. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI held OP-1, OP-2, and OP-3 guilty of contravening Section 3(1) read with Section 3(3)(c)/(d) and vicariously penalized the partners under Section 27(b) read with Section 48 at 10% of average income (granting 75% leniency discount to OP-1), against which Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a dealer/trader can be held liable for horizontal cartelization and bid rigging under Section 3(3)(d) of the Competition Act, 2002 alongside manufacturers based on circumstantial evidence consisting of an email tender distribution matrix and call detail records, and whether being a small-scale industry or family firm constitutes a valid legal ground to set aside penalties under Section 27(b).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Horizontal bid rigging and cartel agreements under competition law can be established through circumstantial and digital communication evidence, including circulating bid pricing charts and high-density call logs around bidding deadlines, even where an enterprise claims to be merely a dealer rather than an original equipment manufacturer. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(3)(d) covers any understanding or collusive action that directly or indirectly results in bid rigging, irrespective of corporate form or principal-agent defenses where the trader exercises independent bidding discretion and shares sensitive pricing data. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The standard of proof is the preponderance of probabilities; an unrefuted trail of an internal bid-sharing spreadsheet across participants' inboxes, corroborated by temporal telephonic communications and identical quoted tender prices, conclusively establishes collusive concerted action. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CCI's findings of bid rigging were fully fortified by documentary and forensic telecommunication evidence, and status as a small-scale enterprise or lower net profit does not warrant interference with statutory penalties under Section 27(b).
operative_order: Both appeals TA (AT) Competition No. 37 of 2017 and TA (AT) Competition No. 38 of 2017 are dismissed, upholding the CCI's order dated 18.01.2017. No orders as to costs.
summary: Appellants Western Electric & Trading Co. and R. Kanwar Electricals challenged the CCI's order finding them guilty of cartelization and bid rigging in tenders floated by Indian Railways and BEML for BLDC fans under Section 3(3)(d) read with Section 48 of the Competition Act, 2002. Penalties were levied at 10% of average income. Appellants argued absence of horizontal competition, principal-agent pricing instructions from Crompton Greaves, and mitigating small-scale status. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, holding that the email containing identical quoted prices, corroborative call detail records, and lack of bona fide explanation conclusively proved collusive bid rigging, rejecting small-scale business status as a defense against statutory penalty.

case_title: Partha Sadhan Bose vs Sugesan Transport Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Partha Sadhan Bose, Suspended Director of E.C. Bose & Co. Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Appellant); Sugesan Transport Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was awarded a shore handling license by Kolkata Port Trust (KoPT) requiring a Rs. 3.52 Crore Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG); Corporate Debtor entered into an MoU dated 11.12.2015 with Respondent No. 1 for Rs. 2.50 Crore financial assistance as margin money for the PBG and proposed formation of an SPV (Seth and Bose Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 1,00,00,000 principal plus bank rate of interest repayable within 30 to 89 days under Clause 1.5 of the MoU (date of default occurring upon expiry of the 89-day term from 11.12.2015, i.e., March 2016). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MoU executed on 11.12.2015; bank guarantee encashed by KoPT on 10.02.2016; Corporate Debtor reissued replacement security cheques through letters dated 06.06.2016; Section 7 petition C.P.(IB) No. 1388/KB/2018 filed in 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MoU dated 11.12.2015 clauses 1.3 and 1.5; Promissory Note dated 11.12.2015 acknowledging receipt of Rs. 1 Crore vide UTR No. CORPR92015121112850002 with interest; Post Dated Cheques issued and renewed by Corporate Debtor; signed Ledger Account of the Corporate Debtor (01.12.2015 to 30.09.2016) acknowledging financial debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted Respondent No. 1's Section 7 petition on 25.10.2019, holding that the loan transaction was independent of the unformed SPV and met the threshold under Section 5(7) & 5(8); Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether money disbursed as margin money to secure a bank guarantee under an MoU containing an independent repayment clause with bank interest within 89 days constitutes a 'financial debt' disbursed against the consideration for time value of money under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and whether the pendency of parallel arbitration proceedings bars admission under Section 7.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unconditional obligation to return disbursed funds alongside bank-rate interest within a defined timeframe constitutes a financial debt disbursed for the time value of money, which remains fully enforceable notwithstanding the non-materialization of collateral business ventures or joint SPVs contemplated in the contract. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) of the IBC requires consideration for the time value of money; where the contract mandates repayment of principal with interest within an outer limit of time, it falls squarely within the commercial effect of borrowing, independent of joint venture covenants. Non-obstante provisions under Section 238 and jurisdictional bar under Section 63 supersede arbitration clauses. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production of promissory notes, banking transaction UTR numbers, post-dated cheques, and acknowledged ledger accounts signed by authorized personnel conclusively establishes the existence of debt and default under Section 7. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The financial debt exceeding the threshold was due and in default, and ongoing arbitration is not a statutory bar to insolvency initiation; hence the admission of the Section 7 petition was lawful and proper.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming NCLT Kolkata Bench's admission order dated 25.10.2019. I.A. No. 4258/2019 is closed.
summary: Partha Sadhan Bose, suspended director of Corporate Debtor E.C. Bose & Co. Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Kolkata Bench's admission of a Section 7 IBC application by Sugesan Transport Pvt. Ltd. The Corporate Debtor had taken funds to provide margin money for a Kolkata Port Trust bank guarantee under an MoU stipulating return within 89 days with bank interest, supported by promissory notes and cheques. The Appellant claimed the funds represented joint venture/consortium capital tied to an aborted SPV and subject to pending arbitration. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the loan was independent, possessed the commercial effect of borrowing with time value of money under Section 5(8), and overriding IBC provisions rendered parallel arbitration irrelevant.

case_title: Mukesh Maneklal Choksi vs Union Of India & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mukesh Maneklal Choksi (Appellant, Chartered Accountant and Statutory Auditor); Union of India through Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Regional Director Western Region (Respondent No. 1); Zen Shaving Limited (Respondent No. 2, Corporate Entity). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory audit engagements and preparation/issuance of independent auditor reports for Respondent No. 2 company for Financial Years 2014-15 and 2015-16. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Issuing clean audit reports on 05.09.2015 and 05.09.2016 without inspecting or requisitioning statutory books of accounts, registers, or financial records of Respondent No. 2, while IPO proceeds aggregating Rs. 3,95,50,000 raised in 1996 had been siphoned off. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IPO prospectus issued 10.10.1996; Appellant appointed auditor on 12.03.2014; audit reports issued on 05.09.2015 and 05.09.2016; MCA inspection ordered 20.03.2017; inspection reports submitted 10.05.2018 and 13.08.2018; Section 140(5) petition filed 26.11.2018; NCLT ad-interim order 03.01.2019; final NCLT order 06.02.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Inspection reports noting untraceable shadow directors, non-listing on stock exchanges, and siphoning between 1996 and 2004; letter dated 10.03.2014 from previous auditor S.M. Bhatt & Associates stating the company had ceased business with no books produced; absence of evidence showing Appellant received illicit benefits or actively colluded in siphoning. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench under Section 140(5) disqualified Appellant from acting as an auditor for any company for 5 years, ordered refund of remuneration, and directed prosecution under Section 447; Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an auditor who acts negligently by issuing audit reports without calling for books of accounts of a dormant/defunct company can be penalized under the second proviso to Section 140(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 and held liable under Section 447 without positive evidence of fraudulent intent, collusion, or abetment.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Disqualification and penal action against an auditor under Section 140(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires proof of deliberate fraudulent conduct, collusion, or abetment with the company's management; mere professional negligence or reliance on a predecessor's procedure without mens rea does not satisfy the statutory threshold of fraud. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The second proviso to Section 140(5) is triggered only if an auditor has acted in a fraudulent manner or abetted or colluded in any fraud by, or in relation to, the company or its directors. Negligent performance of duties cannot be equated with fraudulent action. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of positive documentary or oral evidence demonstrating collusion, sharing of siphoned proceeds, or intent to deceive stakeholders, professional lapses do not satisfy the evidentiary test for fraud under Section 447. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The siphoning of IPO funds occurred between 1996 and 2004 long before Appellant's appointment in 2014, and Appellant's failure to inspect non-existent books was professional negligence rather than fraud, rendering the NCLT disqualification unsustainable.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned order of NCLT Mumbai Bench dated 06.02.2019 is set aside. No order as to costs.
summary: Mukesh Maneklal Choksi, statutory auditor of Zen Shaving Ltd., appealed against NCLT Mumbai Bench's order disqualifying him from acting as auditor for 5 years, directing refund of audit fees, and ordering prosecution under Section 447 pursuant to Section 140(5) of the Companies Act, 2013. The NCLT found he issued clean audit reports for FY 2014-15 and 2015-16 without reviewing books of accounts while public funds were siphoned. NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the order, ruling that although the auditor's conduct was negligent, the siphoning occurred long before his appointment, and negligence without evidence of deliberate fraudulent intent, active collusion, or personal gain does not justify disqualification under Section 140(5).

case_title: Pacific World Shipping PTE Ltd vs Dadi Impex Pvt Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pacific World Shipping Pte Ltd. (Appellant/Operational Creditor); Dadi Impex Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Corporate Debtor - MSME); Anand Prakash Choudhari & Manju Choudhari (Successful Resolution Applicants/Promoters); State Bank of India (Respondent No. 2/Lead Financial Creditor); Dhiren S Shah (Respondent No. 3/Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of freight and vessel charter services by Appellant to Corporate Debtor under charter agreements thrice in 2017 for salt export operations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in unpaid demurrage and freight charges aggregating Rs. 9,22,53,131.72 paise. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 9 upon application of Percula Shipping and Trading INC in CP No. 1562/I&BC/MB/MAH/2017; Appellant filed Form B on 05.06.2018; replacement RP appointed 15.11.2018; 17th CoC meeting approved plan on 11.03.2019; NCLT approved plan with modifications in MA 1090/2019 on 22.05.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor average liquidation value was Rs. 41.35 Crores; total admitted Financial Creditor claims were Rs. 48,48,87,117; CIRP cost originally proposed at Rs. 9.36 Crores (reduced by NCLT to Rs. 2.00 Crores); liquidation value of Operational Creditors was determined to be NIL under Section 53 waterfall. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench approved the MSME promoters' Resolution Plan on 22.05.2019 with modifications, restricting directors' salaries and pruning CIRP costs by Rs. 7.36 Crores to be distributed pari passu to Operational Creditors; Appellant challenged the approval before NCLAT as discriminatory and tokenistic.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan offering operational creditors a token 2% dividend (augmented by redirected CIRP costs) while financial creditors receive 100% restructuring violates Section 30(2)(b) and Section 53 of the IBC, and whether the commercial wisdom of the CoC in approving an MSME promoter-driven plan can be interfered with by appellate tribunals.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appellate review of an approved resolution plan is strictly confined within statutory boundaries, and the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors regarding differential percentage allocations between financial and operational creditors cannot be interfered with where operational creditors receive at least their statutory liquidation value. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 30(2)(b) read with Section 53, operational creditors are entitled to the minimum amount payable under a hypothetical liquidation distribution; where liquidation value is less than the secured financial debt and CIRP costs, the statutory entitlement of operational creditors under Section 53 is nil. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Establishing compliance requires verifying that liquidation valuation was conducted by independent registered valuers and that the minutes of CoC meetings demonstrate substantive deliberation over stakeholders' objections prior to the requisite supermajority vote. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The commercial wisdom of the CoC to accept debt restructuring from MSME promoters to preserve the company as a going concern is inviolable, and the NCLT's pari-passu enhancement of operational payouts from excess CIRP costs satisfies the requirement of equitable treatment.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, sustaining the approval of the Resolution Plan with the clarification that the Monitoring Committee shall enforce NCLT's modification 'b' by distributing the Rs. 7.36 Crores pruned from CIRP costs proportionately on priority to Operational Creditors under Regulation 38(1).
summary: Operational Creditor Pacific World Shipping Pte Ltd appealed the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order approving a Resolution Plan submitted by the promoter-directors of MSME Corporate Debtor Dadi Impex Pvt Ltd. The Appellant contended that allocating 2% to Operational Creditors while Financial Creditors received 100% restructuring was arbitrary and discriminatory. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that judicial review of the CoC's commercial wisdom is limited under the Essar Steel principles. Since the liquidation value (Rs. 41.35 Crores) fell below admitted financial debts (Rs. 48.48 Crores), the operational creditors' liquidation entitlement was nil. The approval was upheld with directions to disburse the Rs. 7.36 Crores pruned from CIRP costs proportionately to Operational Creditors on priority.

case_title: Orbit Lifescience Pvt Ltd vs Raj Ralhan
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Orbit Lifescience Private Limited (Appellant/Intervener/Third-party owner); Raj Ralhan (Respondent/Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Parabolic Drugs Ltd). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bailment Agreement dated 01.05.2018 executed between Appellant and Corporate Debtor for delivering raw materials/stock to the Corporate Debtor's plant for conversion into finished pharmaceutical products. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claim filed by Appellant of Rs. 16,06,33,009 (comprising Rs. 11,01,32,696 Debtor's Account claim and Rs. 5,05,00,313 raw material/stock claim); RP admitted Rs. 11,62,05,100 and rejected a difference amount of Rs. 4,44,27,909 due to missing entries; Corporate Debtor had counter-claims of unpaid operational expenses of Rs. 2,54,26,007 and salary expenses of Rs. 31,86,651. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Bailment agreement dated 01.05.2018; Section 9 CIRP initiated on 23.08.2018; Form-B submitted on 15.11.2018; CoC stock auditor appointed 05.01.2019; NCLT order passed on 26.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bailment Agreement dated 01.05.2018 Clause 11.2 requiring Appellant to fund operating expenses (power, salary, consumables); audited stock segregation verifying Rs. 3.53 Crores already retrieved; books of accounts showing Appellant's non-payment of agreed operating costs; bailee's statutory lien under Section 170 Contract Act. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench allowed CA No. 171/2019 in part under Section 18(1)(f) explanation, directing release of third-party perishable stock conditional upon Appellant reimbursing Rs. 2.30 Crores Pre-CIRP plant costs to the RP; Appellant appealed against the monetary reimbursement condition and unadjudicated difference claim.
legal_issues: Whether third-party assets held under a bailment contract can be unconditionally retrieved from a corporate debtor undergoing CIRP under Section 18(1)(f) of the IBC without satisfying bailee operational expenses and statutory lien rights under Section 170 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Although assets owned by a third party in possession of the corporate debtor do not constitute assets of the corporate debtor under Section 18(1)(f), release of such assets is subject to reciprocal contractual commitments and statutory bailee liens for costs incurred in relation to those goods. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Explanation to Section 18(1) excludes third-party assets held under contractual arrangements from the estate of the corporate debtor, but does not extinguish the bailee's legal right to retain goods or insist on payment of agreed operational costs incurred to maintain and process such assets. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where claims for differential amounts or stock values are unsupported by the verified books of account of the corporate debtor and stock auditor reports, the Resolution Professional's verification cannot be faulted. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly balanced the competing rights by ordering the urgent release of perishable stock while simultaneously requiring reimbursement of pre-CIRP manufacturing expenses agreed upon under the bailment contract.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, sustaining the NCLT Chandigarh Bench's order dated 26.07.2019 in CA No. 171/2019.
summary: Orbit Lifescience Pvt Ltd appealed an NCLT Chandigarh Bench order regarding goods held by Corporate Debtor Parabolic Drugs Ltd under a Bailment Agreement dated 01.05.2018. While NCLT directed the release of Appellant's raw material under Section 18(1)(f) Explanation, it conditioned release on the Appellant reimbursing approximately Rs. 2.30 Crores in pre-CIRP expenses per contractual terms, and declined to admit an unverified claim difference of Rs. 4.44 Crores. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the RP and Corporate Debtor had a valid lien under Section 170 of the Indian Contract Act for incurred operating expenses, and that the Adjudicating Authority properly balanced the interests of both parties without derailing the resolution process.

case_title: Carnoustie Management India Pvt Ltd vs Cbs International Projects Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Carnoustie Management India Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Alleged Financial Creditor); CBS International Projects Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial assistance up to Rs. 40 Crores allegedly granted under a Loan Agreement dated 11.05.2007 for allotment of real estate plots at NOIDA to the Respondent (then a subsidiary of the Appellant), prior to 100% share divestment via Share Purchase Agreement (SPA) dated 13.08.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged outstanding loan amount of Rs. 34,31,87,965 with claimed interest at 12% to 24% per annum, demanded on 28.03.2018 and defaulted on 13.04.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Purported loan agreement dated 11.05.2007; SPA executed on 13.08.2015; SARFAESI notice dated 30.08.2016; demand notice issued 28.03.2018; reply denying agreement 13.04.2018; Section 7 petition CP No. (IB) 792/PB/2018 dismissed 02.01.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Absence of original Loan Agreement dated 11.05.2007; lack of board resolutions authorizing the loan; balance sheets for FY 2012-13 signed by Appellant's own directors showing no repayment terms; two expert forensic reports dated 29.07.2018 and 04.08.2018 stating the loan document was fabricated; Annual Returns showing Appellant was not even a shareholder on 11.05.2007. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi dismissed the Section 7 petition on 02.01.2019, drawing adverse inference from non-production of the original agreement and finding the debt not disbursed against consideration for time value of money; Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an applicant can claim the status of a 'Financial Creditor' under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8) of the IBC relying on a disputed and unproduced loan agreement, and whether mere book entries or financial advances between parent and former subsidiary constitute 'financial debt' without proof of disbursement for the time value of money.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A party claiming to be a financial creditor must produce authentic, genuine primary documentation establishing that funds were disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money; mere advances or disputed book entries lacking proven repayment terms and loan agreements fail to satisfy the threshold of a financial debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Sections 5(7) and 5(8) of the IBC, the grant of a loan ipso facto does not confer the status of a financial creditor unless the creditor establishes genuine disbursement with commercial consideration for the time value of money. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Failure to produce the primary original loan agreement, coupled with unrefuted expert forensic opinions indicating forgery and lack of supporting board resolutions, warrants adverse inference under evidentiary principles. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: In the absence of genuine loan documentation and proof of commercial terms for time value of money, the Appellant is not a financial creditor, and the Section 7 application was rightly dismissed.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT Principal Bench's dismissal order dated 02.01.2019.
summary: Carnoustie Management India Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Principal Bench's dismissal of its Section 7 IBC petition against its former subsidiary, CBS International Projects Pvt. Ltd. Appellant claimed financial debt of over Rs. 34 Crores based on an alleged Loan Agreement dated 11.05.2007 carrying interest. Respondent produced expert reports proving the loan agreement was forged, demonstrated that the original was never produced, and showed that company balance sheets recorded no repayment covenants. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that mere advancement of funds without authentic documentation proving disbursement against consideration for time value of money does not constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8), disqualifying Appellant from maintaining a Section 7 petition.

case_title: Ranjit Kapoor vs Asset Reconstruction Company India Ltd & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ranjit Kapoor (Appellant/Promoter of Corporate Debtor); Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facilities assigned to Respondent No. 1 vide Assignment Agreements dated 21.07.2014 and 17.04.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor's loan account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 06.11.2011; default amount claimed in Section 7 petition filed on 10.01.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 06.11.2011; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 160(PB)/2018 filed on 10.01.2018; admission order passed on 13.06.2018; first appeal Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 410/2018 dismissed on 30.10.2018; miscellaneous application CA No. 190(PB)/2020 filed on 03.01.2020; impugned order passed on 13.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Assignment Agreement dated 17.04.2015 establishing debt entitlement; earlier dismissal order of NCLAT dated 30.10.2018 confirming debt and default and rejecting fraud allegations under Section 65; invocation of Rule 11 inherent powers to bypass limitation findings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After its Section 7 admission order dated 13.06.2018 was affirmed by NCLAT on 30.10.2018, Corporate Debtor filed CA No. 190(PB)/2020 before NCLT under Rule 11 seeking to stay CIRP and dismiss the petition based on Supreme Court's Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave limitation ruling; NCLT dismissed it on 13.01.2020 as misconceived, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a corporate debtor, after having its challenge against an IBC Section 7 admission order conclusively dismissed in appeal, can maintain an interlocutory application under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules before the Adjudicating Authority to stay proceedings and reopen admission on grounds of limitation, and whether an appeal lies under Section 61 from the dismissal of such an application.
ratio_decidendi: 1.
