ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once an insolvency admission order has achieved finality upon dismissal of statutory appeal, a party cannot initiate successive rounds of litigation before the Adjudicating Authority under the guise of inherent powers, and is barred by principles of equity, finality, and issue estoppel. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 61 of the IBC, the remedy of an aggrieved person against an admission order is an appeal within prescribed limitation; Rule 11 of NCLT Rules cannot be invoked as an indirect mechanism to recall, stay, or review a final admission order. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The doctrine of estoppel by conduct applies where a litigant failed to press or succeed on legal defenses in the primary appeal and later seeks collateral invalidation through interlocutory applications. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The attempt to stay CIRP proceedings via CA No. 190(PB)/2020 was an abuse of process and entirely otiose, rendering the subsequent appeal before NCLAT per se not maintainable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as not maintainable without costs, confirming the NCLT Principal Bench's order dated 13.01.2020.
summary: Promoter Ranjit Kapoor appealed the NCLT Principal Bench's rejection of CA No. 190(PB)/2020, wherein the Corporate Debtor sought a stay of CIRP proceedings and dismissal of Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd.'s Section 7 petition on limitation grounds under Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave. The Section 7 admission order dated 13.06.2018 had already been challenged and affirmed by NCLAT in October 2018. NCLAT dismissed the fresh appeal as not maintainable, holding that once admission is finalized, a corporate debtor cannot invoke inherent powers under Rule 11 to reopen admission or stay CIRP, and is stopped by equity, conduct, and res judicata from pursuing collateral litigation.

case_title: Canara Bank vs Valecha Engineering Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Canara Bank (Appellant/Lender Bank); Valecha Engineering Ltd. (Respondent/Borrower Company under High Court winding up proceedings). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial banking relationship involving overdraft credit facility extended by Appellant to Respondent with outstanding banking dues exceeding Rs. 30 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appropriation of Rs. 15.41 Crores received as TDS income tax refund in Respondent's current account by Canara Bank towards outstanding overdraft liabilities; fixed deposit default subject to Section 73(4) deposit holder proceedings. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court winding-up order passed on 01.03.2018 in CP No. 761/2015; stay granted by High Court appellate division in Appeal No. 126/2018 on 06.04.2018; NCLT impugned order passed in MA No. 907/2019 on 25.06.2019/interim hearing. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: High Court order dated 01.03.2018 finding company indebted and unable to pay debts; bank statement reflecting receipt of Rs. 15.41 Crores TDS refund and appropriation against overdraft; MA No. 907/2019 filed in deposit holders' company petition CP No. 2111/(MB)/2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench allowed MA No. 907/2019 directing Canara Bank to reverse its appropriation of Rs. 15.41 Crores and transfer funds to HDFC Bank in an escrow lien account to repay fixed deposit holders; Canara Bank appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT presiding over an application under Section 73(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 by fixed deposit holders has jurisdiction to direct a secured creditor bank to reverse the appropriation of funds from an overdraft account against its lawful dues, especially when winding-up proceedings are pending before the High Court.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The National Company Law Tribunal exercising limited statutory jurisdiction under Section 73(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot issue mandatory recovery or reversal directions against a creditor bank regarding funds appropriated against debt facilities. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 73(4) empowers NCLT to direct repayment of deposits to depositors by the defaulting company; it does not confer extraordinary jurisdiction to adjudicate third-party banking appropriations or compel lenders to surrender appropriated sums. Under Section 283, custody of assets in winding up remains subject to High Court directions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Demonstrating excess of jurisdiction requires examining whether any substantive statutory power authorizes the Tribunal to adjudicate banker's lien and appropriation in a depositor relief proceeding. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT acted without jurisdiction in ordering reversal of the bank's appropriation; the order is quashed and the bank directed to retain funds in an interest-bearing account subject to High Court directions.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned order of NCLT Mumbai Bench is quashed and set aside. Canara Bank is directed to hold the amount of Rs. 15.41 Crores in an interest-bearing account subject to further directions of the High Court in Company Petition No. 761/2015. No order as to costs.
summary: Canara Bank appealed against an NCLT Mumbai Bench order in MA No. 907/2019 (filed in a depositor petition under Section 73(4) of the Companies Act, 2013) which ordered the bank to reverse an appropriation of Rs. 15.41 Crores from the current account of Valecha Engineering Ltd. and deposit it into an HDFC escrow account to repay fixed deposit holders. The bank had adjusted the TDS refund against an outstanding overdraft of over Rs. 30 Crores while High Court winding up proceedings were pending. NCLAT set aside the NCLT order, holding that NCLT lacked statutory jurisdiction under Section 73(4) to order a bank to reverse debt adjustments, directing Canara Bank to hold the money in an interest-bearing account subject to High Court directions.

case_title: Maharashtra State Electricity Transmission Company Limited vs Sri City Private Limited & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Maharashtra State Electricity Transmission Company Limited (Appellant/Transmission Licensee); Sri City Private Limited & KCR Enterprises LLP (Consortium Successful Resolution Applicants/Respondents 1 & 2); Sai Wardha Power Generation Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 3); V. Venkatachalam (Resolution Professional/Respondent No. 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bulk Power Transmission Agreement (BPTA) dated 28.02.2012 allocating 135.15 MW transmission capacity rights for 25 years through Appellant's transmission network pursuant to MERC Open Access Regulations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in transmission and open access charges owed by Corporate Debtor; claims submitted to and admitted by the Resolution Professional during CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: BPTA executed on 28.02.2012; CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor upon Section 7 petition by Indian Opportunities III Pte Limited; Resolution Plan approved by CoC; Adjudicating Authority accepted plan on 17.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Admitted operational claim catered for in the resolution plan; clause 3(s) of the approved Resolution Plan terminating the 25-year BPTA without any obligation, liability, or penalty on the Corporate Debtor or SRA; commercial wisdom exercised by CoC to shed onerous long-term contracts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench approved the Resolution Plan submitted by the consortium of Respondents 1 and 2 on 17.10.2019; Appellant appealed against Para 3(s) terminating the BPTA as violative of Section 30(2)(e) of IBC.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan approved by the CoC can validly terminate an onerous long-term Bulk Power Transmission Agreement without regulatory approval or termination penalties by invoking the clean-slate doctrine and the overriding effect of Section 238 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the clean-slate doctrine and overriding authority of insolvency law, a resolution applicant taking over a corporate debtor cannot be forced to continue onerous long-term commercial agreements, and a resolution plan may validly terminate such contracts without post-resolution liabilities. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC contains an overriding non-obstante clause that prevails over the provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003; termination of an agreement under a CoC-approved resolution plan does not violate Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court examines whether the CoC exercised its commercial wisdom to relieve the enterprise from uneconomic liabilities to ensure viability and whether admitted pre-CIRP claims were treated in compliance with statutory priorities. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The commercial decision of the CoC to approve the plan providing for termination of the long-term BPTA without penalty is fully protected under law and warrants no appellate interference.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, sustaining the NCLT Hyderabad Bench's approval order dated 17.10.2019.
summary: Maharashtra State Electricity Transmission Company Ltd (MSETCL) challenged an NCLT Hyderabad Bench order approving a Resolution Plan for Sai Wardha Power Generation Ltd submitted by a consortium of Sri City Pvt Ltd and KCR Enterprises LLP. The Appellant contended that Clause 3(s) of the plan, which unilaterally terminated a 25-year Bulk Power Transmission Agreement (BPTA) without penalty, violated the Electricity Act, 2003 and Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that by virtue of Section 238 of the IBC and the Supreme Court's Essar Steel ruling, the successful resolution applicant is entitled to a clean slate, and the CoC's commercial wisdom in terminating onerous long-term contracts to preserve business viability overrides other laws.

case_title: Tds Management Consultants Pvt Ltd vs Sunil Kumar Bansal & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: TDS Management Consultants Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Shareholder-Petitioner); Sunil Kumar Bansal (Respondent No. 1/Promoter-Director); Respondent No. 2 (Promoter-Director/Wife of Respondent No. 1); Punjab National Bank (Respondent No. 3/Lender Bank sought to be impleaded); Respondent No. 4 (Target Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged unauthorized mortgaging of company properties by promoter-directors to secure credit facilities for unrelated personal businesses, allegedly in violation of Section 185 of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Impropriety and ultra vires encumbrance of corporate assets and alleged collusion between bank officials and promoters in an oppression and mismanagement petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP No. 140/Chd/Chd/2019 filed under Sections 241 and 242; NCLT Chandigarh Bench passed interlocutory order refusing notice on 10.12.2019; appeal filed before NCLAT in 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Oppression and mismanagement petition pleadings alleging bank connivance under Section 185(4)(iii); absence of prima facie determination of bank's fraudulent complicity at the preliminary stage. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench declined at the preliminary stage to issue notice to Punjab National Bank (Respondent No. 3); Appellant appealed the non-issuance of notice before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT's refusal to issue notice to a lender bank at the threshold stage of an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 constitutes an appealable substantive grievance when the issue of impleadment was kept open for subsequent consideration.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A discretionary procedural order declining to issue notice to a third party at the preliminary stage does not give rise to an appealable grievance where the Adjudicating Authority has expressly reserved liberty to consider impleadment at a subsequent stage upon appropriate justification. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 185(4)(iii) of the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes penal sanctions for contravention of lending restrictions, but does not mandate the automatic threshold impleadment of financing banks in an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241 and 242 prior to establishing a prima facie case. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Appellate courts will not interfere with interlocutory case management orders unless substantive rights have been conclusively prejudiced or foreclosed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the NCLT kept the issue open for the petitioner to persuade the bench at a subsequent stage, no case was made out to entertain the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT Chandigarh Bench's order dated 10.12.2019.
summary: TDS Management Consultants Pvt Ltd appealed against an order of NCLT Chandigarh Bench in an oppression and mismanagement petition filed under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013. The Appellant had impleaded Punjab National Bank alleging it colluded with directors who mortgaged company properties for private businesses in violation of Section 185(4). The NCLT declined to issue notice to the bank at that stage. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the NCLT had kept the issue open for later consideration upon further material, and a preliminary refusal to issue notice without terminating substantive rights warrants no appellate interference.

case_title: Anubhav Anilkumar Agarwal vs Om Prakash Rohra & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anubhav Anilkumar Agarwal, Promoter/Erstwhile Director of M/s AA Estate Private Limited (Corporate Debtor/Appellant); Om Prakash Rohra (Respondent No. 1/Operational Creditor/Former Deputy General Manager - Contracts); Gaurav Khurana (Respondent No. 2/Interim Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment contract initiated via Appointment Letter dated 02.03.2009 appointing Respondent No. 1 as Senior Executive - Estimation & Contract at a monthly remuneration of Rs. 54,166/- plus benefits, culminating in promotion to Deputy General Manager - Contracts with services rendered for over a decade. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of 14 to 15 months of salary arrears from March 2018; debt fell due on 10.04.2018; total claimed default of Rs. 19,23,795/- (comprising Rs. 17,40,375/- principal and Rs. 1,83,420/- interest at 15% per annum). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Date of default 10.04.2018; salary stopped from December 2018; letters issued by employee demanding unpaid salaries on 31.05.2019 and 17.06.2019; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 3008 (MB) of 2019 filed on 30.07.2019; admission order passed on 14.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appointment letter dated 02.03.2009; warning letters issued by Corporate Debtor on 26.10.2018 and 25.03.2019 alleging absenteeism; Corporate Debtor's internal promotion letter dated 29.01.2019 and employer letter dated 14.03.2019 confirming salary non-credit due to business situations and failure to issue Form 16 since FY 2014-15; deduction of TDS without remittance to the revenue authorities. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted Respondent No. 1's Section 9 petition on 14.11.2019, ruling that alleged pre-existing disputes regarding absenteeism were spurious and illusory under Section 5(6); Appellant challenged the admission before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether unsubstantiated allegations of employee absenteeism and failure to tender a formal resignation letter constitute a genuine 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 5(6) of the IBC so as to bar admission of an operational creditor's Section 9 application for unpaid salary arrears.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Spurious, illusory, or moonshine defenses regarding an employee's performance or attendance raised without departmental disciplinary proceedings or formal inquiry do not constitute a pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6) sufficient to defeat an operational debt claim for unpaid salary. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'dispute' under Section 5(6) requires a real, bona fide controversy regarding debt existence or service quality prior to receipt of a demand notice; bald allegations of absenteeism coupled with failure to formally charge or terminate the employee cannot be used as an evasive shield to withhold admitted operational salary debts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the presence of contemporaneous employer admissions confirming non-payment of salary due to financial difficulties, informal warning letters unsupported by disciplinary action fail to meet the standard of a plausible dispute under the Mobilox Innovations framework. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt and default in statutory salary payments were conclusively established, and the Corporate Debtor's defense was an afterthought; the Section 9 admission order was free from legal infirmity.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming NCLT Mumbai Bench's admission order dated 14.11.2019. Appellant is directed to file a certified copy of the impugned order within one week; all connected IAs are closed with liberty to third-party employee applicants to submit claims before the IRP.
summary: Anubhav Anilkumar Agarwal, erstwhile director of Corporate Debtor AA Estate Pvt Ltd, appealed the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by former employee Om Prakash Rohra for unpaid salary arrears of Rs. 19.23 Lakhs. The Appellant contended that pre-existing disputes existed regarding employee absenteeism, deficient services under warning letters dated 26.10.2018 and 25.03.2019, and resignation without notice. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that absenteeism without formal disciplinary proceedings does not amount to a Section 5(6) pre-existing dispute, particularly when the Corporate Debtor had issued letters acknowledging salary non-credits due to financial distress. The Section 9 admission was upheld.

case_title: Mahalaxmi Spinning & Weaving Mills Pvt Ltd vs Maruti Cotex Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mahalaxmi Spinning & Weaving Mills Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Auction Bidder/Respondent No. 4 before NCLT); Maruti Cotex Ltd. through RP Sujata Chattopadhyay (Respondent No. 1/Corporate Debtor); State of Maharashtra through Superintendent of Police & Police Inspector (Respondent Nos. 2 & 3); JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 4/Secured Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Pre-CIRP SARFAESI e-auction conducted by Respondent No. 4 for sale of Corporate Debtor's property valued at Rs. 100 Crores, wherein Appellant paid Rs. 5 Lakhs initial application fee and Rs. 5 Crores Earnest Money Deposit (EMD). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant backed out from paying the balance purchase consideration citing property description discrepancies; Respondent No. 4 forfeited the Rs. 5 Crore EMD, leading Appellant to initiate DRT recovery proceedings and lodge a police complaint on 04.06.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Police complaint lodged by Appellant on 04.06.2018; CIRP subsequently initiated against Corporate Debtor in CP (IB) 241/(MB)/2018; RP filed MA No. 50/2020 alleging harassment by police; NCLT passed interim directions on 18.02.2020/impugned order; appeal heard and disposed of on 24.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Auction sale remained unconcluded without passage of property title to Appellant; pending DRT proceedings regarding validity of EMD forfeiture; police complaint dated 04.06.2018 predating CIRP; communication Exhibit-G regarding CIRP hindrances; unconditional undertaking by Appellant's counsel not to interfere with CIRP or assert title encumbrances. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In MA No. 50/2020, NCLT Mumbai Bench restrained Appellant from obstructing CIRP and directed police authorities to take strenuous criminal/contempt action against Appellant for maliciously proceeding against the RP under Section 233 of IBC; Appellant appealed to NCLAT against the adverse police direction.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the legal competence under the IBC to direct police authorities to take criminal/contempt action against an unsuccessful pre-CIRP auction bidder who lodged a pre-CIRP police complaint against a secured creditor, when the bidder undertakes not to assert rights over corporate debtor assets or obstruct CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While the Adjudicating Authority may protect the Resolution Professional from mala fide interference under Section 233 of the IBC, adverse penal directions commanding police authorities to take coercive action for contempt against a litigant should be expunged when the party provides a binding judicial undertaking disclaiming interest in the corporate debtor's assets and committing not to interfere with the insolvency process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 233 protects the Resolution Professional from actions taken in good faith during CIRP, but does not serve as a penal tool to direct criminal retribution for disputes that originated prior to the insolvency commencement date where no interference with CIRP is persisted in. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Recording an express, unequivocal undertaking of counsel in open court disclaiming title encumbrances over corporate debtor property is sufficient to vitiate the need for coercive punitive directions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: In view of the Appellant's formal undertaking not to impede CIRP or dispute the Corporate Debtor's title, the directive commanding police to take strenuous action for contempt was expunged and the order modified accordingly.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of by modifying the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order dated 18.02.2020, deleting the direction commanding police authorities to take strenuous action against the Appellant for contempt, while recording the Appellant's undertaking not to interfere with CIRP or claim any encumbrance on the Corporate Debtor's assets. No costs.
summary: Mahalaxmi Spinning & Weaving Mills Pvt Ltd appealed an order of NCLT Mumbai Bench in MA No. 50/2020 in the CIRP of Maruti Cotex Ltd. The Appellant, who had paid Rs. 5 Crores EMD in a pre-CIRP SARFAESI auction that fell through, had filed DRT and police proceedings regarding EMD forfeiture. NCLT restrained the Appellant from obstructing CIRP and directed the police to take strenuous action against Appellant for contempt and harassing the RP under Section 233 of IBC. NCLAT expunged the adverse police direction upon recording the Appellant's solemn undertaking that it would not interfere in CIRP or claim any title or encumbrance over the Corporate Debtor's properties.

case_title: Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited vs TSN Raja RP Of Vbc Industries Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited (IREDA) (Appellant/Secured Creditor); T.S.N. Raja (Respondent/Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s VBC Industries Limited); M/s Orissa Power Consortium Limited (OPCL/Principal Borrower). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loan facility of Rs. 65 Crores extended on 18.11.2015 by Appellant to OPCL, secured by Corporate Debtor VBC Industries Limited creating a mortgage charge over its real property at Plot No. 76, Mouza Bhubaneshwar Sahar, Unit No. 7, Surya Nagar, Khurda, Odisha. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal borrower OPCL had not committed default in payment of loan instalments to IREDA; Corporate Debtor was admitted to CIRP; Appellant submitted claim for the contingent exposure of outstanding loan balances to preserve mortgage security. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Term loan granted 18.11.2015; CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor; claim rejected by RP via email on 03.02.2019; IA No. 208/2019 filed under Section 60(5) dismissed by NCLT on 17.07.2019; CoC approved resolution plan; appeal decided 03.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Term loan agreement dated 18.11.2015; valid mortgage security document over corporate debtor's Bhubaneshwar immovable property; admitted absence of payment default by principal borrower OPCL at the time of claim submission. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP rejected IREDA's claim because OPCL had not defaulted, meaning no mature debt existed; NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissed IREDA's Section 60(5) application on 17.07.2019 upholding RP's rejection; IREDA appealed to NCLAT to protect its mortgage rights prior to resolution plan approval.
legal_issues: Whether a lender holding a valid third-party mortgage over the corporate debtor's assets for a term loan where the principal borrower has not yet defaulted possesses a contingent 'claim' under Section 3(6) of the IBC that must be disclosed to and considered by the Successful Resolution Applicant to prevent extinguishment under the clean-slate doctrine.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To prevent unexpected claims from extinguishing existing encumbrances or springing up after plan approval under the clean-slate doctrine, contingent rights of third-party secured lenders holding mortgaged security over a corporate debtor's assets must be brought to the notice of the prospective resolution applicant and considered by the Adjudicating Authority prior to plan approval. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(6) defines 'claim' broadly to include rights to payment and remedies for breach of contract whether or not fixed, disputed, undisputed, matured, unmatured, secured, or unsecured; an unmatured contingent mortgage right falls within this statutory definition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Supreme Court's Essar Steel doctrine, all existing and contingent claims must be identified during CIRP so that prospective resolution applicants do not face sudden, undecided liabilities after takeover. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While the claim cannot be admitted as an overdue debt since the primary borrower has not defaulted, the existing contingent mortgage right must be disclosed to the Successful Resolution Applicant, and the Adjudicating Authority must hear the applicant and consider the right before approving the plan.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of with directions allowing IREDA to bring its contingent mortgage rights to the notice of the Successful Resolution Applicant via an application before NCLT Hyderabad Bench, and directing the Adjudicating Authority to hear the Resolution Applicant and consider said rights before deciding on plan approval. No costs.
summary: IREDA appealed against NCLT Hyderabad Bench's order upholding the Resolution Professional's rejection of its claim in the CIRP of VBC Industries Ltd. IREDA had sanctioned a Rs. 65 Crore loan to Orissa Power Consortium Ltd, secured by a mortgage over the Corporate Debtor's property. The RP and NCLT rejected the claim because the principal borrower had not defaulted. NCLAT disposed of the appeal by holding that while the claim had not matured, IREDA holds a contingent right under Section 3(6) of the IBC. Applying Essar Steel's clean-slate principles, NCLAT directed that IREDA's contingent mortgage right must be made known to the Successful Resolution Applicant and considered by the Adjudicating Authority prior to approving the Resolution Plan.

case_title: Laxmi Ventures India Ltd vs State Bank Of India & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Laxmi Ventures (India) Limited (Appellant/Corporate Debtor); State Bank of India (Respondent No. 1/Financial Creditor); Sunil Agarwal and Others (Respondent Nos. 2-4/Intervenors claiming 50% shareholding). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Banking credit facilities extended by State Bank of India to Corporate Debtor; intra-shareholder dispute governed by Bombay High Court order dated 26.04.2012 regarding management and accounting of the Bhilai manufacturing unit. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit facilities leading to filing of Section 7 application CP (IB)-3307 (MB)/2019; subsequent complete One Time Settlement (OTS) entered prior to admission with full satisfaction of bank dues. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court interim order dated 26.04.2012; Section 7 petition filed in 2019; OTS arrived at between SBI and Corporate Debtor; 'No Due Certificate' issued by SBI on 01.02.2020; NCLT order in IA 149/2020 passed on 29.01.2020; NCLAT final order passed on 17.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: 'No Due Certificate' dated 01.02.2020 issued by State Bank of India certifying full payment under OTS; Bombay High Court order dated 26.04.2012 in Sunil Agarwal v. Laxmi Ventures; absence of any order admitting the Section 7 petition. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In pending Section 7 petition, 50% shareholders filed IA No. 149/2020 seeking production of OTS documents and impleadment; NCLT Mumbai Bench on 29.01.2020 directed SBI and Corporate Debtor to furnish OTS proposals and acceptance to the intervenors; Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether third-party shareholders have locus standi to intervene in a Section 7 IBC application or compel disclosure of settlement terms between the financial creditor and corporate debtor after the underlying financial debt has been fully settled via OTS prior to admission.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In an insolvency application under Section 7 of the IBC, internal shareholders have no legal standing to intervene or demand production of private compromise terms when the financial creditor and corporate debtor have settled the underlying debt prior to admission, rendering the proceedings infructuous. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Proceedings under Section 7 are exclusively between the financial creditor and the corporate debtor to ascertain debt and default; where a pre-admission settlement renders the petition infructuous, the Adjudicating Authority must permit withdrawal rather than entertain collateral shareholder disputes. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production of a valid No Due Certificate issued by the financial creditor conclusively establishes that no default subsists, extinguishing the subject matter of the Section 7 petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application having become infructuous upon settlement, the direction compelling disclosure of OTS terms to shareholder intervenors was unsustainable and set aside, with the petition standing withdrawn.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and paragraph 3 of NCLT Mumbai Bench's order dated 29.01.2020 directing disclosure of OTS documents is set aside. The Section 7 application filed by State Bank of India stands withdrawn and NCLT is directed to close proceedings, leaving intervenors at liberty to agitate shareholder disputes before the appropriate legal forum. No costs.
summary: Laxmi Ventures (India) Ltd appealed an order of NCLT Mumbai Bench in IA No. 149/2020 in CP (IB)-3307(MB)/2019, which directed SBI and the Corporate Debtor to provide copies of their One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal and acceptance to 50% shareholder-intervenors. SBI confirmed before NCLAT that an OTS was concluded and a No Due Certificate issued on 01.02.2020 prior to admission. NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the disclosure direction, holding that shareholder disputes cannot be entertained within a Section 7 proceeding. The Section 7 petition was declared withdrawn and directed to be closed, with liberty granted to intervenors to seek appropriate relief in independent civil forums.

case_title: Arunkant Rai vs Allahabad Bank & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Arunkant Rai (Appellant/Promoter of Corporate Debtor); Allahabad Bank (Respondent No. 1/Consortium Financial Creditor); Suman Agritech Limited through IRP Navin Khandelwal (Respondent No. 2/Corporate Debtor); IDBI Bank (Lead Bank of Consortium). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium lending credit facilities extended to Corporate Debtor governed by Inter-se Agreement and Consortium Agreement both dated 15.11.2010 executed between Allahabad Bank and IDBI Bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit repayment resulting in Allahabad Bank classifying the Corporate Debtor's loan account as Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 30.09.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Consortium and inter-se agreements dated 15.11.2010; loan declared NPA on 30.09.2016; Section 7 petition CP 1003 (IB)/MB/2019 filed on 11.03.2019; NCLT admission order passed on 27.08.2019; NCLAT appeal decided on 11.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Inter-se Agreement dated 15.11.2010 containing clauses requiring 15 to 30 days prior notice to lead bank (IDBI) before initiating legal action; non-signatory status of the Corporate Debtor to the Inter-se Agreement; bank NPA classification records dated 30.09.2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted Allahabad Bank's Section 7 petition on 27.08.2019 and initiated CIRP; Corporate Debtor's promoter appealed arguing the petition was barred because Allahabad Bank failed to issue the mandatory inter-bank 15-day notice to lead bank IDBI under the consortium agreement.
legal_issues: Whether a corporate debtor can challenge the maintainability of a Section 7 IBC application on the ground that a consortium member bank breached internal inter-se consortium lending agreements requiring prior notice to or consent from the lead bank before taking recovery action.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An inter-se consortium agreement between lending banks is an arrangement solely binding among the participating financial institutions; a corporate debtor who is a non-signatory cannot invoke inter-bank covenants to challenge the maintainability of a Section 7 application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC confers an independent statutory right upon every individual financial creditor to initiate CIRP upon occurrence of default, which cannot be restricted, abridged, or overridden by private consortium covenants. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Breach of inter-bank consortium rules is strictly a matter between the participating banks or regulatory oversight by the Reserve Bank of India, and does not create an evidentiary or legal impediment against the establishment of default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: There is no bar in law preventing a bank that has declared an account as NPA from independently initiating Section 7 proceedings, and the NCLT admission was fully justified.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, sustaining NCLT Mumbai Bench's order dated 27.08.2019 admitting the Section 7 petition.
summary: Arunkant Rai, promoter of Corporate Debtor Suman Agritech Ltd, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai Bench order admitting Allahabad Bank's Section 7 IBC petition. The Appellant contended that under the Inter-se and Consortium Agreements dated 15.11.2010, Allahabad Bank was required to give 15 days' notice to lead bank IDBI before initiating legal action, making the Section 7 petition non-maintainable. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that inter-se agreements between banks do not bind third parties, and the Corporate Debtor cannot claim rights under covenants to which it was not a party. Section 7 gives financial creditors an independent statutory right to trigger insolvency upon default, which cannot be overridden by consortium agreements.

case_title: Urban Infrastructure Trustees Ltd vs Ozone Propex Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Urban Infrastructure Trustees Ltd. (Appellant/Financial Creditor); Ozone Propex Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial debt facility disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money triggering an application under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of financial debt exceeding the threshold limit of Rs. 1 Lakh under Section 4 of the Code. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition filed in January 2019; petition kept pending for over one year; NCLT adjournment order passed on 17.12.2019 deferring adjudication until Karnataka High Court decided a collateral writ petition; appeal heard and disposed of on 03.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form 1 petition filed under Rule 4 with requisite supporting documents; absence of any order of injunction or stay granted by the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka halting the Section 7 insolvency proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench adjourned the Section 7 petition on 17.12.2019 on grounds of sub-judice, deciding to defer adjudication until the Karnataka High Court resolved the pending writ petition; Financial Creditor appealed to NCLAT seeking expeditious statutory disposal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can defer adjudication and keep a Section 7 IBC application pending on grounds of sub-judice due to parallel proceedings before a High Court in the absence of an express interim stay order, contrary to the mandatory 14-day statutory timeline and Supreme Court precedent in Innoventive Industries.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of an explicit judicial stay order issued by a superior constitutional court, the Adjudicating Authority is statutorily mandated to determine debt and default in a Section 7 application within the prescribed timelines, and cannot adjourn proceedings sine die under the pretext of sub-judice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 7(4) and Section 7(5) of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority must ascertain the existence of default within 14 days and either admit or reject the application; mere pendency of collateral matters before a High Court does not toll or suspend this statutory mandate. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying Innoventive Industries, the inquiry at the Section 7 stage is strictly confined to verifying whether default has occurred; if debt is due and unpaid in law or fact, admission is mandatory unless the petition is incomplete. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's postponement was improper given the lack of any High Court stay; the Adjudicating Authority is directed to decide the application expeditiously within the parameters of Innoventive Industries.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of with directions commanding the NCLT Bengaluru Bench to decide the Section 7 application expeditiously in accordance with the law settled in Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank, noting the absence of any stay order by the Karnataka High Court. No costs.
summary: Urban Infrastructure Trustees Ltd appealed against an order of NCLT Bengaluru Bench dated 17.12.2019 which deferred hearing its Section 7 IBC application against Ozone Propex Pvt Ltd on the grounds that collateral proceedings were sub-judice before the Karnataka High Court. The Appellant pointed out that the Section 7 petition had been languishing for over a year without any formal stay. NCLAT disposed of the appeal by directing the NCLT to decide the application expeditiously, emphasizing that in the absence of an express stay from the High Court, the Adjudicating Authority is bound under Section 7 and the Supreme Court's ruling in Innoventive Industries to ascertain debt and default within statutory timelines.

case_title: Panch Tatva Promoters Pvt Ltd vs Gpt Steel Industries Ltd Through RP & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Panch Tatva Promoters Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Applicant/Prospective Resolution Applicant); GPT Steel Industries Ltd. through RP (Respondent No. 1/Corporate Debtor); Committee of Creditors & H-1 Bidder (Respondent Nos. 2 & 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Corporate Debtor wherein competitive resolution plans were submitted, resulting in Respondent No. 3 emerging as Highest Bidder-1 (H-1). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP reaching conclusion period; Appellant submitted an unsolicited Revised Resolution Plan claiming higher value maximization over H-1's plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under CP (IB) No. 157/NCLT/AHM/2018; IA No. 116/2020 filed by Appellant heard on 13.02.2020 and 18.02.2020; impugned listing order passed on 18.02.2020 posting matter to 25.02.2020; appeal decided 24.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Filings in IA No. 116/2020 containing Appellant's revised plan; reply filed by H-1 bidder; absence of any substantive decision on the plan by NCLT on 18.02.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench heard IA No. 116/2020 on 18.02.2020, noted H-1's reply, and listed the matter for further hearing on 25.02.2020 without granting interim stay; Appellant appealed to NCLAT alleging that refusing interim relief before CIRP expired caused substantial grievance.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal lies under Section 61 of the IBC against a routine procedural listing order that defers consideration without granting ex-parte interim relief, when the underlying application seeking consideration of a revised resolution plan remains pending undecided before the Adjudicating Authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal under Section 61 of the IBC against a purely procedural adjournment order is premature and otiose where the Adjudicating Authority has not finally adjudicated substantive rights or decided upon the approval or rejection of a resolution plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(3) restricts appellate scrutiny of resolution plan proceedings to specific statutory grounds; an interlocutory adjournment order does not constitute a legal grievance within the meaning of an appealable order under Section 61. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A party cannot claim to be an aggrieved person entitled to maintain an appeal unless the impugned order causes a substantial legal grievance by wrongfully depriving them of a legal right or concluding the lis. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because IA No. 116/2020 was still sub-judice before the NCLT, appellate interference on merits was unwarranted, and the appropriate course was to direct the Adjudicating Authority to decide the application expeditiously within one week.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as premature and otiose without costs, with a direction to NCLT Ahmedabad Bench to finally dispose of IA No. 116/2020 in CP (IB) 157/NCLT/AHM/2018 within one week from receipt of the order before approving or rejecting any resolution plan. IA Nos. 833 & 834 of 2020 are closed.
summary: Panch Tatva Promoters Pvt Ltd appealed an interlocutory order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dated 18.02.2020 which listed its application IA No. 116/2020 for hearing on 25.02.2020 without granting interim relief. The Appellant had submitted a revised resolution plan offering higher value than H-1 and argued that posting the case without interim protection beyond the CIRP expiry caused serious prejudice. NCLAT dismissed the appeal as premature and otiose under Section 61, holding that a procedural listing order does not decide substantive rights. NCLAT directed the Adjudicating Authority to hear the parties and decide the IA on merits within one week prior to approving or rejecting any plan.

case_title: Maharashtra State Load Dispatch Center vs Sri City Pvt Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Maharashtra State Load Dispatch Center (MSLDC) (Appellant/State Undertaking); Sri City Private Limited & KCR Enterprise LLP (Respondents 1 & 2/Consortium Successful Resolution Applicants); Corporate Debtor under CIRP (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Regulatory grid and load dispatch services provided by Appellant to Corporate Debtor; transmission liabilities treated under the CIRP resolution plan. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of statutory/regulatory dispatch charges; claims dealt with and adjudicated by the Committee of Creditors under the Resolution Plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution Plan approved by NCLT Hyderabad Bench on 17.10.2019; subsequent direction issued 10.01.2019/2020; appeal filed after a delay of 60 days beyond the initial 30-day limitation period (total delay of 90 days); decided on 07.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record showing delay of 60 days beyond the 30-day statutory appeal period; earlier dismissal on merits of identical appeal filed by sister concern MSETCL in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1401 of 2019 on 03.02.2020; CoC approval of the plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench approved the consortium's Resolution Plan on 17.10.2019; Appellant filed appeal challenging plan approval after an un-condonable delay of 60 days, citing its status as a Government of Maharashtra undertaking.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT has statutory jurisdiction under Section 61(2) of the IBC to condone a delay of 60 days beyond the initial 30-day period for filing an appeal on the ground that the appellant is a State Government undertaking, and whether an appeal can be maintained when an identical challenge by a sister concern has already been dismissed on merits.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The appellate tribunal has no statutory power under Section 61(2) of the IBC to condone delay exceeding fifteen days beyond the prescribed thirty-day limitation period, and government entities enjoy no special exemption from this mandatory jurisdictional bar. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The proviso to Section 61(2) restricts condonation of delay strictly to a maximum of 15 days upon demonstration of sufficient cause; delays beyond this 45-day outer limit extinguish the tribunal's jurisdiction to entertain the appeal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the record establishes on its face that the appeal was filed 60 days after expiry of the 30-day limitation period, no inquiry into sufficient cause or governmental status is permissible. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is barred by limitation; furthermore, the CoC's commercial approval of the plan is protected under Essar Steel and the dismissal on merits of the sister concern's appeal leaves no ground for relief.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed both on the ground of limitation and on merits. No costs.
summary: Maharashtra State Load Dispatch Center (MSLDC), a State Government undertaking, appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad Bench order dated 17.10.2019 approving the Resolution Plan submitted by the consortium of Sri City Pvt Ltd and KCR Enterprise LLP. The appeal was filed with a delay of 60 days beyond the 30-day statutory limitation period. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 61(2) of the IBC, the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to condone delay beyond 15 days, irrespective of whether the appellant is a government entity. NCLAT further noted that an identical appeal by its sister concern (MSETCL) had already been dismissed on merits under the Essar Steel doctrine.

case_title: Bank Of India And Anr vs Royal Splendour Developers Pvt Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bank of India (Appellant/Dissenting Financial Creditor with 24.97% voting share); Royal Splendour Developers Pvt. Ltd. through RP Kavitha Surana (Respondent No. 1/Corporate Debtor); Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial project lending and banking credit facilities secured by financial securities and mortgages held by Appellant bank over real estate developer's assets. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit facilities leading to CIRP; Resolution Plan formulated and approved by Committee of Creditors (CoC) by a majority of 70.93%, with Appellant casting a dissenting vote of 24.97% seeking liquidation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC approved Resolution Plan with 70.93% majority; NCLT Chennai Division Bench approved the plan; appeal challenging plan approval dismissed at admission on 17.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Voting results sheet Annexure-E showing 70.93% approval and 24.97% dissent; Resolution Plan provisions ensuring treatment of secured creditor classes; absence of any proposal moved by Appellant in CoC meetings regarding handling of securities upon potential implementation failure. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Division Bench Chennai approved the CoC-sanctioned Resolution Plan; Appellant Bank challenged the approval before NCLAT seeking insertion of a contingency clause governing the fate of its securities should the SRA fail to complete the real estate project.
legal_issues: Whether a dissenting financial creditor can maintain an appeal under the IBC to compel the modification of an approved resolution plan by inserting speculative contingency provisions regarding the enforcement of securities in the event of future implementation default by the successful resolution applicant.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal possesses no residual equity jurisdiction to modify a resolution plan approved by the requisite majority of the Committee of Creditors to insert speculative contingency covenants regarding future business default by the resolution applicant. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Sections 30 and 31 of the IBC and the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel, the commercial decision of the CoC taken by majority vote binds dissenting minority creditors, and adjudicating tribunals cannot assess the subjective fairness of commercial terms so long as the statutory liquidation value of each creditor class is respected. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An objection seeking contractual modifications cannot be entertained in appeal when the appellant failed to table or propose such terms during the deliberative meetings of the Committee of Creditors. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The commercial wisdom of the 70.93% majority CoC approving the plan is sovereign, and the court will not mandate speculative terms regarding hypothetical post-implementation failures.
operative_order: Admission of the appeal is declined, and the appeal is dismissed without costs.
summary: Bank of India, a dissenting financial creditor holding a 24.97% voting share, appealed an order of NCLT Chennai Division Bench approving the Resolution Plan for Royal Splendour Developers Pvt Ltd, which had been approved by a 70.93% CoC majority. The Appellant argued that the plan was flawed because it omitted provisions specifying how the bank's securities would be dealt with if the Successful Resolution Applicant failed to complete the project. NCLAT declined admission and dismissed the appeal, holding that under the Supreme Court's Essar Steel decision, the Tribunal has no residual jurisdiction to alter the commercial wisdom of the CoC or mandate speculative clauses addressing hypothetical future defaults by a resolution applicant.

case_title: M/s Ansal Properties & Infrastructure Ltd. vs. M/s MGF Developments Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s Ansal Properties & Infrastructure Ltd. claimed status as Operational Creditor; Respondent M/s MGF Developments Ltd. was alleged to be Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Parties entered into a Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) dated 08.07.2004 as a consortium (50:50 share) to bid for property development at Netaji Subhash Place (Wazirpur) Metro Station, Delhi, followed by a Concession Agreement dated 02.09.2004 with Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) for a 12-year lease to develop and sub-let shops. Under an agreement dated 22.06.2005, an escrow account in the Respondent's name was opened to manage and distribute 50% revenue share to Appellant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed unpaid dues of Rs. 3,81,19,346.84; default occurred post-09.12.2016 when the Respondent ceased sharing revenues. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 of IBC issued on 24.08.2018; Respondent replied on 12.09.2018 disputing liability. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MoA dated 08.07.2004, Concession Agreement dated 02.09.2004 naming parties jointly as 'Concessionaire', escrow agreement dated 22.06.2005, and DMRC dispute letter dated 20.08.2018 establishing pre-existing disputes. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition (IB-1562/(ND)/2018) filed before NCLT New Delhi Bench-III was dismissed on 17.07.2019 for lack of Operational Creditor-Corporate Debtor relationship, absence of operational debt, and pre-existing dispute.
legal_issues: Whether a consortium partner in a joint development/concession agreement claiming an agreed 50% revenue share qualifies as an 'Operational Creditor' with a claim of 'Operational Debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC against the co-consortium member.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Parties collaborating as consortium members or joint-venture partners in a joint development venture do not render operational services or supply goods to one another; hence, profit- or revenue-sharing claims arising from such agreements do not constitute operational debt under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) requires a claim in respect of the provision of goods or services. Mutual execution and obligations under a joint concession agreement where both parties act collectively as concessionaires exclude the classification of either co-venturer as an operational creditor under Section 5(20). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of underlying contractual instruments (MoA and Concession Agreement) and Section 9 pleadings to ascertain if any direct service or sale of goods was explicitly provided by the claimant to the respondent. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The relationship between consortium co-venturers sharing revenue is not that of an Operational Creditor and Corporate Debtor, and no operational debt exists under Section 5(21), rendering the Section 9 application non-maintainable.
operative_order: The appeal is devoid of merit and accordingly dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary: Ansal Properties & Infrastructure Ltd. entered into a joint consortium agreement with MGF Developments Ltd. to develop commercial space at Netaji Subhash Place Metro Station under a concession from DMRC, sharing revenues 50:50. After revenue transfers ceased post-December 2016, Ansal filed a Section 9 application claiming Rs. 3.81 crores. NCLT dismissed it for lack of operational debt. On appeal, NCLAT affirmed that co-venturers in a joint venture/consortium do not supply goods or render services to each other, rendering the claim ineligible under Section 5(21) of the IBC.

case_title: Bank of Baroda vs. Mr. Sundaresh Bhatt, Resolution Professional
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Bank of Baroda is a Financial Creditor/lender; Respondent Mr. Sundaresh Bhatt is the Resolution Professional of ABG Shipyard Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Non-fund-based credit facilities sanctioned under a Master Restructuring Agreement, against which the Corporate Debtor maintained three Fixed Deposits totaling Rs. 9,73,83,818/- as margin money for Bank Guarantees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following invocation of a Bank Guarantee by a third party on 17.06.2017, Bank of Baroda adjusted and appropriated fixed deposits amounting to Rs. 9,74,62,608/- (inclusive of accrued interest). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor under Section 7 on 01.08.2017 with moratorium declared; lead bank (ICICI Bank) circulated the admission order to all consortium lenders on 03.08.2017; bank closed the FDs on 02.08.2017 with accounting adjustment entries posted on 09.08.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Three FD receipts (Nos. 29100300001777, 29100300001820, 29100300001821); bank internal instruction note dated 01.08.2017 acknowledging pending NCLT admission and inability to adjust margin money without IRP/CoC consent; bank ledger/account statements dated 02.08.2017 and 09.08.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA No. 303 of 2018 in CP(IB) No. 53 of 2017 under Section 60(5) read with Sections 14 & 74 before NCLT Ahmedabad; NCLT allowed the IA, directing reversal of Rs. 9,74,62,608/- with interest into the Corporate Debtor's TRA account.
legal_issues: Whether a lender bank can appropriate margin money held in fixed deposits of a corporate debtor after the commencement of CIRP and imposition of moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, relying on pre-existing bank guarantee invocation or internal instructions issued on the date of admission.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a moratorium is imposed under Section 14 of the IBC upon admission of CIRP, a financial creditor is strictly barred from encashing, appropriating, or adjusting assets/fixed deposits of the corporate debtor towards its dues, irrespective of internal instructions predating knowledge of admission. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 mandates an absolute standstill; internal instructions by a financial creditor do not effectuate appropriation until the accounts are formally closed and adjusted, which, if occurring post-admission, directly violates the statutory moratorium. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective determination of the exact chronological timestamp of actual account closure and adjustment relative to the date and time of the CIRP admission order. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The fixed deposit accounts were closed on 02.08.2017 and entries made subsequent to the declaration of moratorium on 01.08.2017; consequently, the appropriation was unlawful and hit by Section 14 of the IBC.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, confirming the Adjudicating Authority's direction ordering the bank to reverse the appropriated amount of Rs. 9,74,62,608/- with accrued interest into the Corporate Debtor's TRA account.
summary: Bank of Baroda challenged the NCLT Ahmedabad order directing it to refund Rs. 9,74,62,608/- along with interest, which it had appropriated from three fixed deposits held as margin money by ABG Shipyard Limited. CIRP was admitted on 01.08.2017, but the bank closed the FD accounts on 02.08.2017 pursuant to an internal instruction dated 01.08.2017. NCLAT held that internal instructions are irrelevant; since the formal closure and appropriation took effect after the CIRP admission order, it directly violated the statutory moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Sita Ram vs. Samir Kumar Bhattacharya, RP of Stesalit Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Sita Ram is an individual/claimant; Respondent No. 1 Mr. Samir Kumar Bhattacharya is the Resolution Professional of Stesalit Limited (Corporate Debtor, Respondent No. 2); Respondent No. 3 is Chairman of Monitoring Committee; Respondent No. 5 is M/s River Rail JV (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Insolvency proceedings leading to approval of a resolution plan for Stesalit Limited submitted by M/s River Rail JV. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Challenge to the approved resolution plan value and non-consideration of claims. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan approved by NCLT Kolkata on 20.07.2018 in C.P. (IB) No. 512/KB/2017; public notices published on 08.12.2018; letter from Monitoring Committee sent on 21.12.2018; certified copy stamp paper purchased on 22.01.2019; certified copy applied for on 21.02.2019 and received on 25.02.2019; appeal presented on 01.03.2019, refiled after defect curation on 02.07.2019 (116 days delay). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Newspaper publications in 'Dainik Tribune' and 'The Statesman' dated 08.12.2018 circulating in HP; postal records from Haripur Sandoli BO showing dispatch on 21.12.2018; certified copy endorsement showing stamp paper purchased on 22.01.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata approved the resolution plan on 20.07.2018. The Appellant filed an appeal challenging the approval on 01.03.2019 before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal filed beyond the 30-day period and the condonable limit of 15 days under Section 61(2) of the IBC can be entertained based on a plea of lack of personal knowledge and illiteracy when constructive notice was given via public newspaper notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The appellate jurisdiction under Section 61 of the IBC strictly limits condonation of delay to a maximum period of 15 days beyond the statutory 30-day window, and the tribunal possesses no statutory power to condone delay beyond 45 days. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) limitation is mandatory and strictly construed; constructive knowledge of an approved resolution plan is properly imputed to stakeholders upon wide publication in circulating newspapers. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of proof of public notifications and dates of purchase of court stamp paper to assess the veracity and credibility of an appellant's claim of first acquiring knowledge at a later date. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Constructive knowledge was attributable to the Appellant as of 08.12.2018, and stamp paper was procured on 22.01.2019, making the presentation on 01.03.2019 hopelessly barred by limitation beyond the statutory condonable period.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as time-barred. No order as to costs.
summary: Sita Ram challenged the NCLT Kolkata order dated 20.07.2018 approving the resolution plan for Stesalit Limited, presenting the appeal on 01.03.2019. The Appellant contended he learned of the order only on 31.01.2019 due to illiteracy and rural residence. The respondents proved that public notices were published in regional newspapers on 08.12.2018, and records revealed the Appellant purchased stamp papers for a certified copy on 22.01.2019. NCLAT held that constructive knowledge was attributable by 08.12.2018 and dismissed the appeal as barred by limitation under Section 61(2) of the IBC.

case_title: Yamuna Infradevelopers Pvt. Ltd. vs. Rakesh Takyar, Resolution Professional & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Yamuna Infradevelopers Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (through promoter/management); Respondent No. 1 Rakesh Takyar is the Resolution Professional; Respondent No. 2 Oriental Bank of Commerce (OBC) is the sole Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Default on credit facilities extended by Oriental Bank of Commerce leading to CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount under credit facilities resulting in CIRP; Corporate Debtor submitted an OTS proposal which was rejected by OBC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC meeting convened on 03.10.2019 resolving liquidation; subsequent liquidation order passed by NCLT New Delhi. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC meeting minutes dated 03.10.2019 reflecting 100% voting in favor of liquidation after zero resolution plans were received, and rejection of the OTS proposal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed an application for liquidation before NCLT New Delhi after failure to receive resolution plans during CIRP; NCLT ordered liquidation under Section 33, against which the Corporate Debtor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an order of liquidation under Section 33 of the IBC is legally sustainable when the CoC unanimously votes for liquidation after receiving no resolution plans, and whether a pending settlement/compromise offer bars liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When no resolution plans are received during CIRP and the Committee of Creditors resolves with the requisite majority to liquidate the Corporate Debtor, the Adjudicating Authority is bound to pass an order of liquidation under Section 33 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33 mandates liquidation upon CoC recommendation where resolution fails; the Adjudicating Authority has no discretion to stall liquidation merely because an unaccepted settlement or OTS proposal is touted by the debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of procedural compliance regarding failure of CIRP, absence of resolution plans, and valid voting share threshold of the CoC recommending liquidation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidation order suffered from no legal infirmity; however, an eligible person remains entitled to float a scheme of compromise or arrangement under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 during liquidation.
operative_order: The appeal is devoid of merit and dismissed, with observation that eligible persons may submit proposals under Sections 230 and 232 of the Companies Act, 2013 during liquidation.
summary: Yamuna Infradevelopers Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order directing its liquidation under Section 33 of the IBC. During CIRP, no resolution plans were received, and the Corporate Debtor's OTS proposal was rejected by the sole financial creditor, Oriental Bank of Commerce, leading the CoC to approve liquidation with 100% voting on 03.10.2019. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority had no option but to order liquidation, confirmed the order, and dismissed the appeal while clarifying that proposals under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 could still be pursued.

case_title: Doshion Pvt. Ltd. vs. Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Doshion Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Respondent Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. is the Financial Creditor/Assignee. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial debt/credit facilities forming the subject matter of an insolvency petition. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial default forming the basis of petition CP (IB) 63/2018 under the IBC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Hearing concluded and order reserved by NCLT Ahmedabad on 18.12.2019 with one week granted for written submissions; appeal presented prior to pronouncement. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT daily order sheet dated 18.12.2019 stating 'order reserved' in CP (IB) 63/2018 and granting one week to submit written submissions. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition CP (IB) 63/2018 was heard by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench and reserved for orders on 18.12.2019. Corporate Debtor filed an appeal under Section 61 before NCLAT against the order reserving judgment.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC is maintainable against a procedural order of the Adjudicating Authority merely reserving the main petition for orders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory right of appeal under Section 61 of the IBC is available exclusively to an 'aggrieved person' upon the pronouncement of an order determining legal rights, and no appeal lies against an order that merely reserves judgment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(1) and 61(2) presuppose a definitive order affecting the rights of a party; an order reserving judgment does not constitute an appealable pronouncement, nor does it render any party 'aggrieved'. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Face-of-record examination of the impugned order to determine if any substantive adjudicatory finding or determination of rights has occurred. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal against an order reserving the case for pronouncement is ex-facie premature and not maintainable in law.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as not maintainable, without costs.
summary: Doshion Pvt. Ltd. filed an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC challenging an order dated 18.12.2019 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad in CP (IB) 63/2018, whereby the Adjudicating Authority reserved judgment and granted the parties one week to file written submissions. NCLAT held that an appeal under Section 61 lies only from the date of pronouncement of a substantive order affecting rights. Since no final order had been passed, the Appellant could not be deemed an 'aggrieved person', making the appeal ex-facie non-maintainable. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: The Deputy Commissioner Commercial Taxes (Audit) 1, Kalaburagi vs. Surana Industries Ltd. (In Liquidation) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is The Deputy Commissioner Commercial Taxes (Audit) 1, Kalaburagi (Operational/Government Creditor); Respondent is Surana Industries Ltd. (In Liquidation) represented by its Liquidator. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory commercial tax audit assessment and claims lodged in the liquidation proceedings of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Commercial tax dues claimed against the Corporate Debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidator rejected the tax department's claim; statutory appeal under Section 42 filed before NCLT with a delay of 7 days beyond the mandatory 14-day appeal window. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator's rejection letter; absence of a separate formal application seeking condonation of delay along with the Section 42 appeal memo; departmental communication citing confusion in receipt of the rejection order. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Tax authority appealed against the Liquidator's rejection before NCLT Division Bench-I Chennai under Section 42 without a delay condonation application; NCLT dismissed the appeal for unexcused delay. Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can entertain a delayed appeal against a liquidator's rejection of claim under Section 42 of the IBC in the absence of an application for condonation of delay, having regard to the time-bound nature of the liquidation process.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal against the rejection of a claim by a liquidator must be filed strictly within the 14-day limitation period prescribed under Section 42 of the IBC; any failure to file a formal condonation application demonstrating sufficient cause mandates rejection. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 42 limitation is governed by the strict statutory timeline of the liquidation process under the IBC, which mandates conclusion of liquidation within one year; administrative confusion does not constitute sufficient cause. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict compliance standard assessing whether an explicit application for condonation of delay demonstrating cogent and sufficient cause was placed on record. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: In the absence of an application seeking condonation of delay and cogent reasoning for the delay, the Adjudicating Authority rightly dismissed the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for lack of sufficient cause and cogent reasons. No order as to costs.
summary: The Deputy Commissioner Commercial Taxes (Audit) 1, Kalaburagi appealed against an order of NCLT Chennai which declined to entertain its appeal under Section 42 of the IBC against the Liquidator's rejection of tax claims in Surana Industries Ltd. (In Liquidation). The appeal was filed with a 7-day delay beyond the prescribed 14-day statutory period without a formal condonation application, citing internal communication confusion. NCLAT affirmed that liquidation is a strictly time-bound process and dismissed the appeal due to the absence of sufficient cause and a proper condonation application.

case_title: Navin Raheja vs. Shilpa Jain and Others
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ms. Shilpa Jain and Mr. Akash Jain are homebuyer allottees acting as Financial Creditors under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC; M/s Raheja Developers Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Navin Raheja is the Shareholder/Promoter of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of a residential apartment in the project 'Raheja's Sampada' under a joint allotment letter and Flat Buyer's Agreement dated 03.08.2012, requiring handover of possession within 36 months (by 03.08.2015), subject to force majeure. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Allottees disbursed a principal sum of Rs. 86,62,691 on various dates and claimed total default including 18% interest p.a. amounting to Rs. 87,32,108.05 (totaling Rs. 1,73,94,799.05); date of default was alleged as 03.08.2015 upon expiry of 36 months. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor issued a notice of offer of possession along with a demand letter for outstanding dues of Rs. 8,62,851 on 15.11.2016; allottees filed the Section 7 petition in 2018, more than two years post possession notice. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Receipts and ledger account showing payments of Rs. 86,62,691; Flat Buyer's Agreement clauses 4.1 to 4.4 establishing force majeure events including delays in government water supply/clearances and grant of Occupancy Certificate; NOC dated 11.11.2016 indicating arrangement of potable water via tankers due to lack of municipal connection; stay order of NGT impacting construction. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application CP No. (IB) 1321 (PB) of 2018 was admitted by NCLT Special Bench, New Delhi on 20.08.2019 on grounds of delay in handing over possession beyond the stipulated 36 months.
legal_issues: Whether a Corporate Debtor can be held to have committed default under Section 7 of the IBC when an apartment/flat is ready but delivery of possession is delayed due to force majeure events beyond its control, such as delays in statutory/governmental clearances; and whether filing a Section 7 petition after refusing an offer of possession constitutes an abuse under Section 65 as being filed fraudulently or with malicious intent for purposes other than resolution of insolvency.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 7 cannot be admitted where a real estate developer is prevented from timely delivery due to genuine force majeure and administrative delays beyond its control and has offered possession upon completing construction, as an allottee who refuses possession and demands excessive refund acts as a speculative investor misusing insolvency processes. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 read with Section 65 of the IBC and Section 19 of RERA mandates that an allottee is under a statutory obligation to take physical possession within two months of issuance of the occupancy certificate and pay remaining dues; using IBC as a coercive recovery mechanism to seek refund instead of taking possession amounts to initiation for purposes 'other than resolution of insolvency or liquidation'. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority must determine whether the developer's delay falls within contractual force majeure clauses and evaluate if the allottee is a speculative investor seeking to 'jump ship' in a falling market rather than a genuine purchaser seeking resolution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Raheja Developers applied for the Occupancy Certificate in 2013, obtained it, and formally offered possession on 15.11.2016 with a legitimate demand for balance payment, no actionable default occurred on the developer's part, rendering the belated Section 7 petition malicious under Section 65.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 20.08.2019 passed by NCLT New Delhi admitting Section 7 application is set aside; Section 7 application dismissed; Corporate Debtor released from moratorium and restored to its Board of Directors; IRP directed to hand over assets and records; Corporate Debtor directed to pay verified IRP fees/CIRP costs; no costs imposed.
summary: Promoter Navin Raheja appealed against the NCLT order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by allottees Shilpa Jain and Akash Jain against Raheja Developers Ltd. The allottees alleged default for failure to deliver an apartment within 36 months from August 2012, claiming Rs. 86.62 lakhs principal plus interest. The developer proved that delay was caused by government clearance delays covered under contractual force majeure, an Occupancy Certificate was secured, and possession was formally offered on 15.11.2016 with a balance demand of Rs. 8.62 lakhs. The allottees refused possession and demanded refunds. NCLAT held that there was no default by the developer and that the petition was maliciously filed by speculative investors under Section 65 to coerce a refund. NCLAT allowed the appeal and quashed the CIRP.

case_title: Mr. M. Ravindranath Reddy vs. Mr. G. Kishan & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. G. Kishan & Ors. are Lessors/Landlords claiming as Operational Creditors; M/s Walnut Packaging Private Limited is the Licensee/Tenant Corporate Debtor; Mr. M. Ravindranath Reddy is the Director of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Registered lease deed dated 12.05.1998 expiring in 2006 for industrial premises measuring 1667 sq. yards at Kukatpally, Hyderabad, providing for yearly tenancy with 10% annual escalation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed rent for July 2011 to June 2017 totaling Rs. 85,67,290 against which Rs. 55,51,920 was credited, asserting arrears of Rs. 30,15,370; subsequent Demand Notice claimed Rs. 49,51,605 (Rs. 39,98,926 rent + Rs. 9,52,679 interest @18% p.a.), later revised down to Rs. 35,94,090; default alleged from January/July 2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Eviction and termination notice under Section 106 of Transfer of Property Act issued on 15.06.2017; Section 8 Demand Notice under IBC issued on 18.01.2018; Section 9 reply sent by Corporate Debtor on 09.02.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 106 notice claiming rent arrears, mesne profits, and eviction; Corporate Debtor's reply asserting an oral agreement/moratorium for non-enhancement of rent for six years due to business slowdown; civil eviction suit instituted before the jurisdictional civil court. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 134/09/HDB/2018 admitted by NCLT Hyderabad Bench on 21.01.2019 holding that the Corporate Debtor failed to provide documentary proof of the alleged moratorium on rent enhancement.
legal_issues: Whether a landlord who leases immovable property provides 'services' to the corporate debtor so as to qualify as an 'operational creditor' and the unpaid rent as an 'operational debt' under Section 5(20) read with Section 5(21) of the IBC; and whether a Section 106 notice under the Transfer of Property Act issued prior to the Section 8 demand notice constitutes a 'pre-existing dispute' barring admission under Section 9.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Unpaid lease rentals arising from the lease or license of immovable property do not constitute an operational debt under the IBC as letting out premises does not constitute the provision of goods or rendering of services having a direct input nexus to the corporate debtor's output; additionally, prior termination and eviction notices constitute a bona fide pre-existing dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) strictly confines 'operational debt' to claims arising from the provision of goods, provision of services (including employment), or statutory dues to governments/authorities; despite the BLRC Report's suggestions, the Legislature intentionally excluded lease rent from the statutory definition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mobilox Innovations standard; where the corporate debtor establishes a plausible controversy requiring detailed evidence (such as disputed oral moratoriums or eviction proceedings under property law) raised prior to the Section 8 notice, summary IBC proceedings cannot resolve it. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A landlord claiming enhanced lease rent is not an operational creditor under Section 5(20)/(21), and the pre-existing dispute evidenced by the Section 106 TP Act notice warranted dismissal under Section 9(5)(2)(d).
operative_order: Appeal allowed; NCLT Hyderabad order dated 21.01.2019 set aside; Section 9 application dismissed; CIRP and moratorium terminated; Corporate Debtor restored to its Board of Directors; IRP directed to hand over management and records; NCLT directed to fix IRP fees to be borne by the applicant; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Director challenged an order of NCLT Hyderabad admitting an application under Section 9 of the IBC filed by landlords G. Kishan & Ors. against M/s Walnut Packaging Pvt. Ltd. for recovery of alleged unpaid enhanced lease rentals. The NCLAT examined whether leasing immovable property constitutes a 'service' under Section 5(21) of the IBC and whether a pre-existing dispute existed. The Appellate Tribunal held that lease of immovable property does not constitute the provision of goods or services within the statutory definition of operational debt. Furthermore, the landlords' prior issuance of a termination notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act demonstrated a pre-existing dispute. The appeal was allowed, and the admission order was set aside.

case_title: Bijay Kumar Agarwal vs. State Bank Of India and Anr.
