material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India is the Financial Creditor; M/s Gee Pee Infotech Pvt. Ltd. is the Principal Borrower; M/s Genegrow Commercial Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Guarantor/Corporate Debtor; Bijay Kumar Agarwal is the Ex-Director of the Corporate Guarantor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities sanctioned to Principal Borrower comprising AUCA cash credit of Rs. 32 Crores and IBD of Rs. 50 Crores (total Rs. 82 Crores), secured by an unconditional, irrevocable guarantee deed executed by the Corporate Guarantor on 05.10.2011 along with a supplementary deed. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed as on 31.01.2018 was Rs. 162,62,23,609.63 (comprising principal outstanding of Rs. 81,92,38,508.50 and interest of Rs. 80,69,85,101.13); date of default/NPA was 10.01.2014. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 10.01.2014; recovery application O.A. No. 493/2015 filed by SBI before DRT-1 Kolkata; balance confirmation signed by Principal Borrower on 07.04.2014; simultaneous Section 7 petitions filed in 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Guarantee deeds dated 05.10.2011; balance confirmation letters; CIBIL report; DRT application O.A. 493/2015. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: On 02.08.2019, NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted a Section 7 petition against the Principal Borrower Gee Pee Infotech, and simultaneously on the very same day admitted CP (IB) No. 353/KB/2018 against Corporate Guarantor Genegrow Commercial Pvt. Ltd. for the identical debt and default.
legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor can simultaneously proceed with and obtain admission of two separate Section 7 applications under the IBC against both the Principal Borrower and the Corporate Guarantor for the exact same set of debt and default.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While a financial creditor is entitled to initiate simultaneous applications under Section 7 against both the principal borrower and corporate guarantor, once an application is admitted against one corporate debtor, a second application by the same creditor for the identical debt and default cannot be admitted against the other corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the ratio of Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal v. Piramal Enterprises Ltd., the scheme of Section 7 does not contemplate concurrent CIRPs against multiple corporate entities for the identical underlying claim, as it leads to duplication of claims and resolution processes. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the claim metrics and parties revealed identical default amounts (Rs. 162.62 Crores) arising out of the exact same credit facilities and guarantee documents. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because NCLT Kolkata admitted the Section 7 petition against the Principal Borrower on 02.08.2019, the second admission order of the same date against the Corporate Guarantor Genegrow Commercial Pvt. Ltd. for the identical debt was legally unsustainable and void.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 02.08.2019 in CP (IB) No. 353/KB/2018 passed by NCLT Kolkata is set aside; Section 7 application against M/s Genegrow Commercial Pvt. Ltd. dismissed without costs; moratorium lifted; Board of Directors restored; IRP discharged and directed to return records and assets; NCLT to determine IRP fees payable by SBI.
summary: SBI filed Section 7 applications against the Principal Borrower Gee Pee Infotech and its Corporate Guarantor Genegrow Commercial Pvt. Ltd. for a defaulted loan facility of over Rs. 162 Crores (NPA declared on 10.01.2014). On 02.08.2019, NCLT Kolkata admitted both petitions simultaneously. Ex-Director Bijay Kumar Agarwal appealed the admission against the guarantor. Following the precedent in Piramal Enterprises, the NCLAT held that while simultaneous filing is permissible, once a Section 7 petition is admitted against either the principal borrower or the guarantor, a second petition for the identical claim and default cannot be admitted against the other. The appeal was allowed, and the CIRP against the guarantor was set aside.

case_title: QVC Exports Pvt. Ltd. vs. United Tradeco FZC & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Cosmic Ferro Alloys Limited is the Corporate Debtor; QVC Exports Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant) and United Tradeco FZC (Respondent No. 1) are Joint Resolution Applicants / Consortium Partners; Anish N. Nanavaty is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission and approval of a Joint Resolution Plan to acquire the Corporate Debtor providing an upfront payment of Rs. 99.74 Crores, whereby United Tradeco paid Rs. 3,160 Lakhs for 51,00,000 shares (51% at premium) and QVC Exports paid Rs. 340 Lakhs for 34,00,000 shares (34%), with remaining 15% allotted to an ESOP Trust. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable directly to default as the matter arises post-resolution; financial commitment under the plan was fully discharged as agreed. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 16.01.2017; Resolution Plan approved by CoC and sanctioned by NCLT Kolkata on 11.10.2018; Board Resolution by United Tradeco acknowledging 51,00,000 shares on 25.10.2018; Monitory Committee meeting held on 21.06.2019; Share Transfer Agreement dated 31.07.2019; Rectification Application C.A. (IB) No. 1131/2019 filed 13 months later. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan text explicitly allotting 51,00,000 shares to United Tradeco and 34,00,000 shares to QVC; Board resolution of Respondent No. 1 confirming acquisition of 51,00,000 shares @ Rs. 51.96 premium; Minutes of 4th Monitoring Committee meeting; conditional unexecuted Share Transfer Agreement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Thirteen months after plan approval, United Tradeco filed a unilateral rectification application alleging a clerical mistake; NCLT Kolkata on 20.11.2019 allowed the application, increasing United Tradeco's shares to 75,00,000 (75%) and reducing QVC's shares to 10,00,000 (10%).
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under Section 31, Section 60(5) of the IBC or Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to entertain an application for substantial modification and rectification of an approved and implemented Resolution Plan 13 months after its approval; and whether an approved joint resolution plan can be altered upon the unilateral application of one co-applicant without the consent of the other under the guise of correcting a clerical or typographical error.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan has attained finality upon approval and implementation, the Adjudicating Authority possesses no statutory jurisdiction to reopen, alter, or substantially modify its terms under the guise of inherent powers or correcting clerical errors, particularly upon the unilateral request of one consortium member without the consent of the co-applicant. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The jurisdiction under Section 31 and Section 60(5) terminates upon implementation when the plan attains finality; inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules or principles analogous to Section 152 CPC are strictly limited to accidental slips or ministerial arithmetic mistakes and cannot be invoked to grant substantive alterations of ownership or shareholding ratios. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contemporaneous documentary conduct, including formal board resolutions and monitoring committee records ratifying specific share numbers and prices, defeats subsequent self-serving allegations of typographical error. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's order altering the approved shareholding distribution from 34% to 10% was wholly without jurisdiction, ultra vires Section 31, and legally unsustainable.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order of NCLT Kolkata dated 20.11.2019 setting aside the original share distribution is quashed; the original approved Resolution Plan shareholding structure is restored; no order as to costs.
summary: Cosmic Ferro Alloys underwent CIRP, resulting in an approved Joint Resolution Plan submitted by United Tradeco and QVC Exports, granting them 51% (51 lakh shares) and 34% (34 lakh shares) equity, respectively. After the plan was implemented and 13 months had elapsed, United Tradeco filed an application before NCLT Kolkata alleging a clerical error and seeking redistribution to 75% and 10%. The NCLT allowed the rectification. QVC appealed. The NCLAT held that once a plan is approved and implemented, it attains finality and the Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction under Section 31 or Rule 11 to alter substantive shareholding rights under the guise of correcting a typographical error, especially without the co-applicant's consent. The appeal was allowed and the NCLT order was quashed.

case_title: Vivek Jha vs. Daimler Financial Services India Private Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Daimler Financial Services India Pvt. Ltd. is the Non-Banking Financial Company acting as Financial Creditor; Natconn Engineering Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Vivek Jha is the Director and Co-Borrower of the Corporate Debtor (Appellant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan cum Hypothecation Agreement dated 28.03.2013 financing Rs. 34 Lakhs towards the purchase of a Mercedes Benz car (E-250-CDI) valued at Rs. 43,51,403 (with initial down payment of Rs. 9,51,403) carrying interest @ 9.4012% p.a., repayable in 36 monthly instalments of Rs. 1,08,775 each from 30.03.2013 to 30.03.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default began on 30.03.2014 after 11 EMIs; total outstanding claimed in demand notice was Rs. 29,29,149.74. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First default occurred 30.03.2014; Loan recall cum demand notice issued on 06.05.2014 claiming Rs. 28,44,423; part-payment of Rs. 3,00,000 made via cheque on 18.03.2015; second Demand-cum-Insolvency notice issued on 17.08.2017; Section 7 application filed on 16.12.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan cum hypothecation agreement, bank statement showing bounced instalments, cheque dated 18.03.2015 for Rs. 3 Lakhs, postal return endorsements showing 'Addressee Left' matching ROC master data. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 7 petition ex-parte on 03.10.2018 in CP No. (IB) 1802/MB/2017 holding that financial debt and default were established and service on the registered ROC address was complete.
legal_issues: Whether a part payment made by cheque within the three-year period following default and loan recall operates as an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 to compute a fresh period of limitation for a Section 7 application under the IBC; and whether service of petition notices sent by registered post to the official ROC master data address returning with the endorsement 'Addressee Left' constitutes valid service.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A part payment made by cheque towards a debt before the expiration of the three-year limitation period constitutes a valid written acknowledgment of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, renewing the limitation period for an application under Section 7 of the IBC; furthermore, service directed to a company's registered address shown on ROC records is legally effective service which cannot be evaded by abandoning the premises. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to applications under Section 7 (governed by Article 137); an acknowledgment of liability gives rise to a fresh commencement period of three years from the date of payment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Service sent via registered post to the correct official registered address satisfies legal service requirements; bare denials of receipt fail where official company records corroborate the mailing address. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since default occurred in 2014, the interim payment of Rs. 3 Lakhs on 18.03.2015 reset the limitation period to 17.03.2018, rendering the Section 7 application filed on 16.12.2017 well within time.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; impugned admission order dated 03.10.2018 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench affirmed; pending IAs closed; Appellant directed to file a certified copy of the impugned order within four days; no order as to costs.
summary: Director of Corporate Debtor Natconn Engineering appealed against NCLT Mumbai's ex-parte admission of a Section 7 IBC application by Daimler Financial Services regarding a defaulted car loan cum hypothecation agreement of March 2013. The Appellant argued lack of service (as notice returned marked 'Addressee Left') and that the petition was barred by limitation since the initial default and loan recall notice dated back to May 2014. The NCLAT held that delivery of notice to the address appearing on ROC records constitutes valid service in law. Further, a part payment of Rs. 3 lakhs made via cheque on 18.03.2015 acted as an acknowledgment of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, granting a fresh 3-year limitation period. Thus, the Section 7 petition filed on 16.12.2017 was timely. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Unistill Alcoblends Pvt. Ltd. vs. India Brewery & Distillery Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Unistill Alcoblends Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor; India Brewery & Distillery Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Business arrangements comprising an Agreement dated 21.02.2011 for manufacture of India Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL) and an MOU dated August 2011 for supplying High Speed Bottling Unit Equipment, alongside advance funds and raw material provisions for ENA supplies. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed outstanding dues of Rs. 2,38,16,374 (including interest, advance payments of Rs. 47,57,800, raw material charges of Rs. 16,77,827, and Rs. 30,00,000 written-down value of bottling equipment); default occurred upon termination of operations in November 2012. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Commercial arrangement terminated in November 2012; Demand Notice under Section 8 of IBC issued on 05.04.2018; Section 8 reply sent on 14.04.2018; subsequent acknowledgment letter sent by Corporate Debtor on 05.05.2018; Section 9 application filed in 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Repeated written acknowledgment letters from Corporate Debtor dated 15.04.2014, 19.11.2015, 06.07.2017, 14.02.2018, and 05.05.2018 confirming balance dues; Audited Balance Sheet of Corporate Debtor for FY ending 31.03.2017 reflecting Rs. 1,30,05,426 due to Unistill under long-term borrowings; Corporate Debtor's Section 9 Arbitration Act petition filed after Section 8 reply. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru dismissed the Section 9 application in C.P. (IB) No. 147/BB/2018 on 11.01.2019 on the erroneous finding that a pre-existing dispute was deemed to exist prior to the filing of the petition.
legal_issues: Whether the relevant statutory test for a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 8 and Section 9 of the IBC requires the dispute to have existed prior to the issuance of the Section 8 Demand Notice rather than prior to the filing of the Section 9 petition; and whether balance sheet entries and written acknowledgments extending limitation override vague dispute assertions raised subsequent to default.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 8 and Section 9 of the IBC, a defense of pre-existing dispute must be demonstrable from communications raised prior to the issuance of the statutory Section 8 Demand Notice, and cannot be founded on disputes raised retrospectively thereafter. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory threshold under Section 9 requires examining whether a dispute was communicated to the creditor before the receipt of the Section 8 notice; subsequent disputes, arbitration filings, or vague replies cannot invalidate an operational debt admitted in balance sheets and periodic acknowledgment letters. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the corporate debtor consistently acknowledged liability in writing and recorded the debt in its audited balance sheet within successive three-year windows under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, unsupported claims of off-take failures unsupported by pre-notice contemporaneous documents fail the Mobilox test. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed an error of law by assessing dispute existence relative to the date of filing the petition rather than the date of the Section 8 notice; no pre-existing dispute existed prior to 05.04.2018.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; NCLT Bengaluru order dated 11.01.2019 set aside; matter remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority; parties directed to appear on 10.02.2020; liberty granted to Corporate Debtor to settle before that date, failing which NCLT is directed to admit the Section 9 application and initiate CIRP; no costs.
summary: Unistill Alcoblends appealed against NCLT Bengaluru's rejection of its Section 9 IBC application filed against India Brewery & Distillery Pvt. Ltd. claiming operational debt exceeding Rs. 2.38 Crores arising from liquor manufacturing contracts terminated in 2012. NCLT had rejected the plea on the ground that a dispute was 'deemed to exist prior to filing the petition'. The NCLAT overturned the decision, clarifying the legal principle that a pre-existing dispute must exist prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice, not merely prior to petition filing. As the debtor had repeatedly acknowledged the debt in writing and in its FY 2017 balance sheet without raising pre-notice objections, the NCLAT remitted the matter for admission under Section 9 if not settled by 10.02.2020.

case_title: Khetan Granite Private Limited vs. Office Of Registrar Of Companies, Jharkhand
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Khetan Granite Private Limited is the struck-off Appellant Company incorporated in 2012; Registrar of Companies (ROC), Jharkhand is the regulatory Respondent Authority. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate incorporation for operating a business in cutting, polishing, and processing granite, marble, and limestones; acquisition of real estate for factory establishment. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure to file statutory Annual Returns and Financial Statements for Financial Years 2012-13 to 2017-18 onwards; unsecured loans amounting to approximately Rs. 1,05,50,000 availed from related parties. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Show Cause Notice issued by ROC on 20.03.2017; Public Notice STK-5 published on 18.04.2017; striking-off notification published in Official Gazette on 14.07.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Sale Deeds dated 17.04.2015 and 08.06.2015 reflecting acquisition of 518.2 decimals of land for Rs. 21,00,000 and Rs. 23,90,000; land mutation records of 488 decimals in Salanpur, West Bengal; Audited Balance Sheets from 2012-13 to 2017-18 showing non-current and current assets of Rs. 11,10,95,189.20 as on 31.03.2018; Income Tax Return for FY 2017-18; active bank account with Bank of Baroda. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Company's name was struck off under Section 248(1); appeal before NCLT Kolkata Bench in CP (Appeal) No. 465/KB/2019 was dismissed on 27.08.2019 because financial statements reflected 'NIL' operational revenue, failing to prove it was a going concern.
legal_issues: Whether a company possessing substantial immovable assets, land acquisitions, and ongoing factory development but reporting 'NIL' operating revenue during its initial establishment phase qualifies as 'carrying on business or in operation' to justify restoration of its name under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The term 'in operation' or 'carrying on business' under Section 252 is not restricted solely to immediate commercial revenue generation; substantial investment in capital assets, land acquisitions, and project development preparatory to commercial operations demonstrate business operations justifying company restoration to avoid injustice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252(3) allows the Tribunal to order restoration if it is 'just' that the name be restored; acquiring land for factory establishment and holding significant assets cannot be characterized as a defunct status under Section 248. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Physical asset verification through registered title deeds, audited balance sheets showing significant assets, and tax returns satisfy the threshold of an ongoing operational enterprise despite nil current revenue from sales. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The presence of Rs. 11.10 Crores in assets and documented land purchases clearly established that the company was active, rendering the striking-off orders unjust.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; NCLT Kolkata order dated 27.08.2019 set aside; ROC Jharkhand directed to restore the company's name to the Register of Companies; Appellant directed to pay Rs. 1,00,000 costs to ROC within 30 days and file all pending Annual Returns, Balance Sheets from FY 2012-13 onwards along with applicable statutory fees; ROC remains free to take punitive steps under law for late filings; no costs in appeal.
summary: ROC Jharkhand struck off Khetan Granite Pvt. Ltd. under Section 248(1) for failing to file financial returns since FY 2012-13, and NCLT Kolkata dismissed its restoration appeal because operating revenue was 'NIL'. On appeal, the NCLAT observed that the company had purchased 518.2 decimals of land via registered sale deeds in 2015 to construct a factory shed, held assets valued at Rs. 11.10 Crores as on 31.03.2018, and filed income tax returns. The Tribunal held that active asset procurement and project implementation qualify as carrying on business even without immediate revenue generation. The NCLAT ordered restoration subject to payment of Rs. 1 Lakh costs and compliance with pending filings.

case_title: Committee of Creditors, M/s. Smartec Build Systems Pvt. Ltd. vs. B. Santosh Babu & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Committee of Creditors (CoC) of M/s Smartec Build Systems Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant; B. Santosh Babu is the Interim Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); M/s Smartec Build Systems Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Performance of statutory duties by the Interim Resolution Professional during CIRP initiated pursuant to a Section 9 application, running CIRP beyond 30 days, constituting the CoC, and filing for liquidation upon CoC recommendation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-payment of professional fees and incurred CIRP operational expenses to the Interim Resolution Professional. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 9; CoC constituted; CoC resolved to liquidate the company; liquidation ordered by NCLT on 13.11.2019; IRP filed an application for pending fees and expenses on the same date. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Records proving that B. Santosh Babu acted as IRP, formed the CoC, continued management beyond 30 days through to the liquidation order, but was not appointed as the liquidator. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: On 13.11.2019, NCLT Hyderabad ordered liquidation and directed the CoC to pay the fees and costs incurred by the IRP; CoC appealed this cost direction.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors is legally obligated to bear and pay the fees and costs of an Interim Resolution Professional who managed the Corporate Debtor beyond 30 days up to the date of liquidation when not appointed as Liquidator, or whether such expenses must be borne by the operational creditor who initiated the Section 9 proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Committee of Creditors is liable to pay the fees and operational expenses incurred by an Interim Resolution Professional who managed the CIRP beyond the initial 30 days until liquidation, and such burden cannot be shifted to an unsecured operational creditor who initiated CIRP and may receive nothing in liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Where an IRP continues discharging functions beyond 30 days until liquidation but is not appointed as the Liquidator, fees cannot be settled as liquidator remuneration under Section 34(8); hence, CIRP costs must be satisfied by the CoC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted discharge of duties by the IRP in managing operations and moving the liquidation application at the behest of the CoC creates an immediate legal liability for the CoC to satisfy accrued administrative expenses. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC's refusal to bear the approved IRP costs and attempt to transfer the burden onto the operational creditor was entirely meritless and frivolous.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed with costs of Rs. 1,00,000 imposed on the Appellant Committee of Creditors; directions of NCLT Hyderabad Bench dated 13.11.2019 ordering CoC to pay the IRP fees and costs affirmed.
summary: The CoC of M/s Smartec Build Systems Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order directing it to pay the outstanding fees and costs of the Interim Resolution Professional (B. Santosh Babu), who had managed the Corporate Debtor beyond 30 days and moved the liquidation application upon the CoC's recommendation. The CoC argued that the initiating Section 9 Operational Creditor was liable for these costs. The NCLAT rejected the plea, holding that an unsecured operational creditor who is unlikely to recover dues in liquidation cannot be saddled with CIRP costs when the IRP functioned for the benefit of the CoC up to liquidation. Deeming the CoC's stance frivolous, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal with Rs. 1 Lakh costs.

case_title: MM Ramachandran vs. South Indian Bank Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: South Indian Bank Ltd. is the Financial Creditor; M/s Atlas Gold Townships (India) Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; MM Ramachandran is the Promoter/Shareholder of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit/loan facilities extended by the Financial Creditor to the Corporate Debtor in the principal amount of Rs. 220 Crores, rising to Rs. 250 Crores with accrued interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 220 Crores principal (escalating to Rs. 250 Crores including interest); date of default/NPA declaration was 31.12.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 31.12.2015; email acknowledging liability sent on 02.05.2016; signed physical copy posted from Dubai on 16.05.2016 and received by the Bank on 25.05.2016 / 30.05.2016; Section 7 application filed on 10.04.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated 02.05.2016 from the Appellant confirming the borrowings and promising repayment; physical signed letter despatched from Dubai on 16.05.2016 with postal cover produced before the bench; postal receipt and bank records verifying receipt on 25.05.2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application was admitted by NCLT Kochi Bench on 19.11.2019, which was appealed by the Promoter on limitation grounds and alleged non-compliance with Section 7(3)(b).
legal_issues: Whether a genuine email and signed physical letter acknowledging debt dispatched within three years of NPA declaration constitutes a valid acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, extending the limitation period for an application under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A written communication or email acknowledging liability dispatched by a borrower/promoter prior to the expiration of the three-year statutory limitation period following loan default resets limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for a Section 7 IBC application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act operates to compute a fresh three-year limitation period from the date of the written acknowledgment; an unsubstantiated plea of forgery cannot defeat contemporaneous documentary proof. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Physical postal covers corroborating international dispatch, matching signatures, and genuine electronic communications satisfy the evidentiary standard to establish debt acknowledgment under Section 18. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the debt was acknowledged in May 2016 following the December 2015 NPA, the Section 7 petition filed on 10.04.2019 was well within the three-year limitation period.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; NCLT Kochi Bench admission order dated 19.11.2019 upheld; no costs.
summary: Promoter MM Ramachandran appealed against an NCLT Kochi order admitting South Indian Bank Ltd.'s Section 7 IBC petition against Atlas Gold Townships (India) Pvt. Ltd., contending that the account had been declared NPA on 31.12.2015 and the application filed on 10.04.2019 was time-barred. The Bank proved that the promoter sent an email on 02.05.2016 followed by a signed letter dispatched from Dubai acknowledging Rs. 220 Crores principal (escalating to Rs. 250 Crores with interest). The NCLAT rejected the promoter's unsubstantiated plea of forgery, holding that the written acknowledgment extended the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Shri Lalit Aggarwal & Anr. vs. Shree Bihari Forgings Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shri Lalit Aggarwal and Lalit Aggarwal HUF (Appellants); Shree Bihari Forgings Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1 Company); Pramod Goil (Respondent No. 2/Cross-Appellant Director); Registrar of Companies and Canara Bank (pro forma respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operation and management of Shree Bihari Forgings Pvt. Ltd., involving an industrial plant at Pilukhawa, Hapur, term loans and cash credit facilities from Canara Bank, and equity share capital distribution between two promoter groups. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Illegal allotment of 3,66,750 equity shares in three tranches; siphoning of company bank funds; dissipation of all physical factory machinery and assets. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Disputed allotments occurred on 17.12.2007, 28.12.2007, and 27.02.2008; cross-petitions filed before CLB in 2008 (CP No. 15/2008 and CP No. 47/2008); High Court ordered comprehensive audit on 13.05.2013; contempt proceedings initiated on 11.03.2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lack of any board resolutions approving share allotments; admission by Appellant's wife denying consent for share conversion; police report 1727/2013 and false claims that statutory books were lost in transit and burnt in a car; Administrator's report dated 18.11.2015 confirming removal of all plant machinery. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench III on 04.09.2018 dismissed both cross-petitions under Sections 397/398 and ordered winding up of the company on just and equitable grounds under Section 242(1)(b) due to total destruction of substratum and mutual unclean hands.
legal_issues: Whether a company should be wound up on just and equitable grounds under Section 242(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 where warring directors have committed mutual oppression, siphoned assets, carried out unauthorized share allotments without board sanction, and destroyed the entire commercial substratum of the company.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the management of a private company is deadlocked between two directors who have acted in bad faith, suppressed records, engaged in unauthorized share allotments without board sanction, siphoned assets, and caused the complete loss of the company's substratum, winding up under the just and equitable clause is the appropriate remedy. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(1)(b) permits the Tribunal to order winding up where the facts justify it on just and equitable grounds and winding up would not unfairly prejudice members because the substratum has already been completely eroded by mutual malfeasance. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Equitable jurisdiction under oppression and mismanagement provisions requires clean hands; fabricated excuses regarding lost or burnt corporate records combined with physical disappearance of factory assets warrant adverse inferences and judicial dissolution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The complete destruction of company assets, disappearance of records, and invalidity of share allotments rendered the company defunct, fully justifying NCLT's winding-up directive.
operative_order: Both appeals (Company Appeal No. 380 of 2018 and No. 23 of 2019) dismissed; NCLT New Delhi order dated 04.09.2018 upholding winding up affirmed; cost of Rs. 5 Lakh each imposed on Lalit Aggarwal and Pramod Goil payable to the National Defence Fund within one month.
summary: Cross-appeals were filed by warring directors Lalit Aggarwal and Pramod Goil against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing their respective oppression and mismanagement petitions and directing the winding up of Shree Bihari Forgings Pvt. Ltd. on just and equitable grounds. The record revealed that both directors had acted with unclean hands: Aggarwal allotted 3,66,750 shares to his relatives without board approval, while Goil dissipated company factory assets and falsely claimed statutory records were successively lost in transit and burned in a car fire. The NCLAT held that since both directors systematically destroyed the company's substratum and rendered its operations impossible, winding up was fully justified. The appeals were dismissed with costs of Rs. 5 Lakh each.

case_title: Supreme Commotrade LLP & Anr. vs. Shree Sanyeeji Ispat Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Supreme Commotrade LLP (Appellant No. 1) and its partners Om Prakash Murarka and Asha Devi Murarka (Appellants 2 and 3) acting as Financial Creditors; M/s Shree Sanyeeji Ispat Ltd. as Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged oral business loans claimed to be granted by Appellants in 2009 and 2010 (Rs. 20 Lakhs on 30.04.2009, Rs. 30 Lakhs on 20.08.2009, and Rs. 30 Lakhs on 16.12.2010) payable on demand without any written loan agreement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed on 24.10.2018 upon dishonour of three cheques totaling Rs. 80 Lakhs, which had been issued blank on 01.10.2014 and dated by creditors as 22.10.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Disbursements made in 2009 and 2010; balance confirmation letters and undated cheques obtained on 01.10.2014; cheques presented and dishonoured in October 2018; Section 7 application filed on 13.12.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Self-serving unilateral ledger accounts of Appellants; undated cheques issued on 01.10.2014 where dates of 22.10.2018 were subsequently entered by Appellants; cheque bounce memos dated 24.10.2018; total absence of bank statements confirming interest payments or loan contracts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Guwahati Bench dismissed Section 7 application Dy. No. 3(186) of 2018 on 01.03.2019, holding the debt time-barred and finding Appellants barred as unregistered money lenders under the Assam Money Lenders Act.
legal_issues: Whether an acknowledgment of debt executed after the expiration of the 3-year limitation period from the date of loan disbursement can revive a time-barred debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act for Section 7 IBC proceedings; and whether the NCLT in summary IBC proceedings can declare a financial creditor an illegal money lender absent specific pleadings, evidence, or prior judicial decree.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A balance acknowledgment executed after the expiration of three years from the date of advancing a loan cannot revive a debt that is already barred by limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, nor does subsequent dishonour of stale blank cheques create a fresh date of default; additionally, summary IBC proceedings cannot determine money-lender status without trial pleadings or evidence. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act requires acknowledgment to be made 'before the expiration of the prescribed period'; where a loan is payable on demand without a fixed term, limitation begins from the date the loan is made (Articles 19 and 21), and post-limitation acknowledgments are legally void. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Section 7 IBC applications require valid proof of enforceable debt and default; presenting unilaterally dated blank cheques years after a debt is barred cannot establish a live financial default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While the NCLT's finding that the Appellants were money lenders was legally improper in summary proceedings and must be quashed, the dismissal of the Section 7 petition was correct because the claim was barred by limitation.
operative_order: Appeals partly allowed; finding of NCLT Guwahati Bench holding Appellants to be money lenders under the Assam Money Lenders Act is set aside; dismissal of Section 7 application on grounds of limitation affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Supreme Commotrade LLP and its partners appealed against NCLT Guwahati orders dismissing Section 7 applications against three corporate debtors (lead case: Shree Sanyeeji Ispat Ltd.) regarding loans advanced in 2009-2010. The Appellants relied on balance confirmations and blank cheques obtained on 01.10.2014, which were filled in and presented in October 2018 before bouncing. The NCLT dismissed the petitions on limitation and held the creditors were unlicensed money lenders. On appeal, the NCLAT set aside the money-lender finding, ruling that summary IBC proceedings cannot decide money-lender status without trial evidence. However, the NCLAT affirmed the dismissal of Section 7, holding that the acknowledgments obtained in 2014 were executed after the 3-year limitation had already expired, rendering the debt time-barred.

case_title: M/s Ugro Capital Limited vs. M/s Bangalore Dehydration and Drying Equipment Co. Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Ugro Capital Limited (formerly Asia Pragati Capfin Pvt. Ltd.) is the Financial Creditor/Decree-holder; M/s Bangalore Dehydration and Drying Equipment Co. Pvt. Ltd. (BDDE) is the Corporate Debtor/Corporate Guarantor; M/s BT & FC Pvt. Ltd. is the Principal Borrower. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan transaction resulting in a civil suit CS (OS) No. 1030/2012 before the Delhi High Court, wherein a consent decree was drawn against the principal borrower, personal guarantors, and the Corporate Debtor jointly and severally for Rs. 8,04,43,637 with 21% p.a. interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Under decree dated 22.05.2015, Rs. 1 Crore was payable on or before 07.07.2015 and Rs. 4 Crores by 14.08.2015; default occurred on 07.07.2015 when first instalment was missed; total default was Rs. 8,04,43,637 plus 21% interest p.a. from 23.03.2012. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Consent decree passed on 22.05.2015; modification application dismissed by High Court on 06.08.2015; default triggered on 07.07.2015 / 06.08.2015; Section 7 application C.P. (IB) No. 135/IB/2018 filed on 27.06.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certified copies of Delhi High Court decrees dated 22.05.2015 and 06.08.2015; High Court registry inspection report dated 19.08.2019 proving Corporate Debtor took back defected review memo on 17.12.2018 and never re-filed it. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru dismissed the Section 7 petition on 05.07.2019, holding that the decree was sub-judice in review, the creditor had not explained failure to execute in civil court, and selectively pursued the guarantor.
legal_issues: Whether a decree-holder qualifies as a creditor entitled to file a Section 7 IBC application based on an unexecuted consent decree within three years of default under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963; and whether an unfiled/withdrawn review petition in civil court precludes CIRP admission.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A financial creditor holding an unsatisfied money decree is legally entitled to maintain an application under Section 7 of the IBC against a corporate guarantor whose liability is joint and several, without being compelled to execute the decree first in civil court or pursue co-debtors, provided the application is filed within three years from the date of decretal default. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(10) explicitly defines 'creditor' to include a 'decree-holder'; an application under Section 7 based on a defaulted decree is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, computing limitation from the date default occurred under the decree. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The burden to prove the pendency of a review petition lies strictly upon the party asserting it; absent proof of a live judicial stay or pending re-filed review, the decree operates with full legal enforceability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor committed default on 07.07.2015/06.08.2015, and the Section 7 petition filed on 27.06.2018 was within the three-year period under Article 137; NCLT's refusal to admit was erroneous.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order of NCLT Bengaluru dated 05.07.2019 set aside; NCLT directed to pass an order admitting the Section 7 application; parties directed to appear before NCLT on 27.01.2020.
summary: Ugro Capital appealed against an NCLT Bengaluru order rejecting its Section 7 IBC application against Corporate Guarantor BDDE. The claim was based on a Delhi High Court consent decree dated 22.05.2015 / 06.08.2015 for Rs. 8.04 Crores with 21% interest, which defaulted on 07.07.2015. NCLT rejected the petition because the creditor did not execute the decree in civil court and accepted the debtor's false assertion that a review petition was pending. The NCLAT held that under Section 5(10), a decree-holder is recognized as a creditor entitled to initiate Section 7 CIRP. Further, the creditor was within the three-year limitation under Article 137, and inspection proved no review was pending. The appeal was allowed with directions to NCLT to admit the petition.

case_title: iValue Advisors Pvt. Ltd. vs. Srinagar Banihal Expressway Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: iValue Advisors Pvt. Ltd. (MSME) is the Operational Creditor; Srinagar Banihal Expressway Ltd. (SPV for J&K expressway construction) is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Engagement letter dated 21.11.2014 for providing project monitoring consultancy services at a monthly fee of Rs. 22 Lakhs for rehabilitation, strengthening, and four-laning of the Srinagar to Banihal highway. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount claimed was Rs. 73,52,122.92 arising from multiple unpaid invoices issued between 24.11.2014 and 16.02.2017 (specifically four invoices dated 02.01.2017). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised up to 16.02.2017; Demand Notice under Section 8 of IBC issued on 21.01.2019; reply by Corporate Debtor sent on 07.02.2019; MSME Facilitation Council conciliation letter dated 15.10.2019 showing no conciliation or arbitrator had been appointed. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Project monitoring engagement letter; unpaid invoices dated 02.01.2017; TDS deduction certificates where Corporate Debtor deducted tax at source on the invoiced amounts; absence of any contemporaneous dispute raised prior to Section 8 notice. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissed the Section 9 petition holding that the operational creditor's prior reference to the MSME Facilitation Council under Section 18 of the MSMED Act established an admitted pre-existing dispute.
legal_issues: Whether a reference filed by an operational creditor before the MSME Facilitation Council under Section 18 of the MSMED Act for recovery of unpaid invoices constitutes a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 5(6) and Section 9 of the IBC so as to bar admission of an insolvency application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational creditor's invocation of statutory dispute resolution under the MSMED Act to recover unpaid dues does not constitute a 'pre-existing dispute' within the meaning of Section 5(6) of the IBC; the pre-existing dispute must be one raised by the corporate debtor regarding liability or service quality prior to the receipt of the Section 8 demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'dispute' in Section 18 of the MSMED Act relates to recovery of amounts due under Section 17 of that Act, whereas 'dispute' under Section 5(6) of the IBC requires an existing controversy regarding the existence of debt, quality of goods/services, or breach of warranty raised by the debtor prior to the Section 8 notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mobilox test requires the corporate debtor to show contemporaneous evidence of dispute communicated to the creditor before the statutory demand notice was issued. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the corporate debtor never raised any dispute regarding the consultancy services prior to the Section 8 notice, the creditor's approach to the MSME council did not bar Section 9 proceedings.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order of NCLT Hyderabad Bench set aside; matter remitted back to NCLT to admit the Section 9 application on 03.02.2020 unless settled by the Corporate Debtor prior to admission; no costs.
summary: MSME consultant iValue Advisors appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order rejecting its Section 9 IBC application against Srinagar Banihal Expressway Ltd. for unpaid project monitoring dues of Rs. 73.52 Lakhs. The NCLT had dismissed the petition holding that the creditor's reference to the MSME Facilitation Council under Section 18 of the MSMED Act constituted an admitted pre-existing dispute. The NCLAT reversed the order, ruling that approaching the MSME Council to recover dues is merely an available statutory remedy and does not establish a pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6) of the IBC. Since the debtor raised no quality or contractual disputes prior to the Section 8 notice, the matter was remitted for admission under Section 9.

case_title: Vipul Ltd. vs. M/s. Vipul Greens Residents Welfare Association
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vipul Ltd. is the real estate developer/Corporate Debtor (Appellant); M/s Vipul Greens Residents Welfare Association (RWA representing 384 allottees) is the Applicant/Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment and maintenance arrangements under real estate contracts concerning the transfer of 'Interest Bearing Maintenance Security Deposit' (IBMS) and common area maintenance charges. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed on account of non-transfer/refund of IBMS corpus and maintenance deposits collected from residential apartment allottees. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IBC Amendment Ordinance promulgated on 28.12.2019 introducing joint filing thresholds under Section 7(1); Impugned interim order passed by NCLT on 15.11.2019; matter listed for compliance on 25.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Real estate contracts; Form 1 filed under Section 7; RWA claims regarding maintenance deposit accounts; conflicting affidavits regarding individual electricity and common maintenance adjustments. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In a pending pre-admission Section 7 petition, NCLT New Delhi on 15.11.2019 directed the Corporate Debtor to furnish itemized details of maintenance defaults of 384 members and ordered the maintenance corpus of non-defaulting members to be handed over to the RWA.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction prior to admitting an application under Section 7 of the IBC to issue mandatory directions compelling a corporate debtor to hand over maintenance funds to an RWA; and whether an RWA's Section 7 claim regarding maintenance deposits must satisfy the threshold requirements of financial debt and the joint-filing minimum numerical thresholds under Section 7(1).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Prior to the admission of an application under Section 7, an Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction to grant substantive mandatory relief directing the deposit or disbursement of maintenance corpus funds; its jurisdiction at the threshold stage is strictly limited to ascertaining whether the claim constitutes a financial debt and whether an actionable default has occurred. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 7(5) and the 2019 Ordinance, the Tribunal must verify whether the claim qualifies as a financial debt under Section 5(8) disbursed against the time value of money, whether the statutory threshold (100 allottees or 10%) is satisfied, and cannot adjudicate collateral disputes over maintenance offsets. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Innoventive Industries standard restricts the NCLT's pre-admission role to examining Form 1 and its statutory annexures to find default, without conducting civil inquiries or directing asset transfers. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT exceeded its summary jurisdiction by ordering the handover of maintenance deposits prior to deciding the maintainability and default under Section 7.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order of NCLT New Delhi dated 15.11.2019 set aside; matter remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority to determine maintainability under Section 7(1) as amended by the 2019 Ordinance and decide if the claim is a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8); no costs.
summary: Vipul Ltd., a real estate developer, appealed against an interim order of NCLT New Delhi in a Section 7 application filed by the Vipul Greens Residents Welfare Association concerning the non-transfer of Interest Bearing Maintenance Security Deposits (IBMS). Prior to admission, the NCLT had ordered Vipul Ltd. to submit detailed accountings of 384 allottees and hand over the maintenance deposit corpus of non-defaulting allottees to the RWA. Relying on Innoventive Industries, the NCLAT set aside the direction, holding that prior to Section 7 admission, the Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to order the release or handover of disputed maintenance funds. The NCLAT remitted the matter to examine maintainability under the 2019 Amendment Ordinance and verify if the claim constitutes a financial debt.

case_title: V.K. Abdul Rahim vs. The Federal Bank Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Federal Bank Ltd. is the Financial Creditor; M/s Sargam Builders Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; V.K. Abdul Rahim is the Shareholder and Director of the Corporate Debtor (Appellant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility availed in 2009 along with execution of a Bank Guarantee at the instance of the Corporate Debtor, secured by mortgage. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred under both loan and guarantee facilities resulting in loan recall and NPA classification. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 15.01.2013; notice sent by Bank on 15.01.2013; Corporate Debtor sent reply acknowledging debt on 05.02.2013; further written acknowledgment letter sent by Corporate Debtor on 03.02.2016 offering OTS; Corporate Debtor sought to withdraw OTS on 11.03.2016; Section 7 application filed on 31.07.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank recall notice dated 15.01.2013; Corporate Debtor's reply dated 05.02.2013; Corporate Debtor's letter dated 03.02.2016 offering OTS; subsequent withdrawal letter dated 11.03.2016; documents forming part of Original Application filed before DRT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi Bench admitted the Section 7 petition on 20.09.2019, erroneously relying on Article 62 of the Limitation Act (12-year mortgage period) to hold that the petition was within time.
legal_issues: Whether a successive chain of written acknowledgments and OTS offers made within three years of each other extends the period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for a Section 7 IBC application; and whether a debtor's subsequent withdrawal of an OTS proposal nullifies the legal effect of the written acknowledgment contained within it.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, a signed written acknowledgment of liability made prior to the expiration of the limitation period creates a fresh period of limitation of three years; the subsequent unilateral withdrawal of a settlement or OTS proposal does not erase or invalidate the factual acknowledgment of debt contained therein. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 applications are governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act (3-year limit from default/NPA), not Article 62 (mortgage); however, Section 18 applies to Section 7 applications, such that successive written acknowledgments within three-year intervals extend limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the genuineness of signed letters admitting liability is not disputed, the acknowledgment satisfies Section 18 as an admission of existing liability, regardless of whether settlement terms were accepted. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Although the NCLT erroneously relied on Article 62, the debt was kept alive within limitation under Article 137 read with Section 18 through continuous written acknowledgments on 05.02.2013 and 03.02.2016, making the petition filed on 31.07.2018 timely.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; NCLT Kochi Bench order dated 20.09.2019 admitting Section 7 application affirmed on grounds of Section 18 limitation extension; no order as to costs.
summary: Director of Sargam Builders Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Kochi's admission of Federal Bank's Section 7 IBC application, arguing that the debt became NPA on 15.01.2013 and the application filed on 31.07.2018 was time-barred, and that NCLT improperly applied Article 62 (mortgages) instead of Article 137. The NCLAT agreed that Article 137 governs Section 7 filings, but affirmed the admission under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. The debtor had formally acknowledged the debt in letters dated 05.02.2013 and 03.02.2016. The Tribunal held that each acknowledgment created a fresh 3-year limitation window, and the subsequent withdrawal of the OTS offer on 11.03.2016 did not negate the written acknowledgment of liability. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Radhika Mehra vs. Vaayu Infrastructure LLP & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vejas Power Projects Ltd. is the Financial Creditor; Vaayu Infrastructure LLP is the Corporate Debtor; Radhika Mehra is the Partner of the Corporate Debtor (Appellant); Shailen Shah is the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial debt facilities extended by Vejas Power Projects Ltd. to Vaayu Infrastructure LLP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of financial debt giving rise to Section 7 CIRP initiation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT admission order passed on 30.08.2019; Appellant filed Writ Petition (Lodging) No. 3498 of 2019 before Bombay High Court; Bombay High Court granted leave to withdraw on instructions to approach NCLAT; Section 61 appeal filed before NCLAT after a lapse of more than 45 days from receipt/knowledge of the impugned order. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Order sheet of Bombay High Court permitting withdrawal of writ petition without expressing views on merits; affidavit seeking condonation and exclusion of time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application admitted by NCLT Mumbai Bench on 30.08.2019; writ petition filed before Bombay High Court and withdrawn with liberty; appeal filed before NCLAT beyond the 30-day period plus maximum 15-day condonable period.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT has jurisdiction to condone delay beyond the statutory limit of 45 days (30 days plus 15 condonable days) under Section 61(2) of the IBC by applying Section 14 or Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 where the appellant pursued writ proceedings before the High Court.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory time limit under Section 61(2) of the IBC mandates that an appeal must be filed within 30 days, extendable by no more than 15 days upon sufficient cause; this special limitation period overrides general provisions of the Limitation Act, and the appellate tribunal possesses no jurisdiction to condone any delay beyond the outer limit of 45 days. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: By virtue of Section 238 of the IBC, Section 61(2) overrides Section 5 of the Limitation Act; Section 14 of the Limitation Act applies to suits and applications and cannot extend or expand the strict outer limit of 45 days for filing appeals under Section 61. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Calculation of limitation from the date of receipt or knowledge of the order reveals whether the appeal is beyond the non-extendable 45-day outer limit. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appeal was filed beyond 45 days from the date of the impugned order, the Appellate Tribunal was precluded by law from entertaining it.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction as time-barred; liberty granted to Appellant to intervene in pending Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1069-1070 of 2019 filed against the same impugned order; no costs.
summary: A partner of Corporate Debtor Vaayu Infrastructure LLP appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order dated 30.08.2019 admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Vejas Power Projects Ltd. The appellant had initially challenged the admission before the Bombay High Court via a writ petition, which was withdrawn with liberty to approach NCLAT. The appeal was filed after 45 days from the order date. The appellant sought exclusion of time under Section 14 and condonation under Section 5 of the Limitation Act. The NCLAT held that under Section 61(2) read with the overriding mandate of Section 238, the Tribunal cannot condone delay exceeding 15 days beyond the initial 30 days. The appeal was dismissed as time-barred, granting liberty to intervene in a parallel pending appeal.

case_title: Shri Madan Lal Food Products Pvt. Ltd. vs. Union Of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shri Madan Lal Food Products Pvt. Ltd. is the struck-off Appellant Company (incorporated in 1995); Laxmi Narayan and Vinod Kumar are the promoter Directors; Union of India through Ministry of Corporate Affairs and ROC Uttarakhand & UP are the regulatory Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Incorporation for carrying on milling, processing, manufacturing, and producing pulses, rice, cereals, and food grains; acquisition and development of land in Mathura, UP for setting up a rice milling factory. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-filing of statutory annual returns and balance sheets from financial year 2005-2006 onwards. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company incorporated on 18.10.1995; construction permission granted by DM Mathura on 21.01.1996; land acquisition by NHAI on 17.01.2013 with compensation of Rs. 30 Lakhs paid in July 2014; striking off under Section 560/248. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Title and revenue records for Khasra No. 164, Village Ajijpur, Mathura; boundary wall and factory shed construction permits; NHAI acquisition award and compensation deposit of Rs. 30 Lakhs in the company's frozen bank account; valuation report establishing remaining land valued at Rs. 3,63,94,800; medical records showing extensive brain tumor and globlastoma surgeries of family members between 2004 and 2012. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: ROC struck off the company for non-filing of returns; Allahabad High Court transferred the writ challenge to NCLT Allahabad; NCLT Allahabad dismissed the appeal in CP-52/2015 on 01.08.2018 holding the company was not carrying on business.
legal_issues: Whether the name of a company holding substantial immovable assets and active bank deposits derived from land acquisition compensation should be restored under the just and equitable principles of Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013, despite failure to file annual returns due to family medical crises of its directors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a struck-off company possesses substantial valuable immovable assets and maintains an active bank account holding public land compensation funds, and default in regulatory filings was caused by bona fide personal distress of its directors rather than fraudulent motives, it is 'just' under Section 252 that the company's name be restored. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252(3) grants broad equitable power to order restoration if the company was carrying on business, in operation, or if it is otherwise 'just' to restore it, preventing undue prejudice to shareholders and the loss of corporate assets. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Concrete documentary evidence of real estate ownership, official land acquisition awards, and audited accounts showing substantial assets rebut the administrative presumption of defunct status under Section 248. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: With remaining real estate worth over Rs. 3.63 Crores and bank deposits of Rs. 30 Lakhs, NCLT's finding that the company had no business or operations was unsustainable.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; NCLT Allahabad order dated 01.08.2018 set aside; ROC directed to restore the company's name to the Register of Companies subject to payment of Rs. 1,00,000 costs to ROC within 30 days and filing of all outstanding annual returns and balance sheets from 2006 onwards along with statutory fees; ROC remains free to take statutory penal steps.
summary: Madan Lal Food Products Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Allahabad order affirming ROC's decision to strike off the company for non-filing of statutory returns since 2006. The promoter directors demonstrated that filings lapsed due to severe medical emergencies (brain tumors and surgeries) between 2004 and 2012. The company owned factory land in Mathura, received Rs. 30 Lakhs in NHAI acquisition compensation (deposited in its now frozen account), and held remaining land valued at Rs. 3.63 Crores. The NCLAT held that since the company possessed substantial valuable assets and the failure to file was inadvertent, it was just and proper to restore its name to the Register of Companies under Section 252, subject to paying Rs. 1 Lakh costs and filing all pending balance sheets.

case_title: Dipco Private Limited vs. Jayesh Sanghrajka, Resolution Professional of Ariisto Developers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dipco Private Limited is the Financial Creditor/CoC Member (Appellant); Jayesh Sanghrajka is the Resolution Professional of Ariisto Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Aasan Corporate Solutions Pvt. Ltd., IIFL Trustee Ltd., Vistra ITCL (India) Ltd., and HDFC Bank Ltd. are Financial Creditors/Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Verification, collation, and determination of financial debt claims and corresponding voting shares within the Committee of Creditors during the CIRP of Ariisto Developers Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute over the quantum of financial claims admitted and resulting CoC voting share allocations; HDFC Bank claimed its share should increase from 21.26% to 51%; Dipco sought exclusion of Vistra and Aasan claims. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP progressed past 330 days; CoC finalized and voted to approve the Resolution Plan; Miscellaneous Applications M.A. No. 999/2019 and M.A. No. 1124/2019 filed under Section 60(5) at the final stage of CIRP. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan and debenture transaction records supporting claims of Vistra ITCL, IIFL Trustee, and Aasan Corporate Solutions, showing direct disbursal and financial liability; CoC voting records approving the Resolution Plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai on 13.11.2019 rejected M.A. No. 1124/2019, holding that the documents proved liability and directed the RP to proceed with submitting the CoC-approved resolution plan for statutory approval.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority under Section 60(5) of the IBC has jurisdiction to entertain an application seeking re-adjudication and re-collation of claims and voting shares after the Committee of Creditors has approved the Resolution Plan beyond the 330-day statutory timeline.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction to entertain applications challenging claim collation and voting share apportionment once the statutory CIRP period has expired and the Committee of Creditors has already voted on and approved a Resolution Plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Relying on ArcelorMittal India v. Satish Kumar Gupta, Section 60(5) does not empower the NCLT to interfere with the resolution process at an interlocutory applicant's behest prior to the formal determination of plan approval under Section 31; NCLT cannot sit as an appellate forum over claim collation by the Resolution Professional once the plan is approved by the CoC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Basic verification showing that underlying commercial finance documents substantiate financial liability ('documents speak for themselves') precludes disruptive claim recalculations at the concluding stage of CIRP. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The belated challenges were intended to disrupt the resolution process after 330 days had expired and were rightly dismissed by the NCLT.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; order dated 13.11.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai affirmed; Resolution Professional directed to proceed with plan approval; no order as to costs.
summary: Dipco Pvt. Ltd., a financial creditor of Ariisto Developers Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting its Section 60(5) application. Dipco challenged the RP's collation of claims and voting share assignments of financial creditors Vistra ITCL, IIFL, and Aasan Corporate Solutions. By the time the application was taken up, more than 330 days had passed and the CoC had already approved a Resolution Plan. Citing ArcelorMittal, the NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that Section 60(5) does not allow the NCLT to interfere with claim collation or reopen voting allocations after the CoC has approved a resolution plan. Adherence to CIRP timelines is paramount, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Indian Overseas Bank vs. Patel Woods Products Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Indian Overseas Bank is the Financial Creditor (Appellant); M/s Patel Woods Products Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple credit facilities originally sanctioned on 27.04.2004 and renewed/enhanced periodically up to 21.01.2011. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan default resulting in NPA declaration on 27.02.2012 with effective retrospective date of default as 28.10.2010. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 27.02.2012 w.e.f. 28.10.2010; Revival Letters executed on 22.01.2007, 12.05.2007, 31.03.2009, 27.01.2011, and 25.01.2014; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice issued 03.12.2012; symbolic possession taken in 2013; DRT Securitisation Application disposed of on 14.10.2016; Original Application No. 224/2017 filed in DRT-III Delhi in 2017; Section 7 petition filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanction letters, revival letters ending 25.01.2014, Section 13(2) SARFAESI notices, DRT pleadings, and alleged undocumented payments in 2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-V on 09.12.2019 rejected the Section 7 petition as barred by limitation, finding that default occurred on 28.10.2010.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed more than three years after default and the last execution of a revival letter is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963; and whether pursuing an IBC petition primarily for debt recovery while parallel recovery proceedings are pending under SARFAESI and RDDBFI attracts Section 65.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a loan account has defaulted and been declared NPA, an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed more than three years after the date of default and after the last written revival letter is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act; using the IBC as a substitute for debt recovery while holding possession under SARFAESI violates Section 65. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The limitation period for Section 7 triggers on the date of default/NPA; neither SARFAESI actions nor pending DRT proceedings toll or extend limitation for filing an insolvency petition under Article 137. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: General assertions of part-payment unsupported by credible balance acknowledgments within the three-year window fail to extend limitation; simultaneous pursuit of parallel debt recovery mechanisms underscores abuse under Section 65. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The default occurred on 28.10.2010, the last revival letter was executed on 25.01.2014, and the petition filed in 2019 was hopelessly time-barred.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; NCLT New Delhi Bench-V order dated 09.12.2019 rejecting Section 7 application affirmed; observation clarified that orders will not affect the Bank's pending proceedings under the SARFAESI Act or before the DRT; no costs.
summary: Indian Overseas Bank appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order rejecting its Section 7 IBC application against Patel Woods Products Ltd. as time-barred. The loan defaulted on 28.10.2010 and was declared NPA on 27.02.2012. The Bank had taken symbolic possession under the SARFAESI Act in 2013 and filed an application before DRT-III Delhi in 2017. The last revival letter was dated 25.01.2014. The NCLAT upheld the rejection, ruling that the application filed in 2019 was barred by limitation under Article 137. Furthermore, filing an insolvency petition solely for debt recovery while pursuing parallel SARFAESI and DRT actions is not for resolution or liquidation and attracts Section 65. The appeal was dismissed without prejudice to pending DRT proceedings.

case_title: Munish Kumar Bhunsali & Anr vs Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1), Kew Precision Parts Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 2), and Munish Kumar Bhunsali & Anr. are the Appellants/Guarantors and Promoters. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple credit facilities totaling Rs. 2036 Lakhs (Cash Credit, WCDL, Invoice Finance Discounting, and Term Loans I, II, III) were sanctioned and renewed on 07.02.2014 and 05.03.2014, secured by mortgage of immovable property. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred in June 2015; account was classified as NPA on 30.09.2015; claimed default amount as on 17.11.2015 was Rs. 18,65,05,035.86 and grew to Rs. 46,63,35,337.31 as of 27.11.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan was recalled on 09.10.2015; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice was issued on 13.12.2017; Corporate Debtor submitted an unaccepted OTS letter on 12.12.2018 offering Rs. 13 Crores. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DRT Delhi decreed recovery in OA No. 576/2016 on 21.05.2019 for Rs. 16,13,40,574.79; DRT Lucknow set aside earlier SARFAESI action on 10.04.2017; Bank relied on Corporate Debtor's letter to RBI dated 26.03.2016 and OTS proposal dated 12.12.2018 as debt acknowledgments. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition was filed on 30.01.2019 before NCLT New Delhi Bench, which admitted CIRP on 06.09.2019 finding it within limitation from the 12.12.2018 OTS letter and exceeding the Rs. 1 Lakh threshold.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 petition filed on 30.01.2019 was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and whether an unaccepted OTS proposal or SARFAESI/DRT recovery proceedings can extend the limitation period under Section 18 or exclude time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The period of limitation for filing an application under Section 7 of the IBC is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, commencing from the date of default/NPA declaration; an acknowledgement of liability under Section 18 must be made within the subsisting three-year limitation period to keep the debt alive, and an unaccepted settlement proposal or parallel recovery proceedings before a forum of competent jurisdiction do not extend or exclude limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 requires an acknowledgement of a subsisting, legally enforceable liability made before expiry of the prescribed period; an acknowledgment given after the expiry of the three-year limitation period cannot revive a barred claim. Section 14 applies strictly where a party prosecutes in good faith before a forum lacking jurisdiction, which does not cover DRT proceedings where jurisdiction is proper. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The burden is on the creditor to establish that a signed, written acknowledgment of liability was made within the active three-year limitation period from the date of default; conditional, unaccepted settlement communications made after the expiry of the limitation period fail this standard. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The default having occurred in June 2015 and NPA declared on 30.09.2015, the three-year limitation expired in 2018; hence the application filed on 30.01.2019 is time-barred as the unaccepted OTS of 12.12.2018 occurred post-expiry, requiring dismissal of the Section 7 petition.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed without costs; the impugned NCLT admission order dated 06.09.2019 is set aside; the Section 7 petition is dismissed; the Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP; all actions taken by the IRP/RP and CoC are set aside; RP is directed to hand over assets and records to the promoters/directors forthwith; and the matter is remitted to NCLT to determine CIRP costs/fees payable by Kotak Mahindra Bank.
summary: Appellants challenged the NCLT New Delhi order admitting Kotak Mahindra Bank's Section 7 IBC petition against Kew Precision Parts Pvt. Ltd. The loan defaulted in June 2015 and was declared an NPA on 30.09.2015, while the petition was filed on 30.01.2019. The Bank argued that the petition was timely based on an unaccepted OTS letter dated 12.12.2018 and ongoing DRT/SARFAESI proceedings. The NCLAT held that the limitation period under Article 137 expired three years after default/NPA. Because the OTS letter was executed after limitation expired, it could not revive the debt under Section 18, nor did Section 14 apply. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and terminated CIRP.

case_title: B. Sudhakar Reddy & Ors vs B. Manpal Reddy & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Original Petitioners B. Manpal Reddy and G. Alwal Reddy (holding 25% share capital) filed against Corporate Debtor Palamoor Agro Complex Ltd. (Respondent No. 3) and subsequent directors B. Sudhakar Reddy & Ors. (Appellants). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Incorporation of company on 11.05.1994 to develop agro-industrial projects; purchase of 99 acres in Revally/Urukonda and 4.20 acres in Kadtal village funded by personal borrowings and promoter contributions. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in internal corporate management, including unauthorized cash transactions, failure to satisfy creditors leading to criminal conviction of the promoter director, and unauthorized distress sale of company land for Rs. 32 Lakhs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original promoter resigned on 29.11.2001 under an MOU; statutory forms (Form 32) filed on 07.10.2002; balance sheets for FY 1994-95 to 1999-2000 belatedly filed on 02.05.2003; complaint to ROC made on 08.09.2003; SFIO investigation ordered pursuant to High Court order dated 07.07.2011 in CP No. 109/2008; SFIO report submitted on 29.02.2012. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SFIO statutory investigation report proving non-maintenance of cash books/statutory registers, falsification of annual balance sheets, fraudulent share allotment forms filed via misused digital signatures, and sale of court-attached land at an undervalue. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Company Petition CP No. 16 of 2013 was filed under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956 before NCLT Hyderabad, which held Appellants guilty of oppression and mismanagement, set aside filings, ordered deposit of land sale proceeds with 12% interest, and imposed Rs. 2 Lakhs costs per respondent.
legal_issues: Whether the findings of severe mismanagement, fraudulent allotment of equity shares, and illicit transfer of company assets based on an SFIO investigation report under Section 223 of the Companies Act, 2013 were justified, and whether the company petition was barred by delay, laches, or res judicata.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An investigation report prepared by Central Government inspectors constitutes valid and admissible substantive evidence in legal proceedings under Section 223 of the Companies Act, 2013, and acts of running a corporate entity without statutory compliances, falsifying records, and misappropriating corporate property constitute actionable oppression and mismanagement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 223 makes SFIO reports statutory evidence of the facts contained therein, entitling the Tribunal to rely upon its factual findings regarding unauthorized share allotments, falsification of financial statements, and illegal asset striping. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unrebutted forensic findings of unrecorded cash dealings, failure to maintain statutory registers, non-convening of AGMs/Board meetings, and unauthorized alienations of attached company properties establish gross oppression and corporate mismanagement. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellants completely failed to substantiate legitimate share allotments or authorized land alienation, rendering the NCLT Hyderabad's directions and penalty fully lawful and sustainable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs; the impugned NCLT Hyderabad order dated 23.02.2018 is affirmed; all rejected statutory filings stand vacated; statutory compliance for filings must be completed within three months, leaving the ROC free to initiate appropriate punitive actions under the Companies Act, 2013.
summary: Appellants challenged the order of NCLT Hyderabad in CP No. 16 of 2013 which found them guilty of oppression and mismanagement under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 in relation to Palamoor Agro Complex Ltd. Relying upon an SFIO investigation report, the Tribunal uncovered massive statutory defaults, non-maintenance of accounts, falsified share allotments, and the illegal sale of company property at undervalue. The NCLAT confirmed that under Section 223 of the Companies Act, 2013, SFIO findings are admissible evidence. Holding that Appellants failed to rebut the findings of fraud and mismanagement, NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Global Business Corporation vs Punjab National Bank & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Global Business Corporation through sole proprietor Gaganjeet Singh is the Resolution Applicant (Appellant); Punjab National Bank is the sole Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Ashish Agarwal is the Resolution Professional/Liquidator (Respondent No. 2); Kochar Overseas Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor voluntarily initiated insolvency proceedings under Section 10 of the IBC, following which expressions of interest and resolution plans were solicited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was unable to service debts owed to Punjab National Bank; Resolution Applicant submitted an initial plan of Rs. 900 Lakhs, later increased to Rs. 1025 Lakhs, and finally to Rs. 1200 Lakhs via email dated 10.08.2018, conditioned upon releasing promoter personal guarantees. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The initial 180-day CIRP period was extended by 90 days under Section 12(3), expiring finally on 14.08.2018; the final revised bid was submitted on 10.08.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence revealed that Vikramjit Singh, suspended director of Corporate Debtor, was an authorized cheque-signing signatory for the Resolution Applicant's bank accounts; Corporate Debtor had transferred an Innova car to Appellant; Appellant operated from the Corporate Debtor's premises paying rent and utilized its brand name 'Double Bull Basmati'. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In the 7th CoC meeting, PNB with 100% voting share rejected the resolution plan due to Section 29A ineligibility and the condition discharging personal guarantees; NCLT Chandigarh rejected Appellant's CA No. 340/2018, 370/2018, and 371/2018 on 01.11.2018, and ordered liquidation on 30.11.2018.
