legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Applicant was disqualified under Section 29A of the IBC as a related party/connected person of the Corporate Debtor's suspended director, and whether the CoC's commercial decision to reject a conditional resolution plan seeking discharge of promoter personal guarantees and recommend liquidation can be interfered with.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution applicant whose bank accounts are authorized to be operated by a suspended director of the corporate debtor is a related party/connected person ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC, and the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors rejecting a conditional plan with a 100% majority is non-justiciable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A bars any connected person or extended arm acting in concert with the suspended board of directors of the Corporate Debtor; Section 33 mandates liquidation where no viable compliant plan is approved within the statutory period of 270 days. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documentary admission by the applicant that the suspended director had bank signing authority, shared business premises, acquired debtor assets, and utilized its brand name confirms related-party status under Section 29A beyond mere commercial coincidence. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC acted entirely within its statutory commercial discretion in rejecting the conditional plan and opting for liquidation, and CIRP cannot be kept alive indefinitely beyond the mandatory 270-day period.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs; the impugned orders dated 01.11.2018 and 30.11.2018 passed by NCLT Chandigarh rejecting the resolution plan and ordering the liquidation of Kochar Overseas Pvt. Ltd. are upheld.
summary: Appellant Global Business Corporation challenged orders of NCLT Chandigarh rejecting its resolution plan and directing liquidation of Corporate Debtor Kochar Overseas Pvt. Ltd. PNB, holding 100% voting share, rejected the plan because the applicant was a related party under Section 29A (the suspended director operated the applicant's bank accounts and shared brand assets) and because the plan impermissibly mandated the release of personal guarantees. The NCLAT held that the Appellant was ineligible under Section 29A, that CIRP timelines cannot be extended indefinitely beyond 270 days, and that the commercial wisdom of the CoC rejecting the plan was non-justiciable. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Ritu Rastogi Resolution Professional vs Riyal Packers
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ritu Rastogi, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Benlon India Ltd. (Appellant); Riyal Packers, Operational Creditor (Respondent No. 1); and Surender Kumar Chawla, Resolution Applicant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Manufacturing operations of synthetic vial by the Corporate Debtor requiring resolution following default on operational debts owed to Riyal Packers. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default formed the basis of CIRP initiation against Benlon India Ltd.; resolution plan submitted by prospective resolution applicant Surender Kumar Chawla was pending final voting before the CoC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 19.12.2018; public announcement made on 23.12.2018; CoC constituted on 12.01.2019; details of assets/liabilities received belatedly on 12.07.2019; extension of 60 days granted by NCLT on 13.09.2019; CoC authorized extension request on 08.11.2019; statutory 330-day timeline expired shortly before plan voting could conclude. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor was a going concern; two resolution plans were received within the extended time granted on 13.09.2019; valuer delays and delayed asset disclosures hampered earlier progress; CoC required 15-20 days to complete internal institutional approval and voting. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed an application seeking a short 15-20 day extension/exclusion beyond 330 days; NCLT New Delhi Bench-V rejected the application on 27.11.2019 relying on State Bank of India v. Ramdev International/Manibhadra Polycot, declining to apply Essar Steel.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in refusing to grant a short extension/exclusion of 15 to 20 days beyond the 330-day timeline prescribed under Section 12 of the IBC to enable the CoC to vote on an existing resolution plan for a going concern.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a corporate debtor remains a viable going concern and a short period is required to complete voting on a resolution plan submitted within time, tribunals possess discretion under the exceptional circumstances doctrine to grant an extension beyond 330 days to avoid unnecessary liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 outer limit of 330 days must be interpreted in light of the primary objective of the IBC—resolution over liquidation—in accordance with the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel, allowing extensions where procedural delays are non-attributable to applicant negligence. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court assesses whether there is a genuine, imminent prospect of resolution of an active enterprise, whether the resolution plan was timely submitted before the CoC, and whether exceptional circumstances justify the brief extension sought. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT misapplied precedents and failed to implement the Essar Steel principles; granting a short window until 06.02.2020 served the core statutory object of corporate revival.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 27.11.2019 is quashed and set aside; the matter is remitted back; time is granted up to 06.02.2020 for the CoC to finalize voting on the resolution plan and submit the outcome to the Adjudicating Authority; failing which the Adjudicating Authority may proceed in accordance with liquidation provisions.
summary: The Resolution Professional of Benlon India Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order rejecting an application for a 15–20 day extension beyond the 330-day CIRP limit to enable the CoC to vote on a pending resolution plan. The NCLAT noted that the Corporate Debtor was a going concern manufacturing synthetic vials and that the plan had been received within the previously extended period. Applying the Supreme Court's decision in Essar Steel, the Appellate Tribunal held that brief extensions beyond 330 days should be granted in exceptional circumstances to facilitate resolution rather than forced liquidation. The appeal was allowed, granting time until 06.02.2020.

case_title: Ved Contracts Pvt. Ltd vs Pan Realtors Pvt. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ved Contracts Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor (Appellant) and Pan Realtors Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Four work orders awarded between January 2010 and January 2014 for executing civil construction works for the project 'PAN OASIS' at Sector 70, Noida. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor received Rs. 16,83,03,963/- and claimed an outstanding unpaid default of Rs. 2,41,58,130/- (including Rs. 69,00,000/- retention amount) along with interest, GST, and other charges; Corporate Debtor had also raised an unaccepted debit note of Rs. 6,21,164/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC was issued by the Operational Creditor on 05.01.2019 and replied to by the Corporate Debtor. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated 24.10.2018 from Corporate Debtor to Operational Creditor prior to the demand notice stating that the claim of 03.10.2018 was baseless, demanding reconciliation documents, asserting debit notes for incomplete works and defects, and expressly negating the exaggerated claim pending final certified bills. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition filed by Operational Creditor before NCLT New Delhi Bench was dismissed on 18.07.2019 on grounds of a pre-existing dispute raised prior to the Section 8 demand notice.
legal_issues: Whether a pre-existing dispute existed between the parties prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice regarding running bills, defective work, and lack of certified final bills, warranting dismissal of the Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Section 9 application under the IBC must be rejected where a plausible, genuine dispute exists prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice, without requiring the Adjudicating Authority to decide the final merits or likelihood of success of the defense. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpreting Section 8 and Section 9 under the doctrine of Mobilox Innovations, an existing dispute is one that raises a plausible contention needing further investigation, not being patently feeble, spurious, or mere bluster. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Written email communications disputing invoices, raising issues of incomplete work, demanding reconciliation, and denying liability prior to the demand notice establish a bona fide pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Corporate Debtor's email of 24.10.2018 demonstrated a serious dispute regarding uncertified running bills, debit adjustments, and incomplete performance before the demand notice of 05.01.2019, the petition under Section 9 was rightly rejected.
operative_order: The appeal is rejected without costs, affirming the order dated 18.07.2019 passed by NCLT New Delhi rejecting the Section 9 application.
summary: Appellant Ved Contracts appealed against the rejection of its Section 9 IBC application by NCLT New Delhi against Pan Realtors Pvt. Ltd. The appellant claimed outstanding dues of over Rs. 2.41 Crores for civil construction work under multiple work orders. The Corporate Debtor established that on 24.10.2018, well before the Section 8 demand notice of 05.01.2019, it had sent an email rejecting the claim as exaggerated, raising debits for defective and incomplete third-party works, and pointing out the lack of certified final bills. Applying the Mobilox Innovations test, the NCLAT affirmed that a genuine pre-existing dispute existed and rejected the appeal.

case_title: Kundan Care Products Ltd. vs. Mr. Surya Kanta Satapathy & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kundan Care Products Ltd. is an unsuccessful Resolution Applicant (Appellant); Surya Kanta Satapathy is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); Fortis Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 3); Alex Green Energy Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution of Corporate Debtor through CIRP initiated under Section 7 of IBC, with RFRP issued to evaluated resolution applicants. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default led to admission on 18.02.2019; Fortis Chemicals submitted an approved resolution plan of Rs. 11.07 Crores; Appellant originally proposed Rs. 5 Crores, subsequently offering to enhance to Rs. 11.50 Crores after evaluation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 admitted on 18.02.2019; EOI publication on 31.08.2019 with deadline 14.09.2019; Appellant submitted delayed EOI on 23.09.2019 and hard plan on 29.10.2019; RP notified Appellant on 01.11.2019 of ranking 6th; CoC approved Fortis Chemicals' plan on 11.11.2019; NCLT approved plan on 25.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RFRP evaluation criteria stipulated negotiations exclusively with the top three resolution applicants; Appellant scored only 39.40% voting shares, ranking 6th; Appellant's email of 04.11.2019 expressing willingness to negotiate lacked a concrete financial figure. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench approved Respondent No. 3's resolution plan on 25.11.2019 while rejecting Appellant's belated enhancement proposal; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether an unsuccessful resolution applicant who failed to rank within the top three under RFRP evaluation criteria possesses an absolute right to renegotiate or enhance its bid after CoC evaluation, and whether an approved resolution plan can be interfered with outside the grounds specified in Section 61(3) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution applicant has no vested legal right to demand renegotiation or revision of its plan once the CoC evaluates proposals in accordance with pre-established RFRP terms, and the commercial judgment of the CoC cannot be disturbed unless violations under Section 61(3) are established. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Appeals challenging approved resolution plans under Section 61(3) of the IBC are strictly circumscribed by the exhaustive grounds enumerated therein; commercial viability and stakeholder distribution decisions belong exclusively to the CoC under Section 31. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Compliance with objective RFRP terms (limiting negotiations to top three ranked bidders) negates claims of procedural arbitrariness or material irregularity by a lower-ranked applicant. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant had no entitlement to force renegotiation, and failing to demonstrate any violation under Section 61(3), the approved plan cannot be set aside.
operative_order: Both appeals are dismissed without costs, sustaining the NCLT Kolkata order dated 25.11.2019 approving the resolution plan submitted by Fortis Chemicals Pvt. Ltd.
summary: Appellant Kundan Care Products challenged the NCLT Kolkata order approving the resolution plan of Fortis Chemicals for Alex Green Energy Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant, whose Rs. 5 Crore plan ranked 6th under the RFRP evaluation criteria, sought to re-negotiate and increase its offer to Rs. 11.50 Crores, which was higher than Fortis Chemicals' Rs. 11.07 Crore offer. The NCLAT held that resolution applicants have no vested right to renegotiate once evaluated under RFRP terms limiting negotiations to the top three bidders. Affirming the commercial supremacy of the CoC under Essar Steel and finding no violation under Section 61(3), the Appellate Tribunal dismissed both appeals.

case_title: M/s. SEW Infrastructure Ltd. vs M/s. Mahendra Investment Advisors Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. SEW Infrastructure Ltd. is the Financial Creditor (Appellant); M/s. Mahendra Investment Advisors Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Guarantor/Corporate Debtor (Respondent); M/s. Amrit Jal Ventures Pvt. Ltd. is the Principal Borrower. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility extended by Appellant to the Principal Borrower Amrit Jal Ventures, secured by a corporate guarantee furnished by Respondent Mahendra Investment Advisors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred under the financial loan agreement; Appellant sought recovery of the financial debt through corporate guarantee enforcement. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP petition under Section 7 was first filed and admitted against the Principal Borrower; subsequently, another Section 7 petition was filed by the same creditor against the Corporate Guarantor. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The claim and default amount asserted against the Corporate Guarantor were identical to the claim for which CIRP was already initiated and admitted against the Principal Borrower; Respondent also raised defense of being an NBFC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad rejected the Section 7 petition on 24.10.2019 because CIRP had already been admitted against the Principal Borrower for the same debt and default; Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor can trigger and maintain a second CIRP application under Section 7 of the IBC against a Corporate Guarantor for the exact same set of debt and default after an application against the Principal Borrower has already been admitted.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed by a financial creditor is admitted against either the principal borrower or the corporate guarantor, a second application by the same creditor for the identical debt and default cannot be admitted against the other. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 does not permit multiple simultaneous CIRPs against two distinct corporate entities for the identical underlying debt, as driving two companies into insolvency/liquidation for the same claim violates the core tenets of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Establishing that the underlying claim, transaction, and default metrics are identical to those admitted in the prior CIRP against the principal borrower renders the subsequent guarantor petition non-maintainable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 petition against the Corporate Guarantor was rightly rejected since the creditor's identical claim had already triggered CIRP against the Principal Borrower.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, upholding the NCLT Hyderabad order dated 24.10.2019 rejecting the Section 7 application.
summary: Appellant SEW Infrastructure challenged the order of NCLT Hyderabad rejecting its Section 7 IBC application against Corporate Guarantor Mahendra Investment Advisors Pvt. Ltd. The Adjudicating Authority dismissed the petition because a Section 7 application for the identical debt and default had already been admitted against the Principal Borrower, Amrit Jal Ventures Pvt. Ltd. Relying on Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal v. Piramal Enterprises, the NCLAT held that a financial creditor cannot trigger two simultaneous CIRP proceedings against both the principal borrower and the corporate guarantor for the identical debt. The appeal was accordingly dismissed.

case_title: Asim Kumar Misra vs M/s. Sarkar & Chowdhury Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Asim Kumar Misra and connected individual appellants (directors/shareholders); M/s. Sarkar & Chowdhury Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying corporate share transfer dispute in CP No. 151/2014, requiring the registration and transfer of shares of Respondent No. 1 Company pursuant to board commitments. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from the refusal and non-cooperation of company directors to implement and execute the transfer of shares. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Order directing appointment of Special Officer passed on 27.08.2019; NCLT directions issued on 18.09.2018 and 11.12.2019; interim High Court/NCLAT order dated 06.01.2020; NCLT compliance order dated 07.01.2020 fixing inspection on 14.01.2020; review listed for 21.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: In Contempt Application No. 1681/KB/2019, the contemnors appeared in person; directors undertook to comply with the share registration via Special Officer at the corporate office subject to their pending review petition (Misc. A. No. 02/KB/2020). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench issued directions on 11.12.2019 to complete share registration; NCLAT in lead appeal Company Appeal (AT) No. 02/2020 refused to interfere on 10.01.2020; subsequent appeals were filed assailing the same 11.12.2019 order.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal should interfere with interlocutory directions issued by the NCLT enforcing compliance of share registration through a Special Officer during pending contempt and review proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the Appellate Tribunal has already examined an impugned interlocutory order in a lead appeal and declined to interfere given pending review and contempt compliance before the lower forum, subsequent identical appeals by related parties are squarely covered and liable to be disposed of similarly. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421 does not warrant appellate interference where the lower tribunal has merely issued interim ministerial implementation directions while keeping substantive maintainability and review challenges pending for adjudication. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The identity of the impugned order dated 11.12.2019 and prior coordinate ruling of the Appellate Tribunal dated 10.01.2020 in the parent appeal conclusively governs the outcome. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the grievance was identical to that decided in Mackintosh Burn Ltd. v. Sarkar & Chowdhury Enterprises Pvt. Ltd., no ground for interference existed.
operative_order: The appeals are disposed of without costs, declining to interfere with the NCLT Kolkata order dated 11.12.2019.
summary: Appellants filed appeals under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 against an interlocutory order dated 11.12.2019 passed by NCLT Kolkata directing the registration and transfer of shares through an appointed Special Officer in ongoing contempt proceedings. The NCLAT noted that the identical order had already been challenged and upheld in Mackintosh Burn Ltd. v. Sarkar & Chowdhury Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. (Company Appeal (AT) No. 02 of 2020) on 10.01.2020, wherein the Tribunal declined to interfere because undertakings were recorded and a review petition was pending. Holding these appeals covered by that decision, NCLAT dismissed/disposed of them.

case_title: Santosh Wasantrao Walokar & Ors vs Vijay Kumar V. Iyer & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Santosh Wasantrao Walokar (representing workmen/employees), Sneha Traders & Shamrao Baliram (Operational Creditors), Nitin & Murlidhar Agrawal (Unsecured Financial Creditors), Lalchand Maloo (Promoter/Suspended Director), and Deputy Commissioner CGST & Central Excise (Operational Creditor) are Appellants; Vijay Kumar V. Iyer is the RP (Respondent No. 1); Dalmia Cement (Bharat) Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 2); Murli Industries Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company is the Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process initiated against Murli Industries Ltd. under Section 7 of the IBC by Edelweiss ARC, culminating in the submission and approval of a resolution plan by Dalmia Cement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Widespread defaults across multiple creditor classes, including claimed operational debt of Rs. 3,23,03,256/- by grain brokers, Rs. 64,04,86,019/- claimed in unpaid central excise/service tax, and liquidation value assessed by registered valuers at Rs. 231,10,00,000/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court provisional liquidator appointed on 21.03.2017; CIRP initiated in April 2017; High Court granted leave to proceed under IBC on 02.11.2018; CoC approved resolution plan with 100% voting share in 11th meeting on 20.12.2017; NCLT issued interim order proposing modifications on 03.07.2019; final plan approved on 22.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution plan contemplated closure of non-viable paper and solvent extraction units, payment of workmen dues pari passu with financial creditors under amended Section 30(2)(b), in-principle approvals for mining leases from Maharashtra state authorities obtained in September 2019, and rejection/non-verification of claims filed improperly via speed post or lacking documentation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench conditionally approved the resolution plan on 03.07.2019 subject to modifications, which were accepted and confirmed by final order on 22.07.2019; various stakeholders appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT had the power to pass an order seeking acceptance of modifications on 03.07.2019 and approve the resolution plan on 22.07.2019 without acting as an illegal review; whether a conditional resolution plan approved by the CoC's commercial wisdom is valid; and whether unfiled or rejected claims stand extinguished upon plan approval under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in evaluating the feasibility, viability, and conditionalities of a resolution plan is non-justiciable and cannot be interfered with by the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal, and once a resolution plan is approved, all claims that were not submitted, verified, or included in the plan stand extinguished to provide a clean slate to the successful resolution applicant. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 30(2) and 31 circumscribe the adjudicating forum's jurisdiction, precluding judicial reassessment of commercial terms; Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 154 of the NCLT Rules allow rectification of patent errors, and an interim order directing a resolution applicant to confirm acceptance of proposed modifications prior to final approval does not constitute an impermissible substantive review. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Compliance with mandatory Section 30(2) parameters, along with the securing of requisite in-principle governmental approvals for conditional covenants and receipt of 100% CoC voting approval, satisfies all legal standards for plan approval. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The commercial judgment of the CoC to approve Dalmia Cement's resolution plan was valid, the procedure adopted by NCLT Mumbai in its two-stage orders was lawful, and all excluded or unadjudicated claims properly stood extinguished under the Essar Steel doctrine.
operative_order: All connected appeals are dismissed without costs, and the impugned approval order dated 22.07.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench is upheld; open to workmen to negotiate any independent scheme of arrangement with the new management.
summary: Multiple stakeholders appealed against the NCLT Mumbai orders dated 03.07.2019 and 22.07.2019 approving Dalmia Cement's resolution plan for Murli Industries Ltd. Workmen challenged the plan due to closure of certain units, operational creditors and tax authorities challenged claim rejections, and the promoter argued the plan was conditional and that NCLT illegally reviewed its earlier order. The NCLAT held that CoC's commercial wisdom is supreme and covers conditional terms once accepted. Furthermore, the NCLT's 03.07.2019 order was an interlocutory step rather than a substantive review. In line with Essar Steel, all unfiled or omitted claims stand extinguished. The appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Cyrus Investments Pvt. Ltd. & Anr vs Tata Sons Ltd. & Ors
appeal_number: I.A. No. 4331 & 4336 of 2019 in Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 254 & 268 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Registrar of Companies Mumbai (Applicant/Intervenor); Cyrus Investments Pvt. Ltd. and Cyrus Pallonji Mistry (Appellants in main appeals); Tata Sons Ltd. & Ors. (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Reconversion of Tata Sons Ltd. from a deemed Public Limited Company to a Private Limited Company following dismissal of company petition by NCLT. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Administrative and regulatory contest concerning the deletion of observations against RoC Mumbai and alteration of rulings on company status in paragraphs 181, 186, and 187 of the NCLAT judgment dated 18.12.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Tata Sons became deemed public company under Section 43A(1A) on 01.02.1975; Companies Act 2013 enacted; Tata Sons applied via letter on 19.07.2018 to RoC requesting substitution of status to private company under Section 43A(2A); NCLAT delivered main judgment on 18.12.2019; RoC filed amendment applications in December 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RoC relied on MCA Notification S.O. 560(E) dated 30.01.2019 contending Section 43A(2A) survived; RoC argued that since Central Government had not prescribed minimum share capital under Section 2(68) read with Section 2(66), it was obligated to record the conversion without NCLT approval or special resolution under Section 14. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLAT had previously declared RoC's conversion of Tata Sons Ltd. illegal on 18.12.2019; RoC Mumbai moved interlocutory applications seeking amendment/deletion of paragraphs alleging aspersions and errors.
legal_issues: Whether Section 43A(2A) of the Companies Act, 1956 remains operational to permit summary reconversion of a deemed public company to a private company without complying with Sections 14, 18, and 465 of the Companies Act, 2013, and whether grounds existed to amend or delete the findings in the judgment dated 18.12.2019.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 465 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Companies Act, 1956 stands entirely repealed (except Part IX-A), meaning Section 43A(2A) is no longer available, and conversion of any company class requires strict adherence to Section 14 (alteration of articles by special resolution) and Section 18 of the 2013 Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 43A(4) of the 1956 Act itself mandated Central Government approval to revert to private status; in the 2013 Act, Sections 14 and 18 occupy the field, and in the absence of rules prescribing paid-up capital under Section 2(66)/2(68), the Registrar lacks unilateral authority to alter the register or incorporation certificate. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Rectification or amendment of a judgment is permissible only where there is an apparent clerical or manifest factual error on the face of the record, not to rewrite substantive legal findings determining parties' legal status. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RoC's action was contrary to Sections 14 and 18 of the Companies Act, 2013, no aspersions were cast upon the officer, and no legal error existed to warrant amendment of the final judgment beyond correcting a typographical statutory citation in paragraph 171.
operative_order: Both Interlocutory Applications (I.A. Nos. 4331 & 4336 of 2019) are dismissed without costs; prayer for amendment rejected, with only a typographical correction ordered in paragraph 171 to substitute the amended definition of Section 2(68).
summary: The Registrar of Companies, Mumbai, filed applications seeking amendment and deletion of observations made in paragraphs 181, 186, and 187 of the NCLAT's judgment dated 18.12.2019, which had declared the conversion of Tata Sons Ltd. from a public to a private company illegal. The RoC argued that Section 43A(2A) of the 1956 Act was still operational and that no aspersions should lie against the regulator. The NCLAT held that the 1956 Act stood repealed under Section 465 of the 2013 Act and that conversion required compliance with Sections 14 and 18. Clarifying that no personal aspersions were cast and finding no error apparent on record, the NCLAT dismissed both applications.

case_title: Bank of Baroda vs Aban Offshore Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bank of Baroda (originally Vijaya Bank, substituted post-amalgamation) is the Preference Shareholder (Appellant); Aban Offshore Limited is a listed public Corporate Entity (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant subscribed to cumulative extendable non-convertible redeemable preference shares worth Rs. 30,00,000/- on 09.07.2005 and 29.05.2007 carrying 8% to 9% annual dividend coupons, and agreed on 31.10.2011 to roll over redemption for 3 years. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in redemption of principal and dividend payments from FY 2015-16 onwards; total unpaid debt claimed was Rs. 41,68,09,739/- (comprising Rs. 22.50 Crores principal and Rs. 19.18 Crores dividend and overdue interest as of 19.03.2018). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Redemption fell due post-extension; company paid 180% equity dividend in FY 2014-15 but ceased preference payouts thereafter; preference shareholders meeting convened on 07.09.2016; application MA/175/2018 filed by Appellant before NCLT Chennai in 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share subscription certificates, roll-over agreement dated 31.10.2011, balance sheets reflecting failure to redeem preference shares or create Capital Redemption Reserve, and financial disclosures showing dividend distributions to equity holders while withholding preference redemption. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench dismissed Appellant's MA No. 175/2018 on 19.12.2018, holding that under Section 55(3) only the company has locus to petition the Tribunal and that Section 245 class actions do not cover individual preference share redemption.
legal_issues: Whether preference shareholders have locus standi under Section 55(3) or Section 245 of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, to approach the NCLT for enforcement and redemption of unredeemed preference shares upon company default.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The legislative mandate of Section 55 of the Companies Act, 2013 prohibits irredeemable preference shares and obligates redemption; where a company fails to redeem preference shares or file an application under Section 55(3), preference shareholders are not remediless and may invoke the inherent powers of the Tribunal under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules or file a class action under Section 245 as members under Section 2(55). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 55 compulsorily requires timely redemption; although Section 55(3) references petitions made by the company, it cannot be interpreted to leave preference shareholders without judicial recourse; preference shareholders constitute members under Section 2(55) and Section 88, entitling them to seek relief against prejudicial management under Section 245 or via Rule 11. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Undisputed proof of failure to redeem mature preference shares and failure to pay cumulative contractual dividends establishes a prima facie cause of action for member oppression and statutory default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT Chennai Bench erred in holding that preference shareholders lack locus standi to petition for redemption, requiring the dismissal order to be quashed and the matter remanded for merits adjudication.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 19.12.2018 passed by NCLT Chennai Bench in MA/175/2018 is set aside; and the matter is remitted back to the NCLT to decide the application on merits in accordance with law. No order as to costs.
summary: Bank of Baroda appealed against the dismissal of its application by NCLT Chennai seeking redemption of cumulative redeemable preference shares worth over Rs. 41.68 Crores against Aban Offshore Ltd. The NCLT had held that preference shareholders lacked locus standi because Section 55(3) contemplates a petition by the company, and that Section 245 does not cover such claims. The NCLAT reversed, ruling that Section 55 aims to eliminate irredeemable preference capital, ensuring shareholders are not left remediless. Preference shareholders qualify as 'members' under Section 2(55) and can seek redress via Section 55(3), Section 245, or Rule 11 inherent powers. The matter was remanded to the NCLT.

case_title: Anjani Gases vs B.P Projects Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anjani Gases (Sole Proprietorship) is the Operational Creditor (Appellant); B.P. Projects Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Long-standing supply contract commencing prior to 2005 for supply of Natural Oxygen Cylinders, Carbon Dioxide Cylinders, and LPG Gas Cylinders against purchase orders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default alleged on invoices raised from June 2014 onwards; total claimed operational debt was Rs. 1,45,74,133.33 (comprising Rs. 1,10,23,431.38 principal plus 12% interest amounting to Rs. 35,50,701.95). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notices issued under erstwhile law on 17.06.2016 and 13.07.2016; FIR filed on 07.09.2016; Section 8 demand notice under IBC served on 31.03.2018; Corporate Debtor replied on 13.04.2018; Section 9 petition filed in 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor filed a criminal FIR on 07.09.2016 under Sections 120-B, 406, 420, and 506 IPC against the Corporate Debtor's directors for wrongful loss of Rs. 1,10,23,403.63, proceedings of which were stayed by Calcutta High Court on 17.01.2017; Corporate Debtor's reply dated 13.04.2018 asserted that Rs. 86,30,000/- plus an excess amount of Rs. 5,56,889/- had been paid during 2014-2016 and disputed the absence of contractual holding/rental charges. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the Section 9 application in CP(IB) No. 802/KB/2018 on 03.05.2019 on grounds of serious pre-existing disputes requiring regular adjudication.
legal_issues: Whether a criminal complaint/FIR lodged by an operational creditor alleging fraud and cheating for the exact amount claimed as operational debt, combined with disputes over ledger reconciliation and excess payments, constitutes a pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC must be rejected where an active, plausible dispute exists prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice, as IBC proceedings are summary in nature and cannot be utilized as a substitute for debt recovery or resolution of criminal and complex accounting controversies. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2)(a) read with Section 5(6) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) mandates dismissal of an insolvency petition when notice of dispute has been received; the definition of dispute is illustrative and encompasses serious contested claims of cheating, criminal breach of trust, and disputed running accounts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Mobilox standard, the Adjudicating Authority evaluates whether the defense is genuine, plausible, and supported by pre-existing documentary controversy rather than an afterthought or spurious defense. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The filing of a criminal FIR on 07.09.2016 by the operational creditor for the identical sum of Rs. 1,10,23,403.63 and pending High Court quashing proceedings conclusively demonstrated a pre-existing dispute prior to the Section 8 notice of 31.03.2018, requiring rejection of the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, sustaining the order dated 03.05.2019 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench rejecting the Section 9 application.
summary: Appellant Anjani Gases appealed against the NCLT Kolkata order rejecting its Section 9 IBC application for recovery of Rs. 1.45 Crores against B.P. Projects Pvt. Ltd. The Corporate Debtor resisted the petition on grounds of a pre-existing dispute, showing that the Appellant had lodged an FIR on 07.09.2016 alleging cheating and breach of trust for the exact claimed sum of Rs. 1.10 Crores, which was stayed by the Calcutta High Court. The Corporate Debtor also disputed invoices and claimed excess payments. Applying the Mobilox Innovations doctrine, the NCLAT affirmed that serious, bona fide disputes preceded the Section 8 demand notice, making summary insolvency proceedings inappropriate. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: DLF Ltd. & Anr vs Satya Bhushan Kaura & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: DLF Ltd. (Appellant No. 1); Rajdhani Investments & Agencies Pvt. Ltd., formerly Haryana Electrical Udyog Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant No. 2, promoter entity); Satya Bhushan Kaura and Subhash Chander Kaura, legal heirs of late Devki Nandan Kaura (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Late Devki Nandan Kaura held 150 equity shares (split/bonus adjusted to 6,000 shares) in DLF Ltd.; DLF issued a rights issue between 29.12.2005 and 18.01.2006, followed by a limited-time opportunity up to 26.09.2007 under an arrangement with Appellant No. 2 to transfer rights entitlement shares (60,000 shares) at Rs. 2/- per share to existing holders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unjustified refusal and default by Appellants to transmit the 6,000 equity shares and allot/transfer the 60,000 rights shares despite tender of consideration of Rs. 1,20,000/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demise of original shareholder on 27.08.1987; company accepted will on 09.11.1987; Respondents sought rights allotment on 25.05.2007 and 01.06.2007; DLF demanded court order and indemnity bond on 06.08.2007; Respondents submitted indemnity on 19.11.2007; DLF deferred decision pending court order on 30.11.2007; District Court granted Letter of Administration on 31.01.2012 (decree on 25.04.2012); DLF refused transfer on 17.09.2012; petition filed in December 2013. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Correspondence establishing that DLF agreed to process transfer upon receipt of court order, utilized the filed indemnity bond in its Red Herring Prospectus to demonstrate absence of shareholder complaints, but subsequently refused transfer claiming rights debentures were non-heritable. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench allowed CP No. 17/58/2013 on 11.12.2018 under Section 58(5), directing DLF to register transfer of 60,000 shares upon payment of Rs. 2/- per share and transmit 6,000 shares, which Appellants appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the petition under Section 58(4) was barred by limitation or laches given the passage of time since the shareholder's death, and whether a listed company can refuse transmission and rights share transfer after compelling the legal heir to obtain a Letter of Administration under the doctrine of approbation and reprobation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate entity that instructs a legal heir to obtain a formal succession decree or letter of administration and confirms that transfer decisions will await such judicial order is precluded under the doctrine of approbation and reprobation from asserting that the claim is barred by limitation once the decree is produced. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 58(4) and Section 58(5) empower the Tribunal to direct rectification and registration of share transfers where a company has without sufficient cause refused transfer or transmission; the right to entitlement shares flowing from valid shareholding is heritable upon establishing legal representation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A valid Letter of Administration issued under Section 290 of the Indian Succession Act completely discharges the company from competing third-party claims, rendering repeated insistence on indemnity bonds and affidavits vexatious and oppressive. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: DLF's refusal to register the transfer and transmission after receipt of the District Court's decree was arbitrary, without sufficient cause, and justified both specific compliance directions and punitive costs.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the NCLT Chandigarh order dated 11.12.2018 is upheld; Respondent No. 1 directed to pay share consideration within 15 days; Appellants directed to transfer/arrange transfer of 60,000 shares within 30 days of payment; Respondent No. 1 to transfer Respondent No. 2's share within 30 days thereafter; and costs of Rs. 5,00,000/- imposed on Appellants payable to the National Defence Fund within 15 days.
summary: DLF Ltd. and its promoter entity appealed an NCLT Chandigarh order directing them to transfer 60,000 rights issue shares and transmit 6,000 split shares to the legal heirs of late Devki Nandan Kaura under Section 58 of the Companies Act, 2013. The appellants argued limitation and contended rights entitlements were non-heritable. The NCLAT rejected these pleas, finding that DLF had itself directed the legal heirs in 2007 to obtain a court order and could not resile from that position under the doctrine against approbation and reprobation once the Letter of Administration was secured in 2012. Characterizing the listed company's continued resistance as shareholder harassment, NCLAT dismissed the appeal with Rs. 5,00,000/- costs.

case_title: Sri Munisuvrata Agri International Ltd vs Bank Of Baroda & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sri Munisuvrata Agri International Ltd., formerly LMJ International Ltd. (Corporate Applicant/Appellant); Bank of Baroda (Lead Consortium Bank, Respondent No. 1); Sleepwell Industries Co. Ltd., Swiss Singapore Overseas Enterprises Pte. Ltd., and family shareholders (Objectors/Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Working Capital Consortium Agreement dated 15.02.2018 involving 10 consortium banks and multiple international commodities trading and charter contracts. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Applicant declared financial debt default of Rs. 536,92,00,000/- against total debt raised of Rs. 544,00,00,000/-, and admitted disputed operational liabilities exceeding Rs. 256 Crores (including Rs. 167 Crores in income tax demands). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Arbitral awards rendered in favor of foreign creditors in 2013; Supreme Court directed encashment of bank guarantees on 20.04.2018; company changed name on 23.04.2018; registered office relocated on 26.04.2018; Section 10 petition filed immediately on 27.04.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Applicant suppressed its former name 'LMJ International Ltd.' in Form-6 and petition affidavits violating Section 12(3) of Companies Act, 2013; unproduced EGM approval dated 10.04.2018 was challenged as manufactured; forensic financial disclosures indicated fraudulent asset-stripping, family arbitral execution evasions, and siphoning of capital. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the Section 10 petition on 15.11.2018 on grounds of lack of valid shareholder authorization and fraudulent filing intended to evade decree enforcement.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 10 of the IBC filed by a corporate applicant can be maintained where the petition is initiated fraudulently and with malicious intent to defeat arbitral awards, evade Supreme Court orders, and suppress historical identity in violation of statutory provisions.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for voluntary insolvency resolution under Section 10 of the IBC is not maintainable if instituted fraudulently with malicious intent to thwart execution of decrees and evade legitimate creditor recoveries rather than for bona fide resolution or liquidation of the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10 must be read alongside Section 65 of the IBC; the procedural mechanism cannot be abused as an engine of fraud to secure a moratorium shield against judicial enforcement decrees, and non-compliance with statutory disclosure mandates (such as prior corporate names under Section 12(3) of the Companies Act) vitiates bona fides. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Clear circumstantial and documentary evidence showing rapid name change, surreptitious address transfer, concealment of previous corporate identity, and filing within 24 hours of adverse Supreme Court orders proves fraudulent and malicious initiation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 10 petition was filed in abuse of process and was rightly dismissed by NCLT Kolkata, without barring independent creditor proceedings under Section 7.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs; the NCLT Kolkata order dated 15.11.2018 is upheld; and Adjudicating Authority is clarified to be free to adjudicate Bank of Baroda's Section 7 petition independently on its own merits.
summary: Corporate Applicant Sri Munisuvrata Agri International Ltd. (formerly LMJ International Ltd.) appealed the dismissal of its Section 10 IBC application by NCLT Kolkata. Creditors and dissenting shareholders established that the applicant had suffered massive arbitral awards and Supreme Court adverse enforcement orders, whereupon it changed its corporate name and registered office within days to file for insolvency and avoid decree execution, while suppressing its former identity. The NCLAT held that the petition was filed fraudulently and with malicious intent to defraud creditors rather than for genuine corporate resolution. The dismissal was upheld, permitting consortium banks to pursue their Section 7 petitions.

case_title: Mr. Mukesh Mehta & Ors. vs Silver Land Developers Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mukesh Mehta and family ('Mehta Group', holding 50.2% shares) are Appellants/Petitioners; Silver Land Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Entity, Respondent No. 1); Shah Group (holding 49.8%, Respondents No. 2 to 4); and J.M. Financial Services (Secured Creditor/Mortgagee, Respondent No. 5). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development project known as 'Silver Point' undertaken by Respondent No. 1 Company financed by credit facilities from secured lender J.M. Financial Services secured via mortgage. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent No. 1 committed default in repayment to secured creditor J.M. Financial Services, resulting in loan recall, NPA classification, and proposed sale of mortgaged commercial units. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company incorporated on 16.08.1989; internal management disputes erupted in 2019; interim application MA No. 3779/2019 filed in CP No. 488/2019; impugned interim order passed on 28.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Allegations that Shah Group forcibly ousted Mehta Group and colluded with J.M. Financial Services to alienate mortgaged units in 'Silver Point' at undervalue without company consent under Section 59 of Transfer of Property Act; lender agreed before NCLT to maintain status quo for 14 days to allow appellants to produce higher-paying buyers. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP under Sections 241, 242, and 245 before NCLT Mumbai seeking restraint against asset sales; NCLT granted a 14-day status quo for appellants to procure better buyers while preserving lender rights and conditioning any collusive sale on final adjudication; Appellants appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT properly exercised its equitable discretionary jurisdiction under Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 in passing an interim status quo order allowing the secured creditor to exercise recovery rights after 14 days if the petitioner failed to introduce better prospective purchasers.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Adjudicating Authority possesses wide equitable discretion to regulate the affairs of a company through interim orders, and an interim order balancing the statutory recovery rights of a secured lender against minority oppression claims by granting opportunity to bring a higher buyer is just and equitable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(4) permits interim orders that are just and equitable without deciding complex substantive title or mortgage enforcement questions at an interlocutory stage; Section 421(2) restricts interference where the interlocutory arrangement was passed essentially on concession/fair agreement of parties. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Prima facie assessment of balance of convenience and urgency where an account is NPA and the secured lender agrees to defer realization to test the market value asserted by the complainant shareholder. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The interim order protected the company and its shareholders while safeguarding secured lender rights, with any collusive transaction expressly made subject to final review; hence no appellate interference was warranted.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, sustaining the interim order dated 28.11.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in MA No. 3779 of 2019.
summary: Appellants ('Mehta Group', 50.2% shareholders) challenged an interim order of NCLT Mumbai in their oppression petition regarding Silver Land Developers Pvt. Ltd. Appellants alleged that the respondent directors colluded with secured lender J.M. Financial Services to sell mortgaged units at undervalue. Before the NCLT, the lender agreed to wait 14 days to allow appellants to bring a buyer offering a higher price, leading to an interim status-quo order. Appellants appealed, claiming the lender lacked authority to sell. The NCLAT held that under Section 242(4), the NCLT has broad powers to pass just and equitable interim orders, and that substantive mortgage questions must await final trial. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Ashok Kumar Sachdeva vs Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ashok Kumar Sachdeva, Director of Corporate Debtor (Appellant); Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd., Assignee Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Himanshu Jetley, Interim Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2); Sachdeva And Sons Rice Mills Ltd., Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities originally sanctioned by erstwhile Bank of Punjab (later Centurion Bank of Punjab) to Corporate Debtor on 24.09.2002, subsequently assigned to Kotak Mahindra Bank on 27.09.2007. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account defaulted and declared NPA on 31.12.2004; Section 7 petition filed demanding outstanding dues of Rs. 1,28,65,40,328.38. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NPA declared on 31.12.2004; SARFAESI notice issued on 17.02.2005; original DRT application filed in September 2006; possession notice issued on 17.09.2012; sale notice issued on 20.06.2014; balance sheet signed on 03.09.2015; Section 7 application filed on 21.09.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Financial Creditor relied on continuous recovery litigations pending before DRT Chandigarh/Mumbai and balance sheet for FY ending 31.03.2015 signed on 03.09.2015 as Section 18 debt acknowledgment; however, no subsequent balance sheets were produced. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed on 21.09.2018 was admitted by NCLT Chandigarh on 29.07.2019 holding that ongoing recovery proceedings and balance sheets kept limitation alive; Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed more than 13 years after the loan account was declared NPA is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and whether pending DRT proceedings or a balance sheet signed more than three years prior to filing can revive the limitation period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 7 of the IBC is governed strictly by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, giving a three-year period running from the date of default/NPA declaration; pursuing recovery proceedings before a DRT does not extend the limitation period for filing an insolvency application, and any acknowledgment under Section 18 must itself fall within the subsisting limitation period and cannot rescue an application filed more than three years after the acknowledgment date. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Article 62 applies only to mortgage suits and not to applications under Section 7; Article 137 is the sole applicable provision; the intent of the IBC is not to give a fresh lease of life to time-barred debts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Even assuming a signed balance sheet serves as an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18, the creditor must prove the Section 7 petition was filed within three years from the date of such balance sheet signature. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the default occurred on 31.12.2004, and even the last relied balance sheet signed on 03.09.2015 fell outside the three-year window preceding the filing on 21.09.2018, the petition was hopelessly time-barred and liable to dismissal.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned admission order dated 29.07.2019 passed by NCLT Chandigarh is quashed and set aside; the Section 7 application is dismissed; Corporate Debtor is released from moratorium and CIRP; RP directed to restore management and records to the Board of Directors; and Adjudicating Authority to determine CIRP costs and fees payable by Kotak Mahindra Bank.
summary: The Director of Corporate Debtor Sachdeva And Sons Rice Mills Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh order admitting Kotak Mahindra Bank's Section 7 IBC application. The Corporate Debtor had defaulted and was classified as an NPA on 31.12.2004, whereas the Section 7 petition was filed on 21.09.2018 claiming over Rs. 128 Crores. The Bank argued limitation was extended by ongoing DRT proceedings and a balance sheet signed on 03.09.2015. Applying Supreme Court precedents in B.K. Educational Services, Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave, and Jignesh Shah, the NCLAT held that Article 137 applies from default, DRT actions do not extend limitation, and the petition was filed more than three years even after the 2015 balance sheet. The admission was reversed.

case_title: Amit Kumar Gupta vs Lgw Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Amit Kumar Gupta, promoter-director holding 17.58% (Appellant); LGW Ltd., family company (Respondent No. 1); Sanjay Kumar Gupta and branch holding 82.42% (Respondents No. 2 to 4); and Jinesh Shah (Respondent No. 5). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Governance and control of closely held family company LGW Ltd. (formerly Laxmi Glass Works P. Ltd.) under corporate statutes. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate governance deadlocks and severe factional disputes among promoter brothers culminating in moves to unseat the minority promoter from directorship. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company incorporated on 31.08.1984; special removal notice under Sections 115 and 169 issued on 06.02.2017 for EOGM on 15.03.2017; NCLT passed ex parte interim order on 14.03.2017 restraining implementation of EOGM resolutions; EOGM held on 16.03.2017 voting for removal; interim order extended for 2 years; Respondents filed IA No. 1229/KB/2019; NCLT passed impugned order on 04.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Initial removal notice lacked an explanatory statement; ex parte interim protection led to deadlock lasting over two years, paralyzing company projects; Respondents issued fresh compliant notices and consented to have an independent court officer chair the fresh meeting. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench allowed IA No. 1229/KB/2019 on 04.10.2019, directing a fresh EOGM under the chairmanship of an independent Special Officer (Mr. S.M. Gupta) to decide on director removal; Appellant appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT had the jurisdiction under Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 to modify its earlier ex parte interim restraint and order a fresh EOGM under the supervision of an independent Special Officer to consider the removal of a director under Section 169.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority possesses full legal authority under Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 to modify its earlier ex parte interim orders in response to changed circumstances, and directing an EOGM to be conducted under the chairmanship of an independent court-appointed Special Officer is a just and equitable measure to resolve corporate deadlock. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(4) vests the Tribunal with wide powers to make any interim order it thinks fit for regulating the conduct of company affairs; Section 169 statutory rights of the majority shareholders to remove a director cannot be permanently paralyzed by an interim order. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where both factions agree to hold an EOGM under an independent Special Officer, objections by a minority director that the company is a quasi-partnership exempt from Section 169 are untenable at an interlocutory stage. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's direction appointing a Special Officer to oversee a fresh EOGM with proper statutory notices was fully justified and free from procedural infirmity.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT Kolkata order dated 04.10.2019 directing the convening of a fresh EOGM under the chairmanship of Special Officer Mr. S.M. Gupta.
summary: Appellant Amit Kumar Gupta (17.58% shareholder) appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order in IA No. 1229/KB/2019 directing the convening of a fresh EOGM under an independent Special Officer to consider his removal from directorship of LGW Ltd. under Section 169 of the Companies Act, 2013. The appellant argued that this contradicted a prior ex parte order dated 14.03.2017 and undermined a quasi-partnership family company. The NCLAT held that Section 242(4) empowers the Tribunal to modify interim orders to regulate corporate affairs and eliminate business paralysis. Since proper statutory notice was now provided and the meeting was to be supervised by an independent chair, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Universal Heat Exchangers Ltd vs K. Ramakrishnan
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Universal Heat Exchangers Ltd. and promoter directors/allottees (Appellants); K. Ramakrishnan, S. Visvanathan, and V.R. Narayanamurti, overseas non-resident minority shareholders (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate capitalization and share allotment in a closely held public limited company; Respondents had originally invested Rs. 1,40,00,000/- acquiring 4,00,000 equity shares (representing a 27% equity stake). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Severe oppression and dilution whereby two impugned share allotments—20,00,000 shares on 09.04.2007 at Rs. 10/- and 5,55,555 shares on 27.09.2010 at Rs. 18/-—reduced Respondents' holding from 27% down to 9.86%, while increasing the promoters' family stake to 90.14%. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First allotment executed on 09.04.2007; second allotment executed on 27.09.2010; CP No. 42/2012 filed before CLB Chennai on 17.04.2012; transferred as TCP No. 96/2016 before NCLT Chennai. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Complete lack of postal or delivery proof showing service of EGM notices or rights issue offers upon the non-resident Respondents; financial evidence demonstrating siphoning of corporate funds via unsecured loans of Rs. 8.96 Crores from directors while routing Rs. 4 Crores to interested parties under Section 301, accompanied by an arbitrary 30% reduction in equipment selling prices. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench held on 10.07.2018 that the share allotments were oppressive and invalid, set them aside, ordered refund of monies to allottees, and directed rectification of the Register of Members, which Appellants appealed.
legal_issues: Whether preferential share allotments that drastically dilute a minority shareholder group from 27% to below 10% without offering pre-emptive rights or establishing proof of service of EGM notices constitute actionable oppression under Section 397/398, and whether the petition was barred by limitation or laches.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Disproportionate allotment of shares undertaken without offering proportionate participation to existing minority shareholders in violation of Section 81 of the Companies Act, 1956, and without serving requisite notices, constitutes an act of oppression and mismanagement that cannot be shielded by claims of limitation or company business exigencies. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 81 mandates proportional pre-emptive rights to existing equity holders; non-compliance invalidates the allotment, and minority shareholders cannot be forced into an exit without safeguarding their statutory rights. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The burden of proving lawful service of EGM and rights offer notices rests entirely on the company; mere assertion of dispatch without documentary delivery receipt fails to establish compliance. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The share allotments of 2007 and 2010 were illegal and oppressive as they stripped minority voting protection without notice, justifying cancellation of the allotments and rectification of the member register.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs; the NCLT Chennai order dated 10.07.2018 is upheld; Appellants directed to comply with the directions to set aside the allotments, refund subscription sums, and rectify the register, with liberty to obtain independent valuation for a minority buyout.
summary: Appellants challenged the order of NCLT Chennai setting aside two share allotments made in 2007 and 2010 by Universal Heat Exchangers Ltd. that diluted the overseas minority respondents' shareholding from 27% down to 9.86%, while increasing the promoter family's control to 90.14%. The respondents also demonstrated siphoning through unsecured related-party transactions. The Appellants claimed limitation and business justification. The NCLAT held that the company failed to produce proof of service of notice for the meetings and violated pre-emptive rights under Section 81 of the Companies Act, 1956. Affirming that such dilution constitutes gross oppression, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Spade Financial Services Limited & Anr. vs. Hari Krishan Sharma & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Spade Financial Services Ltd. (Appellant No. 1) and its wholly owned subsidiary AAA Landmark Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant No. 2) acted as purported Financial Creditors; AKME Projects Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor promoted by Anil Nanda; Yes Bank Ltd. and Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. are contesting Financial Creditors in the CoC; Hari Krishan Sharma is the original Operational Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purported inter-corporate deposits (ICDs) totaling Rs. 66 Crores granted between June 2009 and January 2013 under an MoU dated 12.08.2011 bearing 24% interest, alongside a Development Agreement dated 01.03.2012 and subsequent Agreement to Sell dated 25.10.2012 for joint development of project AKME Raaga. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed under ICDs and agreements aggregating Rs. 109.11 Crores by Spade and Rs. 52.96 Crores by AAA, with alleged default arising prior to CIRP initiation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor on 18.04.2018 under Section 9; first CoC meeting convened on 01.06.2018 where exclusion applications were initiated. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Out of ICDs granted by Spade, Rs. 43.06 Crores was directly credited to the personal account of Arun Anand; Arun Anand served as Group CEO and strategic advisor of Anil Nanda Group while his brother-in-law Sonal Anand was a Whole-Time Director in holding company JIPL; JIPL held shares in Spade until 2017; and side letters revealed the 2012 Agreement to Sell was a camouflage for partnership profit sharing. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IRP initially rejected the claims of Spade (lack of time value of money) and AAA (belated filing), but NCLT New Delhi Bench-III accepted their financial creditor status; subsequently, on applications CA-268/2018 and CA-337/2018 filed by Yes Bank and Phoenix ARC, NCLT excluded Spade and AAA from the CoC on 19.07.2019 as related parties.
legal_issues: Whether Spade Financial Services Ltd. and AAA Landmark Pvt. Ltd. are related parties to the Corporate Debtor under Section 5(24) and disqualified from representation, participation, and voting in the Committee of Creditors under the first proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Entities whose key managerial personnel operate in concert with the corporate debtor's promoter through an entangled web of collusive transactions, consulting roles, and family affinities during debt creation constitute related parties and cannot gain backdoor entry into the CoC even if formal directorships were severed prior to CIRP initiation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(24)(h), (f), and (m)(i) must be interpreted purposively to include advisory influence, board control, and policy-making participation during the debt origin period, preventing circumventive resignation before CIRP from washing away related-party disability under the first proviso to Section 21(2). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of pervasive managerial nexus, inter-corporate fund diversions to personal accounts, camouflaged joint development agreements, and common director-shareholder patterns across affiliate entities. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Arun Anand and Anil Nanda orchestrated collusive transactions across sister entities while exercising de facto operational and managerial dominance, Appellants are related parties and legally barred from the CoC.
operative_order: The appeal is rejected, confirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 19.07.2019 excluding Spade Financial Services Ltd. and AAA Landmark Pvt. Ltd. from participation and voting in the Committee of Creditors of AKME Projects Ltd., with no order as to costs.
summary: Spade Financial Services Ltd. and AAA Landmark Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT order excluding them from the Committee of Creditors of AKME Projects Ltd. as related parties under Section 5(24) and Section 21(2) of the IBC. Existing financial creditors Yes Bank and Phoenix ARC objected to their CoC inclusion on grounds that promoter Arun Anand was deeply intertwined with Corporate Debtor promoter Anil Nanda through past managerial posts, family connections, and sham ICDs. NCLAT held that the web of collusive transactions and managerial participation rendered both entities related parties attempting backdoor control, affirming their exclusion from the CoC and dismissing the appeal.

case_title: M/s. Medeor Hospitals Limited vs. Registrar of Companies, Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Medeor Hospitals Ltd. (formerly Rockland Hospitals Ltd.), an unlisted public limited company wholly owned by VPS Healthcare Pvt. Ltd., as Appellant; Registrar of Companies, Delhi as Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate restructuring seeking conversion from a public limited company to a private limited company under Section 14(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to eliminate unnecessary compliance burdens since no public funding was sought. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: No financial default; 35 creditors comprising 87% of total debt gave no-objection certificates, while objectors held barely 0.05% of direct debt and 1.39% contingent debt. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board meeting and EOGM approving conversion convened on shorter notice on 14.08.2017; intimation to ROC on 25.08.2017; initial petition CP No. 71/14/ND/2017 filed on 30.10.2017 and withdrawn on 06.12.2017; second petition CP No. 80/14/ND/2018 filed on 19.12.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Written consent of 100% of shareholders for shorter EOGM notice under Section 101, Board Resolution of parent holding company dated 17.06.2017, ICAI order exonerating new statutory auditor M/s Dayanand Yadav & Co., and subsequent No Dues Certificates from objectors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench rejected the conversion petition on 28.08.2018 citing premature filing under Rule 68(1), suspicion over immediate balance sheet sign-off by new auditors, resignation of two independent directors, and pending arbitrations.
legal_issues: Whether the conversion petition was barred by limitation under Rule 68(1) of NCLT Rules, 2016, and whether auditor appointment formalities, independent director resignations, and pending arbitrations legally precluded conversion of a wholly owned public company to a private limited company.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A petition for conversion to a private company filed after the expiration of three months from the special resolution date complies with Rule 68(1), and conversion cannot be denied on hyper-technical governance objections where 100% shareholder consent exists and creditor interests remain unimpaired. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'not less than three months' in Rule 68(1) mandates filing post three months from the special resolution; Section 101 proviso allows general meetings on shorter notice if consented to by not less than 95% of voting members. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unanimous shareholder consent on record, absence of prejudice to third-party arbitral proceedings which survive conversion by operation of law, and formal exoneration of statutory auditors by regulatory authorities. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The shortcomings identified by NCLT were minor, inconsequential, and fully explained; conversion does not extinguish pre-existing liabilities or prejudice pending arbitrations.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 28.08.2018 passed by NCLT New Delhi is set aside, and the special resolution dated 14.08.2017 converting Medeor Hospitals Ltd. from a public limited company to a private limited company is formally approved, with no order as to costs.
summary: Medeor Hospitals Ltd. appealed against NCLT New Delhi's rejection of its petition for conversion from a public limited company to a private limited company under Section 14 of the Companies Act, 2013. NCLT had rejected the conversion citing alleged delay under Rule 68(1), shorter notice for the EGM, swift auditor balance-sheet sign-offs, and pending arbitrations. NCLAT held that the second petition filed post three months satisfied Rule 68(1), 100% of shareholders consented in writing to shorter notice, and arbitral disputes or director resignations in a wholly owned subsidiary do not impede conversion. The appeal was allowed, approving the conversion.

case_title: Bridge E-Solutions Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Bridge Solutions Group Inc.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bridge E-Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (Company), Rajendra Kumar Gupta, Varun Gupta, and Dipayan Chandra Sarkar as Appellants/Directors; Bridge Solutions Group Inc. (US entity holding 51% majority equity) as Respondent/Petitioner. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Majority equity investment and managerial arrangement wherein Respondent held 25,500 shares (51%) for funding support while Indian resident Appellants managed regulatory compliance and operational affairs. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unilateral increase of authorized share capital from Rs. 5 Lakhs to Rs. 40 Lakhs without bona fide commercial necessity, resulting in dilution of Respondent's shareholding from 51% to 47%, accompanied by unauthorized salary disbursement of Rs. 3,22,220 to Rajendra Gupta's wife. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Disputed EGM convened on 27.09.2013 passing the capital increase resolution without valid prior 21-day notice; company petition initially filed before CLB New Delhi in 2015 and transferred to NCLT Allahabad. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Courier receipt produced by Appellants was illegible without delivery acknowledgement; foreign inward remittance of 30,000 USD occurred on 02.04.2013 towards invoices months before the alleged EGM; and internal ledger entries for director share subscriptions lacked matching bank credits. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench held on 20.09.2018 that the capital expansion and dilution constituted oppression and financial mismanagement, declared the 27.09.2013 resolution void, and ordered independent forensic audit and valuation.
legal_issues: Whether the unilateral increase of authorized share capital diluting the majority shareholder to a minority without proof of commercial necessity, proper notice, or actual capital infusion constitutes oppression and mismanagement under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An increase in share capital and allotment of shares carried out without established corporate need, without proper statutory notice to majority shareholders, and without verified fund infusion constitutes an oppressive device designed to reduce majority shareholders to a minority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 397 and 398 encompass conduct that breaches fiduciary standards, manipulates corporate democracy, and orchestrates share dilutions via fabricated or unnotified meetings to the prejudice of fellow shareholders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Self-serving ledger entries uncorroborated by banking deposits cannot prove share subscription; courier receipts lacking verifiable delivery tracking fail the burden of demonstrating statutory notice under company law. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The purported capital increase was an illegal maneuver aimed at diluting the Respondent, coupled with fund siphoning via clandestine family payroll, justifying nullification and forensic audit.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Allahabad order dated 20.09.2018 declaring the EGM resolution of 27.09.2013 void, cancelling Form-II with the ROC, and upholding the appointment of an independent auditor and valuer, with no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants appealed an NCLT Allahabad judgment declaring an increase in authorized share capital from Rs. 5 Lakhs to Rs. 40 Lakhs void and finding acts of oppression and mismanagement under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956. The majority US shareholder's equity had been diluted from 51% to 47% via an EGM resolution purportedly passed without valid notice or capital infusion, while unauthorized salary was paid to the director's wife. NCLAT affirmed that the capital increase lacked genuine business need, failed statutory notice requirements, and lacked bank-verified fund infusion, dismissing the appeal and upholding the direction for an independent forensic audit.

case_title: Morgan Securities & Credits Pvt. Ltd. vs. Resolution Professional of Videocon Industries Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Morgan Securities & Credits Pvt. Ltd. as Appellant/Financial Creditor; Videocon Industries Ltd. through its Resolution Professional as Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan transaction culminating in an Arbitral Award dated 29.04.2013 for Rs. 76.45 Crores in favor of Morgan against the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose upon non-satisfaction of the arbitral award, leading Morgan to file a claim of Rs. 325 Crores in CIRP, of which the RP admitted Rs. 76.45 Crores giving Morgan a 0.13% CoC voting share. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Delhi High Court under Section 9 ordered deposit of Rs. 20 Crores bank guarantee on 13.11.2013; Allahabad Bank furnished guarantee on 06.12.2013; CIRP initiated on 06.06.2018; Section 34 challenge dismissed and Division Bench affirmed retention on 07.02.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Allahabad Bank executed the guarantee at the instance, expense, and security of the Corporate Debtor, renewed periodically until December 2018; guarantee proceeds of Rs. 20 Crores were encashed and deposited with the High Court Registrar General. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai on 11.11.2019 directed the Registrar General to release the Rs. 20 Crores to the RP as an asset of the Corporate Debtor, but observed it constituted a 'security interest' in Morgan's favor, prompting cross-appeals.
legal_issues: Whether an encashed bank guarantee of Rs. 20 Crores lying with the High Court Registrar General constitutes an asset of the Corporate Debtor subject to CIRP moratorium under Section 14, and whether it creates a prioritized 'security interest' in favor of the award-holder during CIRP and liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Funds deposited by way of a bank guarantee procured by a debtor company to secure an arbitral challenge remain the debtor's asset upon insolvency, and an unsecured arbitral creditor cannot claim an exclusive security interest or priority charge over such funds once its full claim is admitted into the CIRP pool. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 moratorium prohibits the enforcement of any lien or priority arrangement against debtor assets, and interim judicial security deposits do not mutate into statutory 'security interests' under the IBC to bypass the collective resolution or liquidation waterfall under Section 53. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Establishing the provenance of the bank guarantee as issued on debtor credit and counter-security, coupled with claimant's unconditional participation in the CoC based on the underlying arbitral debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Rs. 20 Crores forms part of the Corporate Debtor's general resolution asset pool, and NCLT's categorization of the sum as a security interest in favor of Morgan was erroneous.
operative_order: Company Appeals No. 1366, 1367, and 1368 of 2019 filed by Morgan Securities are dismissed; Company Appeal No. 20 of 2020 filed by the Resolution Professional is allowed, setting aside the observation that the Rs. 20 Crores is a security interest in Morgan's favor and directing the amount to be added to the debtor's general assets.
summary: Morgan Securities challenged an NCLT Mumbai order directing that Rs. 20 Crores encashed from a bank guarantee and deposited with the Delhi High Court during Section 34 arbitration proceedings be remitted to Videocon's Resolution Professional. The RP cross-appealed against NCLT's finding that the amount constituted a security interest in Morgan's favor.
