NCLAT held that because the bank guarantee was procured on the debtor's account and Morgan had submitted its claim for the entire arbitral award in the CIRP, the funds represented corporate assets subject to CIRP administration. NCLAT dismissed Morgan's appeals, allowed the RP's appeal, and set aside the security interest characterization.

case_title: M/s. Hyderabad Pollution Controls Limited & Ors. vs. S. Radhakrishnan & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Hyderabad Pollution Controls Ltd., S.G. Nair (MD), and family members as Appellants; S. Radhakrishnan (brother of S.G. Nair) and family as Respondents/Original Petitioners. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Transfer and division of 30% equity shareholding held by outgoing founding shareholder N.A. Nayar between two brother-factions to ensure a 50:50 equal balance in the corporate enterprise. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Disputed breach of the tripartite Share Transfer Agreement dated 08.04.2010, failure of Appellants to pay agreed consideration of Rs. 2.5 Crores, and illegal removal of Respondent as Director. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Share transfers executed on 27.02.2007; subsequent settlement agreement executed on 08.04.2010; CLB interim injunction granted on 18.05.2011; company petition CP No. 40/2011 transferred to NCLT Hyderabad as TP No. 50/HDB/2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Violation of CLB status quo orders dated 18.05.2011 via unapproved share transfers and removal of Respondent as Director without statutory process; S.G. Nair exceeding 70 years of age without special resolution under Section 196(3)(a); and Ministry of Corporate Affairs inspection reports revealing fabrication of corporate records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad on 26.10.2017 found S.G. Nair guilty of oppression and mismanagement, upheld the validity of the 08.04.2010 agreement, set aside post-2011 transfers, and directed equal 50:50 shareholding division.
legal_issues: Whether the Share Transfer Agreement dated 08.04.2010 was valid and enforceable in summary company proceedings, and whether unilateral transfers and removal of a director in violation of CLB interim status-quo orders constituted actionable oppression and mismanagement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Corporate actions executed in deliberate defiance of binding judicial status-quo orders, including clandestine share manipulation and unlawful directorship ousters, constitute severe oppression and mismanagement warranting equitable division of corporate control. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 397 and 398 empower company tribunals to dismantle contrived transfers, enforce binding family compromise agreements, and restore parity where actions of dominant directors breach corporate democracy. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Failure to demonstrate payment of consideration, uncorroborated allegations of coercion against registered settlements, and documented violations of judicial stay orders establish bad faith and oppression. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Share Transfer Agreement dated 08.04.2010 was legally binding, and all subsequent share transfers and managerial alterations performed in violation of CLB interim directions were null, void, and properly reversed.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding NCLT Hyderabad's order dated 26.10.2017 confirming the 50:50 share division under the agreement of 08.04.2010 and nullifying subsequent unilateral corporate acts, with no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants challenged an NCLT Hyderabad judgment directing an equal 50:50 shareholding division between two brother-directors in Hyderabad Pollution Controls Ltd. pursuant to a Share Transfer Agreement dated 08.04.2010. Appellant S.G. Nair had alleged coercion and filed civil suits, simultaneously removing the Respondent as director and transferring shares in direct breach of CLB interim status-quo orders dated 18.05.2011. NCLAT found that the 2010 agreement was fully binding and that Appellants committed continuous oppression and mismanagement by defying judicial status quo orders and fabricating records. NCLAT affirmed NCLT's judgment and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Mr. R. Balarami Reddy vs. Mr. Sutanu Sinha, Resolution Professional of IVRCL Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. R. Balarami Reddy (former Executive Director Finance, Joint MD, and related party) as Appellant; Mr. Sutanu Sinha, Resolution Professional of IVRCL Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in liquidation), as Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Managerial employment contract providing increased remuneration and promotion to Joint Managing Director in an NPA company subject to lender approvals and Companies Act ceilings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim of Rs. 1,06,28,584 submitted in Form D for alleged unpaid managerial salary and refund of excess remuneration recovered by the debtor (Rs. 33,84,835 in November 2017 and Rs. 21,69,702 from subsequent period). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board and AGM approvals in September 2016; CIRP commenced under Section 7 in CP (IB) No. 294/7/HDB/2017; CoC meetings rejecting excess pay held on 26.04.2018 and 07.08.2018; RP rejection email sent on 21.05.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's books showed excess remuneration as an advance/receivable due to absence of Central Government approval; lender bank approvals required under Schedule V were expressly refused by the CoC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 673/2018 under Section 60(5) of the IBC before NCLT Hyderabad, which allowed remuneration for CIRP services but rejected pre-CIRP claims exceeding statutory limits; Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a managerial person can claim arrears of remuneration or refund of excess salary paid in anticipation of Central Government approval under Section 197 of the Companies Act, 2013 as an admissible debt in CIRP when lenders and CoC refuse consent.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A claim for managerial remuneration exceeding limits prescribed under Section 197 of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be admitted by a Resolution Professional in CIRP absent mandatory approvals from corporate lenders and the Central Government. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 197(1) of the Companies Act mandates that managerial pay beyond prescribed ceilings requires lender NOC and Central Government approval; amounts paid without sanction are held in trust and must be refunded to the corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To sustain a claim in Form D, the creditor must present an enforceable debt legally payable on the insolvency date supported by requisite statutory sanctions, rather than conditional expectations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because neither the consortium lenders nor the CoC granted approval for excess managerial remuneration, the RP rightly rejected the pre-CIRP claim and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, affirming NCLT Hyderabad Bench's order dated 07.03.2019 rejecting the Appellant's pre-CIRP claim for excess managerial remuneration, with no order as to costs.
summary: The former Joint Managing Director of IVRCL Ltd. appealed an NCLT Hyderabad order rejecting his Section 60(5) application for admitting a pre-CIRP salary claim of Rs. 1,06,28,584. The RP had rejected the claim because the remuneration exceeded the statutory caps under Section 197 of the Companies Act, 2013 and lacked mandatory approvals from lenders and the Central Government, leading the company to recover earlier excess disbursements. NCLAT held that in the absence of lender and Central Government approvals, excess managerial compensation is unrecoverable and cannot be admitted as an operational debt in CIRP, affirming the dismissal.

case_title: State Tax Officer vs. Mr. Chandra Prakash Jain, Resolution Professional of M/s. Mekaster Engineering Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Tax Officer, Office of Assistant Commissioner of State Tax, Unit-46, Gujarat as Appellant; Chandra Prakash Jain, Resolution Professional, and M/s. Mekaster Engineering Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in liquidation) as Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory sales tax and Value Added Tax (VAT) assessments creating statutory tax, interest, and penalty liabilities against the Corporate Debtor under the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total statutory VAT tax assessment dues with interest and penalties lodged as a claim before the Resolution Professional during CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP (IB) 46 of 2017 initiated CIRP against Mekaster Engineering Ltd.; Appellant filed Inv. P 19 of 2019 before NCLT; impugned order passed on 13.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant relied upon the statutory charge created under Section 48 of the Gujarat VAT Act, 2003 asserting a first charge over corporate debtor properties, and provided claim bifurcation of penalty and interest at page 15 of its application. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 13.09.2019 directed the RP to consider the bifurcated claim but rejected the State's prayer to be categorized as a 'Secured Creditor', treating it strictly as an Operational Creditor; Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether statutory first charge provisions under Section 48 of the Gujarat VAT Act, 2003 elevate the State Tax Department to the status of a 'Secured Creditor' under Section 3(30) and Section 3(31) of the IBC, or whether IBC Section 53 read with Section 238 overrides state tax liens.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory first charges created under State taxation enactments yield to the distribution priority specified under Section 53 of the IBC, and tax authorities cannot claim status as secured creditors over debtor assets. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC has overriding effect over Section 48 of the Gujarat VAT Act; consequently, government tax dues fall within operational debts rather than secured debts under Section 3(30) read with Section 3(31). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Direct application of the larger bench ruling in Tourism Finance Corporation of India Ltd. v. Rainbow Papers Ltd. subordinating statutory first charges to the IBC waterfall scheme. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The State Tax Officer is an Operational Creditor and cannot assert secured status or first charge priority in corporate insolvency proceedings.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench order dated 13.09.2019 declining secured creditor status to the State Tax Department, with no order as to costs.
summary: The State Tax Officer, Gujarat appealed an order of NCLT Ahmedabad holding that the Tax Department could not be treated as a Secured Creditor in the insolvency proceedings of Mekaster Engineering Ltd. The Appellant contended that Section 48 of the Gujarat VAT Act, 2003 created a statutory first charge making it a secured creditor. Relying on its larger bench precedent in Tourism Finance Corporation of India v. Rainbow Papers Ltd., NCLAT held that Section 238 of the IBC overrides state statutes and Section 48 cannot prevail over the Section 53 waterfall mechanism, maintaining that tax departments remain operational creditors and dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Hind Dyes Manufacturing Company Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Kanji Bhanji Shah & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Hind Dyes Manufacturing Company Pvt. Ltd., Dipti Umesh Barai, and Rajiv Harendra Chandarana as Appellants; Kanji Bhanji Shah and Vadilal Kunverji Gada as Respondents/Petitioners. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Equity participation and directorships dating back to December 2010, followed by disputed share transfers and alleged unnotified resignations in February 2012. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression allegations centered on the clandestine removal of Respondents as directors, denial of access to statutory records, and attempted asset stripping of the company. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Share transfer application dated 03.06.2011 received on 04.06.2011; complaint to ROC filed on 22.04.2016 and closed on 06.11.2017; company petition CP No. 2440/241-242/MB/2018 filed before NCLT Mumbai; interim order passed on 22.01.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share certificates bearing signatures of two directors produced by Respondents; ongoing continuous denial of statutory inspection despite legal notices dated 11.04.2018 and 30.04.2018; and mutual allegations of forged share scrips. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Division-II granted interim relief on 22.01.2019 ordering production of statutory books for inspection and restraining alienation of company assets pending final hearing; Appellants appealed to vacate the injunction.
legal_issues: Whether an interim injunction restraining alienation of corporate assets and permitting inspection of statutory records under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 is maintainable when title to shares and directorship status are disputed by the management.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Company tribunals possess ample interim jurisdiction under Section 242 to preserve corporate assets and ensure record transparency pending final adjudication of oppression and mismanagement petitions where prima facie shareholding thresholds are satisfied. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 241 read with Section 244 applies to shareholders agitating continuous acts of oppression, and interlocutory protective orders preserving the status quo of assets do not determine final substantive rights. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Physical possession of original share certificates bearing company director signatures satisfies threshold standing for seeking interim protective reliefs. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The interim order restraining asset alienation was purely interlocutory and essential to prevent irreparable harm while the main petition remained pending for final hearing before NCLT.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, affirming NCLT Mumbai Division-II's interlocutory order dated 22.01.2019, leaving all substantive contentions open for final determination by NCLT, with no order as to costs.
summary: Hind Dyes Manufacturing Co. Pvt. Ltd. and its directors appealed an interim order passed by NCLT Mumbai under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013, which directed statutory inspection of records and restrained the company from alienating assets pending final hearing. Appellants claimed Respondents were neither directors nor legitimate shareholders and alleged forged share certificates. NCLAT found that Respondents held physical share certificates satisfying Section 244 eligibility, the interim status-quo order was essential to preserve corporate assets, and no grounds existed to interfere with NCLT's interim directions, dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Sales Tax Department, State of Maharashtra vs. New Phaltan Sugar Works Ltd. & Anr. (with Ambey Iron Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sales Tax Department, State of Maharashtra as Appellant/Operational Creditor; New Phaltan Sugar Works Ltd. and Ambey Iron Pvt. Ltd. through their Resolution Professionals/Successful Resolution Applicants as Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory assessment of Value Added Tax liabilities and sales tax dues payable by the Corporate Debtors under the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act, 2002. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from unpaid statutory tax assessments, where CoC-approved resolution plans drastically scaled down the Department's claims to 1% in Comp. App. 155/2020 and NIL in Comp. App. 156/2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Orders approving resolution plans passed by NCLT Mumbai on 28.11.2019 (MA 3271/2019) and 14.10.2019 (MA 82/2019); appeals filed on 21.01.2020 and 20.01.2020 respectively with delays condoned under Section 61(2). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plans allocated 1% and NIL recovery to the Sales Tax Department, which the Department challenged based on the statutory first charge created over debtor assets under Section 37 of MVAT Act, 2002. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench approved the resolution plans; Appellant challenged the approval orders asserting immunity from plan haircuts and priority over general operational creditors.
legal_issues: Whether statutory tax dues creating a first charge under Section 37 of the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act, 2002 prevail over IBC provisions, and whether the CoC's commercial wisdom in allocating 1% or NIL payment to statutory operational creditors can be judicially disturbed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in allocating plan payouts to operational creditors is non-justiciable, and statutory first charges created by State taxation enactments are subordinated to the IBC framework by virtue of non-obstante supremacy. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Statutory government tax dues represent 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC; Section 37 of the MVAT Act yields to the overriding effect of Section 238 of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Binding authority of the Supreme Court judgment in Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Ltd. v. Satish Kumar Gupta barring adjudicating authorities from altering commercial distribution matrices. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Sales Tax Department is an Operational Creditor whose statutory first charge stands eclipsed under the IBC, rendering the approved Resolution Plans lawful and immune to challenge.
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 155 of 2020 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 156 of 2020 are dismissed, affirming the orders of NCLT Mumbai Bench approving the respective resolution plans, with no order as to costs.
summary: The Sales Tax Department, Maharashtra challenged NCLT Mumbai orders approving resolution plans for New Phaltan Sugar Works Ltd. and Ambey Iron Pvt. Ltd., which reduced its tax claims to 1% and NIL respectively. The Appellant contended that Section 37 of the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act, 2002 conferred a first charge over debtor assets, preventing its claims from being extinguished as ordinary operational debt. Following the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel, NCLAT held that statutory tax claims constitute operational debts under Section 5(21), the IBC overrides state tax priorities via Section 238, and the CoC's commercial wisdom regarding distribution is final and non-justiciable, dismissing both appeals.

case_title: Aalborg CSP A/S vs. Solar Atria Cleantech Private Limited
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 167 of 2019 & Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 168 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Aalborg CSP A/S (Appellant/Operational Creditor), a Danish engineering supplier; Solar Atria Cleantech Private Limited (Respondent/Corporate Debtor), a renewable project developer. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Two Supply Contracts executed on 16.03.2016 for design, manufacture, and delivery of steam generating heat exchanger lines consisting of evaporators, steam drums, superheaters, reheaters, and spares for the 'Karnataka Project' and 'Aurum Project'. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: In the Karnataka Project, Corporate Debtor paid the H1 advance milestone of USD 165,000 but defaulted on milestone H2 (USD 165,000) and milestone H3 (USD 220,000) plus contractual interest; in the Aurum Project, the initial down payment (H1) was never remitted. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised in April 2016 and December 2016; termination notices issued on 01.12.2017 effective 08.12.2017; Section 8 demand notices dispatched on 15.03.2018; Section 9 petitions filed under CP(IB) No. 143/BB/2018 and CP(IB) No. 144/BB/2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor acknowledged debts via WhatsApp messages from its representative Karthik Raju admitting banking disbursement delays, an email dated 21.11.2017 requesting mutual termination and cost determination due to regulatory hurdles, and an email dated 13.12.2017 asserting that the USD 165,000 H1 payment was sufficient to cover expenses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench on 11.01.2019 dismissed both applications under Section 9, holding that contractual milestone disputes and advance payment claims fall outside summary insolvency jurisdiction and do not constitute 'operational debt' under Section 5(21).
legal_issues: Whether a purchaser's plea that milestone-based design and engineering services were covered by initial advance payments constitutes a genuine pre-existing dispute under Section 9(5)(2)(d) of the IBC, and whether non-payment of an initial down payment to activate a contract creates an actionable operational debt under Section 9.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A debtor's evasive attempts to seek contract termination or negotiate fee reductions driven by third-party regulatory or financing setbacks do not constitute a genuine pre-existing dispute when milestone deliverables were demonstrably furnished; however, IBC mechanisms cannot be deployed to enforce executory contracts where no preparatory services or goods were ever supplied due to failure to pay initial triggering advances. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Operational debt under Section 5(21) requires the actual rendition of services or provision of goods; milestone payments for technical designs and purchase order placements satisfy this definition, whereas an unfulfilled contract that never commenced execution due to lack of a notice-to-proceed/down-payment does not qualify. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The standard laid down in Mobilox Innovations v. Kirusa Software requires separating genuine dispute evidence from patently feeble arguments, mere bluster, or evasive restructuring maneuvers. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Karnataka Project petition presented undisputed performance of H2/H3 design milestones and clear default, necessitating admission; the Aurum Project petition failed as no underlying goods or services were rendered.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 167 of 2019 is dismissed, affirming the rejection of CP(IB) No. 143/BB/2018. Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 168 of 2019 is allowed, setting aside the rejection order in CP(IB) No. 144/BB/2018; the Adjudicating Authority is directed to admit the Section 9 petition and initiate CIRP on 17.02.2020 unless settled prior thereto, with interim status quo imposed on Corporate Debtor assets; no costs.
summary: Aalborg CSP A/S challenged NCLT Bengaluru's dismissal of two Section 9 petitions against Solar Atria Cleantech Pvt. Ltd. concerning two contracts for steam generating heat exchanger lines. For the Karnataka Project, Aalborg completed technical design milestones H2 and H3 after receiving the H1 down payment, while Atria defaulted citing financing issues. For the Aurum Project, no down payment was made and work never started. NCLAT held that Atria's defense in the Karnataka Project was feeble bluster masking commercial distress rather than a genuine dispute, ordering admission of CIRP. Conversely, NCLAT upheld dismissal of the Aurum Project appeal because the executory contract never commenced, meaning no operational debt under Section 5(21) had arisen.

case_title: Mr. K.N. Mahesh Prasad vs. M/s. MedinnBelle Herbalcare Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. K.N. Mahesh Prasad, CEO/promoter of M&A advisory firm Genesis Management Consultancy Services Pvt. Ltd., as Appellant/purported Financial Creditor; M/s. MedinnBelle Herbalcare Pvt. Ltd. (brand owner of 'Endura Mass') as Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Advisory agreement dated 06.12.2016 for arranging M&A transactions on success-fee basis, followed by a Memorandum of Understanding dated 16.01.2018 under which the Appellant personally advanced a short-term loan of Rs. 1.70 Crores to enable the Corporate Debtor to acquire an infringing trademark 'NPD Endura Mass' required as a pre-condition for an asset buyout by Piramal Enterprises Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal claim of Rs. 1.70 Crores advanced via RTGS with no agreed interest provision, repayable upon deal consummation with Piramal or within three months. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Cheque No. 004178 presented and dishonored on 12.03.2018 ('signature not as per mandate'); replacement Cheque No. 000725 dishonored on 13.03.2018 ('exceeds arrangement'); Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act notice issued on 28.04.2018; Section 7 IBC petition filed thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MoU dated 16.01.2018 confirming a short-term advance repayable from deal proceeds, dishonored cheques, and counter-allegations that Appellant colluded with trademark rival Sanjay Kumar Chetwani to orchestrate an artificial acquisition transaction. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi dismissed the Section 7 petition on the ground that the advance was a simple loan completely devoid of any element of time value of money, thus failing to constitute 'financial debt'.
legal_issues: Whether a short-term advance extended without interest or financial return to facilitate a collateral trademark acquisition constitutes a 'financial debt' disbursed against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An advance of funds that carries no interest component, is not accepted under a credit or loan facility, and lacks any commercial effect of borrowing disbursed against consideration for the time value of money cannot be categorized as a financial debt under Section 5(8). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: To fall within Section 5(8)(f), an amount raised must have the commercial effect of a borrowing; a pure and simple short-term advance devoid of interest or financial return does not fulfill the foundational statutory criteria of disbursement against consideration for the time value of money. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of transaction documentation to ascertain whether borrowing mechanics, interest stipulations, discounted notes, or commercial returns are present, or whether the transaction represents an unremunerated advance entangled in disputed advisory dealings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Rs. 1.70 Crores transaction was not borrowed against payment of interest or under any commercial credit facility, disentitling the applicant from initiating CIRP as a Financial Creditor.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for absence of merit, affirming NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi's dismissal of the Section 7 application, with no order as to costs.
summary: Mr. K.N. Mahesh Prasad appealed against an order of the NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi dismissing his Section 7 application against M/s. MedinnBelle Herbalcare Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant, acting as an M&A consultant, advanced Rs. 1.70 Crores under an MoU dated 16.01.2018 to help the Corporate Debtor settle a disputed trademark claim with a third party to satisfy a buyer condition in a prospective buyout. The cheques issued by the debtor were dishonored. NCLAT held that the disbursement carried no interest, was not made under a credit facility, and completely lacked the attribute of time value of money under Section 5(8) of the IBC. Finding that the advance did not constitute a financial debt, NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Earth Gracia Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. vs. Connoisseur Infrabuild Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Earth Gracia Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor undergoing CIRP represented by its RP Ms. Manisha Rawat) as Appellant/Financial Creditor; Connoisseur Infrabuild Pvt. Ltd. (group entity) as Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Inter-corporate fund transfers across affiliated group entities conducted between 2013 and 2015 via direct banking and RTGS channels without a formal written loan agreement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial debt claimed based on fund transfers where the last transfer took place on 29.12.2015; no date of default or specific evidence of default was substantiated in Part V of Form 1. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Inter-corporate transfers made during 2013, 2014, and up to 29.12.2015; three-year limitation period expired on 28.12.2018; Demand Notice issued belatedly prior to Section 7 application; impugned order passed on 09.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audited balance sheet for the financial year ending 31.03.2015 and unilateral internal ledger extracts; no written acknowledgment of debt executed by the Respondent prior to 28.12.2018 under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, nor any part-payment under Section 19. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Resolution Professional filed a Section 7 petition seeking initiation of CIRP against the sister company to facilitate joint resolution and asset maximization; NCLT New Delhi Bench-V rejected the application on 09.12.2019 as barred by limitation.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 petition filed more than three years after the last fund transfer without an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 or part-payment under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 is maintainable, and whether the necessity of group insolvency consolidation can override statutory limitation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A financial debt barred by the law of limitation ceases to be payable in law, and an application under Section 7 of the IBC cannot be sustained where default is shown beyond three years without valid acknowledgment or revival under the Limitation Act, 1963. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying Innoventive Industries v. ICICI Bank, Section 7(5) mandates that the Adjudicating Authority must be satisfied that a default has occurred in respect of a debt due and payable in law and fact; commercial group consolidation arguments cannot bypass statutory limitation periods. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Part IV and Part V of Form 1 must establish a legally enforceable claim and positive evidence of default occurring within three years preceding the application; unacknowledged balance sheets older than three years fail Section 18 scrutiny. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the last fund transfer occurred on 29.12.2015 and no acknowledgment occurred before 28.12.2018, the claimed amount was legally irrecoverable and the petition was rightly rejected.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, affirming the order dated 09.12.2019 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-V rejecting the Section 7 application as barred by limitation, with no order as to costs.
summary: The Resolution Professional of Earth Gracia Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. appealed the dismissal of a Section 7 application filed against sister company Connoisseur Infrabuild Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant contended that the companies required consolidated CIRP to prevent liquidation and that limitation ran from the date of demand. NCLAT held that the last fund transfer occurred on 29.12.2015 and the three-year limitation under the Limitation Act expired on 28.12.2018 without any valid acknowledgment under Section 18 or part-payment under Section 19. Affirming the NCLT New Delhi order, NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that time-barred claims are not payable in law and cannot trigger Section 7 insolvency.

case_title: Smt. Akula Nagalaxmi vs. M/s. Crompton Greaves Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Smt. Akula Nagalaxmi (purchaser/transferee) as Appellant; M/s. Crompton Greaves Ltd. (issuer company) as Respondent No. 1; Rupesh K. Sanghvi (registered transferor) as Respondent No. 2; M/s. Zen Securities Ltd. (broker) as Respondent No. 3. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purchase of physical equity shares on the National Stock Exchange through broker bills (Bill No. 3119 dated 23.04.1998, No. 23080 dated 09.10.1997, and No. 5207 dated 07.05.1998) followed by lodgment for transfer. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent No. 1 failed and refused to register the lawful transfer of 700 equity shares in the Appellant's name, placing 150 shares under 'stop transfer' and withholding all accrued dividends and corporate benefits since 1998. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: 1,450 shares (jointly covering Appellant and husband) dispatched to company on 30.05.1998 via Sanchar Courier (Note No. L115288); legal notice issued on 12.03.1999; OS No. 73/1999 decreed ex-parte on 31.01.2000; ex-parte decree set aside by High Court in CRP No. 4758/2006; transferred company petition CP No. 45/111A/MB/2011 decided by NCLT on 02.05.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Production of share certificate numbers, registered folios, courier receipts, broker purchase contracts, and precedent Company Law Board order dated 28.09.2010 in CP No. 69/2008 directing transfer of identical husband's shares. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed the Section 111A rectification petition on 02.05.2018 on grounds of limitation, misjoinder of subsequent electronic transferees, and asserting that complicated questions of title belong exclusively in Civil Court.
legal_issues: Whether a company petition under Section 111A of the Companies Act, 1956 for rectification of the register of members and transfer of lodged physical shares is maintainable before the Tribunal, and whether dematerialization and subsequent transfers to third parties oust the Tribunal's summary jurisdiction in favor of a Civil Court.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An investor who lawfully purchases shares through a recognized stock exchange and dispatches original share scrips for statutory registration cannot be relegated to a civil court due to the company's continuous inaction, negligence, or subsequent improper dematerialization of the disputed scrips. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 111A vests wide statutory jurisdiction in the Company Law Board (and successor Tribunals) to rectify the register of members and rectify fraudulent or wrongful refusals to transfer, precluding companies from setting up summary procedure bars caused by their own historic defaults. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Establishing legitimate purchase through verified broker contract notes, registered courier dispatch proof, and identical adjudicated outcomes of co-dispatched share bundles. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Crompton Greaves failed to notify non-receipt or rejection in 1998, subjecting the shareholder to decades of avoidable litigation, and must effectuate the transfer upon standard indemnity documentation.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of in favor of the Appellant; the impugned order of NCLT Mumbai is set aside; Respondent No. 1 is directed to register the transfer of the 700 shares in favor of the Appellant upon receipt of requisite declarations, indemnity bond, and relevant papers, and issue shares with all accrued corporate benefits in accordance with law; no costs.
summary: Smt. Akula Nagalaxmi appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing her Section 111A petition seeking registration and transfer of 700 Crompton Greaves shares purchased on the NSE in 1998. NCLT had dismissed the petition holding that the shares had since been dematerialized, transferee parties were omitted, and title disputes required a Civil Court decree. NCLAT held that the investor had fully substantiated her purchase via broker bills and courier lodgment receipts from 1998, and that the company had unlawfully delayed action while transferring an identical tranche of shares to her husband. Setting aside NCLT's order, NCLAT directed Crompton Greaves to effectuate the share transfer and release all accrued corporate benefits upon standard indemnity submission.

case_title: Mr. Sandeep Goel vs. M/s. Ahuja Cotspin Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Sandeep Goel, sole proprietor of NYSA Enterprises, as Appellant/Operational Creditor; M/s. Ahuja Cotspin Pvt. Ltd. as Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and supply of cotton/textile yarn materials amounting to 325 MT under booking contracts negotiated via mediator Rakesh Rathi. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational creditor claimed an outstanding liability of Rs. 28,17,421 against goods supplied; corporate debtor asserted counter-losses of Rs. 4,00,00,000 arising from short and non-delivery of booked material. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Winding up notice under Section 434(1)(a) issued by Appellant on 27.02.2017; reply disputing delivery and claiming Rs. 4 Crore losses issued on 31.03.2017; Section 8(1) demand notice issued on 08.09.2017; reply to Section 8 notice sent on 21.12.2017; Section 9 petition decided on 25.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate debtor's reply dated 31.03.2017 to the pre-IBC winding-up notice explicitly documenting non-delivery of booked cotton consignments causing business damages of Rs. 4 Crores, raised long before the Section 8 notice. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed the Section 9 application on 25.11.2019 upon finding a genuine pre-existing dispute raised in the winding-up correspondence; Operational Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a detailed commercial dispute regarding breach of supply quantities and consequential business losses raised in response to a pre-IBC winding-up notice constitutes a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 9(5)(2)(d) of the IBC despite partial acknowledgment of ledger balances.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a corporate debtor has raised specific, documented grievances regarding short delivery of goods and substantial consequential losses in response to a winding-up notice prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice, a bona fide pre-existing dispute exists warranting rejection of a Section 9 petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(2)(d) read with the Mobilox doctrine mandates rejection of an insolvency petition if the dispute is plausible and raised prior to the Section 8 notice, irrespective of whether the debtor's defense will ultimately succeed in civil adjudication. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Existence of a contemporaneous paper trail demonstrating that the controversy concerning breach of contract and damages was agitated well before the statutory demand notice was dispatched. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor's reply of 31.03.2017 disputing deliveries and asserting Rs. 4 Crores in damages established a substantial pre-existing dispute, rendering the Section 9 petition unsustainable.
operative_order: Delay of 15 days is condoned; the appeal is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Chandigarh Bench judgment dated 25.11.2019 rejecting the Section 9 application, with no order as to costs.
summary: Mr. Sandeep Goel, proprietor of NYSA Enterprises, appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order dismissing his Section 9 insolvency petition against M/s. Ahuja Cotspin Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant argued that the Corporate Debtor had acknowledged a liability of Rs. 28,17,421 in communications. The record showed that in reply to a winding-up notice on 31.03.2017—months before the Section 8 demand notice—the debtor had formally raised grievances regarding short supply of 325 MT of yarn resulting in damages of Rs. 4 Crores. Applying the Mobilox Innovations standard, NCLAT held that a genuine pre-existing dispute existed prior to the demand notice, precluding summary insolvency proceedings, and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: M/s. Fairwood Infra & Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s. Wave Megacity Centre Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Fairwood Infra & Services Pvt. Ltd. (Project Management Consultant) as Appellant/Operational Creditor; M/s. Wave Megacity Centre Pvt. Ltd. (Real Estate Developer) as Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Project Management Consultancy Agreement executed on 09.09.2015 for supervising and providing consultancy services for developer's project against invoice payments. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed contractual dues of Rs. 1,51,54,735 based on accepted and unpaid invoices; Corporate Debtor claimed a counter-recovery of Rs. 32,82,404 based on contractual Built-Up Area (BUA) fee caps under Clause 10.1. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Dispute letter/email sent by Corporate Debtor on 16.12.2016; rebuttal email sent on 08.02.2017; Section 8 demand notice issued on 21.12.2018; Section 8 reply invoking arbitration sent on 13.03.2018; CP IB-406/(ND)/2018 dismissed by NCLT on 14.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's email dated 16.12.2016 disputing fee calculations on Built-Up Area terms, attached reconciliation sheet asserting Rs. 32,82,404 recoverable from Fairwood, and an arbitral award subsequently passed in favor of the debtor pending Section 34 challenge. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-III dismissed the Section 9 petition on 14.06.2019 citing pre-existing contractual disputes raised prior to the statutory demand notice; Operational Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a dispute concerning the contractual formula for fee computation (invoice-based vs. built-up area method) communicated via email prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice constitutes a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 9 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the corporate debtor has disputed the calculation methodology of consultancy fees and asserted counter-claims under contractual reconciliation clauses prior to the issuance of a Section 8 notice, the claim involves a bona fide pre-existing dispute outside the purview of summary Section 9 proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 of the IBC cannot be converted into a debt-collection mechanism when genuine contractual interpretation issues and cross-claims are communicated prior to statutory demand notices. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Email correspondence and reconciliation sheets pre-dating the statutory demand notice demonstrating real, unresolved commercial controversy between the contracting parties. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor's email of 16.12.2016 raised a genuine, substantial dispute concerning contractual fee caps and counter-recoveries, justifying the dismissal of the Section 9 application.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, affirming the NCLT New Delhi Bench-III order dated 14.06.2019 rejecting the Section 9 application, with no order as to costs.
summary: Fairwood Infra & Services Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT New Delhi's dismissal of its Section 9 insolvency application against Wave Megacity Centre Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant sought payment of Rs. 1,51,54,735 for project management consultancy invoices. The Respondent resisted, showing that via an email dated 16.12.2016—well before the Section 8 notice—it had calculated fees under the contractual Built-Up Area formula and claimed a counter-recovery of Rs. 32,82,404 from the Appellant, culminating in an arbitral award under Section 34 challenge. NCLAT held that the contemporaneous communications clearly established a pre-existing contractual dispute, rendering the Section 9 petition unmaintainable and dismissing the appeal.

case_title: PNB Housing Finance Ltd. vs. J.S.S. Buildcon Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor/Appellant is PNB Housing Finance Ltd.; Corporate Debtor/Respondent is J.S.S. Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. (Promoter/Developer); third parties are 14 individual allottees/borrowers. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan agreements and Tripartite Agreements executed between PNB Housing Finance Ltd., individual allottees, and J.S.S. Buildcon Pvt. Ltd., wherein loan amounts sanctioned to allottees were disbursed directly to the account of the Corporate Debtor for booking units in an infrastructure/housing project, with residential units mortgaged as security. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by 14 individual borrowers totaling an aggregate disbursed principal amount of Rs. 6,50,37,015/- disbursed between 19.09.2014 and 01.10.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Individual loan agreements entered into between September 2014 and October 2015; Section 7 petition was filed following payment defaults by allottees. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements containing repayment clauses (Clause 2.9) and delay penalties (Clause 2.10) treating borrower failure to pay EMI/PEMI as an event of default under Article 7.1; Tripartite Agreement dated 15.12.2014 stipulating builder's obligation to cancel allotments and refund disbursed sums to PNBHFL upon written intimation/instructions, but no record of written instructions, cancellation of allotments, or notices issued to individual allottees was produced. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed by PNB Housing Finance Ltd. was dismissed by NCLT New Delhi Bench holding that loans were availed individually by borrowers, tripartite arrangements were purely by way of security, and no direct financial debt was owed by the Corporate Debtor to PNBHFL.
legal_issues: Whether a housing finance institution that disbursed loans to a developer on behalf of individual allottees pursuant to tripartite agreements qualifies as a Financial Creditor of the corporate developer under Section 5(8) entitled to maintain a Section 7 application against the developer upon default by individual allottees.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A housing finance creditor holding a mortgage over properties allotted to individual home-buyers under tripartite agreements cannot initiate corporate insolvency resolution against the developer as a financial creditor for defaults committed by individual borrowers unless a direct, independent financial debt and default are established against the developer. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) read with Section 7 of the Code requires a direct debtor-creditor financial debt relationship between the applicant and the corporate debtor; mortgage/security arrangements under tripartite pacts securing borrower obligations do not transform the mortgagee into a financial creditor of the developer absent fulfillment of specific contractual cancellation/refund triggers. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict construction of loan covenants; the creditor failed to produce evidentiary proof of having issued written intimation or instructions cancelling allotments to trigger developer refund liabilities under the tripartite contract. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The primary default arises under individual loan agreements as distinct events of default by borrowers; hence, the Section 7 petition against the corporate developer based solely on its status as mortgagor/developer in a tripartite agreement is not maintainable.
operative_order: Delay of one day in preferring the appeal was condoned; the appeal preferred by PNB Housing Finance Ltd. was dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: PNB Housing Finance Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its Section 7 IBC application against developer J.S.S. Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. PNBHFL disbursed housing loans aggregating Rs. 6.50 Crores directly to the builder under tripartite agreements on behalf of 14 individual allottees who subsequently defaulted on EMIs. NCLAT held that defaults occurred on individual loan agreements between the bank and borrowers, and the tripartite agreement served merely as security creating a mortgage. As PNBHFL failed to show written intimation cancelling allotments to trigger any refund obligations by the builder, it could not be treated as a Financial Creditor of the developer under Section 5(8). The dismissal was upheld.

case_title: Oriental Bank of Commerce vs. M/s Ruchi Global Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor/Appellant is Oriental Bank of Commerce; Corporate Debtor/Respondent is M/s Ruchi Global Limited; other consortium members are Dena Bank (Lead Bank), Punjab National Bank, and Jammu & Kashmir Bank. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Non-fund-based Letter of Credit facilities granted by the Appellant Bank to the Corporate Debtor as part of a Consortium of Banks secured by a Third Supplemental Inter Se Agreement dated 27.01.2012 securing an individual credit facility of Rs. 34.15 Crores out of a total consortium facility of Rs. 343.44 Crores, further secured by Deeds of Guarantee and borrower undertakings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit facilities leading to classification of Corporate Debtor's account as Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 31.08.2017 with an outstanding default amount of Rs. 8,22,36,542/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account classified as NPA on 31.08.2017; notice sent by Appellant Bank to Corporate Debtor on 05.09.2017; Section 7 application dismissed by NCLT on 14.02.2019; NCLAT appeal decided on 31.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Third Supplemental Inter Se Agreement dated 27.01.2012 among consortium banks; bank account statements showing account was out of order in Appellant's books; default notice dated 05.09.2017; Corporate Debtor did not dispute the existence of debt and default. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed by Oriental Bank of Commerce was dismissed on 14.02.2019 by Adjudicating Authority holding that the Appellant failed to issue prior 30-day notice to Lead Bank (Dena Bank) as mandated under the Inter Se Consortium Agreement dated 27.01.2012, granting liberty to file afresh.
legal_issues: Whether an inter se agreement between member banks of a lending consortium requiring prior notice to the lead bank creates a legal bar preventing an individual financial creditor from maintaining an application under Section 7 of the IBC against the corporate debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An inter se agreement between member banks of a lending consortium binds only the contracting banks; third-party corporate debtors cannot enforce or take advantage of its contractual clauses to impede a statutory petition under Section 7 of the Code. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 confers an independent statutory right upon any financial creditor to initiate insolvency resolution individually or jointly; contractual inter se consortium stipulations cannot override, alter, or restrict this statutory right. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Undisputed existence of financial debt and default on record satisfies the statutory requirement for admission under Section 7; lack of compliance with inter-bank notice covenants is irrelevant to adjudication against the debtor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The failure to give notice to the lead bank under an inter se consortium pact does not constitute a legal bar to maintaining a Section 7 petition, rendering the dismissal order unsustainable.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order of NCLT dated 14.02.2019 quashed and set aside. Matter remitted to the Adjudicating Authority with directions for parties to appear on 24.02.2020 to consider any settlement, failing which the Adjudicating Authority shall admit the Section 7 application. No costs.
summary: Oriental Bank of Commerce appealed against the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 7 IBC application against M/s Ruchi Global Limited for a default of Rs. 8.22 Crores. The NCLT had dismissed the petition holding that the bank failed to provide prior notice to the lead consortium bank (Dena Bank) under a Third Supplemental Inter Se Consortium Agreement. The NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that an inter se consortium agreement binds only the participating banks, and the corporate debtor, not being a party, cannot invoke its terms. Relying on precedent, NCLAT held that contractual inter se arrangements cannot override the statutory right of a financial creditor to trigger Section 7 individually, remanding the matter for admission absent settlement.

case_title: S.A. Pharmachem Pvt. Ltd. vs. Alok Industries Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Operational Creditors (S.A. Pharmachem Pvt. Ltd. and batch appellants); Respondent No. 1 is Corporate Debtor (Alok Industries Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 is Resolution Professional; Respondent No. 3 is Reliance Industries Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Committee of Creditors also appeared. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods and materials by the Operational Creditors during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) to maintain the Corporate Debtor as a going concern, along with pre-CIRP supply invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Disputed non-payment/adjustment of invoices for goods supplied during CIRP, apprehension of set-off against pre-CIRP dues, and non-payment of CIRP costs (amounts not quantified in order). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan approved by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 08.03.2019; RP sent email regarding invoice adjustments on 21.11.2018; Interlocutory Applications rejected by NCLT on 18.11.2019; Appeal decided on 22.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated 21.11.2018 from RP directing settlement of payments of October-November 2018 against running invoices; approved Resolution Plan allocating funds for CIRP costs and operational creditors; submission by RP/Monitoring Committee confirming compliance with CIRP cost disbursements. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditors filed Interlocutory Applications during plan implementation seeking payment of CIRP costs; NCLT Ahmedabad Bench rejected the applications on 18.11.2019, prompting this batch appeal.
legal_issues: Whether individual operational creditors can maintain independent claims or interlocutory applications for CIRP costs and goods supplied during CIRP before the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal after the resolution plan has been finally approved and attained finality without challenge.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a corporate resolution plan is approved by the Adjudicating Authority and attains finality without appeal or challenge, it becomes binding on all stakeholders, extinguishing all independent stakeholder claims outside the distribution scheme framed in the plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Approvals under Section 31 render the resolution plan universally binding across all classes of creditors; implementation and fund allocation of approved CIRP costs rest entirely within the jurisdiction of the Monitoring Committee, not piecemeal judicial determination. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of an explicit challenge to the approval order dated 08.03.2019, representations by the Monitoring Committee and Resolution Professional affirming CIRP cost coverage preclude contradictory individual claims. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Individual claims of operational creditors cannot be adjudicated afresh post-approval, and all pre-existing and CIRP dues stand resolved strictly in accordance with the terms of the sanctioned plan.
operative_order: All connected appeals (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 66, 67, 69, 70, 71, 73, and 74 of 2020) dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary: S.A. Pharmachem Pvt. Ltd. and other operational creditors appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench order dated 18.11.2019 rejecting their interlocutory applications for CIRP costs for goods supplied during the CIRP of Alok Industries Ltd. The Appellants contended that their post-commencement operational dues were improperly set off against pre-CIRP claims. The NCLAT held that because the resolution plan approved on 08.03.2019 had not been challenged and attained finality, it was completely binding on all stakeholders. Distribution of CIRP costs is solely within the purview of the Monitoring Committee, barring any independent individual claim adjudications before the Tribunal. The appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Aurora Accessories Pvt. Ltd. vs. Ace Acoustics & Audio Video Solutions Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor/Appellant is Aurora Accessories Pvt. Ltd. (landlord/lessor); Corporate Debtor/Respondent is Ace Acoustics & Audio Video Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (tenant/lessee). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lease of immovable property by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor under a lease agreement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Arrears of lease rent amounting to Rs. 38,52,937/-, which accumulated with interest to a total claimed default of Rs. 49,09,072/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original Section 9 petition CP(IB) No. 15/GB/2019 dismissed by NCLT Guwahati Bench on 09.08.2019; NCLAT appeal decided on 28.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease agreement and records establishing arrears of lease rent and accrued interest. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 9 application before NCLT Guwahati Bench for outstanding lease rentals; NCLT dismissed the petition on 09.08.2019 holding lease rent arrears do not qualify as 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) and lessor is not an 'operational creditor' under Section 5(20).
legal_issues: Whether a claim arising out of unpaid arrears of lease rent for immovable property constitutes an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC so as to entitle the landlord/lessor to initiate CIRP under Section 9.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The leasing of immovable property does not constitute the supply of goods or the rendering of services, and consequently, rental arrears arising from lease agreements do not qualify as operational debt under the Code. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) strictly confines operational debt to claims in respect of the provision of goods or services, including employment and government dues; it excludes claims relating to immovable property rentals. Section 5(20) is correspondingly limited. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Application of the three-judge bench binding authority in Mr. M. Ravindranath Reddy vs. Mr. G. Kishan & Ors. defining the essential subject-matter limits of Section 5(21). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A Section 9 petition cannot be maintained for recovery of lease rentals, affirming the order of the Adjudicating Authority dismissing the application.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, granting liberty to the Appellant to pursue ordinary remedies for recovery of rent dues in accordance with law.
summary: Aurora Accessories Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Guwahati Bench order dismissing its Section 9 application against Ace Acoustics & Audio Video Solutions Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid lease rent arrears totaling Rs. 49,09,072/- including interest. Relying on its three-judge bench precedent in Mr. M. Ravindranath Reddy vs. Mr. G. Kishan & Ors., the NCLAT affirmed that leasing of immovable property does not amount to the provision of goods or rendering of services within the statutory ambit of Section 5(21) of the IBC. Consequently, rental arrears do not constitute an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21), rendering a Section 9 petition non-maintainable. The appeal was dismissed with liberty to seek ordinary legal remedies.

case_title: M/s. Loyal Credit and Investment Ltd. vs. M/s. Cosmopolis Properties Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor/Appellant is M/s. Loyal Credit and Investment Ltd.; Corporate Debtor/Respondent is M/s. Cosmopolis Properties Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying commercial and financial transactions giving rise to arbitral proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim grounded upon an arbitral award dated 28.06.2016 passed in favor of the Appellant (exact monetary quantum not specified in the appellate order). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Arbitral Award passed on 28.06.2016; challenge petition under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 filed and pending before Madras High Court; Section 7 petition rejected by NCLT Chennai Bench on 13.11.2019; NCLAT appeal disposed of on 02.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Arbitral award dated 28.06.2016; documentation of ongoing Section 34 challenge proceedings pending adjudication before the High Court of Judicature at Madras. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 7 application based on an arbitral award; NCLT Chennai Division Bench rejected the application on merits on 13.11.2019 in an ex-parte hearing session after counsel failed to appear in the second call.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC is maintainable when the purported financial debt/default is predicated on an arbitral award that is actively contested and pending adjudication in an application under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a claim of debt is founded upon an arbitral award that is sub judice and challenged under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, it cannot be deemed an indisputable, crystallized default to sustain an application under Section 7 of the Code. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'default' under Section 3(12) and Section 7 of the IBC contemplates a clear, non-contingent liability due and payable; an arbitral award under active challenge in a competent court lacks the final executable character required to establish default for insolvency initiation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pendency of Section 34 arbitration challenge proceedings before a High Court establishes the contested and uncrystallized nature of the underlying liability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the arbitral award is subject to Section 34 challenge, default cannot be legally alleged under Section 7, rendering the insolvency application non-maintainable.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs, with observations that the NCLT and NCLAT orders shall not prejudice the determination of rights pending before the High Court of Judicature at Madras in the Section 34 petition.
summary: M/s Loyal Credit and Investment Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Chennai order dated 13.11.2019 rejecting its Section 7 application against M/s Cosmopolis Properties Pvt. Ltd. The creditor asserted default based on an arbitral award passed in its favor on 28.06.2016. The Corporate Debtor had challenged the award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 before the Madras High Court, which was pending. NCLAT held that given the sub judice Section 34 challenge, a definitive default cannot be established to sustain a Section 7 CIRP petition. The dismissal was affirmed while preserving the appellant's rights in the High Court proceedings.

case_title: Jindal Stainless Ltd. vs. Cosmic Ferro Alloys Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jindal Stainless Ltd. (Appellant/Operational Creditor), Cosmic Ferro Alloys Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Corporate Debtor represented through RP Anis Niranjan Nanavati), and United Tradeco FZC & QVC Exports Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 2/Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods/materials under commercial arrangements attracting statutory Central Sales Tax/VAT Form-C declarations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed in Form-B totaling Rs. 3,18,82,894, comprising principal and interest of Rs. 2,54,42,448 and statutory liability arising from non-issuance of Form-C amounting to Rs. 64,40,446 as on 15.01.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form-B submitted during CIRP; RP verified claims and placed list of creditors before the CoC on 13.08.2018; Resolution Plan approved by NCLT on 11.10.2018; Appeal decided on 10.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Proof of claim Form-B (Annexure-A4), outstanding summary ledger as on 15.01.2018, Form-C outstanding summary, approved Resolution Plan (Annexure-8) waiving all statutory sales tax/VAT liabilities, and RP's verification admitting Rs. 2,66,98,711 against which Rs. 1,00,00,000 was disbursed in full and final settlement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 IBC application was admitted against the Corporate Debtor, culminating in CIRP completion and NCLT approval of Respondent No. 2's Resolution Plan; Appellant filed an application before NCLT Kolkata Bench challenging non-consideration of Form-C liability and alleged discrimination, which was dismissed without granting relief.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal can interfere with or modify an approved Resolution Plan to mandate the new management to issue statutory Form-C certificates or reconsider operational debt calculations approved under the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An approved resolution plan duly sanctioned by the Committee of Creditors and the Adjudicating Authority cannot be substantively altered, recalculated, or burdened with additional contractual or statutory directions by an appellate forum in the absence of patent statutory illegality. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30 and Section 31 of the IBC accord primacy to the commercial wisdom of the CoC; operational debt settlements incorporating blanket waivers of accrued statutory taxes/VAT approved under a resolution plan operate as a full, final, and binding extinguishment of all residual claims against the reconstituted corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The standard of patent illegality or jurisdictional breach; courts will not conduct a fresh evidentiary or mathematical inquiry into claim verification once the Resolution Professional has processed claims and the CoC has approved the distribution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan legitimately provided for waiver and final settlement of operational and statutory claims, barring the appellate court from directing the successful resolution applicant to issue Form-C declarations or alter admitted settlement values.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs; liberty reserved to the Appellant to present its case before the concerned sales tax/VAT authorities in accordance with law.
summary: Jindal Stainless Ltd. appealed against an NCLT order declining relief regarding its operational claim of Rs. 3.18 Crores against Cosmic Ferro Alloys Ltd., specifically seeking a direction for the reconstituted corporate debtor to issue VAT 'Form-C' certificates for Rs. 64.40 Lakhs. The NCLAT held that the resolution plan submitted by United Tradeco FZC & QVC Exports Pvt. Ltd. had been duly approved by the CoC and the Adjudicating Authority, providing full settlement and statutory waivers. Refusing to encroach upon the commercial wisdom of the CoC or modify the plan without any demonstrated illegality, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

case_title: M/s B.E. Billimoria and Company Ltd. vs. M/s Vikram Ispat Udyog
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s B.E. Billimoria and Company Ltd. (Appellant/Corporate Debtor) and M/s Vikram Ispat Udyog (Respondent/Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of Tiscon TMT Steel Coils/Bars between 25.08.2015 and 19.12.2015 aggregating to an invoice value of Rs. 2,16,73,188. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor made part-payments of Rs. 1,17,93,537, leaving an unpaid principal operational debt of Rs. 98,79,591 plus contractually stipulated delayed interest at 24% per annum. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 read with Rule 5 issued on 19.08.2017; Corporate Debtor submitted reply denying liability; Section 9 petition CP (IB)-1544(MB)/2017 filed thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Supply invoices, delivery challans, Section 8 demand notice and reply, and joint consent statements submitted before NCLT on 25.01.2019 accepting an agreed payment schedule and mutually delegating determination of delayed payment interest rate to the Adjudicating Authority. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor initiated CIRP under Section 9; during pendency before NCLT Mumbai Bench, parties settled the principal claim but referred the delayed interest rate to the Tribunal, which directed payment of 12% interest and granted liberty to revive upon default; Corporate Debtor appealed arguing NCLT exceeded jurisdiction by acting as a recovery court.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority, while disposing of a Section 9 application pursuant to an amicable settlement between parties, possesses the jurisdiction under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to award interest on delayed payments when both parties have expressly consented to its adjudication.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where litigating parties in an insolvency proceeding enter into an amicable settlement and jointly empower the Tribunal to determine a disputed ancillary term such as delayed payment interest, the Tribunal may validly exercise its inherent powers to fix a reasonable interest rate to meet the ends of justice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While IBC proceedings are fundamentally resolution and not debt recovery mechanisms, Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 confers inherent jurisdiction to pass consequential and equitable orders to give effect to consensual party arrangements and prevent abuse of process. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mutual consent and estoppel; an order cannot be assailed as jurisdictional overreach by a party that expressly submitted the determination of interest to the Adjudicating Authority's discretion. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority acted well within its inherent jurisdiction in fixing interest at 12% per annum (reduced from 24%) pursuant to the explicit agreement of both parties.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's direction to pay interest @ 12% per annum.
summary: M/s B.E. Billimoria and Company Ltd. appealed an NCLT Mumbai Bench order in a Section 9 IBC proceeding that directed it to pay 12% interest per annum on delayed payments to operational creditor M/s Vikram Ispat Udyog following an amicable settlement of an unpaid balance of Rs. 98,79,591. The Appellant argued that the NCLT had exceeded its jurisdiction under the IBC by acting as a recovery court. The NCLAT held that because both parties had explicitly agreed to abide by the Tribunal's interest rate determination, the NCLT validly exercised its inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Yogendra Vasupal vs. S. Kannan & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Yogendra Vasupal (Appellant/Erstwhile Director), S. Kannan (Respondent No. 1/Liquidator), Amazon Internet Services Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 2/Cloud Service Provider), Karthigeyan Srinivasan (Respondent No. 3/Erstwhile IRP/RP), Sachit Singhi (Respondent No. 4/Director), and Inasra Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in Liquidation). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed cloud data hosting services from Amazon Internet Services Pvt. Ltd. to preserve corporate records, financial books, and operational databases. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-quantified financial default leading to CIRP and subsequent liquidation, coupled with failure of the erstwhile management to settle cloud hosting service charges, resulting in suspension/deletion of digital records. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation ordered by NCLT Chennai Bench; Liquidator filed M.A. No. 172 of 2019 seeking production of financial statements for years ended 31.03.2017 and 31.03.2018; impugned order passed directing compliance within three weeks. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Non-availability of physical books; email correspondence between Amazon and the Corporate Debtor showing non-payment of subscription fees leading to data withholding/deletion; partial restoration of cloud data confirmed by Amazon. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 Liquidator filed M.A. No. 172 of 2019 before NCLT Chennai alleging non-cooperation; NCLT found dereliction of duty by Directors and the erstwhile RP, directed data handover within three weeks, and referred the RP to IBBI; Appellant appealed seeking expunction of adverse remarks.
legal_issues: Whether erstwhile directors and resolution professionals can evade statutory obligations to maintain, finalize, and hand over accounts and corporate data to the liquidator by citing data deletion by third-party cloud service providers, and whether adverse observations for dereliction of duty were justified.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Erstwhile corporate management and insolvency professionals remain under an absolute, non-delegable duty to co-operate with the liquidator and reconstruct or retrieve corporate books of account, and cannot deflect statutory responsibility onto third-party technical vendors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 19 and Section 34/35 of the IBC impose mandatory obligations on corporate personnel to provide information and records necessary for liquidation; inter-se finger-pointing between directors, the RP, and third-party IT service providers constitutes dereliction of statutory duty. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Duty of active compliance; where technology permits retrieval and third-party cloud hosts have restored accessible backups, assertions of impossibility of compliance are legally untenable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority was fully justified in directing all stakeholders to furnish corporate data and in recording observations of dereliction of duty against the erstwhile directors.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs; parties are strictly directed to comply with the directions of the Adjudicating Authority to furnish accounts and data, failing which the Adjudicating Authority may initiate penal/coercive proceedings.
summary: The Appellant, an erstwhile director of Inasra Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (in liquidation), challenged an order of NCLT Chennai Bench in M.A. No. 172 of 2019 which observed dereliction of duty on the part of directors and the erstwhile IRP/RP and directed them to submit books of account for FY 2016-17 and 2017-18 to the Liquidator. The Appellant attributed missing corporate data to cloud hosting vendor Amazon Internet Services Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT rejected the Appellant's contentions, ruling that corporate officers cannot engage in blame games or evade statutory information-sharing duties under the IBC when data retrieval is feasible. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Bhagyanagar Boards & Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Vijay Kumar Goyal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bhagyanagar Boards & Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (Appellants/Respondents in Company Petition) and Vijay Kumar Goyal & Ors. (Respondents No. 1 to 3/Original Petitioners). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Compulsory acquisition of company land and demolition of compound structures by Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC), resulting in statutory compensation payout. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute over custody and preservation of GHMC compensation of Rs. 9,99,18,703; Appellants deposited Rs. 9,87,61,429 into Fixed Deposits and expended Rs. 11,57,274 on wall repairs and site restoration following municipal demolition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Transferred Petition T.P. No. 06/HDB/2016 pending before NCLT Hyderabad; Interlocutory Application I.A. No. 1103 of 2019 filed seeking escrow deposit; interim order passed directing deposit of Rs. 9,99,18,703; Company Petition scheduled for final hearing on 04.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Fixed Deposit receipts totaling Rs. 9,87,61,429 tendered under identification Document 'X', prior Company Law Board order (Annexure A-32) directing safe custody of compensation, and municipal demolition records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents 1 to 3 filed IA No. 1103 of 2019 in TP No. 06/HDB/2016 under Sections 241-242; NCLT Hyderabad directed Appellants to place entire compensation of Rs. 9,99,18,703 in a separate Fixed Deposit; Appellants appealed claiming the full sum had already been secured except for legitimate repair expenses.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in directing the deposit of the gross compensation amount of Rs. 9,99,18,703 without accounting for sums legitimately expended on property repairs and the actual amount secured in existing Fixed Deposits.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Interim preservation orders in oppression and mismanagement disputes must realistically account for demonstrably incurred bona fide maintenance expenses and modify deposit directives to align with actual, verifiable sums kept in secure, interest-bearing instruments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242 powers to pass interim conservatory orders to safeguard company assets require balancing asset security with operational reality, provided the corporate corpus is insulated against encumbrance or siphoning pending final hearing. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Physical verification of bank instruments; production of valid fixed deposit certificates before the appellate court discharges the burden of proving that funds are held in safe custody. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Rs. 9,87,61,429 had already been invested in Fixed Deposits and Rs. 11,57,274 was utilized for site repairs, the NCLT deposit order must be modified to require the deposit of the expended balance while keeping existing FDs unencumbered.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of with modification substituting the required deposit figure in Para 7 of the Impugned Order to Rs. 11,57,274; existing Fixed Deposits totaling Rs. 9,87,61,429 to be renewed periodically with interest and kept strictly unencumbered; NCLT directed to dispose of the Company Petition expeditiously, preferably within two months.
summary: Bhagyanagar Boards & Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an interim order of NCLT Hyderabad in an oppression and mismanagement petition directing it to deposit Rs. 9,99,18,703 received as municipal land acquisition compensation into a separate Fixed Deposit account. The Appellants demonstrated that Rs. 9,87,61,429 had already been placed in bank Fixed Deposits, while the residual Rs. 11,57,274 was spent on reconstructing demolished boundary walls. The NCLAT modified the order by directing the Appellants to deposit the balance Rs. 11,57,274, maintain and renew the existing FDs without creating any encumbrance, and requested the NCLT to decide the main petition within two months.

case_title: Reliance India Power Fund vs. Raj Kumar Ralhan, Liquidator of Su Kam Power Systems Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Reliance India Power Fund / Reliance Capital Trustee Co. Ltd. (Appellant/Shareholder/Claimant) and Mr. Raj Kumar Ralhan (Respondent/Liquidator of Corporate Debtor M/s Su Kam Power Systems Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Pre-CIRP Share Subscription / Shareholders' Agreement entered into between the Appellant and the Corporate Debtor containing an arbitration clause. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Pre-existing dispute over contractual terms resulting in arbitral claims prior to CIRP; corporate debtor entered liquidation, extinguishing resolution possibilities. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Arbitration commenced prior to insolvency; CIRP commenced staying proceedings under Section 14; Liquidation ordered by NCLT Principal Bench on 03.04.2019 in CP (IB)-540(PB)/2017; Liquidator appeared once before arbitral tribunal; Appellant moved CA No. 1096(PB)/2020 on which impugned order was passed on 11.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Shareholder Agreement (Annexure A-3), Liquidation order dated 03.04.2019 directing investigation under Section 35(1), and arbitral records showing the dispute primarily concerned inter-shareholder issues. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CA No. 1096(PB)/2020 seeking directions to compel the Liquidator to actively defend pending arbitration proceedings under Section 35(1)(k); NCLT dismissed the application; Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether Section 35(1)(k) of the IBC imposes an absolute, mandatory duty on a Liquidator to contest or defend every pending arbitral proceeding, or whether the Liquidator has the discretionary administrative authority to elect not to participate.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory power of an insolvency liquidator to institute or defend legal proceedings is discretionary rather than mandatory, vesting the liquidator with managerial authority to decide whether defending a claim serves the economic interests of the liquidation estate. 2.
