STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 35(1)(k) of the IBC, which empowers the liquidator to 'institute or defend any suit, prosecution or other legal proceedings,' encompasses the conscious prerogative to abstain from defending litigation that involves disputes where the corporate debtor's estate has no beneficial interest. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective business discretion; an external claimant cannot legally compel an officer of the court to expend estate assets defending an arbitral dispute that primarily concerns inter-shareholder conflicts. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidator legitimately exercised his statutory discretion under Section 35(1)(k) in opting not to contest the arbitration, and the claimant cannot compel the liquidator to participate.
operative_order: The appeal is found devoid of substance and dismissed at the admission stage without costs.
summary: Reliance India Power Fund appealed against an order of NCLT New Delhi (Principal Bench) refusing to compel the Liquidator of Su Kam Power Systems Ltd. to participate in and defend an ongoing arbitration proceeding initiated prior to CIRP under a shareholder agreement. The Appellant contended that Section 35(1)(k) of the IBC imposes a mandatory statutory duty on the liquidator to defend all legal proceedings. The NCLAT rejected this interpretation, holding that the statutory duty under Section 35(1)(k) includes the conscious administrative discretion to refrain from contesting proceedings where the corporate debtor has no viable commercial stake. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: M/s Regal Engineers & Construction (P) Ltd. vs. M/s Endee Shelter Properties Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Regal Engineers & Construction (P) Ltd. (Appellant/Operational Creditor) and M/s Endee Shelter Properties Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Construction contract under which Corporate Debtor engaged Appellant as a contractor for civil construction works on its real estate development. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed default of Rs. 1.88 Crores for unpaid running construction invoices; Corporate Debtor disputed the sum and raised a counter-claim of Rs. 45 Lakhs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Operational Creditor issued Legal Notice on 21.05.2018; Corporate Debtor replied on 05.06.2018; Section 8 statutory demand notice (Form 3) issued on 05.07.2018 and received on 12.07.2018; Section 8 reply served on 21.07.2018; Section 9 petition rejected by NCLT Chennai on 31.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Legal Notice dated 21.05.2018, Corporate Debtor's reply dated 05.06.2018 alleging defective work in Block 3 and asserting a counter-claim of Rs. 45 Lakhs, Section 8 demand notice and reply, and a consultant's valuation report from November 2017 showing payable amount of Rs. 1,19,82,975. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 application before NCLT Chennai (Division Bench-I); NCLT rejected the petition on 31.12.2019 holding that a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding quality and incomplete work had been raised prior to the Section 8 notice; Operational Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a consultant's interim valuation report of executed works overrides a corporate debtor's prior written disputes regarding defective workmanship and counter-claims so as to permit admission of a Section 9 application under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational debt petition under Section 9 of the IBC is non-maintainable if the Corporate Debtor has raised a genuine, pre-existing dispute regarding quality of work and counter-claims prior to the issuance of the Section 8 statutory demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'dispute' under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC is not restricted to pending arbitration or litigation, but includes any bona fide contestation raised in pre-notice correspondence that is plausible and not a patently feeble or moonshine defense. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Plausibility standard established in Mobilox Innovations; a third-party consultant's quantity valuation report does not bar a debtor from contesting performance quality or setting up counter-claims, which insolvency tribunals cannot adjudicate. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor had raised a genuine pre-existing dispute and counter-claim by its reply dated 05.06.2018, prior to the Section 8 notice of 05.07.2018, warranting dismissal of the Section 9 application.
operative_order: Delay of 8 days condoned; appeal dismissed at the admission stage with no order as to costs.
summary: M/s Regal Engineers & Construction (P) Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT Chennai rejecting its Section 9 IBC application against M/s Endee Shelter Properties Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid construction invoices of Rs. 1.88 Crores. The Appellant contended that a consultant's payment summary from November 2017 confirming payable dues of Rs. 1.19 Crores negated the existence of any dispute. The NCLAT held that the Corporate Debtor had raised specific disputes regarding defective workmanship in Block 3 and asserted a counter-claim of Rs. 45 Lakhs in its reply dated 05.06.2018, prior to the Section 8 demand notice of 05.07.2018. Confirming that insolvency tribunals cannot adjudicate contractual quality disputes, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Rashesh Purohit vs. Punjab National Bank & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rashesh Purohit (Appellant/Director/Promoter), Punjab National Bank (Respondent No. 1/Financial Creditor), and Corporate Debtor (in CIRP represented by IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Overdraft credit facility availed by the Corporate Debtor from Punjab National Bank in or around January 2017 for business working capital. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in overdraft repayment exceeding the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Lakh, resulting in the loan account being classified as Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 12.10.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Overdraft availed January 2017; NPA declared 12.10.2018; Section 7 application filed and admitted by NCLT; Appellate notice issued 16.12.2019 to explore settlement; appeal decided 17.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Overdraft facility loan sanction documents, default and NPA classification record dated 12.10.2018, failed settlement communications offering reduced payouts over prolonged periods, and RBI Circular dated 01.01.2019 regarding MSME debt restructuring. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: PNB initiated Section 7 proceedings; Corporate Debtor resisted on grounds of GST-related economic stress and requested restructuring under RBI's MSME circular; NCLT admitted the petition; Appellant appealed on the ground that the bank was legally bound to offer a one-year restructuring under the RBI circular.
legal_issues: Whether Reserve Bank of India circulars mandating the consideration of MSME restructuring through One Time Settlement (OTS) operate as a statutory bar to the admission of an application under Section 7 of the IBC against a defaulting corporate debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Sectoral or central bank guidelines for debt restructuring do not supersede the statutory framework of the IBC or create an embargo on a financial creditor's right to initiate corporate insolvency resolution upon default. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC operates independently; once the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that a financial debt exceeding the threshold is legally due and in default, admission is mandatory irrespective of collateral restructuring circulars. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Dual-criteria test of existence of debt and occurrence of default; banking regulations and non-statutory circulars cannot be interposed to dispute admitted default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor had an admitted default exceeding Rs. 1 Lakh and was classified as an NPA; grievances regarding RBI MSME circular compliance must be addressed to the regulator and cannot vitiate Section 7 admission.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of without interfering in the impugned order of admission. No orders as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, a director of the Corporate Debtor, challenged an NCLT order admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Punjab National Bank following default on an overdraft facility classified as an NPA on 12.10.2018. The Appellant argued that because the debtor was an MSME, the bank was mandated by the RBI Circular dated 01.01.2019 to grant a one-year debt restructuring through an OTS. The NCLAT held that RBI circulars do not create a legal bar to the maintainability or admission of a Section 7 application under the IBC. Given the undisputed debt and default exceeding Rs. 1 Lakh, the admission order was upheld and the appeal dismissed.

case_title: M/s Vertex Customer Management India Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s Abhibus Services (India) Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Vertex Customer Management India Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Operational Creditor) and M/s Abhibus Services (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Service agreement for providing business process outsourcing and customer care services to the patrons/passengers of the Corporate Debtor's bus ticketing platform. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed default on service fees amounting to Rs. 1,83,87,559. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Customer care deficiency grievances raised by Corporate Debtor; contract terminated; Section 8(1) demand notice issued; Section 9 petition filed and rejected by NCLT on 05.11.2019; communication of order on 06.01.2020; appeal dismissed 26.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Pre-notice communications showing dissatisfaction with customer care service, contract termination notice, Section 8(1) demand notice, and invoices claiming Rs. 1,83,87,559. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed a Section 9 application before the Adjudicating Authority; NCLT rejected the petition on 05.11.2019 on grounds of a pre-existing dispute regarding service deficiency raised prior to the Section 8 demand notice; Operational Creditor appealed arguing the termination notice was unlawful.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority and Appellate Tribunal have the jurisdiction under Section 9 of the IBC to adjudicate upon the validity or legality of a contract termination notice when deficient service was raised prior to the Section 8 demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Neither the NCLT nor the NCLAT possesses jurisdiction in summary insolvency proceedings to determine the validity of a contractual termination notice or resolve substantive disputes regarding deficient performance of services. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 8(1) read with Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC, where written contestation concerning the quality of service is raised prior to the issuance of a statutory demand notice, the bar of pre-existing dispute is triggered, precluding admission of CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Threshold test of pre-existing controversy; it is sufficient for the Corporate Debtor to demonstrate that grievances regarding service quality were communicated prior to the demand notice, without requiring the Tribunal to conduct a full trial on contractual breach. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because customer care service deficiencies were raised before the Section 8 notice, the Section 9 petition could not be admitted, and legality of contract termination falls outside the purview of the IBC.
operative_order: Delay condoned; appeal dismissed with no order as to costs, granting liberty to the Appellant to seek appropriate legal remedies before the competent civil forum.
summary: M/s Vertex Customer Management India Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 9 IBC application claiming Rs. 1,83,87,559 for customer care services provided to M/s Abhibus Services (India) Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had rejected the petition after finding that the Corporate Debtor had raised grievances regarding defective service prior to the Section 8 notice. The Appellant contended that the termination of its contract was wrongful. The NCLAT affirmed that insolvency tribunals have no jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the validity of contract terminations, and that documented dissatisfaction regarding service quality prior to the demand notice constitutes a valid pre-existing dispute barring CIRP admission. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Sanjay Gupta, R.P. of Topworth Pipes & Tubes Pvt. Ltd. vs. Committee of Creditors, Topworth Pipes & Tubes Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sanjay Gupta (Appellant/Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Topworth Pipes & Tubes Pvt. Ltd.) and Committee of Creditors of Topworth Pipes & Tubes Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Topworth Pipes & Tubes Pvt. Ltd. seeking resolution plans for revival of the manufacturing corporate debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to admission of Section 7 application on 11.12.2018; extension sought for exclusion of 89 days from the statutory CIRP period. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 11.12.2018; interim protection granted by NCLAT on 21.10.2019 restraining liquidation order; total elapsed period exceeded 330 days by decision date of 03.02.2020; directions issued to proceed under Section 33(1) within two weeks. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Rejection records of earlier resolution plans by the CoC, lack of any approved resolution plan within the statutory period, and calculation demonstrating completion of over 330 days of CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed an appeal against NCLT's refusal to exclude 89 days from the 270-day CIRP period; NCLAT initially restrained the NCLT from passing a liquidation order to give the CoC time to evaluate pending plans, but no viable plan materialized.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal can grant an exclusion or extension of the CIRP timeline beyond the outer statutory limit of 330 days under amended Section 12 of the IBC when no approved or viable resolution plan is available before the Committee of Creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When the statutory maximum timeline for CIRP under Section 12 has lapsed and no viable resolution plan has been approved by the Committee of Creditors, statutory liquidation under Section 33(1) must be initiated without further enlargement of time. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Amended Section 12 mandates resolution within 330 days inclusive of litigation; once this outer limit is breached without a pending, legally approvable plan, the Adjudicating Authority and CoC are obligated under Section 33(1) to initiate liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict temporal threshold and plan availability test; discretionary timeline exclusions cannot be granted on speculative hopes of revival once all received plans have been rejected and the maximum outer timeline has expired. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: With more than 330 days elapsed and all plans rejected by the CoC, refusal to interfere with the impugned order was mandated, requiring the RP to convene an urgent CoC meeting to seek liquidation.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of without interfering in the impugned order, with a direction to the RP to urgently convene a CoC meeting within two weeks to initiate liquidation steps before the Adjudicating Authority under Section 33(1) of the IBC.
summary: The Resolution Professional of Topworth Pipes & Tubes Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT order seeking exclusion of 89 days from the statutory CIRP period to enable the CoC to consider resolution plans. Although the NCLAT initially stayed liquidation proceedings on 21.10.2019 to provide time for resolution, all submitted plans were ultimately rejected by the CoC and the process exceeded 330 days. The NCLAT held that in light of amended Section 12 and the absence of any viable plan, the statutory timeline had expired, necessitating liquidation under Section 33(1). The RP was directed to convene a CoC meeting within two weeks to apply for liquidation.

case_title: IRK Raju vs. Immaneni Eswara Rao & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shri IRK Raju (Appellant/Promoter/Director), Immaneni Eswara Rao (Respondent No. 1), M/s Ice TV Private Limited (Respondent No. 2/Operational Creditor), and M/s Sreedevi Digital Systems Private Limited (Respondent No. 3/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and supply of 45,000 units of Digital Set-Top Boxes (DSTBs) between 10.06.2014 and 22.08.2014 for digital cable TV networking in Visakhapatnam, purportedly governed by two separate Memorandums of Understanding dated 22.11.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational creditor claimed Rs. 2,36,18,518 plus 24% interest from 21.12.2016, bifurcated into Rs. 1,06,38,500 under the 1st MoU (supply invoices) and Rs. 1,29,80,018 under the disputed 2nd MoU (customs duty reimbursement). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Goods supplied June–August 2014; MoUs dated 22.11.2015; Demand Notice issued 24.01.2018 giving 15 days' notice; NCLT Amaravati Bench admitted Section 9 application on 04.10.2019; NCLAT final judgment on 30.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: 1st MoU dated 22.11.2015 detailing invoice numbers and VAT; contested 2nd MoU dated 22.11.2015 not on company letterhead and lacking signature boxes; Section 8 notice demanding payment within 15 days; tender of Rs. 1,06,38,500 plus Rs. 10,00,000 by Appellant before NCLAT which was refused by Respondent No. 2. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Amaravati admitted Respondent No. 2's Section 9 application on 04.10.2019; Appellant appealed under Section 61 contending the petition was filed fraudulently with malicious intent under Section 65(1) based on a fabricated second MoU.
legal_issues: Whether a private supplier's claim for reimbursement of customs duty qualifies as an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC, and whether a Section 9 application based on disputed statutory reimbursements and non-compliant Section 8 notices amounts to fraudulent initiation under Section 65.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A claim for reimbursement of statutory dues paid by a private supplier on behalf of a buyer does not constitute an operational debt payable to that supplier, and invoking Section 9 to enforce disputed reimbursement claims while refusing principal settlement constitutes misuse under Section 65. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(21), statutory dues constitute 'operational debt' only when payable directly to the Central Government, State Government, or a local authority, as affirmed by substituting 'repayment' with 'payment'; a private third party cannot claim operational creditor status for tax reimbursements. Additionally, a Section 8(1) demand notice must strictly comply with Form 3 and provide a 10-day notice period rather than 15 days. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict statutory compliance and bona fide creditor test; where invoices show supply claims but ancillary MoUs for duty reimbursement are suspicious and disparate, the petition demonstrates malicious intent to extract money rather than seek corporate resolution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Customs duty reimbursement is not operational debt due to Respondent No. 2, the demand notice was legally defective, and the Section 9 petition was maliciously maintained, warranting reversal of CIRP.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 04.10.2019 set aside; Corporate Debtor released from CIRP and management restored to Board of Directors; IRP directed to hand over records and assets; matter remitted to Adjudicating Authority to determine IRP fees and costs to be paid by Respondent No. 2. No costs.
summary: Shri IRK Raju appealed against the NCLT Amaravati Bench order admitting an application under Section 9 of the IBC filed by Ice TV Pvt. Ltd. against Sreedevi Digital Systems Pvt. Ltd. claiming Rs. 2.36 Crores, which included Rs. 1.29 Crores as customs duty reimbursement. The NCLAT held that customs duty reimbursement claimed by a private party does not constitute an operational debt under Section 5(21), as statutory dues must be payable directly to the government. Observing that the demand notice was defective and Respondent No. 2 refused full payment of genuine invoice dues to extract money, the Tribunal set aside the CIRP admission under Section 65.

case_title: Rishabh Jain vs. S.S. Enterprises & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rishabh Jain (Appellant/Managing Director), M/s Home Connect Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 2/Corporate Debtor), and S.S. Enterprises through Proprietor Ranjan Kumar Bajaj (Respondent No. 1/Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Advance of financial assistance totaling Rs. 90 Lakhs structured across three successive MOUs dated 05.09.2017, 12.09.2017, and 13.09.2017 (superseding earlier ones), coupled with security plots and post-dated interest cheques. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of principal loan amount of Rs. 90,00,000 along with agreed monthly interest at 2% per month following expiry of an 11-month lock-in period and one month's notice. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MOUs executed on 05.09.2017, 12.09.2017, and 13.09.2017; demand and notice issued on 27.11.2018; Section 7 application (IB-1094/ND/2019) admitted on 25.10.2019; appeal decided on 27.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Third MoU dated 13.09.2017 acknowledging receipt of Rs. 90 Lakhs as a loan bearing 2% monthly interest, 11 post-dated cheques of Rs. 1,80,000 each for monthly interest, dishonored repayment cheques, and notice dated 27.11.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed a Section 7 petition after cheques were dishonored; NCLT New Delhi Bench admitted the petition on 25.10.2019, holding that the transaction was financial assistance notwithstanding the use of the words 'security deposit'; Appellant appealed claiming the transaction was operational.
legal_issues: Whether funds disbursed under a Memorandum of Understanding labeled as a 'security deposit' against a contemplated construction contract constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC when the funds carried assured monthly interest and repayment guarantees.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Nomenclature used in commercial agreements does not determine the legal nature of a transaction; where money is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money with assured monthly interest, it constitutes a financial debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) encompasses transactions having the commercial effect of a borrowing; referring to funds as a 'security deposit' against an unexecuted contract does not convert a loan carrying regular interest into an operational debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: True intent standard; the court examines the substance of the agreement over its form, specifically looking at interest obligations, repayment schedules, and security collateral such as post-dated interest cheques. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The deposit of Rs. 90 Lakhs carried 2% interest per month and was repayable on demand after a lock-in period, establishing an admitted financial debt and default under Section 7.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs; impugned order of admission dated 25.10.2019 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench is affirmed.
summary: Rishabh Jain, Managing Director of Home Connect Developers Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT New Delhi Bench order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by S.S. Enterprises for an outstanding sum of Rs. 90 Lakhs plus interest. The Appellant argued that the amount was a security deposit for a civil construction contract and should be classified as an operational debt secured by four villa plots. The NCLAT examined the third MoU dated 13.09.2017 and held that because the transaction carried an assured monthly return of 2% interest backed by post-dated interest cheques, it had the commercial effect of a borrowing with time value of money, fully satisfying Section 5(8). The admission was upheld.

case_title: Sameer Gulati vs. Salasar Techno Engineering Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sameer Gulati (Appellant/Ex-Director), Netsoft Consulting Services Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), and Salasar Techno Engineering Ltd. (Respondent/Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purchase Order dated 12.06.2018 for the supply and installation of 28 telecom towers, later revised to 24 towers, with terms stipulating 15% advance and the balance upon progressive completion. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed on unpaid supply and erection invoices amounting to Rs. 16,02,500, reduced by post-notice part-payments of Rs. 7,37,500 (20.05.2019) and Rs. 1,27,500 (06.06.2019), leaving a balance in default exceeding Rs. 1 Lakh. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Purchase Order dated 12.06.2018; Section 8 Demand Notice issued on 07.05.2019; Reply sent on 20.05.2019; NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI admitted Section 9 petition on 03.12.2019; appeal decided on 30.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Purchase Order dated 12.06.2018; balance confirmation email dated 31.12.2018; Corporate Debtor's email dated 26.04.2019 acknowledging outstanding balance of INR 8,65,000 for 23 towers while noting the 24th tower was on hold due to local municipal resistance. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI admitted Respondent's Section 9 petition on 03.12.2019 finding no pre-existing dispute and an admitted default; Appellant appealed offering to settle dues by cheque.
legal_issues: Whether an email from a corporate debtor acknowledging an admitted balance while noting that work on one installation site was put on hold due to third-party local authority issues constitutes a pre-existing dispute under Section 8 and 9 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An external execution delay or temporary hold on works caused by third-party local authorities, acknowledged concurrently with an admission of outstanding balance, does not constitute a pre-existing dispute between the commercial parties under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9, a 'dispute' must relate to a genuine contestation regarding price, quality, delay, or breach of contract between the contracting parties; factual third-party site impediments do not amount to a legal dispute over debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented acknowledgment standard; internal emails explicitly stating an outstanding balance while explaining a site suspension confirm the debt and default rather than establish a defense. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor failed to demonstrate any pre-existing contractual dispute; once the Committee of Creditors is constituted, the appellate court cannot set aside admission on mere settlement offers, leaving parties to seek withdrawal under Section 12A.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of without interfering with the impugned order of admission dated 03.12.2019; IRP directed to process withdrawal under Section 12A of the IBC if the Corporate Debtor moves an application as per regulations. No costs.
summary: Sameer Gulati, ex-director of Netsoft Consulting Services Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Salasar Techno Engineering Ltd. for unpaid telecom tower installation dues. The Appellant argued that an email dated 26.04.2019 established a pre-existing dispute regarding a 24th tower on hold and offered to clear the remaining balance in court. The NCLAT held that site delays due to local public resistance do not constitute a pre-existing dispute under the IBC, and the email in fact confirmed an unpaid liability. Since the CoC had already been formed, the Tribunal refused to reverse admission and directed the parties to explore settlement under Section 12A.

case_title: Mark Splendour Nonwovens Pvt. Ltd. vs. Dakota Chemicals India Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mark Splendour Nonwovens Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Corporate Debtor) and Dakota Chemicals India Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial supply of industrial chemicals by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed on unpaid invoices forming the basis of a Section 9 application filed on 30.06.2018 exceeding the statutory minimum threshold. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 application filed on 30.06.2018; ex-parte orders passed by NCLT on 12.04.2019 and 03.05.2019; recall application dismissed on 06.06.2019; appellate order passed on 24.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Affidavit of service filed by Operational Creditor showing notice served at the registered office in Bhiwadi, Alwar, Rajasthan; Corporate Debtor's application citing managing director's base in Gurgaon and non-receipt of notice as ground for default. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Jaipur Bench proceeded ex-parte against the Corporate Debtor on 12.04.2019 and refused to recall the ex-parte order on 06.06.2019; Corporate Debtor appealed; NCLAT initially stayed admission of CIRP on 15.07.2019 before vacating the stay on 03.01.2020.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in refusing to recall an ex-parte order against a corporate debtor in a Section 9 petition when the application was still pending admission and the corporate debtor sought an opportunity to file objections on terms of costs.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Because corporate insolvency resolution under Section 9 carries severe commercial consequences, an Adjudicating Authority should afford the corporate debtor a final opportunity to present its defense on the merits upon reasonable terms of costs, provided the application has not yet been admitted. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Service of statutory notice at the registered office constitutes valid legal service, and corporate officers cannot evade participation by claiming they operate from alternate locations; however, natural justice favors adjudication on the merits over ex-parte disposition prior to admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Balance of prejudice standard; procedural delay caused by a party's lack of diligence can be compensated by costs to ensure full factual adjudication before admitting a company into CIRP. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor showed lack of diligence, but in the interests of justice, it is entitled to participate and file its reply subject to paying compensatory costs of Rs. 75,000.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of; parties directed to appear before NCLT Jaipur on 17.02.2020; Appellant permitted to file reply to Section 9 application subject to paying Rs. 75,000 costs to Respondent; failing payment or reply, NCLT to proceed to dispose of Section 9 application as per law.
summary: Mark Splendour Nonwovens Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an order of NCLT Jaipur Bench refusing to recall ex-parte orders passed in a pending Section 9 IBC application filed by Dakota Chemicals India Pvt. Ltd. The Corporate Debtor claimed non-receipt of notices because its director operated from Gurgaon rather than its registered office in Bhiwadi. The NCLAT observed that service at the registered office was proper and the appellant was not diligent. Nevertheless, recognizing the grave consequences of CIRP, the Appellate Tribunal granted one final opportunity to file a reply and contest the Section 9 petition on the merits, conditional upon payment of Rs. 75,000 in costs.

case_title: Ms. Pavithra & Anr. vs. Monitoring Committee & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ms. Pavithra & Anr. (Appellants/Shareholders and Suspended Directors), Monitoring Committee (Respondent No. 1), Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited (Original Financial Creditor), M/s Hi-Tech Bio Products Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant), and M/s Sri Srivathsa Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Implementation of an approved Resolution Plan under Section 31 providing for infusion of Rs. 21.66 Crores and reconstitution of the Board of Directors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on financial facilities assigned to Arcil leading to admission under Section 7 on 13.11.2018, culminating in plan approval on 19.07.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 13.11.2018; Resolution Plan approved on 19.07.2019; Section 60(5) implementation order passed on 16.10.2019 (impugned order); Appeal filed in January 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan dated 19.07.2019, RoC statutory records showing Appellant directors' DINs, and Section 60(5) directions to replace erstwhile directors with nominees of the Resolution Applicant. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Special Bench Chennai admitted the Section 7 petition on 13.11.2018 and approved the resolution plan on 19.07.2019; subsequently, on 16.10.2019, NCLT directed the Registrar of Companies to strike off the erstwhile directors' names; Appellants filed appeals challenging both the initial admission order of 13.11.2018 and the implementation order of 16.10.2019.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal challenging the initial Section 7 admission order after more than a year is maintainable under Section 61(2) of the IBC, and whether erstwhile directors can challenge implementation directions removing their names from the ROC once a resolution plan has attained finality.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal against an order under the IBC filed beyond the outer statutory limit of 45 days (30 days plus 15 days condonable delay) is barred by limitation, and once a resolution plan achieves finality, erstwhile directors must vacate office to allow implementation of the approved plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) contains an inflexible statutory cap on limitation that strips the Appellate Tribunal of jurisdiction to condone delays exceeding 15 days; Section 31 makes an approved resolution plan binding on all stakeholders, including erstwhile directors and shareholders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Temporal jurisdiction bar and res judicata/finality; absent a timely challenge to plan approval, derivative attacks against routine implementation orders under Section 60(5) are non-maintainable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The challenge to the 2018 admission order was time-barred, and the order directing RoC to replace erstwhile directors was a mandatory consequence of the finalized resolution plan.
operative_order: Appeals dismissed without costs; the challenge to the order dated 13.11.2018 is dismissed as barred by limitation, and the challenge to the implementation order is rejected on the merits.
summary: Shareholders and suspended directors of Sri Srivathsa Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. challenged the NCLT Chennai's initial Section 7 admission order dated 13.11.2018 and a subsequent implementation order dated 16.10.2019 directing the RoC to strike off their names as directors to facilitate management handover to Hi-Tech Bio Products Pvt. Ltd. under an approved resolution plan. The NCLAT dismissed the challenge to the 2018 order as barred by limitation under Section 61(2), reaffirming that delays beyond 15 days cannot be condoned. The Tribunal also held that because the resolution plan approved on 19.07.2019 had attained finality, erstwhile directors had no legal right to obstruct implementation.

case_title: Ponneri Steel Industries vs. Gulam Mustafa Enterprises Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Ponneri Steel Industries (Appellant/Operational Creditor) and M/s Gulam Mustafa Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purchase Order dated 17.01.2018 for supply and delivery of TMT steel bars to the Corporate Debtor's construction project site. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of principal invoice amounts under Invoices Nos. 1907, 1908, and 1909 dated 22.01.2018, together with accrued interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Purchase Order dated 17.01.2018; Invoices raised and goods delivered 22.01.2018; Corporate Debtor confirmed zero shortage on 06.02.2018; Section 8 notice issued; NCLT Bengaluru Bench rejected Section 9 application on 26.07.2019; NCLAT judgment on 29.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Purchase Order containing Term 11 permitting site engineer to reject inferior goods, invoices stamped 'Security Material Inward' and signed by site supervisors without demurral, and Corporate Debtor's email dated 06.02.2018 confirming no shortage. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru rejected the Section 9 application on 26.07.2019 on the ground that the Appellant failed to produce quality certificates to prove goods met contractual standards; Operational Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can place the burden of proving the quality of supplied goods on the operational creditor when the corporate debtor accepted deliveries without demurrer and raised no objection prior to the Section 8 demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once an operational creditor proves delivery of goods accepted by the corporate debtor's agents without demurrer, the burden shifts entirely to the corporate debtor to establish by pre-notice contemporaneous communication that the goods were defective. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 and 9 do not require an operational creditor to affirmatively certify or prove quality standards at the threshold; quality claims qualify as a 'dispute' under Section 8(2)(a) only if raised prior to receipt of the statutory demand notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Burden of proof allocation; where inward delivery receipts are stamped and acknowledged without complaint, a contractual rejection clause cannot be invoked ex post facto by the Adjudicating Authority to dismiss a complete Section 9 petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed a reversible legal error by imposing an unstatutory quality-proving burden on the supplier; the Corporate Debtor had admitted delivery and shortage-free receipt, mandating admission.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 26.07.2019 set aside; parties directed to appear before NCLT Bengaluru on 18.02.2020 to settle, failing which NCLT shall admit the Section 9 application and proceed with CIRP.
summary: Ponneri Steel Industries appealed an order of NCLT Bengaluru rejecting its Section 9 IBC petition against Gulam Mustafa Enterprises Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid TMT steel bar supplies. The NCLT had dismissed the petition holding that the creditor failed to substantiate that the materials supplied were of contractual quality as required under Term 11 of the purchase order. The NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that when goods are received on-site with 'Security Material Inward' endorsements without objection, the burden rests on the corporate debtor to establish a pre-existing dispute communicated prior to the Section 8 notice. The dismissal was set aside and the matter remitted for admission.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Sical Logistics Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Appellant/Operational Creditor) and M/s Sical Logistics Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational services/transactions under which State Bank of India claimed operational creditor status against the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed on outstanding operational dues where the specific date of default occurred over eleven years earlier on 10.04.2008. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Date of default occurred on 10.04.2008; Section 9 application filed post-2016; NCLT Chennai Division Bench-I dismissed the application on 19.11.2019; NCLAT condoned 7 days' filing delay and dismissed the appeal on 08.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 9 petition pleadings and default records fixing the date of default as 10.04.2008, with no acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act on record. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: State Bank of India filed a Section 9 application; NCLT Chennai dismissed the petition on 19.11.2019 as barred by limitation under Section 238A read with Article 137; Appellant appealed arguing limitation had not been specifically pleaded by the Corporate Debtor.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the independent jurisdictional obligation to dismiss an insolvency application as time-barred under Section 238A of the IBC and the Limitation Act even if the defense of limitation was not raised by the corporate debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority has an independent statutory duty under Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963 read with Section 238A of the IBC to dismiss any application filed beyond the three-year limitation period, irrespective of whether limitation has been set up as a defense. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238A of the IBC incorporates the provisions of the Limitation Act, 1963 to insolvency proceedings; Article 137 governs Section 9 applications, prescribing a strict three-year period from the date of default. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Facial bar of limitation; when the petition's own averments identify a default occurring more than three years prior to filing without establishing any statutory acknowledgment or extension, the petition is dead on arrival. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because default occurred on 10.04.2008, the Section 9 petition was hopelessly time-barred, and the Adjudicating Authority was competent and obligated to reject it sua sponte.
operative_order: Delay of 7 days in preferring the appeal condoned; appeal dismissed on the merits without costs.
summary: State Bank of India appealed against an order of NCLT Chennai Bench-I dismissing its Section 9 IBC application against Sical Logistics Ltd. as barred by limitation. The date of default specified in the application was 10.04.2008. SBI argued on appeal that the Corporate Debtor had not raised the plea of limitation before the Tribunal. The NCLAT rejected this contention, holding that under Section 238A of the IBC read with Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the Adjudicating Authority has an independent statutory duty to dismiss any claim instituted beyond the prescribed three-year period regardless of party pleadings. The dismissal was upheld.

case_title: M/s. Emgee Infrastructure Holdings (India) Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s. Navayuga Engineering Company Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Emgee Infrastructure Holdings (India) Pvt. Ltd. is the sub-contractor acting as the Operational Creditor; M/s. Navayuga Engineering Company Ltd. is the principal contractor acting as the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sub-contracting works governed by Work Order Nos. 07 and 08 dated 26.08.2013 and 30.08.2013 (relating to period 01.10.2013 to 31.03.2014) and Work Order No. 26 dated 25.03.2014 (relating to period 01.04.2014 to 31.03.2015), against which monthly Running Account (RA) bills were raised. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed for unpaid RA bills where work under Work Order No. 07 was to be completed by 25.08.2013, Work Order No. 08 by 29.08.2013, and Work Order No. 26 by 24.03.2015; default was pegged to have occurred as far back as 25.08.2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC was issued on 16.06.2018; Section 8(2) reply notice denying liability due to sub-standard work was issued on 29.06.2018; rejoinder filed on 08.01.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor relied on a balance confirmation certificate issued by the Corporate Debtor on 28.12.2018 and part payments; Corporate Debtor relied on contract terms establishing time was of the essence and showing only 70% of work was completed with sub-standard quality. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application was filed before NCLT Amaravati Bench and dismissed vide order dated 03.12.2019 on the ground of pre-existing dispute.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is barred by limitation when the underlying default occurred more than three years prior to the filing of the application, and whether subsequent balance confirmation or part-payments towards incomplete work revive or shift the date of default for limitation purposes.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for initiating corporate insolvency resolution process under Section 9 of the IBC must be filed within a three-year period of limitation from the original date of default, and failure to initiate recovery or insolvency proceedings within three years renders the petition barred by time. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 read with the law of limitation requires default to be within three years; a balance confirmation or certificate issued after the expiration of the limitation period does not shift or re-trigger the accrual of the original default date. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of contractual completion milestones set out in work orders and running account bills to identify the exact date of breach and default; proof of part-payment towards previously executed portions of work (70%) does not constitute debt acknowledgement or cure limitation for the remaining claimed default amount. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The work orders having stipulated completion on or before 25.08.2013, the default arose on that date; because the operational creditor took no action for nearly five years, the application filed beyond three years was hopelessly barred by limitation.
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal found no merit in the appeal, affirmed the dismissal of the Section 9 petition, and dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 79 of 2020 with no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, M/s. Emgee Infrastructure Holdings (India) Pvt. Ltd., filed an appeal against the NCLT Amaravati Bench's order dated 03.12.2019, which had rejected its Section 9 application against M/s. Navayuga Engineering Company Ltd. on the ground of a pre-existing dispute concerning sub-standard work. The NCLAT examined the underlying work orders from August 2013 and determined that the default had occurred as far back as 25.08.2013. Holding that subsequent balance confirmations or part-payments for 70% completed works could not extend the statutory limitation period, the NCLAT ruled the application barred by limitation and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Suman Chakraborty vs. Anhui Technology Imp. & Exp. Co. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor: Anhui Technology Imp. & Exp. Co. Ltd.; Corporate Debtor: M/s Pantel Technologies Pvt. Ltd.; Appellant: Suman Chakraborty (Shareholder of Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of materials and goods by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed under Section 9 application pursuant to unpaid supply invoices; specific amount and default date not specified in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 8(1) demand notice was issued by the Operational Creditor on 10th June, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor relied on an email dated 30th September, 2016 demonstrating substandard and faulty materials supplied prior to the demand notice, alongside a letter dated 10th July, 2017 showing sales proceeds could not be realized due to bad quality and short supply; the Operational Creditor relied on a Letter of Guarantee dated 14th February, 2017 and an email dated 18th July, 2017 asserting corporate debtor's readiness to pay. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition was filed by the Operational Creditor and admitted by NCLT New Delhi on 19th September, 2019, which initiated CIRP against the Corporate Debtor.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction under Section 9 of the IBC to adjudicate claims and counter-claims regarding debt admission when there is documented evidence of a pre-existing dispute concerning goods quality prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC cannot be admitted if there exists a genuine pre-existing dispute between the parties raised prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice under Section 8(1). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory threshold for 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 8 and Section 9 requires only that a dispute concerning quality or performance was raised prior to the Section 8(1) notice; the Adjudicating Authority cannot evaluate subsequent promises or admissions of liability to override such an existing dispute. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority under Section 9 is not a court of competent jurisdiction to determine claims, counter-claims, or resolve contested factual disputes over the quality of goods. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because communication detailing defective and substandard supplies dated 30th September, 2016 preceded the 10th June, 2017 demand notice, a pre-existing dispute was established, making the Section 9 admission order incompetent and liable to be set aside.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 19th September, 2019 passed by NCLT New Delhi is set aside, and the Section 9 application is dismissed; Corporate Debtor is released from the rigours of CIRP to function through its Promoters and Directors; IRP directed to immediately hand over assets and records; matter remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to determine IRP fees and costs within three weeks; appeal allowed with no costs.
summary: An appeal was filed by a shareholder of Pantel Technologies Pvt. Ltd. challenging the NCLT New Delhi's order admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by Anhui Technology Imp. & Exp. Co. Ltd. The appellant contended that an email dated 30th September 2016 raised genuine disputes regarding substandard goods prior to the Section 8 demand notice issued on 10th June 2017. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority is not a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate contested claims or counter-claims. Establishing that a dispute concerning product quality existed prior to the statutory demand notice, NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the CIRP admission.

case_title: Ritusree Basu vs. Punjab National Bank & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor: Punjab National Bank; Corporate Debtor: M/s Hotel East Palace Pvt. Ltd.; Appellant: Ritusree Basu (Director/Shareholder of Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loan and working capital credit facilities of Rs. 15 Crores sanctioned and availed in July, 2012. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount claimed was Rs. 16,60,32,532/- (including interest up to 31st December, 2016); the loan account was classified as Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 28th January, 2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice issued on 14th January, 2017 recalling the entire loan; OTS-related communications issued on 4th June, 2019, 3rd July, 2019, and 15th July, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank loan recall and demand notice dated 14th January, 2017; bank letters regarding OTS eligibility and rejection/revision letters dated 4th June, 2019 and 15th July, 2019; DRT order dated 12th December, 2019 in parallel SARFAESI proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed in August, 2018 (CP (IB) No. 1139/KB/2018); admitted by NCLT Kolkata Bench on 13th December, 2019 on finding an outstanding debt, occurrence of default, and a complete application.
legal_issues: Whether the pendency of One-Time Settlement (OTS) negotiations or parallel debt recovery proceedings before the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) under the SARFAESI Act constitutes a valid legal obstruction to the admission of an application under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Ongoing negotiations for an amicable settlement, such as an OTS, or parallel recovery actions before debt recovery forums cannot bar or restrict the statutory jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority to initiate CIRP where financial debt and default are established. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC mandates that once the Adjudicating Authority ascertains the existence of a financial debt, default, and completeness of the petition format and annexures, it is legally bound to admit the petition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Satisfaction of the statutory criteria under Section 7 requires only prima facie verification of debt due and default from the records submitted by the financial creditor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application was complete and default was undisputed; hence, pending settlement talks and DRT directions posed no legal bar, rendering the admission lawful and the appeal devoid of merit.
operative_order: The appeal lacks merit and the NCLAT declines to admit the appeal; the impugned order dated 13th December, 2019 admitting the Section 7 application is affirmed, and the appeal is dismissed.
summary: Punjab National Bank initiated Section 7 CIRP against Hotel East Palace Pvt. Ltd. over a defaulted term and working capital facility of Rs. 15 Crores (NPA declared on 28th January 2016; claim of Rs. 16.60 Crores). A director/shareholder appealed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench's admission order dated 13th December 2019, arguing that the bank had initiated OTS discussions and DRT proceedings under the SARFAESI Act were ongoing. The NCLAT held that pending OTS proposals or DRT proceedings do not obstruct Section 7 proceedings. Once debt and default are established and the application is complete, admission is mandatory. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Kaushal Ramesh Mehta vs. Metallica Industries Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants: Kaushal Ramesh Mehta and Pratik Ramesh Mehta (claimants seeking status as Secured Financial Creditors); Corporate Debtor: Metallica Industries Ltd.; Resolution Professional and Committee of Creditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged agreement/arrangement entered into by the Appellants for the purchase of a portion of the Gala (Project) of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary metrics and specific default dates were not specified in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: No statutory demand notices under Section 8 were involved; Resolution Plan was approved with 85.89% voting share by the Committee of Creditors and approved by the Adjudicating Authority on 16th October, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Purported arrangement/agreement for purchase of the Gala project; rejection of claim and status as 'Secured Financial Creditor' by the Resolution Professional; lack of any direct privity of contract between Appellants and the Corporate Debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor was undergoing CIRP wherein the RP and CoC approved a resolution plan; NCLT Mumbai Bench approved the plan on 16th October, 2019, leading to the statutory appeal under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal against an order approving a resolution plan can be sustained in the absence of demonstrable grounds enumerated under Section 61(3) of the IBC, and whether a property purchase claimant can challenge the plan without establishing privity of contract with the Corporate Debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An approved resolution plan can only be challenged on the strictly limited statutory grounds enumerated under Section 61(3) of the IBC; in the absence of privity of contract with the corporate debtor, a claimant lacks standing to seek relief against an approved plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(3) provides an exhaustive list of grounds—including contravention of law, material irregularity by the RP, non-provision for operational creditors or CIRP costs, or non-compliance with IBBI criteria—which must be affirmatively established by the appellant. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Appellants must demonstrate that their challenge falls squarely within the statutory grounds of Section 61(3) and establish direct contractual privity with the corporate debtor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellants failed to prove any ground under Section 61(3) and failed to demonstrate privity of contract with the corporate debtor; hence, the appellate tribunal had no basis to interfere with the CoC-approved resolution plan.
operative_order: Both appeals (Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1437 of 2019 and 1438 of 2019) are dismissed for want of merit, with no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants Kaushal Ramesh Mehta and Pratik Ramesh Mehta challenged the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order dated 16th October 2019 approving a Resolution Plan with 85.89% CoC voting share for Metallica Industries Ltd. The appellants claimed to have purchased a part of the Corporate Debtor's Gala Project and contested the Resolution Professional's rejection of their claim as Secured Financial Creditors. The NCLAT held that appeals against approved resolution plans are restricted strictly to the grounds enumerated under Section 61(3) of the IBC. Finding no grounds made out and noting an absence of privity of contract between the appellants and the Corporate Debtor, the NCLAT dismissed the appeals.

case_title: Eastern Electrodes & Coke Pvt. Ltd. vs. Bhaskar Shrachi Alloys Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor: Eastern Electrodes & Coke Pvt. Ltd.; Corporate Debtor: Bhaskar Shrachi Alloys Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of Electro Carbon Paste (ECP) and Tamping Paste by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor pursuant to supplies made and invoices raised in the year 2014. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Debt claimed under 2014 supply invoices; specific default amount and exact date not explicitly quantified in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC was issued on 01.02.2018; Section 8 reply disputing quality was issued by the Corporate Debtor on 12.02.2018; a prior demand letter was sent on 27.07.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's urgent supply request email dated 08.10.2014; Operational Creditor's email dated 09.10.2014 requiring quality intimation within 48 hours; letter of complaint dated 10.10.2014 and email dated 13.10.2014 concerning inferior quality and tip breaking; unaccepted Confirmation of Accounts letter dated 03.04.2015 bearing disputed and uncertain seal and signature without original production. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 application on 29.03.2018 before NCLT Kolkata Bench; NCLT rejected the application on grounds of a pre-existing dispute regarding product quality and the claim being barred by limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the subsequent placement of urgent orders for goods by a corporate debtor negates a pre-existing dispute regarding quality raised prior to the Section 8 demand notice, and whether an unreplied demand letter or a disputed confirmation of accounts can extend the three-year period of limitation under Section 9 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An urgent order placed by a corporate debtor out of commercial necessity does not waive or extinguish a prior genuine dispute over goods quality; furthermore, a unilateral demand letter that goes unreplied does not constitute an acknowledgment of debt to extend limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: For the purposes of Section 8 and Section 9 of the IBC, a 'pre-existing dispute' exists where contemporaneous correspondence demonstrates genuine quality contestations prior to the demand notice; an 'acknowledgment of debt' under the law of limitation cannot be inferred from mere silence or failure to reply to a demand notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To establish an acknowledgment of debt extending limitation beyond three years from the invoice date, an applicant must produce reliable, authenticated, and undisputed documents bearing verified signatures; secondary or uncertain copies with disputed seals are insufficient. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was rightly rejected as the claim was barred by limitation (filed more than three years after the 2014 invoices without valid acknowledgment) and precluded by documented pre-existing disputes regarding quality.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for want of substance and merit, affirming the order of the Adjudicating Authority; no order as to costs.
summary: Eastern Electrodes & Coke Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench's order rejecting its Section 9 IBC application against Bhaskar Shrachi Alloys Ltd. concerning unpaid 2014 invoices for Electro Carbon Paste. The NCLT had rejected the petition on grounds of pre-existing quality disputes and limitation. The appellant argued that urgent repeat orders placed in October 2014 waived the quality dispute and that limitation was extended by a 2015 balance confirmation and an unreplied 2017 demand letter. The NCLAT held that placing urgent orders does not extinguish pre-existing quality disputes, an unreplied demand letter does not constitute an acknowledgment of debt, and unproven balance confirmations cannot extend limitation. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: M/s. Lloyd Insulations (India) Ltd. vs. M/s. Sintex Prefab & Infra Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor / Appellant: M/s. Lloyd Insulations (India) Ltd.; Corporate Debtor / Respondent: M/s. Sintex Prefab and Infra Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Execution of tank fabrication works and associated erection and construction services rendered by the Operational Creditor for the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt arising from unpaid claims for services rendered; precise quantum and date of default not recorded in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Dates of Section 8 demand notice and reply are not specified in the appellate order. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email communication dated 25th July, 2014 sent by the Corporate Debtor establishing that tank fabrication was incomplete and work was deficient due to poor workmanship and failure of the Appellant to retain its erection gang. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application filed by the Appellant was rejected by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench by order dated 2nd January, 2020 on the ground of pre-existence of dispute.
legal_issues: Whether contemporaneous email correspondence demonstrating incomplete work and poor workmanship constitutes a pre-existing dispute under Section 9 of the IBC, and whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal possesses jurisdiction to determine the merits or genuineness of such a dispute.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the record reveals an existing dispute regarding deficient performance or poor workmanship prior to the statutory notice, the insolvency application under Section 9 must be rejected, as tribunals under the IBC cannot conduct a trial on the merits of the dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A 'pre-existence of dispute' under Section 9 is satisfied where contemporaneous correspondence establishes that the debtor questioned the completion and workmanship of the contractual service prior to the demand notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority and Appellate Tribunal are not courts of competent jurisdiction to assess whether a dispute raised by the respondent is factually genuine or substantiated on the merits; the inquiry is strictly limited to whether a plausible dispute existed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the email dated 25th July, 2014 evidenced incomplete fabrication and deficient workmanship, a pre-existing dispute was established, warranting dismissal of the Section 9 application.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for lack of merit; no order as to costs.
summary: M/s. Lloyd Insulations (India) Ltd. appealed an order of the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dated 2nd January 2020 which rejected its Section 9 IBC application against M/s. Sintex Prefab and Infra Limited on the ground of a pre-existing dispute. The dispute was founded upon an email dated 25th July 2014 highlighting incomplete tank fabrication and deficient workmanship by the appellant's erection gang. The NCLAT affirmed that contemporaneous correspondence established a pre-existing dispute regarding the services rendered. It held that neither the Adjudicating Authority nor the Appellate Tribunal is a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate whether such a dispute is genuine on the merits. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Sandeep Dipak Chatterjee vs. FR Tech Innovations Private Limited Through its Resolution Professional Dr. Arun Mohan & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Sandeep Dipak Chatterjee (42% shareholder of Corporate Debtor); Corporate Debtor: FR Tech Innovations Private Limited; Financial Creditor / Respondent No. 2: Mr. Karan Lalwani; Resolution Professional: Dr. Arun Mohan. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial investment / debt disbursed by the Financial Creditor into the Corporate Debtor with an agreed return / interest component. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount of Rs. 1,13,01,328/- (including interest); the default occurred on 26th December, 2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Default date was 26th December, 2018; Section 7 admission order passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench on 14th November, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Undisputed records of non-payment of Rs. 1,13,01,328/- from 26th December, 2018; appearance of legal counsel (Mr. Sumit Agarwal and Mr. M. Rajguru) on behalf of the Corporate Debtor before the Adjudicating Authority. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditor filed Section 7 application; NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the application on 14th November, 2019; shareholder appealed claiming lack of knowledge, absence of opportunity for the debtor, connivance of another shareholder, and disputing the character of the debt.
legal_issues: Whether an investment carrying repayment and interest obligations constitutes a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and whether a shareholder's unsubstantiated allegation of lack of opportunity and intra-shareholder connivance can invalidate an admission order under Section 7.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When financial disbursals carry interest and repayment obligations, an undisputed default therein constitutes a financial debt under the IBC; unsubstantiated allegations of lack of notice or connivance between shareholders cannot overturn an admission where the debtor was duly represented by counsel. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The definition of 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) includes investments and disbursals that are subject to commercial repayment and interest commitments, the default of which entitles the creditor to invoke Section 7. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mere allegations of procedural denial of natural justice and collusion among corporate stakeholders fail when the record unequivocally demonstrates that advocates entered appearances on behalf of the corporate debtor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt and default of Rs. 1,13,01,328/- occurring on 26th December, 2018 were undisputed, the transaction qualified as a financial debt, and the Corporate Debtor was duly heard, justifying admission under Section 7.
operative_order: Delay of 15 days condoned and Interlocutory Application No. 477 of 2020 disposed of; the appeal is dismissed for lack of merit; no order as to costs.
summary: Sandeep Dipak Chatterjee, a 42% shareholder of FR Tech Innovations Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order dated 14th November 2019 admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by financial creditor Karan Lalwani. The appellant contended that the Corporate Debtor was denied an opportunity to be heard, that another shareholder connived with the creditor, and that the investment did not constitute a financial debt. The NCLAT rejected these contentions, observing that advocates had duly represented the Corporate Debtor before the NCLT. Finding an undisputed default of Rs. 1,13,01,328/- occurred on 26th December 2018 qualifying as a financial debt, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Directorate of Economic Offences vs. Binay Kumar Singhania & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant: Directorate of Economic Offences (DEO) through its delinquent officer; Respondent No. 1: Binay Kumar Singhania (Liquidator / former Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 4: Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory investigation / regulatory proceedings conducted by the DEO alongside the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process and subsequent liquidation of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; appeal arises from an ancillary penal cost order imposed within insolvency proceedings. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court directions regarding cooperation issued during resolution; NCLT passed liquidation order and imposed the monetary liability on the Appellant. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record showing alleged contumacious non-cooperation by an officer of the DEO with the Resolution Professional despite directions from the High Court; absence of any causal connection between the DEO officer's conduct and the statutory grounds for liquidation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: While passing an order of liquidation against the Corporate Debtor, the Adjudicating Authority penalized the Appellant by imposing a liability to pay Rs. 5 Lakhs for non-cooperation with the Resolution Professional; DEO appealed specifically against the penalty.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction under the IBC to impose monetary penalties or costs on a statutory investigating authority for alleged contumacious conduct and non-cooperation with a Resolution Professional as part of an order of liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority exceeds its statutory jurisdiction by imposing monetary penalties or costs on a third-party regulatory body for non-cooperation while adjudicating a liquidation application, where no nexus exists between the alleged conduct and the statutory grounds for liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory jurisdiction to pass an order of liquidation under the IBC is governed strictly by independent statutory criteria; it cannot be expanded into summary contempt or penal jurisdiction to punish third-party statutory authorities. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Liability for contempt or non-compliance with High Court directions must be addressed before the appropriate judicial forum having contempt jurisdiction, not by penal cost impositions attached to an insolvency liquidation order without statutory nexus. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority lacked jurisdiction to slap the DEO with a penalty of Rs. 5 Lakhs under the guise of costs during liquidation, requiring that portion of the order to be set aside.
operative_order: The appeals are allowed to the limited extent of setting aside the penalty/cost liability of Rs. 5 Lakhs imposed on the Appellant; the unassailed order of liquidation remains undisturbed.
summary: The Directorate of Economic Offences (DEO) appealed against the Adjudicating Authority's order imposing a penalty of Rs. 5 Lakhs on it for failing to cooperate with the Resolution Professional pursuant to High Court directions while ordering liquidation of the Corporate Debtor. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction by linking an alleged contumacious conduct with the liquidation order when no nexus existed between the two. The court observed that any alleged contempt of High Court orders could not be penalized by the NCLT under the guise of costs in an insolvency proceeding. The appeal was allowed to the extent of setting aside the monetary penalty.

case_title: Pradeep Kumar Goenka vs. Shubham Capital Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pradeep Kumar Goenka is the Appellant (erstwhile Resolution Professional), while Shubham Capital Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. are Respondents, with Skipper Furnishings Pvt. Ltd. identified as an entity related to the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debtor had issued corporate guarantees in favor of financial institutions, specifically ICICI Bank and an uninvoked corporate guarantee of Rs. 75 Lakh in favor of Magma Fincorp Ltd. in relation to Skipper Furnishings Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Exact principal/interest default metrics are not recorded in the order, but the guarantee to Magma Fincorp Ltd. stood at Rs. 75 Lakh. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Information Memorandum containing guarantee details was prepared during the CIRP timeline prior to approval proceedings concluding on 2019-12-20. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Page 78 of the Paper Book containing the Information Memorandum demonstrated that the Resolution Professional included the corporate guarantee for ICICI Bank but omitted to consider the Magma Fincorp guarantee in arriving at claim metrics or voting share calculations. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: By order dated 2019-12-20, the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) made critical observations against the RP's selective reporting in the Information Memorandum under Regulation 36(2)(l); the RP appealed to expunge these remarks.
legal_issues: Whether the adverse observations made by the Adjudicating Authority in paragraphs 33, 34, and 48 regarding the Resolution Professional's failure to disclose and consistently treat uninvoked corporate guarantees in the Information Memorandum constitute individual personal aspersions warranting expunction.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Critical judicial observations evaluating the functional correctness, consistency, or statutory omission of an insolvency professional's official acts do not constitute personal aspersions or stigmatizing strictures requiring expunction if they address procedural viability and statutory duties. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 36(2)(l) of the CIRP Regulations requires full disclosure of all corporate guarantees given by the corporate debtor in the Information Memorandum to ensure viability and prevent failure of the resolution plan, irrespective of whether the guarantees are invoked. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An objective examination of the impugned text to determine whether the tribunal attributed individual malafides/personal misconduct versus characterizing an official act as contradictory or skewed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that the Adjudicating Authority's remarks addressed only the contradictory and unbalanced administrative conduct of the RP rather than casting personal aspersions, rendering the appeal without merit.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs.
summary: The erstwhile Resolution Professional appealed against critical remarks in paragraphs 33, 34, and 48 of the NCLT's order dated 20 December 2019 concerning his failure to properly disclose and account for an uninvoked Rs. 75 Lakh corporate guarantee in the Information Memorandum under Regulation 36(2)(l). The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority's observations evaluated administrative and statutory actions that produced contradictory outcomes rather than casting individual personal aspersions against the Appellant. Confirming that findings of fact on claim submissions do not cast personal stigma, the Appellate Tribunal declined to interfere and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Mr. Vipin Agarwal vs. Mr. Satyaprakash Aggarwal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Satyaprakash Aggarwal and two other applicants are Financial Creditors, Vistar Metal Industries Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor, and Mr. Vipin Agarwal is the Director/Appellant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Disbursement of loans by the Financial Creditors to the Corporate Debtor for time value of money, with the Corporate Debtor regularly deducting and paying TDS on the accrued interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amounts comprised Rs. 1,31,00,000/- on 2016-05-15 for Financial Creditor 1, Rs. 40,00,000/- on 2017-03-15 for Financial Creditor 2, and Rs. 30,00,000/- on 2017-05-15 for Financial Creditor 3. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Letters proposing repayment schedules were executed by the Corporate Debtor on 2015-12-15; subsequent post-dated cheques were presented and dishonoured on the respective default dates in 2016 and 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Undertaking letters dated 2015-12-15, dishonoured cheques, bank dishonour memos, and evidence of TDS deduction on interest payments. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditors filed a Section 7 application; the NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the application on 2019-10-14, which was appealed by the Director on grounds of absence of financial debt.
legal_issues: Whether a transaction qualifies as a financial debt under Section 5(8) when no formal interest is allegedly payable, but loan funds were disbursed for time value of money and the corporate debtor deducted and paid TDS on interest.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where funds are disbursed for time value of money and utilized by an entity, the statutory deduction and deposit of Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on interest constitutes conclusive evidence of the commercial nature of borrowing under financial debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) read with Section 5(7) encompasses loans where consideration for the time value of money is manifested through interest, which is evidenced by the debtor's own compliance in deducting TDS on such interest. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Dishonour memos coupled with contemporaneous tax deduction records (TDS on interest) establish both disbursal for time value of money and the occurrence of default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor having deducted TDS on interest and defaulted on dishonoured cheques, the debt constitutes financial debt and the applicants are Financial Creditors, validating admission under Section 7.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for lack of merit without costs.
summary: A director of Corporate Debtor Vistar Metal Industries Pvt. Ltd. challenged the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order dated 14 October 2019 admitting a Section 7 application filed by Satyaprakash Aggarwal and others for defaults totaling over Rs. 2.01 Crores across three creditors. The Appellant contended the debt lacked an interest component and did not qualify as a financial debt under Section 5(8). The NCLAT rejected the plea, observing that the Corporate Debtor had disbursed loan funds for time value of money, defaulted on cheques issued under settlement letters dated 15 December 2015, and consistently deducted TDS on interest, firmly establishing financial debt and default.

case_title: R. S. Fuel Pvt. Ltd. vs. Ankit Metal & Power Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s R. S. Fuel (P) Ltd. is the Operational Creditor/Appellant, and M/s Ankit Metal & Power Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying contracts and purchase orders for the commercial supply of coal by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed for unpaid coal consignments; specific claimed monetary default sum is not quantified in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Operational Creditor issued a legal notice on 2016-08-29; Corporate Debtor's advocate issued a detailed dispute reply on 2016-09-22; formal Section 8(1) demand notice was issued much later on 2017-09-30. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's reply letter dated 2016-09-22 demonstrating contemporaneous disputes regarding substandard quality of coal failing to meet purchase order specifications and delayed supplies. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application before NCLT Kolkata Bench, which dismissed it on 2019-11-21 due to pre-existing dispute.
